## 🤖 New release * `vta-sdk`: 0.29.0 -> 0.30.0 (✓ API compatible changes) * `vti-common`: 0.14.0 -> 0.15.0 (✓ API compatible changes) * `cnm-cli`: 0.12.2 -> 0.12.3 * `pnm-cli`: 0.13.2 -> 0.14.0 * `vta-audit`: 0.2.0 -> 0.2.1 * `vta-keys`: 0.3.0 -> 0.3.1 * `vta-policy`: 0.2.12 -> 0.2.13 * `vta-webvh`: 0.1.14 -> 0.2.0 * `vta-service`: 0.21.0 -> 0.22.0 (✓ API compatible changes) * `vtc-client`: 0.4.0 -> 0.4.1 (✓ API compatible changes) * `vta-cli-common`: 0.11.5 -> 0.11.6 * `vti-secrets`: 0.2.2 -> 0.2.3 * `vta-config`: 0.3.13 -> 0.3.14 * `vta-keyspaces`: 0.2.1 -> 0.2.2 * `vta-support`: 0.2.12 -> 0.2.13 * `vta-backup`: 0.2.0 -> 0.2.1 * `vta-vault`: 0.4.0 -> 0.4.1 * `vta-sweepers`: 0.3.0 -> 0.3.1 * `vta-tee`: 0.1.10 -> 0.1.11
Changelog

## `vta-sdk`

## [0.30.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-sdk-v0.29.0...vta-sdk-v0.30.0) — 2026-08-27 ### Added - **vta**: Close the CI cache class, map the 0.5.0 lifecycle, cover more tasks ([#1134](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1134)) Three things belonging to the same release. - **vta**: Bound the replay record by the acceptance window, not by capacity ([#1127](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1127)) The follow-up #1126 named. VTI now honours SPEC §7.2's same-bound rule: the acceptance window and the duplicate-execution record's retention are one instant, derived from one policy. #1126 shipped the ReplayGuard without a window, leaving the record bounded by InMemoryReplayGuard's capacity. That is not "no expiry so entries live forever" — it is LRU, which makes the window load-dependent: on a quiet service the protection is effectively unbounded, but under burst the eviction horizon can fall below any sensible acceptance window and a replay executes a second time. The defence was weakest exactly when the service was busiest. Ten minutes rather than the library's five: this service routes over a mediator that can hold a message while a recipient reconnects. It is the same 600s the retired replay::check_and_record used as its dedup TTL, now bounding acceptance as well as retention. Most of the diff is the fixture migration the window forced, and none of it was the policy being wrong. 65 envelopes carried no issuedAt at all — with a window set, a document with neither issuedAt nor expiresAt cannot be placed in time and is refused, which is what §7.2 requires. 12 more carried fixed literals already days stale. One subtlety: the first pass used to_rfc3339(), which renders the offset as +00:00 where TrustTask's typed DateTime round-trip renders Z. That broke a signed fixture's proof — a document signed in one spelling and verified after the other is a different document, which is the §8.4 distinction #1126 added idConflict for, arriving as a signature failure instead. Every stamp now uses to_rfc3339_opts(SecondsFormat::Secs, true). ### Fixed - **vta**: Refuse a swap-key without linkProof by name, not as malformed ([#1137](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1137)) Coverage 77 to 79 of 109, and a fifth request-side divergence. - **vta**: Re-case the extended error codes the Trust Tasks registry moved ([#1122](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1122)) * fix(vta)!: emit the re-cased extended error codes the registry now declares trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#279 re-cased 200 extended error-code local parts to lowerCamelCase per SPEC §4.10 rule 4 — only the part after the `:` moved, the namespace is unchanged. This service still produced the snake_case spellings for 32 of them, so every one of those rejects carried a code the registry no longer defines and no conforming consumer can branch on. Every site here is an **emitter**: this repo decides what to send, and the registry decides what is correct to send, so each moves to the new spelling with no compatibility arm. The matcher side — where this repo reads a code a peer produced and cannot control that peer's deploy order — is handled separately in the following commit. Three of the vault emitters build their namespace by interpolation (`vault/{verb}:not_found`, `vault/{verb}:version_conflict`, `vault/{op}:not_found` in `vault_not_found`, `check_expected_version` and `refuse_if_not_active`), so the codes they produce do not appear as literals anywhere. Those helpers cover `vault/delete:{notFound,versionConflict}` and the `notFound` conflation the three consumer-facing use paths rely on for enumeration resistance. - **vta**: Take keyId from the wire instead of minting one ([#1123](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1123)) First of the three stopgaps #1121 unblocked. `keys/create/0.1` publishes `keyId` as of trust-tasks-rs 0.12.1 (dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#275), so the caller names the key and the binding no longer has to invent one. #1118 minted `internal-` at the binding for an internal key. That was a deliberate deviation from a SHOULD I wrote in #275 — a maintainer offering internal keys and receiving no `keyId` SHOULD reject — taken because the alternative was a security feature nobody could use: an internal key has no derivation path to be named after, the operation layer refuses one without an id, and the wire had no member to carry it. The comment at that site said to delete it when the bump landed. - **vta**: --internal creates an internal key ([#1118](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1118)) `pnm keys create --internal` printed a non-recoverable-key warning, required the operator to type "i understand this key cannot be recovered", and then created an ordinary seed-derived key — recoverable from the mnemonic, included in backups, exportable. The operator was told the opposite of what happened. `CreateKeyRequest` carries `internal`, `key_id` and `derivation_path`; the CLI set them and `VtaClient::create_key` built its wire body with `internal: None` hardcoded, `key_id` never read, and `derivation_path` as `unwrap_or_default()` — `""` for absent, which worked only because the operation layer reads `""` as absent. The operation layer was always right: `derivation_path` is an `Option` there that auto-derives, and `internal` short-circuits to a CSPRNG key. It could not have worked even with the flag forwarded. The spine rejected the document, because `keys/create/0.1` was `additionalProperties: false` with no `internal` member (fixed upstream in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#269, which also added `internal` to `KeyOrigin` — the value that makes the outcome checkable); and an internal key needs an explicit `key_id`, which neither the wire type nor the specification had (dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#275). Forwards `internal` and `derivation_path`, makes `CreateKeyBody`'s `derivation_path` optional to match the specification and the operation layer, and mints a `key_id` for an internal key at the trust-task binding, which has no `keyId` member to carry one yet. That minting is a deliberate, temporary deviation from a SHOULD in the specification, taken because `keyId` needs trust-tasks-rs 0.12.1 and this workspace cannot move to 0.12: `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.19.12 pins `trust-tasks-rs ^0.11` and `vta_sdk::acl_setup` hands it a generated `MediatorAcl`, so two nodes in one graph fail to compile. The id is returned on the record and `keys/rename/0.1` can change it; the site says to delete the branch when the bump lands. `an_internal_key_is_actually_internal` asserts `origin == "internal"` — the check the CLI already made and that always silently failed. ### Chore - **deps**: Trust-tasks-rs 0.12 and the TDK crates that carry it ([#1121](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1121)) Verified locally against a path-patched affinidi-tdk-rs before those crates published (affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#743); VTI's graph collapses to a single trust-tasks-rs 0.12.1 node and the workspace compiles. Bumps trust-tasks-rs 0.11.17 -> 0.12 with the four sibling crates that moved with it — capability-client 0.10 -> 0.11, https 0.10 -> 0.12, didcomm 0.10 -> 0.12, proof 0.10 -> 0.11 — and the TDK crates whose public API carries trust-tasks-rs types: affinidi-tdk 0.8.5 -> 0.9, affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.19 -> 0.20, affinidi-messaging-test-mediator 0.2 -> 0.3. They move together because two trust-tasks-rs nodes in one graph do not warn, they fail to compile: `expected MediatorAcl, found a different MediatorAcl`. One source change. `classify_git_trust_reply` gained a required `expected_thread_id` in capability-client 0.11, because acting on an uncorrelated reply lets whichever document arrives next decide the fate of a write it has nothing to do with. The `replies` registry already keys its waiter on `doc.id`, so this is defence in depth — and `correlation_thread` is the library's own SPEC §4.9 rule (`threadId` falling back to `id`) rather than this call site's guess at it. Three marked stopgaps become deletable once this lands, each of which names this bump at its site: the freshness stand-in from #1117 in favour of `FreshnessPolicy`/`validate_freshness`, the minted `key_id` branch from #1118 in favour of the wire `keyId`, and `replay::check_and_record` in favour of `ReplayGuard`. They are left alone here so this change is a dependency move and nothing else. ### Test - **vta**: Cover the did-templates and policy families ([#1128](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1128)) Coverage 48 -> 58 of 109 (44% -> 53%). Two families, one real defect.
## `vti-common`
## [0.15.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vti-common-v0.14.0...vti-common-v0.15.0) — 2026-08-27 ### Added - **vta**: Stop error messages from being a probing oracle ([#1130](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1130)) Framework 0.5.0 makes the message-sanitization rule normative for every code, not just `identityMismatch`: a `message` MUST NOT reveal consumer-internal state, the contested value of a mismatched party, or resolver, verifier, or key-status internals. Every rejection is emitted on the same path, to the same possibly-unauthenticated party, generally before any authorization decision has been reached. This service violated two of the three. `app_error_to_reject` passed `AppError::Internal`'s cause into the `message` verbatim, so a caller learned "ATM not configured — server cannot pack DIDComm envelopes" or "log entry has no update_keys" — the deployment's shape, its configuration, and which invariant just broke. The catch-all arm was the quieter half: it rendered whatever `Display` an error happened to have, so a variant added later would publish itself with nobody choosing to. Both now land on one fixed string and log the cause for the operator. `DiProofError`'s `Display` rendered the underlying verifier error, and that reaches the wire through `PermissionDenied`. A caller could read which cryptosuite ran and how verification failed. The detail moves to a `cause()` that is deliberately not reachable through `Display`, since the defect was that the wire rendering and the operator rendering were one function. `notFound`, `malformedRequest` and `permissionDenied` pass through unchanged: they describe the caller's own request back to it, which is not consumer-internal state. `an_internal_error_does_not_say_internal_error_twice` asserted the cause was on the wire. Its subject was a doubled prefix, which the fixed string also settles; it is now `an_internal_error_reveals_no_internal_state`, joined by `the_catch_all_arm_is_opaque_too`.

## `vta-audit`
## [0.2.1](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-audit-v0.2.0...vta-audit-v0.2.1) — 2026-08-27 ### Added - **audit**: Bound the operator reason an audit row keeps ([#1132](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1132)) Framework 0.5.0 requires every free-text member to carry a bound. Most of that is upstream schema work, but one free-text path is this workspace's own and was bounded by nothing: the operator `reason` that `record_with_detail` writes into the audit log. The cost here is worse than the wire cost 0.5.0 argues from. The row goes into a hash-chained, append-only log, so an oversized `detail` is permanent and cannot be trimmed later without breaking the chain that makes the log evidence. Truncated at 4096 characters rather than rejected, and that choice is the substance: this runs after the operation it records has already happened, so refusing the row would trade an over-long reason for no audit record at all — losing the evidence to protect its formatting. The cut is marked, because a silently shortened reason reads as the operator's own words. Cut on a character boundary: byte-slicing panics mid-codepoint, and would do so on the first operator who wrote a reason in a language this workspace did not anticipate. The rest of the free-text rule is upstream and already in hand: 1013 of 1067 registry free-text members carry no maxLength, and dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#296 is open across 275 files to fix exactly that. Taking the latest trust-tasks-rs today would not bound free text — 0.14.0 predates it.
## `vta-policy`
## [0.2.13](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-policy-v0.2.12...vta-policy-v0.2.13) — 2026-08-27 ### Added - **vta**: Mint the consent ceremony's correlator instead of deriving it ([#1133](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1133)) * feat(vta): mint the consent ceremony's correlator instead of deriving it Framework 0.5.0, *Identifier correlation and linkability*: `id`, `threadId` and `ceremony.enactment` MUST be freshly minted and unguessable, and MUST NOT be derived from subject data. The `task-consent/granted` notice threaded on `wire_digest` — a function of the task payload, and the same string the document carries as `payloadDigest`. The challenge is 256 bits of randomness, so the digest is not guessable from the payload; this is not the "UUIDv5 over a subject identifier" case. The mediator is the exposure. `threadId` is routing metadata, and the mediator also forwards documents carrying `payloadDigest`; with the same value in both it can tie the routing it performs to the digest it carries and link the refusal, the approval pushes and the notice into one ceremony with named counterparties. `PendingTaskConsent` gains a minted `correlator`, created alongside the challenge. The notice threads on it and the body still carries `payloadDigest` unchanged, so a requester matching on the digest is unaffected. The requester is told the correlator in the `auth:consent_required` refusal beside the digest it already receives. Smaller than it first looked: the request push to approvers already threaded on the request document's own id, so only the requester-facing notice was derived. The notice is produced but never consumed in this workspace and is explicitly non-load-bearing — the grant check at re-submit is the real gate.

The bound is 4096 bytes of JCS or 16 immediate members — 0.5.0's default where a specification declares none — applied in `reject_with`, the single funnel every rejection passes through, rather than at the thirty `details: Some(...)` construction sites. A new site cannot be added that skips it. An oversized `details` is ignored and never grounds to discard the `code`: the code is what the receiving party needs, and dropping the rejection because its annex was too long would turn a verbose policy into an unexplained failure. An uncanonicalisable `details` is dropped too — it cannot be measured, so it does not go out. - **vta**: Stop error messages from being a probing oracle ([#1130](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1130)) Framework 0.5.0 makes the message-sanitization rule normative for every code, not just `identityMismatch`: a `message` MUST NOT reveal consumer-internal state, the contested value of a mismatched party, or resolver, verifier, or key-status internals. Deletes trust_tasks/replay.rs and the hand-rolled freshness bounds from #1117. They land together because ConsumeChecks bundles them in one argument: SPEC §7.2 makes the acceptance window and the replay record's retention the same bound, and splitting them is how a deployment ends up with a ten-minute record against an unbounded window believing it has a replay defence. This service had exactly that. The retired module keyed on (actor, id) and kept no digest, which cost two things. It never produced idConflict — item 11 requires a different document under an accepted id to be rejected, and with no digest that case was silently absorbed as a retry, the one outcome §7.2 and §8.4 both rule out. And the key was wrong: §7.2 fixes it as the document id alone, so actor-scoping let two callers each spend the same id. A duplicate is also no longer answered with taskFailed, which §7.2 forbids outright. A failed outcome releases the claim, mirroring the idempotency layer beside it; a successful one records its response so a retry is answered with the result. The Err arm fails closed with a retryable unavailable, and the non_exhaustive ReplayVerdict gets an arm that refuses rather than executes. No acceptance window yet, and that was measured rather than assumed: with_max_age(10 minutes) scoped to consequential tasks failed 41 assertions across 10 suites with expired, because the suite is full of documents stamped hours or days in the past. Fixing those alters what the service accepts and belongs in a change whose subject is the window. ### Fixed - **vta**: Say which fact refused a retire-orphan, and cover the slot paths ([#1138](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1138)) Coverage 79 to 81 of 109, and a misleading refusal message found by trying to make the task succeed. `servers/retire-orphan` routes two very different facts to the same `NotOrphaned` variant, and the message asserted one of them for both: "slot X has a record in this VTA, so it is not an orphan … use webvh/dids/delete for one it still controls." The variant already carries `did: Option`, which distinguishes them. `Some` means the VTA still controls the slot, and the message was right. `None` means the slot is not in the host's listing at all — so the message told an operator the VTA held a record it had never heard of, and pointed them at `dids/delete` for a DID that does not exist. Both now say what happened and name different next actions. The `Option` was there the whole time; only the message ignored it. The stub host now answers `GET /api/dids` with one slot the VTA has no record of, rather than an empty list. That makes both reconcile arms non-empty in one call — host_only is the stub's slot, agent_only is the minted DID — where an empty list proved one arm and a list echoing the VTA's own records would prove neither. It is also what makes retire-orphan reachable: a slot is retireable precisely when it is host-only. Covers `vta/webvh/servers/{retire-orphan,remove}`. `remove` runs last, after `dids/delete`, because removing the server registration invalidates every path above it — the order an operator actually uses. - **vta**: Refuse a swap-key without linkProof by name, not as malformed ([#1137](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1137)) Coverage 77 to 79 of 109, and a fifth request-side divergence. - **vta**: Carry ecosystem-local capabilities under ext, not in the closed enum ([#1136](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1136)) Coverage 76 to 77 of 109, and a real conformance defect found by covering the device family. `device/register/0.2` put `credentialWrite` in the response's `capabilities` array. The published `Capability` enum does not define it, so the response failed its own schema. This was already known and half-fixed: a filter dropped `sign-trust-task` with a comment saying it is "absent from the wire schema's closed `Capability` enum". `CredentialWrite` was added later, the filter was not extended, and it went straight out. Fixed by carrying both under `ext["org.openvtc"].capabilities` rather than dropping them. Dropping is what the old filter did, and it is lossy in the direction that matters: omitting a capability from a listing is a safety claim, and it was not a true one — the device held `sign-trust-task` and the response said it did not. SPEC §4.5.1 provides the extension slot and `DeviceBinding` declares one, so no upstream change is needed; widening the framework's closed vocabulary with two ecosystem-specific concepts would be the wrong fix anyway. The filter is now positive: `PUBLISHED_CAPABILITIES` lists what the published enum defines and everything else is local, so a capability added tomorrow lands in `ext` by default rather than leaking one variant at a time. The local values are camel-cased at the source, because `wire_v0_2` re-cases kebab to camel only at declared enum field paths and an `ext` member is invisible to it — otherwise the response would answer `deviceAdmin` beside `sign-trust-task`, in two dialects at once. Two blockers recorded in earlier PRs turned out to be one line each. `passkey-vms/enroll-challenge` needs `public_url`, not a WebAuthn relying party — the RP is derived from the public origin. `device/*` needs one ACL row, not a provisioned integration — the entry is the enrolment the device is completing. Both notes were mine; a refusal that names a procedure reads as needing the whole procedure when it needs that procedure's residue. - **vta**: Re-case the extended error codes the Trust Tasks registry moved ([#1122](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1122)) * fix(vta)!: emit the re-cased extended error codes the registry now declares trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#279 re-cased 200 extended error-code local parts to lowerCamelCase per SPEC §4.10 rule 4 — only the part after the `:` moved, the namespace is unchanged. This service still produced the snake_case spellings for 32 of them, so every one of those rejects carried a code the registry no longer defines and no conforming consumer can branch on. Every site here is an **emitter**: this repo decides what to send, and the registry decides what is correct to send, so each moves to the new spelling with no compatibility arm. The matcher side — where this repo reads a code a peer produced and cannot control that peer's deploy order — is handled separately in the following commit. Three of the vault emitters build their namespace by interpolation (`vault/{verb}:not_found`, `vault/{verb}:version_conflict`, `vault/{op}:not_found` in `vault_not_found`, `check_expected_version` and `refuse_if_not_active`), so the codes they produce do not appear as literals anywhere. Those helpers cover `vault/delete:{notFound,versionConflict}` and the `notFound` conflation the three consumer-facing use paths rely on for enumeration resistance. - **vta**: Take keyId from the wire instead of minting one ([#1123](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1123)) First of the three stopgaps #1121 unblocked. `keys/create/0.1` publishes `keyId` as of trust-tasks-rs 0.12.1 (dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#275), so the caller names the key and the binding no longer has to invent one. #1118 minted `internal-` at the binding for an internal key. That was a deliberate deviation from a SHOULD I wrote in #275 — a maintainer offering internal keys and receiving no `keyId` SHOULD reject — taken because the alternative was a security feature nobody could use: an internal key has no derivation path to be named after, the operation layer refuses one without an id, and the wire had no member to carry it. The comment at that site said to delete it when the bump landed. - **vta**: --internal creates an internal key ([#1118](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1118)) `pnm keys create --internal` printed a non-recoverable-key warning, required the operator to type "i understand this key cannot be recovered", and then created an ordinary seed-derived key — recoverable from the mnemonic, included in backups, exportable. The operator was told the opposite of what happened. `CreateKeyRequest` carries `internal`, `key_id` and `derivation_path`; the CLI set them and `VtaClient::create_key` built its wire body with `internal: None` hardcoded, `key_id` never read, and `derivation_path` as `unwrap_or_default()` — `""` for absent, which worked only because the operation layer reads `""` as absent. The operation layer was always right: `derivation_path` is an `Option` there that auto-derives, and `internal` short-circuits to a CSPRNG key. It could not have worked even with the flag forwarded. The spine rejected the document, because `keys/create/0.1` was `additionalProperties: false` with no `internal` member (fixed upstream in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#269, which also added `internal` to `KeyOrigin` — the value that makes the outcome checkable); and an internal key needs an explicit `key_id`, which neither the wire type nor the specification had (dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#275). Forwards `internal` and `derivation_path`, makes `CreateKeyBody`'s `derivation_path` optional to match the specification and the operation layer, and mints a `key_id` for an internal key at the trust-task binding, which has no `keyId` member to carry one yet. That minting is a deliberate, temporary deviation from a SHOULD in the specification, taken because `keyId` needs trust-tasks-rs 0.12.1 and this workspace cannot move to 0.12: `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.19.12 pins `trust-tasks-rs ^0.11` and `vta_sdk::acl_setup` hands it a generated `MediatorAcl`, so two nodes in one graph fail to compile. The id is returned on the record and `keys/rename/0.1` can change it; the site says to delete the branch when the bump lands. `an_internal_key_is_actually_internal` asserts `origin == "internal"` — the check the CLI already made and that always silently failed. ### Chore - **deps**: Trust-tasks-rs 0.12 and the TDK crates that carry it ([#1121](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1121)) Verified locally against a path-patched affinidi-tdk-rs before those crates published (affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#743); VTI's graph collapses to a single trust-tasks-rs 0.12.1 node and the workspace compiles. Bumps trust-tasks-rs 0.11.17 -> 0.12 with the four sibling crates that moved with it — capability-client 0.10 -> 0.11, https 0.10 -> 0.12, didcomm 0.10 -> 0.12, proof 0.10 -> 0.11 — and the TDK crates whose public API carries trust-tasks-rs types: affinidi-tdk 0.8.5 -> 0.9, affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.19 -> 0.20, affinidi-messaging-test-mediator 0.2 -> 0.3. They move together because two trust-tasks-rs nodes in one graph do not warn, they fail to compile: `expected MediatorAcl, found a different MediatorAcl`. One source change. `classify_git_trust_reply` gained a required `expected_thread_id` in capability-client 0.11, because acting on an uncorrelated reply lets whichever document arrives next decide the fate of a write it has nothing to do with. The `replies` registry already keys its waiter on `doc.id`, so this is defence in depth — and `correlation_thread` is the library's own SPEC §4.9 rule (`threadId` falling back to `id`) rather than this call site's guess at it. Three marked stopgaps become deletable once this lands, each of which names this bump at its site: the freshness stand-in from #1117 in favour of `FreshnessPolicy`/`validate_freshness`, the minted `key_id` branch from #1118 in favour of the wire `keyId`, and `replay::check_and_record` in favour of `ReplayGuard`. They are left alone here so this change is a dependency move and nothing else. ### Test - **vta**: Cover the did-templates and policy families ([#1128](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1128)) Coverage 48 -> 58 of 109 (44% -> 53%). Two families, one real defect.

title: fix(vta): say which fact refused a retire-orphan, and cover the slot paths
body:
Coverage **79 → 81 of 109**, and a misleading refusal message fixed — found,
again, by trying to make a task succeed.

## A refusal that asserted the opposite of the truth

`servers/retire-orphan` refuses a slot it cannot confirm is orphaned. Two very
different facts reach the same `NotOrphaned` variant, and its message asserted
one of them for both:

```
slot `X` has a record in this VTA, so it is not an orphan.
use `webvh/dids/delete` for one it still controls.
```

The variant already carries `did: Option<String>`, which distinguishes them:

- **`Some`** — the VTA still controls the slot. The message is right, and
  `dids/delete` is the correct next action.
- **`None`** — the slot is not in the host's listing at all. The VTA has never
  heard of it, so the message told the operator "slot X has a record in this
  VTA" about a slot it has no record of, and pointed them at `dids/delete` for a
  DID that does not exist.

Both now say what actually happened, and name different next actions: delete it,
or re-run reconcile because the report was for another server or has gone stale.

The `did: Option` was there the whole time; only the message ignored it.

## The stub host now reports a host-only slot

Previously it answered `GET /api/dids` with an empty list, deliberately, to
exercise reconcile's *missing-on-host* arm. It now answers with **one slot the
VTA has no record of**, which is strictly better:

- `host_only` — that slot;
- `agent_only` — the DID the test mints.

Both arms non-empty in one call, where an empty list proved one and a list
echoing the VTA's own records would prove neither.

It is also what makes `retire-orphan` reachable at all: **a slot is retireable
precisely when it is host-only**, so there was no way to cover the success path
while the host claimed to hold nothing.

## Newly covered

`vta/webvh/servers/{retire-orphan,remove}`.

`remove` runs last, after `dids/delete` — removing the server registration
invalidates every path above it, so the test follows the order an operator
actually uses rather than a convenient one.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings` — **exit 0**
- `./scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` — 28 suites, **0 violations**, coverage **81/109**
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast` — exit 0
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — exit 0

Refs #1059

title: spec(registry): gate SPEC §7.3 item 19 instead of counting it
body:
Auditing the five remaining backlog items. **Four were already closed**, and two of the counts I had been carrying were wrong in both directions.

| Item | quoted | actual |
|---|---|---|
| Unbounded free-text members | ~68 | **0 live** (17 in retired specs) |
| Redundant `permissionDenied` | 90 | **0 live** (4 in retired specs) |
| Security & Privacy sections | open | **37/37** sensitive specs have one |
| `max_age` follow-up | open | **done** — all three bindings default to `FreshnessPolicy::consequential` |
| Five proof-required responses unsigned | open | **genuinely open** — VTI-side, see below |

## Why there was nothing to fix

Every remaining instance of the first two sits in a `retired` spec. SPEC §5.3 freezes a retired specification's schema *at the moment of retirement*; adding `maxLength` narrows which documents validate, which §5.2 would require a MAJOR increment for — on a spec that is terminal and can take none.

Their live successors already bound them: `confirm/request/0.1` → `task-consent/request/0.1`, which bounds `note` at 500 and `reason` at 1024. **Exempt, not debt.**

## …and that is the problem

#296 and #301 bounded 112 members and left the corpus at zero. Nothing stopped the next spec from reintroducing one. The error-code shadowing rule has a gate; the `issuedAt` floor has a gate; item 19 had a number quoted in a backlog. **A count is not a check.**

This adds the missing lint on the same shape as its two neighbours — a `check*` function, a frozen/offending/conforming counter, an explicit §5.3 exemption, and a failure message stating the rule, the fix, and the pattern to copy.

## Detection is by name, deliberately

Only strings with no closed shape (no `enum`/`const`/`format`/`pattern`/`$ref`/`contentEncoding`) whose member name is in the free-text vocabulary. `did`, `contextId` and `cursor` are unbounded strings too — but bounding an identifier is §10.2's job at the transport, and a lint demanding `maxLength` on all **863** of them would be ignored. That is how the last backlog got its size.

## Verified it fires

A gate that never fires is worthless — this repo has already paid once for a guard that only proved a valid state *existed*.

```
$ # remove maxLength from 'note' in the DRAFT task-consent/request/0.1
Free-text bounds (§7.3 item 19): 336 spec(s) clean; 17 frozen in 12 retired spec(s); 1 unbounded
Build failed with the following problems:
  - task-consent/request/0.1/payload.schema.json: free-text member(s) 'note' declare no 'maxLength'. …

$ # restored
Free-text bounds (§7.3 item 19): 337 spec(s) clean; 17 frozen in 12 retired spec(s); 0 unbounded
Done.
```

The frozen count stays 17 throughout, so the §5.3 exemption holds while the live rule bites.

## Still open, and not in this PR

**The five proof-required responses that return unsigned** — `audit/list`, `auth/whoami`, `credential-exchange/present`, `trust-task-discovery`, `vta/memory/list`. All five specs do require proof on the response; the gap is in VTI, where e.g. `audit/list` returns `Json(AuditListResponse{…})` — a bare payload with no envelope and no proof.

Not attempted here: it needs the VTI 0.12 → 0.17 upgrade first, it spans `vtc-service` and `vta-sdk`, it needs a decision about which key the service signs responses with — and VTI's working tree is currently on another branch with uncommitted changes.

title: spec(registry): gate SPEC §7.3 item 19 instead of counting it (#319)
body:
spec(registry): gate SPEC §7.3 item 19 instead of counting it (#319)

* fix(ci): exempt workspace path dependencies from the wildcard ban

`cargo deny` has failed on main since #316. That PR deliberately dropped
the `version` field from `trust-tasks-https`'s dev-dependency on
`trust-tasks-proof`, because `cargo publish` resolves any dev-dependency
carrying one from the registry — constraining publication order, while
release-plz does not count dev-dependency edges when ordering the
publish. That mismatch half-published 0.17.0. Path-only is the right fix
for it.

But a path dependency with no version is what cargo-deny reports as a
wildcard, so the release fix turned the bans check red:

    error[wildcard]: found 1 wildcard dependency for crate
    'trust-tasks-https'

Set `allow-wildcard-paths = true`, which narrows the ban to registry
crates. That is where an unpinned requirement is an actual supply-chain
risk: a path dependency resolves in-tree and cannot float to something
the author did not intend. The comment records why the version field is
absent, so a future reader does not "fix" it back and re-break the
release.

Verified locally with cargo-deny 0.19.8: advisories ok, bans ok,
licenses ok, sources ok.

title: fix(ci): exempt workspace path dependencies from the wildcard ban
body:
**`cargo deny` is red on `main`** ([run 33031926033](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/actions/runs/33031926033)), and has been since #316 merged. Found while raising #317, whose CI it blocks. Two commits.

## 1. The wildcard ban and the release fix are in direct conflict

#316 deliberately dropped the `version` field from `trust-tasks-https`'s dev-dependency on `trust-tasks-proof`. That fix is correct: `cargo publish` resolves any dev-dependency carrying a `version` from the registry, which constrains publication order — while release-plz does **not** count dev-dependency edges when ordering the publish. That mismatch is what half-published 0.17.0.

But a path dependency with no version is precisely what cargo-deny reports as a wildcard:

```
error[wildcard]: found 1 wildcard dependency for crate 'trust-tasks-https'
```

**Fix:** `allow-wildcard-paths = true`, narrowing the ban to registry crates — where an unpinned requirement is an actual supply-chain risk. A path dependency resolves in-tree and cannot float to something the author did not intend, so the check was never buying anything there. The comment records *why* the `version` field is absent, so a future reader doesn't helpfully add it back and re-break the release.

## 2. `deny.toml` was not in the Rust workflow's `paths` filter

Found because the first commit's own PR ran no Rust CI: `deny.toml` was absent from the filter, so **the file that decides what the supply-chain check bans was the one file that change could not be tested by.** This is the same gap the filter's existing comment records for `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1`, `-capability-client` and `-ceremony`.

Adding it makes the fix self-validating, which is how the `cargo deny | pass` on this PR was produced rather than asserted.

## Verified

Locally with cargo-deny 0.19.8 — `advisories ok, bans ok, licenses ok, sources ok` — and now in CI: all twelve checks pass, including `cargo deny`, `cargo test (stable, full workspace)`, `trust-tasks-codegen drift` and `publication order is satisfiable`.

Independent of #317, which is docs-only and needs this merged (or its check re-run) to go green.

title: docs(spec): say what identifierScope is, and that it is not a scope taxonomy
body:
Companion to [`dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#6`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec/pull/6), which carries the same clarification into the framework specification proper. Addresses [`dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#5`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec/issues/5).

Two files, +8/−1. **No binding, crate, or package is affected.**

## What and why

`identifierScope` and the DTG credentials specification's proposed declared correlation scope ([`dtgwg-cred-spec#22`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22)) read as two vocabularies competing for one axis, with `community` and `linked` having no target here. Working through it, they are not competing — but neither document said so, and the member's name invites the misreading.

`identifierScope` is a machine-readable restatement of §10.5 item 1, which is **binary**: relationship-scoped, or reused across relationships and justified. Not a taxonomy of correlation width. Two consequences now stated in the text:

- It is declared by a **specification about a party role**, before any identifier exists — not by a holder about an identifier it controls. The two are assertions about different subjects; neither overrides the other. This is what lets #22 land in any form without this member moving.
- **A bounded-recognisability identifier is cross-relationship for item 1's purposes** — the joins item 1 forecloses are available to any two of that set who compare what they hold — so it is declared `public` and carries the justification obligation in full. That answers the reported gap without growing the enum.

## Changes here

1. `SPEC.md` — the same three paragraphs as the framework PR, adapted to this copy's `*VID*` emphasis and `[§10.5]` link conventions.
2. `specs/spec.meta.schema.json` — **`description` string only.** It previously called the member "the identifier correlation scope this party's VID is expected to have", which is exactly the reading the framework PR corrects.

## Why this touches no code

The enum is unchanged at three values, so all 56 existing declarations (37 `pairwise`, 19 `public`) stay valid, and `spec.meta.schema.json` is excluded from both generators **by name**:

- `scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs` — `NOT_PAYLOAD_SCHEMAS = new Set(["spec.meta.schema.json", "trust-task.schema.json"])`
- `trust-tasks-codegen/src/main.rs` — walks `payload.schema.json` only

No `IdentifierScope` or `identifier_scope` symbol exists in any `.rs` or `.ts` in the workspace. The one Rust site that opens the meta schema is a `#[test]` reading the *slug* allowlist, which early-returns on the published crate. So: no `codegen-drift`/`bindings-drift` exposure, no lockstep version bump, and none of the struct-literal breakage an additive *payload* member would cause.

## Validation

- `npm run validate` — 349 specs, 66 shared schemas, **no errors** (warnings are pre-existing `additionalProperties` ones).
- `node scripts/build-registry.mjs` — clean, `SPEC.md → website/SPEC.md` synced. The website copy is gitignored, so the diff stays at the two source files.
- The `checkIdentifierScopeJustification` lint is unaffected: it keys on `identifierScope === 'public'`, and this PR adds no value and moves no declaration.

Say what identifierScope is, and that it is not a scope taxonomy (#317)

Carries the framework text of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#6 into
this repository's copy of SPEC.md, and aligns the meta-schema
description with it.

Addresses trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#5: the framework's
identifierScope and the DTG credentials specification's proposed
declared correlation scope (trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#22) read as two
vocabularies for one axis, with `community` and `linked` unmappable
here. They are not competing, and neither document said so.

identifierScope is a machine-readable restatement of §10.5 item 1,
which is binary: relationship-scoped, or reused across relationships
and justified. It is not a taxonomy of correlation width. It is
declared by a specification about a party role, not by a holder about
an identifier it controls, so the two are assertions about different
subjects and neither overrides the other. An identifier recognisable
within a bounded set is, for item 1's purposes, cross-relationship, so
it is declared `public` and carries the justification obligation in
full.

The meta-schema change is to the `description` string only. The enum
stays at three values, so all 56 existing declarations remain valid,
and spec.meta.schema.json is excluded from both binding generators by
name — scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs via NOT_PAYLOAD_SCHEMAS, and
trust-tasks-codegen, which walks payload.schema.json only. No generated
binding, crate, or package is affected, and no version bump is needed.

npm run validate: 349 specs, no errors. Registry build clean.

title: Replace the four VID types with a declared correlation scope
body:
## Summary

The four VID types (R-DID, M-DID, C-DID, P-DID) each encode two independent
things in one name: **what the identifier is attached to**, and **how widely it
may be correlated**. Only the second is what implementers and users need to
reason about, and the first is already carried by the credential the identifier
appears in.

This proposes replacing the four types with a single declared property — the
scope over which an identifier may be correlated — and letting roles be
conferred by credentials, where they already are.

Raised as a follow-up to #21, which is a symptom of the same thing.

## The problem, concretely

The role axis is redundant with the credential type. A VMC's subject is a
member; a VRC's issuer is a party to a relationship. The credential says so.
Naming the identifier again duplicates that, and the duplication is where the
ambiguity lives, because the two can disagree.

Put an M-DID in a VRC — which §VRC explicitly permits — and both names apply.
Is it a membership DID or a relationship DID? The specification has to
disambiguate in prose, and that prose is #21.

The confusion is not hypothetical. In our implementation the word "persona" had
come to mean the membership DID, because a P-DID has no implementation and an
M-DID is described in the glossary as "a type of persona". An entire issue
(`OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1054`) was spent establishing which
identifier the specification was actually talking about.

## Proposal

One axis, monotonic from narrowest to widest, declared by the holder:

| Scope | Known to | Replaces |
|---|---|---|
| `pairwise` | exactly one counterparty | R-DID |
| `community` | one community | M-DID (not reused) |
| `linked` | a set the holder chooses | M-DID (reused), P-DID |
| `public` | unbounded, published, meant to be found | C-DID |

And the accompanying principle: **roles are conferred by credentials, scope is
declared by the holder.** An identifier is not "a membership DID"; it is an
identifier that *has* a membership credential. The VMC makes it a membership.
The name never did.

## What this buys

**The uniqueness requirement becomes definitional.** §Unilateral Relationship
Identification currently needs a normative MUST — "a new, unique R-DID for
every single entity they connect with" — plus a Privacy Consideration
explaining it. Under a scope axis, an identifier declared `pairwise` and used
with two counterparties simply is not pairwise. There is nothing left to
require.

**The public-community case stops being an anomaly.** A public open-source
community declares `community` or `public` and is done. No "bootstrapping", no
recommended migration, none of the framing problem raised in #21.

**C-DID stops being a special case.** A community's DID is a `public`-scoped
identifier that happens to be held by an organisation, not a fourth kind of
thing.

**Verifiers get the inference stated rather than implied.** Seeing `pairwise`
licenses exactly one conclusion: this identifier tells you nothing beyond this
relationship. That is the guarantee the whole model rests on, and today it is
only reachable by knowing what "R" stands for.

## Evidence from implementing it

We did not set out to propose this. Implementing pairwise publication in the
VTC forced an `IdentifierForm::{Attributed, Pairwise}` enum into existence,
because the code had to answer "how wide is this identifier claiming to be?"
and the four-type taxonomy does not answer that question — it answers a
different one. The community profile then needed a field declaring which form
the community expects, and the policy input needed to carry it.

A reference implementation independently reaching for a vocabulary the
specification does not have is the strongest evidence we can offer that the
vocabulary is missing.

## Where the four types are load-bearing, and should stay

Roles are not purely redundant. Two of them have real machinery:

- **Membership** is established by a VMC issued from a C-DID.
- **Persona** is asserted via a VPC.

Those mechanisms should stay exactly as they are. What should go is naming them
as *DID types*, which is the part that collides. Keeping the machinery and
dropping the type names costs nothing and removes the ambiguity.

## Costs, honestly

- It is a vocabulary change to a specification's core terms, which is more
  expensive than any fix in #21. Working Draft 01 is the cheapest moment it
  will ever be.
- R-DID / M-DID / C-DID / P-DID are established shorthand in this working
  group's conversation. They can survive as informal shorthand while the
  normative model uses scope — the same way people say "a web cert" without the
  specification defining that term.
- Declaring scope is not itself a correlation risk: the identifier *value* is
  what correlates. Declaring `pairwise` tells a verifier not to store it as a
  stable key, which helps.

## Requested

Whether the working group considers this in scope for WD02. We are willing to
write the specification text and to report back on what it takes to implement,
since we have already built the two-level version of it by accident.

title: identifierScope and the credential spec's identifier taxonomy should be settled as one axis
body:
## Summary

Framework 0.5.0 added `parties[].identifierScope` — `pairwise | public | any` (`spec/body.md:795`, merged 2026-08-26 in #2). The DTG credentials specification is concurrently considering replacing its four VID types with a declared correlation scope ([`trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#22`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22)), whose proposed values are `pairwise | community | linked | public`.

A witnessed exchange carries credentials under the credential specification's vocabulary inside Trust Task documents under this one. One identifier, two axes, no mapping between them. Raising it here because I wrote the 0.5.0 field, so the divergence is mine, and because it is cheapest to reconcile before the field gains dependants.

Flagged by @albertoleon7794 while testing the credential spec's proposal against a second implementation ([comment](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5432781147)).

## The two axes are not the same kind of thing

Worth separating before deciding whether they should be one vocabulary, because they answer different questions:

|  | This framework's `identifierScope` | cred-spec #22's scope |
|---|---|---|
| Declared by | a Trust Task **specification** | an identifier's **holder** |
| Applies to | a party **role** in that specification | one identifier **instance** |
| Force | descriptive, explicitly not prescriptive (`:797`) | a claim about the identifier itself |

So this is not straightforwardly two vocabularies competing for one slot. A specification saying "this role expects a pairwise identifier" and a holder saying "this identifier is pairwise" are different assertions, and a consumer may reasonably want both.

## The gap that remains either way

`pairwise` and `public` correspond across the two. **`community` and `linked` have no target here.** Neither is `pairwise` — more than one counterparty may recognise the identifier — and neither is `public`, because the set is bounded and enumerable.

The available choices for a producer holding such an identifier are both lossy:

1. **Omit the declaration.** Then `:797` bites: a consumer *"MUST treat an absent or unresolvable declaration as no less correlatable than `public`"*. A bounded identifier is reasoned about as unbounded — the fail-safe working as designed, on an input it was not designed for.
2. **Declare `any`.** That is present and resolvable, so the fail-safe does not fire, but `any` means "the specification takes no position" — the bound is erased rather than overstated.

Either way the fact that the identifier is bounded, and to what, cannot be expressed. That is the substance of the problem, and it does not depend on which axis is right.

## What I am asking

1. Is `pairwise | public | any` intended to be the same axis the credential specification is deciding, or deliberately a coarser spec-level one?
2. If the same: should the two be settled together, and which vocabulary is the base? #22 is unresolved, so neither is committed yet.
3. If deliberately different: should this framework say so, and define how a role-level expectation relates to an instance-level declaration? A consumer seeing both needs to know which governs and what a mismatch means.
4. Independently of 1–3, is the `community`/`linked` gap worth closing here, given the fail-safe is load-bearing?

Happy to write whichever way the group lands, including reverting or widening the 0.5.0 field. I would rather change it now than after Trust Task specifications start declaring against it.

Related: [`dtgwg-cred-spec#22`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22) (the proposal), [`#23`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/23) (edges whose halves declare different scopes — the case that most needs a shared axis, since such an edge crosses both specifications).

title: fix(vta)!: refuse a swap-key without linkProof by name, not as malformed
body:
Coverage **77 → 79 of 109**, and a **fifth** request-side divergence — the same
shape as the four before it, and the second one that turned out to be a *good
policy reported with the wrong code*.

## `acl/swap-key`: right policy, wrong answer

`SwapKeyBody::link_proof` was a bare `String`, so a producer that omitted it got
`malformedRequest`.

The schema makes it optional, and says why:

> Cryptographic evidence — **required by some maintainers** — that the new VID
> consents to taking over. … Producers omit this when the consumer's policy
> doesn't require it.

So this deployment requiring it is **exactly the split the specification
describes**, and the existing comment already said so: "The spec marks this
optional at the framework level, but the FPN deployment policy requires it."

What was wrong is the *answer*. `malformedRequest` tells a producer its document
is the wrong shape, sending it to re-read a schema that will agree with the
producer. It now parses and is refused with `acl:link_proof_required`, naming
what this maintainer wants.

**The security posture is unchanged** — a swap with no proof of possession is
still refused, on both the Trust Task and DIDComm paths.

That is the second of these (after `auth/revoke-session`'s `all` in #1134) where
the service's behaviour was right and only the reporting was wrong. Worth
separating from the other three (`derivationPath`, `internal`, `enabled`), which
were plain bugs.

## Also covered

- `vta/credentials/{issue,revoke}` — chained, because revoke needs an id only an
  issue produces.
- `vta/contexts/update-did`.

## What is asserted, and what is not

`swap_key_without_a_link_proof_names_the_policy` covers the **refusal**, not the
success. The success path needs a real VP-JWT signed by the new subject *and*
`currentSubject` equal to the authenticated caller — a second keypair and a
signing ceremony. Recorded in the test so it is a known cost rather than an
oversight.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings` — **exit 0**
- `./scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` — 28 suites, **0 violations**, coverage **79/109**
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast` — exit 0
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — exit 0

BREAKING CHANGE: `SwapKeyBody::link_proof` is `Option<String>`. An
`acl/swap-key` request without one is refused as `taskFailed` /
`acl:link_proof_required` instead of `malformedRequest`; it is still refused.

Refs #1059

title: Say what identifierScope is, and that it is not a scope taxonomy
body:
Addresses #5. Prose only, one file, +7. **No schema change and no code change** — see the blast-radius note at the bottom.

## The problem

#5 reported that this framework's `parties[].identifierScope` (`pairwise | public | any`) and the DTG credentials specification's proposed declared correlation scope (`pairwise | community | linked | public`, [`dtgwg-cred-spec#22`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22)) look like two vocabularies for one axis, with `community` and `linked` having no faithful target here. A witnessed exchange carries credentials under that vocabulary inside Trust Task documents under this one, so the two meet on a single identifier.

Working through it, they are **not** competing vocabularies — but nothing in the text says so, and the member's name actively invites the misreading.

## What this says

**`identifierScope` is a machine-readable restatement of Identifier Correlation and Linkability item 1**, which is a binary rule: an identifier is relationship-scoped, or it is reused across relationships and needs justification. The three values mirror that rule plus abstention. It is not a taxonomy of correlation width and does not claim to be one.

Two consequences, both now stated:

1. **It is declared by a specification, about a party role** — before any identifier exists — not by a holder about an identifier it controls. Where a holder declares something about its own identifier under another specification, the two are assertions about different subjects. Neither overrides the other, and a divergence is not itself a conformance failure. That is what makes the two axes compose rather than compete, and it means #22 can land in any form without this member needing to move.

2. **A bounded-recognisability identifier is a cross-relationship identifier for item 1's purposes.** A VID that one community's members can recognise is reused across relationships, and the joins item 1 forecloses are available to any two of them who compare what they hold. So it is declared `public` and carries the justification obligation in full.

That second point answers the reported `community`/`linked` gap by deciding it rather than by growing the enum. The framework deliberately does not grade width: the bound may be unknown to the parties and may grow, and item 1 does not turn on it. A specification needing to record the bound states it in its justification — which the existing lint already asks for.

It also makes the fail-safe in the following paragraph correct rather than overstated. Treating an unresolvable declaration as "no less correlatable than `public`" is not a bug applied to bounded identifiers; under item 1 a bounded identifier **is** on the `public` side.

## Blast radius

Verified before writing:

- The enum stays at three values. `specs/spec.meta.schema.json` is unchanged, so the 37 `pairwise` and 19 `public` declarations across the registry stay valid.
- `spec.meta.schema.json` is excluded from **both** binding generators by name — `scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs` (`NOT_PAYLOAD_SCHEMAS`) and `trust-tasks-codegen/src/main.rs`, which walks `payload.schema.json` only. No `IdentifierScope` symbol exists in any `.rs` or `.ts` in the workspace.
- No crate or package version bump, no `codegen-drift`/`bindings-drift` exposure, no struct-literal breakage.

A companion PR carries the same text into `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`'s copy of `SPEC.md` and aligns the meta-schema description.

`npm run render` clean.

title: Name the asymmetric edge: two halves may declare different correlation scopes
body:
## Summary

The specification assumes both halves of a DTG edge are the same kind of thing.
When two communities with opposite disclosure policies form an edge, they are
not: one half is published under an attributed, correlatable identifier and the
other under a pairwise one. The four VID types cannot name this edge, and
nothing states what an implementation should conclude about its privacy.

This is not the mixed-scope community case (a community that uses different
identifier kinds internally). It is two communities, two policies, and one edge
whose halves legitimately disagree.

## Detail

A DTG edge is two VRCs, one in each direction. Each party issues its own half
and chooses the identifier it appears under. Neither can impose that choice on
the other, and neither needs to.

Take a deliberately public community — an open-source project whose whole value
is that contributions trace back to named people — and a deliberately private
one, where members are known to each other only by per-counterparty identifiers.
A member of each forms a relationship with a member of the other:

- Half 1 is issued by the public member under an attributed identifier, into a
  graph anyone can read.
- Half 2 is issued by the private member under an R-DID that only their
  counterparty can map to them.

Both halves are conformant. The edge is one edge.

**1. The taxonomy has no word for it.** Under the four VID types, an implementer
must ask whether this is an R-DID edge or an M-DID edge. It is one of each.
There is no answer, because the question presumes both halves are the same kind.
This is a stronger argument for the structural change proposed in #22 than the
mixed-scope community case is: there, one authority chooses; here, no single
party is entitled to choose.

**2. Nothing says an edge's effective privacy is the minimum of its halves.**
The private member declared the scope of *their own* identifier, and that
declaration is honoured — only their counterparty can resolve it. But their
counterparty publishes the other half into a public, correlatable graph, so the
pairwise identifier now sits next to a named person in a place anyone can read.

The private member has no say in where the other half is published, and no way
to discover it. §Privacy Considerations 2 addresses R-DID uniqueness — reuse
across counterparties — which is a different failure. Nothing addresses the case
where a *correctly unique* R-DID is correlated by what the other party does with
its own half.

The rule that seems to be missing: **an edge's effective disclosure is the
maximum of its two halves; a declared scope binds only its own holder.** Neither
sentence appears in the specification, and an implementation that computed
privacy from one half alone would be wrong in a way nothing warns it about.

## Why it matters

Cross-community edges are the interesting case for a trust spanning layer — an
edge inside one community is governed by one policy and needs no reconciliation.
If the specification only describes edges whose halves agree, it describes the
case that does not need it.

An implementation reading the current text will reasonably conclude that a
pairwise-declared identifier stays pairwise. In the cross-community case it does
not, and the party who loses privacy is the one who followed the guidance.

## Requested clarification

1. Does the specification acknowledge that the two halves of one edge may
   declare different scopes, and is that a conformant edge?
2. Should it state that a declared scope constrains only its own holder's
   disclosure, and that an edge's effective disclosure is the maximum of its
   halves?
3. Should that appear as a Privacy Consideration, or normatively?

**Proposed answer**, for the group to react to rather than open cold: name it.
State that scope is declared per identifier and experienced per edge, that
halves may legitimately differ, and add the maximum rule as a Privacy
Consideration. Under the declared-scope model in #22 this falls out of the
vocabulary; under the four types it needs prose.

## Context

Raised while implementing the VRC path in
`OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure`. The cross-community analysis is set
out in full, with the graph drawn from a single shared edge list, in the
["Across communities" section of the DTG conformance
review](https://docs.fpp.storm.ws/dtg-conformance-infographic.html) (items
X1 and X2). Related: #21 (edge verifiability), #22 (declared correlation
scope).

title: VRC edge-verifiability conditions exist only in the glossary and contradict the body
body:
## Summary

The glossary definition of the VRC states conditions for edge verifiability that
appear nowhere in the body, contradict the body's Privacy Considerations, and
contradict the body's own bidirectional edge model. The VMC definition carries
half of the same construction.

The VRC entry (`spec/terms-definitions/verifiable_relationship_credential.md`)
has not been revised since the Working Draft 01 migration (#3), while the body's
treatment of R-DIDs, M-DIDs and the ZKP constructions has moved on. An
implementer reading the two together gets opposite instructions.

## Detail

The glossary entry reads:

> A VRC may contain either R-DIDs or M-DIDs. A VRC is only verifiable as a DTG
> edge in the context of a specific VTN if: a) it contains M-DIDs for both
> peers, b) both peers have signed the VRC using their M-DID private keys,
> c) both M-DIDs are verifiable via VMCs issued by VTCs, and d) those VTCs are
> recognized as VTN trust anchors in that VTN.

Three problems.

**1. It inverts the body's identifier guidance.** The body recommends the
opposite of condition (a):

- §VRC: "R-DIDs are RECOMMENDED for privacy; M-DIDs are allowed for
  bootstrapping (see Privacy Considerations)."
- §Unilateral Relationship Identification: "The valid application of this
  specification requires that each entity MUST generate a new, unique R-DID for
  every single entity they connect with, even within the same community."
- §Privacy Considerations 1: "Migration from M-DID-based to R-DID-based edges is
  recommended post-bootstrapping for enhanced privacy."

So the body tells an implementer to migrate to R-DID edges, and the glossary
tells the same implementer that an R-DID edge is not verifiable as an edge. Read
together, the privacy-preserving construction the body recommends is the one
that forfeits VTN-level edge verifiability.

**2. It is not reconciled with the Community-Anchored ZKP.** §Community-Anchored
Zero-Knowledge Proof states plainly that "Community membership is **not** a
precondition for issuing, holding, or presenting a VRC," and then defines a
construction in which the holder proves that "the VRC issuer possesses a VMC
from the *same* C-DID" *without revealing the specific DIDs*. That is the same
predicate the glossary's conditions (c) and (d) express by disclosure. If the
ZKP construction satisfies VTN-level edge verifiability, the glossary's
requirement for M-DIDs in the credential is unnecessary; if it does not, the
body should say so, because the ZKP section currently reads as though it does.
(Related: #9, on whether the linkages those constructions require are encoded at
all.)

**3. Condition (b) contradicts the bidirectional edge model** — and the first
sentence of the glossary entry itself. §VRC: "two VRCs (one each direction) form
a complete DTG edge," and the schema has a single `issuer` and a single `proof`.
The glossary entry opens by calling a VRC "one half of a bidirectional peer-to-
peer trust relationship" and then requires that "both peers have signed the VRC"
— which describes a single dual-signed credential, not two.

**4. The VMC entry carries the same unsourced construction.**
`verifiable_membership_credential.md`: "A VMC is only verifiable as a DTG edge in
the context of a specific VTN if the issuing VTC is recognized as a VTN trust
anchor on that VTN." Whether or not that one is correct, "only verifiable as a
DTG edge in the context of a specific VTN" is a normative-sounding constraint
that exists in no normative section. `grep` for it returns only these two
glossary files.

## Why it matters

This is not theoretical. In `OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1054` we are
deciding whether relationship credentials published to a community should carry
pairwise R-DIDs or membership M-DIDs, and the current VTC policy requires both
parties to be identifiable current members — which is the glossary's rule.
Choosing correctly requires knowing whether an R-DID edge is a first-class DTG
edge or a degraded one, and the specification currently answers both ways
depending on which file is read.

## Requested clarification

1. Is VTN-level edge verifiability intended to be a defined property of the
   specification at all? If so, it belongs in a normative section, not only in
   the glossary.
2. If it is: does a VRC carrying R-DIDs, presented with a community-anchored
   ZKP, satisfy it? Our reading of §Community-Anchored ZKP is that it should,
   and that condition (a) is a bootstrapping-era artifact.
3. Should condition (b) be struck as inconsistent with the two-VRC edge model,
   or does it describe an alternative single-credential form that the body does
   not define?
4. Should the VMC entry's edge-verifiability sentence be moved to the body or
   removed?

Happy to open a PR against `spec/terms-definitions/` and the relevant body
sections once the group has a view on (1) and (2) — the answer to (2) in
particular changes what the fix looks like rather than just where it lands.

title: Add a privacy consideration for the effective disclosure of an edge
body:
Addresses #23. One paragraph, one file.

The rule proposed in #23 and supported by both @mitchuski and @albertoleon7794: **a choice of identifier constrains only its own holder's disclosure, and an edge's effective disclosure is the wider of its two halves.**

## Why it is missing today

Privacy consideration 2 covers R-DID reuse — an issuer's own failure, which the issuer can avoid. This is the other case: a *correctly* unique R-DID that is correlated to a named party because the counterparty published the opposing half under an M-DID into a readable graph. The party who loses privacy is the one who followed the specification's recommendation, through an action it neither controls nor can discover. Nothing currently warns an implementation that computing an edge's privacy from the half it issued gives the wrong answer.

## Two corrections to the framing in #23

I filed #23 as a cross-community problem. Two people have since improved on that, and the text reflects them rather than my original framing:

- @albertoleon7794's classifier returns **no answer** — not a wrong one — when asked whether a mixed edge is an R-DID or an M-DID edge, and, more usefully, showed the same failure is reachable **inside a single community** passing through the migration consideration 1 recommends. So it is not a cross-community special case, and the text says so.

title: Define edge verifiability normatively and strike it from the glossary
body:
Closes #21.

#21 asked four questions and offered a PR once the group had a view on Q1 and Q2. Both now have concordant answers from the ZKP task force ([#21 comment](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/21#issuecomment-5427885485)) and from a second implementation with runnable verifiers ([#21 comment](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/21#issuecomment-5432779043)), so here is the text. It is offered for the editors to react to rather than as a settled outcome.

## What changes

A normative **Edge Verifiability** section is added to Edge Credentials, and both glossary entries are reduced to a pointer at it. Three files, +26/−2.

The section defines the property **with respect to a verifier** rather than in the abstract: a credential is an edge to a verifier when its proof verifies and the verifier can establish that the issuer holds a VMC from a VTC in the anchor set that verifier accepts. A VTN is the common case of such an anchor set, but no VTN need exist. That phrasing is @mitchuski's, who reports the reference circuits already state it that way; it should also serve #24, where the two peers anchor in different VTNs or in none.

## Against the four questions

**Q1 — is edge verifiability a defined property at all?** Now yes, in a normative section. Previously it appeared only in two glossary files.

**Q2 — does a VRC carrying R-DIDs with a community-anchored ZKP satisfy it? Yes.** The anchor predicate may be satisfied by disclosure *or* by proof, and the two are equivalent. Glossary condition (a) — M-DIDs for both peers — is dropped. It would have excluded the construction the specification recommends on privacy grounds, and, as @albertoleon7794 noted, it would have made the specification's own VRC example (`did:peer` to `did:peer`, no membership credential) not an edge.

Per Mitch's qualifier, a note records that the linkage the proof route depends on — that the party controlling the R-DID is the party holding the VMC — is not yet encoded, so that route states an intended design goal until #9 lands. That bears on the proof's witness data, not on whether the edge counts, and the note says so.

**Q3 — strike the dual-signature condition? Yes.** The schema defines one `issuer` and one `proof`, so condition (b) could not be satisfied by *any* credential, including the M-DID edges it existed to bless. The section states instead that each half is signed by its own issuer and evaluated independently, and that the halves need not satisfy it by the same route — which is also the seam #23 needs.

**Q4 — the VMC sentence.** Same unsourced construction, same treatment.

## Scope

Deliberately excluded: the framing of M-DID edges as a bootstrapping state rather than a valid terminal form (raised in a [#21 comment](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/21#issuecomment-5424663130)). It is a real problem but a separable one, and only Q1–Q4 have three-party agreement. Happy to follow up if the editors want it in the same pass.

Also excluded: anything that depends on #22. This fix is written to hold whether or not the four VID types survive.

## Validation

`npm run render` is clean; the dangling-definitions list is byte-identical to `main`, and every `[[ref:]]` in the new section resolves. `VTN trust anchor` remains referenced from two other glossary entries, so removing the references here does not orphan it.

title: Use did:webvh in examples and state what each VID role needs of a DID method
body:
## Summary

Two related changes to how this specification treats DID methods.

**The examples showed `did:web` for durable issuers.** The VTC (`chess-club.example`), the witness service, and the IDVC issuer were all `did:web`. That method resolves to a document with no verifiable history: a verifier can establish which key is authoritative *now*, but not which key was authoritative *when the credential was signed*, and there is no recovery path on key compromise. Since DTG credentials may be presented long after issuance, and [Security Considerations](https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-cred-spec/#security-considerations) requires verifiers to validate the verification method, `did:web` understates what the specification assumes of a C-DID.

These examples now use [`did:webvh`](https://identity.foundation/didwebvh/), whose DID log publishes an append-only history of document versions, commits to successor keys via `nextKeyHashes`, and may be witnessed. Pairwise subjects are unchanged and stay on `did:key` / `did:peer`.

**The specification was silent on what it needs from a DID method.** It mandates none — correctly, and this PR does not change that — but it also never said what it relies on a method to provide, leaving implementers no basis for choosing one. The new informative `DID Method Considerations` subsection separates the two property sets, which pull against each other:

| | Durable (C-DID, M-DID) | Pairwise (R-DID, P-DID) |
|---|---|---|
| Key history | Verifiable, so signing-time key state is recoverable | Not required |
| Rotation | Without changing the identifier | Not required |
| Successor keys | Pre-rotation or equivalent commitment | Not required |
| Creation cost | Amortised over the identifier's life | Cheap, no registration step |
| Resolution origin | Independent of a single operator | **Not shared across identifiers** |
| Service endpoints | Discoverable (VTA, `credentialStatus`, trust registry) | Not required |

The conclusion is that implementations should expect to use more than one method rather than seeking one that serves every role. Nothing here requires an `issuer` and a `credentialSubject.id` to share a method, and the examples now reflect that.

## Privacy consideration 7

Correlation does not require the credentials themselves. Where several of a party's R-DIDs or P-DIDs resolve through common infrastructure — a shared web origin, a shared registry, or a shared set of witnesses observing their updates — that infrastructure can associate identifiers the credential structure was designed to keep apart, and can observe when each is used.

The existing considerations (1–3) cover correlation through credential *content*; none covered correlation through the *resolution layer*. This makes DID method choice for pairwise roles a privacy decision, not only a key management one — and it is the reason the table above marks "no shared resolution origin" as the property that distinguishes the two sets.

## Notes for reviewers

- **Entirely informative.** No normative requirement is added, changed, or removed. No schema changes.
- **No method is mandated.** `did:webvh` appears in examples and as an illustration of a method satisfying the durable-role properties; the text is written in terms of properties so that other methods can be assessed against it. This is deliberate — it is what makes a later conformance statement for, say, a KERI-based method cheap to write.
- **SCIDs in the examples are illustrative placeholders**, truncated in the house style used elsewhere for `did:key` and `did:peer` values. They are not real, resolvable SCIDs.
- Independent of #19; the two touch different parts of the document.

title: trust-tasks-v0.17.0
body:
### Changed

- **versioning**: Release the trust-tasks-rs-exposing crates in lockstep ([#315](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/315))


### Specifications

- Bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength (§7.3) ([#296](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/296))

* spec: bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength

  SPEC.md §7.3 (framework 0.5.0) requires that any member holding free
  text declare a `maxLength`. 92 free-text string members across 83 draft
  schemas carried none, leaving the wire contract unbounded and every
  consumer to invent its own ceiling — or none, which is what §10.3
  (schema-validation DoS) exists to prevent.

  Bounds are chosen per member from the vocabulary the registry already
  uses rather than applied uniformly:

    256   `label`, `comment` — a display name or an OpenSSH key comment;
          matches the existing 256 on provision/integration `label` and
          the `name` members alongside it.
    500   requester-authored prose that a surface renders to a human who
          is deciding something; matches task-consent/request/0.1 `note`,
          the registry's considered consent-surface bound.
    1024  `reason`, `description`, `message` — operator or service prose
          recorded for audit or returned as a diagnostic; matches the six
          existing `reason: 1024` and the `description: 1024` in policy/
          and vtc/endorsement-type.
    16384 chat/message `text` — the task's actual content rather than
          metadata about it; matches the corpus's long-form bound on
          vault `secureNotes`.

  All amended specifications are `status: draft`, so the change is made in
  place per SPEC §5.2. Deliberately untouched:

    * 17 members in `retired` specifications, frozen by SPEC §6.4.
    * messaging/_shared/0.1 `AuditEntry.detail` and did-management/
      _shared/0.1 `DomainEntry.label` — shared $defs reachable from a
      retired specification, so bounding them would change a frozen
      specification's effective wire contract.
    * vault/_shared/{0.1,0.2,0.3} `TspMessageEnvelope.message` — opaque
      base64url TSP bytes, not free text.

  The `label` description in vault/_shared/*/vault-entry.schema.json said
  the wire spec enforced no maximum length. It now does, so the sentence
  is corrected rather than left contradicting the schema it annotates.

  `npm run validate` re-checks all 533 fenced example documents against
  the amended schemas; none is rejected by a new bound.
