title: fix(vta)!: carry ecosystem-local capabilities under ext, not in the closed enum
body:
Coverage **76 → 77 of 109**, and a real conformance defect found by covering
the device family — plus two blockers that turned out not to be blockers.

## The defect: an ecosystem-local capability leaked into a closed enum

`device/register/0.2` put `credentialWrite` in the response's `capabilities`
array. The published `Capability` enum does not have it, so the response failed
its own schema.

The interesting part is that **this was already known and half-fixed**. There
was a filter dropping `sign-trust-task` with a comment saying it is "absent from
the wire schema's closed `Capability` enum". `CredentialWrite` was added later
(the vault-credential lifecycle), the filter was not extended, and it went
straight out.

### Fixed by carrying them, not dropping them

Dropping is what the old filter did, and it is lossy in the direction that
matters: omitting a capability from a listing is a **safety claim**, and it was
not a true one — the device held `sign-trust-task` and the response said it did
not.

SPEC §4.5.1 has an extension slot for exactly this, and `DeviceBinding`
declares one. Both local capabilities now travel under
`ext["org.openvtc"].capabilities`, so a reader sees the device's real authority
and the closed enum stays closed.

**No upstream change.** Widening the framework's vocabulary with two
ecosystem-specific concepts would be the wrong fix even if it were cheaper:
that enum is closed on purpose, and `ext` is the mechanism the specification
provides for precisely this.

### The filter is now positive, not negative

`PUBLISHED_CAPABILITIES` lists what the published enum defines, and anything
else is treated as local. A capability added to this workspace tomorrow lands
in `ext` by default rather than leaking — which is the exact failure mode that
produced this bug, one variant at a time.

### Casing

The local values are camel-cased at the source. `wire_v0_2` re-cases enum
values kebab→camel for the 0.2 wire, but only at **declared enum field paths**
— an `ext` member is invisible to it. Without this the response would answer
`deviceAdmin` beside `sign-trust-task`, in two dialects at once.

## Two "blockers" that were not

Both were recorded in earlier PRs as needing heavy fixtures. Both were one line:

- **`passkey-vms/enroll-challenge`** — I recorded this as needing a WebAuthn
  relying party. It needs **`public_url`**: the RP is *derived* from the VTA's
  public origin (`require_public_url` → `build_webauthn`), and the fixture left
  it unset. Setting the origin is the whole prerequisite.
- **`device/*`** — recorded as needing a provisioned integration, because
  `register` refuses a DID with no ACL entry ("complete provision-integration +
  acl/swap-key first"). It needs one **row**: the entry *is* the enrolment the
  device is completing, and seeding it is what a swapped-in long-term key leaves
  behind.

Worth stating plainly because I wrote both of those notes: a refusal message
that names a *procedure* ("complete provision-integration first") reads as
needing the whole procedure, when what it needs is that procedure's residue.

## Newly covered

`device/{register,heartbeat,set-wake}` (on the non-deprecated `0.2` URIs),
`passkey-vms/enroll-challenge`.

Still uncovered, with the reason in the test: `passkey-vms/{enroll-submit,
revoke}` need a real authenticator attestation over the challenge, and the
`services` write paths need a live DIDComm handshake.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings` — **exit 0**
- `./scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` — 28 suites, **0 violations**, coverage **77/109**
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast` — 54 suites, 0 failures
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — exit 0

BREAKING CHANGE: `device/register` and the other device responses carry
`credentialWrite` / `signTrustTask` under `ext["org.openvtc"].capabilities`
instead of omitting them (`signTrustTask`) or emitting them in the closed
`capabilities` enum (`credentialWrite`).

Refs #1059

title: fix(release): drop the version from the dev-dependency that half-published 0.17.0
body:
## What happened

The 0.17.0 release published **four of eight** crates and then died:

```
failed to select a version for the requirement `trust-tasks-proof = "^0.17"`
candidate versions found which didn't match: 0.13.0, 0.12.1, 0.12.0, ...
required by package `trust-tasks-https v0.17.0`
```

| published at 0.17.0 | still on old versions |
|---|---|
| `trust-tasks-rs` | `trust-tasks-proof` 0.13.0 |
| `trust-tasks-didcomm` | `trust-tasks-tsp` 0.14.0 |
| `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` | `trust-tasks-https` 0.16.0 |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | `trust-tasks` 0.2.0 |

## Why

`cargo publish` resolves any dev-dependency that carries a `version` from the registry. So a versioned dev-dependency on a workspace sibling constrains publication order **exactly as a normal dependency does** — while release-plz does **not** count dev-dependency edges when it orders the publish. It packaged `trust-tasks-https` before `trust-tasks-proof` had uploaded.

That question was explicitly open in `rust.yml`'s comment ("its documentation does not state whether that order counts dev-dependencies"). It is now settled, the expensive way: it does not.

The edge has been there since #284. It survived only because the requirement named an *older, already-published* version. Lockstep versioning moved it to `^0.17`, which did not exist yet — turning a latent ordering bug into a half-published release. **That is a consequence of the lockstep change I made in #315**, and this is the fix `rust.yml` already prescribed for exactly this case.

## Fix

Drop `version`, keep `path`. Cargo then strips the dependency from the published manifest, so it imposes no ordering constraint at all. Verified `cargo check -p trust-tasks-https --all-targets --all-features` still passes — the example builds in-tree from `path`.

## The guard becomes a gate

Asserting the graph is acyclic was **necessary but not sufficient**: a valid order existing does not mean release-plz will use it. The job now fails on *any* intra-workspace dev-dependency carrying a version — the condition that actually is sufficient.

Verified both directions against real `cargo metadata`:

```
pre-fix:   offenders: [('trust-tasks-https', 'trust-tasks-proof', '^0.17')]  -> exit 1
post-fix:  offenders: none                                                   -> exit 0
```

## Completing the release

crates.io uploads cannot be undone, so the four published crates stay. Once this merges, re-running the workflow publishes the remaining four at 0.17.0 — `release_always` resumes and skips what is already up. No version renumbering is needed.

### Added

- **specs**: Require issuedAt on every live consequential spec, and make the §7.3 item 17 floor fatal ([#302](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/302))

* spec: make the §7.3 item 17 freshness floor a hard failure

- **rs**: Make SPEC §7.3 item 17's issuedAt MUST expressible ([#300](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/300))

Framework 0.5.0's §7.3 item 17 says a Trust Task specification defining a
  consequential Trust Task MUST require the `issuedAt` member, raising §4.2's
  SHOULD to a MUST for documents conforming to it. There was no way to declare
  that: the meta-schema had `proofRequirement` for the `proof` envelope member
  and nothing equivalent for `issuedAt`, so the MUST was unexpressible and none
  of the 209 consequential specs in the registry could comply.

  Adds `issuedAtRequirement` to the front-matter meta-schema, modelled on
  `proofRequirement` — same two forms (a single `requirement`, or a per-variant
  `request`/`response` pair), same enum, same `rationale`. It governs an envelope
  member, admits a per-variant reading because request and response are relied on
  differently, and reading one declaration now teaches the other.

  Declared rather than derived, with the derived floor checked and reported:

    * `sideEffects` and `exposure` are DESCRIPTIVE (§7.3 items 13/14). Deriving
      `issuedAt`-REQUIRED from them would mean that correcting `sideEffects.level`
      from `none` to `mutating` for accuracy silently changed which documents
      every consumer of that spec must reject.
    * §2 makes the *handler* authoritative for consequentiality, not the front
      matter — so a value computed from the front matter would enforce something
      the front matter does not authoritatively state.
    * A non-consequential spec may legitimately require `issuedAt` anyway; a
      derived-only mechanism cannot express that.
    * Deriving would flip 209 specs' wire behaviour in one commit, invisibly.

  So the build derives the floor instead of substituting for the declaration.
  `npm run validate` prints a `Freshness floor (§7.3 item 17)` line counting the
  consequential specs that have not declared it (currently 0/209), *fails* on a
  spec that declares something weaker than REQUIRED, and escalates the undeclared
  case to a hard error under `TT_STRICT_ISSUED_AT=1` — the ratchet that becomes
  the default once the registry has caught up.

  Enforcement reaches consumers the same way `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` does:

    * `Payload::IS_ISSUED_AT_REQUIRED` (Rust) and `SpecPolicy.isIssuedAtRequired`
      (TypeScript), emitted per variant by both generators from the front matter.
    * `TrustTask::enforce_spec_policy` / `enforceSpecPolicy` reject a document
      with no `issuedAt` as `malformedRequest`. Not `expired`: §8.3 defines no
      dedicated code, `expired` names a document that was once acceptable, and
      §7.2 item 13 already uses `malformedRequest` for the other freshness
      rejections.
    * The trait constant has a default of `false`, so hand-written impls — the
      crate's own `trust-task-error`, hand-modelled in `error.rs` because it is
      in the codegen's SKIP_SLUGS, and every downstream impl — keep compiling.
    * `check-bindings` compares the new key across front matter, Rust and
      TypeScript, so the two languages cannot drift on it.

  Distinct from `FreshnessPolicy::require_issued_at`, which is a *consumer's*
  own posture applied to every document it sees. This is the *specification's*
  requirement, published in the registry and not the consumer's to relax.

  No specification declares `issuedAtRequirement` yet — that is a follow-up,
  spec by spec. The generated Rust tree is therefore byte-identical (the const is
  emitted only on override) and the generated TypeScript gains one
  `isIssuedAtRequired: false` line per policy object. Nothing that was accepted
  before is rejected now.

  Also documents the declaration in CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md, and teaches
  `npm run new-spec` to emit it on a scaffold whose declared classes make the
  task consequential.



### Changed

- **versioning**: Release the trust-tasks-rs-exposing crates in lockstep ([#315](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/315))


### Fixed

- **rs**: Enforce both halves of the SPEC §6.1 slug reservation ([#293](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/293))

* fix(rs): enforce both halves of the SPEC 6.1 slug reservation

  TypeUri rejected a published framework specification and accepted a reserved
  one, in the same function pair:

    REJECTED  trust-task-control     published since 0.1; its Type URI would not parse
    PARSES    trust-ceremony-evil    reserved by 6.1, accepted from any party

  is_reserved_namespace checked only the trust-task half of
  ^trust-(task|ceremony)($|-|/), so the ceremony half of the reservation — which
  exists precisely so the ceremony layer has a namespace no other party can claim
  first — protected nothing. And is_allowed_framework_slug listed five slugs
  where specs/spec.meta.schema.json lists seven, so two published specs sat
  inside the reservation with no permission to be there.

  The allowlist is one of two hand-maintained copies. The new test reads the
  meta-schema's copy and fails naming the missing slug if they drift again;
  verified by removing trust-task-control and watching it fail.

  Found while retiring trust-task-ok ([#292](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/292)), which swept for references to the
  slug and noticed the two lists disagreed.



### Specifications

- Bound the remaining free-text payload members and state who reads them ([#301](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/301))

SPEC.md §7.3 (framework 0.5.0) item 19 has three parts. PR #296 closed most
  of part 1 for eight member names (`reason`, `note`, `detail`, `description`,
  `message`, `text`, `label`, `comment`), 92 members in all. Sweeping the whole
  corpus rather than a name list finds **48 more** unbounded free-text members
  across 27 draft specifications and 10 shared schemas, under names the earlier
  sweep did not look for: `purpose`, `deviceLabel`, `displayName`, `explanation`,
  `summary`, `title`, `name`, `blurb`, `filename`, `trace`, `error`, `lastError`,
  `deniedReason`, `displayHint`, `consequences`, `rpName`, `userName`,
  `userDisplayName`.

  The one the earlier review named specifically is here: `task-consent`'s
  `Effect.summary` — the member its own schema calls "the ONLY member a consent
  surface is guaranteed to be able to render" — was unbounded on the surface a
  human reads to approve an action. It is now 500, the same figure as the `note`
  beside it.

  Bounds are drawn from the vocabulary the corpus already uses and sized per
  member, not applied uniformly:

      64   WebAuthn entity names (`rp.name`, `user.name`, `user.displayName`,
           `rpName`, `userName`, `userDisplayName`) — the length WebAuthn tells
           authenticators to truncate to, so a longer value would be silently
           cut on the device rather than carried.
     128   `purpose` where it names a decision slot or a declared intent. This
           is consistency repair, not a new judgement: policy/activate/0.1 and
           policy/active/0.1 already declared `maxLength: 128` on the request
           member while the response that echoes it declared none.
     256   display labels and names — `deviceLabel`, `displayName`,
           `displayHint`, `label`, `title`, `name`, `blurb`, `filename`;
           matches #296's reasoning that a display name is not prose.
     500   consent-surface prose a human reads while deciding — `Effect.summary`,
           `consequences[]`, credential-exchange `purpose`, `deniedReason`;
           matches task-consent/request/0.1 `note`.
    1024   operator or service diagnostic prose — `explanation`, `trace[]`,
           `error`, `lastError`, and vta/credentials/issue `purpose`.

  **Part 3 of the MUST is the half nobody had done.** Item 19 also requires each
  specification to state who reads a free-text value, whether the recipient is
  expected to retain it, and whether it is trusted. Prose is added to the
  `## Security & Privacy` section of all **37** draft specifications that reach a
  newly bounded member — the 27 whose own payload schema moved, plus 10 that
  reach one through a shared `$def`. `vta/credentials/issue/0.{1,2}` had no such
  section at all and now carry one containing the item 19 statement; both remain
  on the Security & Privacy debt allowlist, because neither yet has the four
  sub-headings the repo lint wants. The other 35 sections were extended in place.

  Deliberately untouched, matching #296's own carve-outs:

    * `messaging/_shared/0.1` `AuditEntry.detail` and `did-management/_shared/0.1`
      `DomainEntry.label` — shared `$defs` reachable from a retired specification,
      so bounding them would move a frozen specification's wire contract. These
      are the only two shared schemas in this change's blast radius that a
      retired spec reaches; the ten this PR edits are draft-only.
    * Members item 19's own last paragraph excludes: identifiers, opaque handles,
      digests and references; and values carried verbatim from an external
      vocabulary — DNS domains, did:webvh agent-name local parts, DID logs, Rego
      source, RFC 6901 pointers, HTTP header and cookie names, APNs topics, IANA
      media types, BCP 47 language tags, and maintainer- or community-defined
      role and kind vocabularies.

  Two members were bounded where the schema's own description calls the value an
  undeclared closed set (`nature`, `wired` in vtc/ceremonies/list) — deliberately
  left alone, because the right fix there is the closed enumeration item 19
  prefers, not a length.

  All 48 members sit in `status: draft` specifications and are amended in place
  per SPEC §5.2. `npm run validate` re-checks all 533 fenced example documents
  against the amended schemas; none is rejected by a new bound.

  **Still open, and deliberately not in this PR:** item 19's "SHOULD be OPTIONAL"
  half. 18 of the 48 members bounded here are REQUIRED — `CredentialCreationOptions`
  `rp.name`/`user.name`/`user.displayName`, credential-exchange `purpose` (both
  copies), `Effect.summary`, `ContextRecord.name` and vta/contexts/create `name`,
  the three `enroll-challenge` WebAuthn names, `CommunityProfile.name`,
  `CommunityProfileView.name`, `CommunityProfileSnapshot.name`, and the four
  decision-slot `purpose` members. Added to the 13 #296 found, that is 31.
  Making any of them optional is a wire-compatibility change and belongs in its
  own PR; several (purpose binding, `Effect.summary`) are required by design and
  the specification should say so rather than change.

  This is **breaking**, on the same terms #296 judged itself so: typify emits a
  bounded member as a validating newtype, so `Option<String>` becomes
  `Option<PayloadDeviceLabel>`, `Option<PayloadDeniedReason>`,
  `Option<AttachmentRefFilename>` and so on, and the newtype rejects in
  `Deserialize` a document the library previously accepted. `@openvtc/trust-tasks`
  generates unchanged *types* — TypeScript has no length refinement — but its
  embedded schemas now reject over-long values at runtime. No version is bumped
  and no changelog is written: release-plz computes both from this title.

- Bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength (§7.3) ([#296](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/296))

* spec: bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength

  SPEC.md §7.3 (framework 0.5.0) requires that any member holding free
  text declare a `maxLength`. 92 free-text string members across 83 draft
  schemas carried none, leaving the wire contract unbounded and every
  consumer to invent its own ceiling — or none, which is what §10.3
  (schema-validation DoS) exists to prevent.

  Bounds are chosen per member from the vocabulary the registry already
  uses rather than applied uniformly:

    256   `label`, `comment` — a display name or an OpenSSH key comment;
          matches the existing 256 on provision/integration `label` and
          the `name` members alongside it.
    500   requester-authored prose that a surface renders to a human who
          is deciding something; matches task-consent/request/0.1 `note`,
          the registry's considered consent-surface bound.
    1024  `reason`, `description`, `message` — operator or service prose
          recorded for audit or returned as a diagnostic; matches the six
          existing `reason: 1024` and the `description: 1024` in policy/
          and vtc/endorsement-type.
    16384 chat/message `text` — the task's actual content rather than
          metadata about it; matches the corpus's long-form bound on
          vault `secureNotes`.

  All amended specifications are `status: draft`, so the change is made in
  place per SPEC §5.2. Deliberately untouched:

    * 17 members in `retired` specifications, frozen by SPEC §6.4.
    * messaging/_shared/0.1 `AuditEntry.detail` and did-management/
      _shared/0.1 `DomainEntry.label` — shared $defs reachable from a
      retired specification, so bounding them would change a frozen
      specification's effective wire contract.
    * vault/_shared/{0.1,0.2,0.3} `TspMessageEnvelope.message` — opaque
      base64url TSP bytes, not free text.

  The `label` description in vault/_shared/*/vault-entry.schema.json said
  the wire spec enforced no maximum length. It now does, so the sentence
  is corrected rather than left contradicting the schema it annotates.

  `npm run validate` re-checks all 533 fenced example documents against
  the amended schemas; none is rejected by a new bound.



**No version has been taken for this entry yet, deliberately.** The change below
is breaking under the rules at the top of this file, so releasing it moves the
leading component and drags the six dependent crates with it — the workspace
event the callout above says to plan rather than discover. Three specification
PRs are in flight against the same registry; whoever sequences that cascade
assigns the number and dates this heading.

### Changed

- **BREAKING.** 92 free-text payload members across 83 draft schemas now declare
  a `maxLength`, which SPEC.md §7.3 requires of any member holding free text.
  Two consequences, both observable by a consumer:

  1. **Type change.** A `String` member that gains a `maxLength` is generated by
     typify as a validating newtype, so `Option<String>` becomes
     `Option<PayloadReason>`, `Option<AclEntryLabel>`, and so on. Reads through
     `Deref` are unaffected; construction and assignment are not.
  2. **Behavioural change.** The newtype enforces its bound in `Deserialize`, so
     a document carrying an over-long value — one this library previously
     accepted — is now rejected. This is the "alters behaviour against an
     unchanged wire format" case named at the top of this file.

  #### Migration

  A builder setter takes the newtype rather than a `String`:

  ```rust
  // before
  let entry = grant::AclEntry::builder()
      .subject("did:web:carol.example")
      .role("moderator")
      .label("Carol — content moderation".to_string())
      .try_into()?;

  // after
  let entry = grant::AclEntry::builder()
      .subject("did:web:carol.example")
      .role("moderator")
      .label(grant::AclEntryLabel::try_from("Carol — content moderation")?)
      .try_into()?;
  ```

  The conversion is fallible precisely because the bound is real: a value longer
  than the schema permits now fails where it is authored rather than at the far
  end of the wire. Reading a member still derefs to `&String`, so
  `label.as_deref().map(String::as_str)` recovers an `Option<&str>`.

  Bounds were chosen per member from the vocabulary the registry already uses —
  256 for a display `label` or an OpenSSH key `comment`, 500 for requester
  prose a surface renders to a human deciding something (matching
  `task-consent/request/0.1` `note`), 1024 for `reason` / `description` /
  `message`, and 16384 for a `chat/message` `text` body. Members in `retired`
  specifications are untouched, frozen by SPEC §6.4.

title: chore: release @openvtc/trust-tasks 0.16.0
body:
Release PR for the npm package, the counterpart to the release-plz PR for the
crates. **Merging this is the release**: the `publish-npm` job in
`publish.yml` sees a version that is not on npm, publishes it with OIDC
provenance, and tags `trust-tasks-ts-v0.16.0`.

- `@openvtc/trust-tasks`: `0.15.0` → `0.16.0` (`breaking`)
- derived from the conventional commits in `trust-tasks-ts-v0.15.0..HEAD` touching `specs/`,
  `trust-tasks-ts/` or `scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs`

This branch is regenerated from `main` on every push, so do not commit to it —
edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

title: ci: patch the npm Release PR over REST instead of `gh pr edit` (#314)
body:
ci: patch the npm Release PR over REST instead of `gh pr edit` (#314)

`gh pr edit` resolves editable metadata before it writes — assignees,
reviewers, milestones and organization teams — so it asks GraphQL for
`login`, `name` and `slug`. Those fields need `read:org`; the release
token has `repo`, which is the scope it should have.

The failure mode was the bad one. The branch had already been force-pushed
to 0.16.0 when the edit failed, so the job died leaving PR #303 titled
"release @openvtc/trust-tasks 0.15.1" over a branch that releases 0.16.0 —
a release PR whose description contradicts its diff.

Patching title and body over REST resolves no metadata and is satisfied by
`repo`. `{owner}/{repo}` is expanded by gh from the checkout.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>
author: stormer78

title: ci: patch the npm Release PR over REST instead of `gh pr edit`
body:
The `release-ts-pr` job failed in [run 32991642096](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/actions/runs/32991642096):

```
GraphQL: Your token has not been granted the required scopes to execute this query.
The 'login' field requires one of the following scopes: ['read:org'], but your token
has only been granted the: ['repo'] scopes.
... 'name' ... 'slug' ...
```

## Why

`gh pr edit` resolves *editable metadata* before it writes — assignees, reviewers, milestones and organization **teams** — so it queries GraphQL for `login`, `name` and `slug`. Those need `read:org`. The release token has `repo`, which is the scope it ought to have: it pushes a branch and moves a PR, it does not read the org.

## Why this one mattered more than a red check

The branch had **already been force-pushed** when the edit failed:

```
+ 882be144...aeaa866f release-ts -> release-ts (forced update)
```

So the job died leaving **#303 titled `release @openvtc/trust-tasks 0.15.1` over a branch that releases 0.16.0** — a release PR whose description contradicts its own diff. That is the one state a release PR must never be in, because the title is what a reviewer reads before merging a publish.

## Fix

Patch title and body over REST. It resolves no metadata and is satisfied by `repo`; `{owner}/{repo}` is expanded by gh from the checkout, so no new env var:

```sh
gh api --silent -X PATCH "repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/$existing" \
  -f title="$title" -f body="$(cat "$body_file")"
```

`gh pr create` on the other branch of the `if` already has a `--label`-less fallback, so it is unaffected.

title: test(vta): cover the webvh family by extending the stub host
body:
Coverage **64 → 76 of 109 (59% → 70%)**. Twelve tasks, almost all of the webvh
family, by extending the stub host rather than by writing more assertions.

## Why these were the hard ones

They were left until last because they looked like they needed a live hosting
server. Most did — and the stub host that already exists
(`MockVta::start_with_webvh_host`) was three endpoints short of covering them.

The non-obvious part is **which** tasks need a host:

- `webvh/servers/*` and the `dids` write paths — obviously.
- **`agent-name/*`** — not obviously. The names are *local* records, so they
  read like cheap local reads. Every one of them refuses a **serverless** DID
  ("agent names require a hosted DID"), and a DID seeded straight into the
  keyspace is serverless. Only a real mint against a host qualifies.
- **`passkey-vms/*`** — same shape, different reason: they refuse a DID that is
  not **VTA-managed**, so the fixture's own `did:key` signing identity does not
  qualify either.

That is why this batch is one test against a minted DID rather than a dozen
small ones.

## Three endpoints added to the stub host

Each was found by running the real client against it and reading what it asked
for. Two of the three had a shape that could not be guessed:

| endpoint | the detail that bites |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/me/domains` | `createdAt` is **Unix seconds**, not RFC 3339 — the VTA converts when relaying into the canonical `DomainEntry`, which does want a string. A string here fails the decode with "error decoding response body". |
| `GET /api/dids` | answers **empty** on purpose: reconcile's job is to report the difference between two sets, so an empty host list exercises the *missing-on-host* arm. A stub echoing the VTA's own records back would only ever prove the empty-difference path. The run logs `host_only=0 agent_only=1`, which is the arm under test. |
| `POST /api/agent-names/{update,remove,check}` | `remove` is its own verb, not an `update` state — releasing a name returns it to the pool, which is a different act from parking it. |

## A note on debugging this after #1130

Every one of these failures arrived as `internalError: the consumer could not
complete this task` — because #1130 stopped `internalError` from carrying its
cause to the wire, which is exactly what Framework 0.5.0 requires.

That is the sanitisation working, and it has a cost: the cause is in the
operator's log, so debugging these meant attaching a subscriber rather than
reading the response. Worth knowing before someone concludes the errors became
useless. They did not move — they moved *audience*.

## Coverage boundaries recorded, not left implicit

Three families stay uncovered with the reason written into the test, so the
next person does not re-derive it:

- `passkey-vms/{enroll-challenge,enroll-submit,revoke}` — answer `unavailable`
  because this fixture configures no WebAuthn relying party. Covering them
  needs an RP and a soft authenticator, which the `admin_passkeys` suites
  already stand up on the VTC side.
- `device/*` — `device/register` refuses a DID not already in the ACL, so the
  family needs a provisioned integration.
- `services/{enable,update,disable,rollback}` — publish a WebVH LogEntry *and*
  run a live DIDComm handshake against the running service.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings` — **exit 0**
- `./scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` — 28 suites, **0 violations**, coverage **76/109**
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast` — 54 suites, 0 failures
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — exit 0

Refs #1059

title: refactor(versioning)!: release the trust-tasks-rs-exposing crates in lockstep
body:
## The bug release-plz sized the pending release ([#312](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/312)) as: | crate | proposed | correct | |---|---|---| | `trust-tasks-rs` | 0.14.0 → **0.15.0** | ✅ breaking, right | | `trust-tasks-https` | 0.16.0 → 0.16.1 | ❌ patch | | `trust-tasks` | 0.2.0 → 0.2.1 | ❌ patch | | `trust-tasks-proof` | 0.13.0 → 0.13.1 | ❌ patch | | `trust-tasks-didcomm` | 0.15.0 → 0.15.1 | ❌ patch | | `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` | 0.14.0 → 0.14.1 | ❌ patch | | `trust-tasks-tsp` | 0.14.0 → 0.14.1 | ❌ patch | | `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.14.0 → 0.14.1 | ❌ patch | Every dependent exposes `trust-tasks-rs` types in its **own public API** — `trust-tasks` re-exports the whole crate with `pub use trust_tasks_rs::*`, and the bindings take and return `TrustTask

` / `TrustTaskCode`. So the core's breaking change is *their* breaking change, and they were about to ship it as a patch. ## Reproduced, not theorised A probe consumer holding the caret ranges it had before this release: ``` error[E0308]: expected `TrustTask`, found a different `TrustTask` note: there are multiple different versions of crate `trust_tasks_rs` in the dependency graph ``` `^0.14` admits `0.14.1`, so that break arrives on a routine `cargo update` with **no version signal at all**. VTI is exactly such a consumer. crates.io versions are immutable — publishing it would have been permanent. ## Why `semver_check` didn't catch it It can't. `cargo-semver-checks` compares each crate's rustdoc against *that crate's own* published baseline and does not track type identity across dependency versions — so it cheerfully reports "✓ API compatible changes" for a crate whose public API just changed underneath it. A green semver check says nothing about breaks arriving through a public dependency. ## The fix A `version_group` makes the relationship the code already had explicit: the eight crates share one version, so a break anywhere in the unit is a break everywhere. `version_group` alone was **not** enough, and I verified that before settling on this. Applied to today's versions it lands the whole group on `0.16.1` — still a patch for `trust-tasks-https`, still broken. It needs a shared floor, which is why this lands as a breaking change. Verified end to end with a local `release-plz update`: ``` trust-tasks-rs 0.14.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks 0.2.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks-https 0.16.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks-proof 0.13.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks-didcomm 0.15.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks-didcomm-v1 0.14.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks-tsp 0.14.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks-capability-client 0.14.0 -> 0.17.0 trust-tasks-ceremony 0.2.0 (unchanged) trust-tasks-codegen 0.1.0 (unchanged) ``` `0.17.0` is a correct breaking signal from every one of the eight. From then on release-plz's highest-next-version rule keeps it right by itself: once they share a floor, a break in the core dominates the group. ## Not in the group - **`trust-tasks-ceremony`** — has no `trust-tasks-rs` dependency at all, so it versions independently. (`version_group` across the whole workspace would have swept it to 0.16.1 for no reason.) - **`trust-tasks-codegen`** — `publish = false`. ## Also here Each crate gains a `# Versioning` doc section explaining the public-dependency relationship, and `release-plz.toml` carries the reasoning. This trap is invisible in the diff of any single crate, so it needs to be written down where the next person will hit it. ## Consequence for #312 Do **not** merge #312 as it stands. Once this is on `main`, re-run the workflow and it regenerates with 0.17.0 across the unit.

title: Specify both VMC directions so membership requires member consent
body:
The spec asserted in five places that two VMCs form a complete membership edge, but the normative schema required `issuer` to be the VTC/VTN C-DID and the subject to be the member, making the reverse credential unconstructible. Issue #8 correctly flagged this as a structural contradiction rather than an editorial one.

The pair is deliberate: the member-issued VMC is the member's consent artifact. A community can always issue a credential naming someone as a member, but it cannot produce the acknowledgement without that party's signature, so requiring both directions makes an unconsented membership claim unprovable. That rationale appeared nowhere in the text, which is why the contradiction was reachable in the first place.

So the prose was right and the schema was the defect. The two directions are now distinguished by issuer and subject rules rather than by a new credential type, matching how the VIC's two variants are handled.

- `spec/body.md`: VMC schema gains direction-qualified issuer/subject rules and a `digest` binding the acknowledgement to the grant, reusing the existing VWC digest algorithm verbatim; a second worked example; a new "Membership Edge Completion" subsection carrying the completeness, ordering and verifier rules plus the consent rationale; and a lifecycle editor's note deferring revocation to the planned Trust Task Protocols spec.
- `spec/body.md`: the per-direction witnessing rule generalised from VRCs to both edge-credential subtypes, so a witnessed membership edge has a defined `credentialSubject.id` binding.
- `spec/body.md`: new Security Consideration for unconsented membership assertion; "Digest integrity" extended to cover the VMC acknowledgement digest.
- `spec/terms-definitions/`: seven files corrected, including the "always ... C-DID" clause in `verifiable_membership_credential.md` that was the term-level source of the contradiction, and the CTA being "automatically" made a member without acknowledging.
- `CONTEXT.md`: VMC entry rewritten to describe both directions.

The verifier rule is deliberately direction-sensitive, which is the part worth reviewing closely: a member presenting their own community-issued VMC is accepted alone, since the act of presenting is itself the consent. A blanket "both always" would have broken the Community-Anchored ZKP and PHC constructions, which rely on the member holding only the community-issued half.

Resolves #8

title: fix(vtc)!: wrap the last three responses the schemas nest
body:
Stacked on #1093, and finishes the envelope family: after this, **no VTC
route returns a bare row or array where its published schema wraps one.**

## `ceremonies/list` — a top-level array

`Json<Vec<CeremonyManifest>>` where `vtc/ceremonies/list/0.1` says
`{ceremonies: […]}`. An array cannot grow a sibling member later without
breaking every reader, which is the whole reason the spec asks for an
envelope. `fetchCeremonies` in the admin SPA moves with it.

## `community/profile/show` — more than an un-flatten

`CommunityProfileResponse` used `#[serde(flatten)]`, putting every profile
field at the top level. Reading the published schema rather than assuming
the fix: the response is `{profile: …}` and **`additionalProperties: false`**,
and `registryStatus` is defined *inside* the canonical `CommunityProfile`
component ("Populated on reads; not settable") — not beside it.

So un-flattening alone would have left `registryStatus` a sibling of
`profile`, which the schema forbids. It now nests inside the profile object,
where the component puts it. The SPA's `ProfileResponse` interface splits
into `Profile` + a `{profile: Profile}` wrapper, and `getProfile` unwraps.

## `members/update` — the bare row

Returned `MemberResponse` where the spec says `{member: …}`. Reuses
`MemberEnvelope` from #1093, so `update` and `show` now publish the same
shape. The admin SPA calls `patchJson<unknown>` and ignores the body, so
nothing there moves.

## Coverage

`GET /v1/ceremonies` had **no HTTP-level test at all** — the same gap that
hid the `endorsements/show` drift in #1093. New `tests/ceremonies_list.rs`
covers it: one test asserts the top level is an object and reads the
manifests through `ceremonies`, so removing the envelope fails rather than
passing on a payload that merely contains the right data; one pins that the
route needs a session.

Six existing tests read the old shapes and failed as soon as the handlers
changed — two profile reads (`community_profile`, `install_flow`) and four
`members_crud` PATCH assertions. All six now read through the envelope and
would fail without it.

## Conformance witness

`KNOWN_DRIFT_COUNT` stays **26**. All three entries keep their row with the
fixture updated to what now ships and the note narrowed to what still
diverges — in every case an unspecced member that belongs upstream, not a
shape this service controls:

- `ceremonies/list` — envelope fixed; each manifest still carries
  `factsTemplate`. The admin UI renders the simulator from it, so dropping
  it is not an option; it goes upstream.
- `community/profile/show` — nesting fixed and `registryStatus` correctly
  placed; the profile still carries `communityDid`, `createdAt` and
  `relationshipIdentifierDefault`, none of which the canonical component
  defines. `communityDid` is the one a consumer most needs, and its absence
  from the component is the same root cause as the `config/export`,
  `config/import` and `profile/update` entries — one upstream change clears
  four rows.
- `members/update` — envelope fixed; request still carries `label` and the
  row still carries the same five unspecced members as `list`.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast`
- `cargo fmt --all --check`
- `npm run lint` in `admin-ui`

Note that `semver checks` fails on this branch as it does on every recent PR
(#1092 and #1093 both). The failing items are identical across all three —
thirteen `vta-sdk` / `vta-service` entries, none touched here. That gate is
skipped on `main`, so nothing ever forces it back to green; worth fixing
separately, because a real API break would currently land invisibly inside
that noise.

BREAKING CHANGE: `GET /v1/ceremonies` returns `{ceremonies: […]}` instead of
a bare array. `GET /v1/community/profile` returns `{profile: {…}}` with
`registryStatus` inside the profile, instead of the profile fields flattened
at the top level. `PATCH /v1/members/{did}` returns `{member: …}` instead of
the bare row. Every in-repo consumer moves with them in this PR; all three
were returning something their published schemas did not describe.

Refs #1059

title: feat(vta)!: close the CI cache class, map the 0.5.0 lifecycle, cover more tasks
body:
Three things that belong to the same release, taken together: the CI cache
class, the last 0.5.0 item VTI owns, and a coverage batch that found a fourth
request-side divergence.

## 1. The stale-`target/` cache class, closed

#1133 fixed the MSRV job after it failed on a commit a clean-room checkout
compiled without complaint. **Six other jobs had the identical bug**: Check,
Test, Clippy, Feature combos, Enclave build, Mobile build.

Every crate here is a **path** dependency, so a source-only change does not move
`Cargo.lock` and therefore does not move a key built from
`hashFiles('**/Cargo.lock')`. The job restores a `target/` built from *other*
source and reuses stale artifacts. The failure then names a field that is
plainly there in the diff, so it reads as the author's bug.

`target/` is dropped from all six. The registry and git caches stay: they are
content-addressed by package version, so a stale entry is impossible by
construction. Each site carries the reason, because the next person to see a
slow job will otherwise put it back.

The direction of risk is worth stating: this causes **false red, not false
green** — git checkout gives fresh mtimes on changed sources, so a stale
artifact cannot hide a real break. It costs time and trust, not correctness.

## 2. The document lifecycle, mapped onto this consumer's transports

0.5.0 adds a normative state table and requires **a transport binding to map it
onto its own protocol**. Upstream
[#294](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/294) does that
for the five published binding crates — and **does not reach this workspace**,
which uses exactly one item from them (`status_for_code`) and dispatches through
its own spine.

So the mapping is written where the code is. All three transports converge on
`dispatch_trust_task_core`, so it is one state machine with three renderings:
`received` at the transport boundary, `validated` across freshness → recipient →
schema, `accepted` at the `ReplayGuard` claim, `responded`/`errored` at
`success_response`/`reject_with`.

**Two states are named as absent rather than left ambiguous.** `suspended`:
there is no `trust-task-control` surface here, so nothing can suspend a task in
flight. `cancelled`: nothing stops a task on the consumer's own initiative once
accepted — a policy refusal happens *before* acceptance and is therefore
`errored`.

On **silence signifies no state**: this service's one deliberate silence is
conformant. A duplicate whose first execution recorded no response is answered
`204`, which is §7.2's fire-and-forget disposition, and the in-flight case is
`202` precisely so the two are not conflated. The producer-side half of that
rule binds the SDK, not the spine — which is why `receive_next` returns
`Ok(None)` on timeout: "nothing arrived", not "nothing happened".

## 3. Coverage 62 → 64, and a fourth request-side divergence

`auth/revoke-session/0.1` is `sessionId` **XOR** `all`. `RevokeSessionRequest`
required `sessionId`, so a conforming client sending `{"all": true}` got
**`malformedRequest`** — telling the client its *shape* is wrong when the shape
was fine.

This VTA implements only the named-session arm. That is a legitimate limit, but
an unimplemented option deserves to be **named as unimplemented**: `all: true`
now parses and is refused with `auth:revoke_all_unsupported`, and "both or
neither" is still malformed because the `oneOf` says so.

Fourth of this class, after `derivationPath` (#1123), `internal` (#1118) and
`enabled` (#1128). All four share a shape a response gate structurally cannot
see: the request never reaches a handler, so nothing about the *response* is
wrong.

Newly covered: `keys/derive-and-sign`, `messaging/ping`, and the refusal path
above.

### Two families that look cheap and are not

Recorded in the tests so the next person does not spend the same afternoon:

- **`device/*`** — `device/register` refuses a DID that is not already in the
  ACL ("complete provision-integration + acl/swap-key first"), so every path
  behind it needs a provisioned integration, not a seeded row.
- **`auth/revoke-session` success** — needs a real session row, and its other
  arm is one this VTA refuses by design.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings` — **exit 0**
- `./scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` — 28 suites, **0 violations**, coverage **64/109**
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast` — 54 suites, 0 failures
- `cargo test -p vta-sdk` — exit 0
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — exit 0

BREAKING CHANGE: `RevokeSessionRequest::session_id` is `Option<String>` and the
type gains `all`. `auth/revoke-session/0.1` with `all: true` is now accepted as
a document and refused as unsupported, rather than rejected as malformed.

Refs #1059

title: ci: give --force-with-lease a ref it can actually check
body:
Third iteration on this step. Worth saying so plainly rather than patching quietly.

| PR | Bug |
|---|---|
| #304 | guarded on `pr_head_branch`, an output that does not exist — step never ran |
| #311 | `--depth=1` made the amend write a **root commit**; `persist-credentials: false` meant no push auth |
| this | amend was correct, both assertions passed — push rejected `stale info` |

## The bug

`--force-with-lease` resolves its expected value from the remote-**tracking** ref. #311 pushed to a bare authenticated URL, which has no tracking ref, so git refuses:

```
! [rejected]   HEAD -> release-plz-2026-08-26T16-57-34Z (stale info)
```

The protection silently became an outage.

Reproduced locally:

```
anonymous URL:                       ! [rejected] (stale info)
explicit lease + named remote:       + f7b566d...a87bc0b (forced update)   exit 0
```

## Fix

Authenticate `origin` itself rather than pushing to a bare URL, and pass the lease value explicitly:

```
git push --force-with-lease="$BRANCH:$(git rev-parse "origin/$BRANCH")" origin "HEAD:$BRANCH"
```

The check now compares against the commit actually fetched rather than nothing. **Keeping it real matters** — the lease is what stopped #311's malformed root commit from reaching the branch. The two assertions added in #311 (parent unchanged, trailer present) both passed this run, so the amend itself is now correct.

body:
ci: give --force-with-lease a ref it can actually check (#313)

Third iteration on this step, and worth stating why rather than quietly
patching again.

#304 added it, guarding on an action output that does not exist, so it never
ran. #311 fixed a shallow fetch that turned the amend into a root commit, and
a missing push credential. This run got further: the amend was correct and
both new assertions passed, then the push was rejected with 'stale info'.

--force-with-lease resolves its expected value from the remote-TRACKING ref.
Pushing to a bare authenticated URL gives it no such ref, so it refuses — the
protection silently becomes an outage. Reproduced locally: anonymous URL is
rejected 'stale info'; an explicit lease value against a named remote pushes
cleanly.

Fixed by authenticating  itself and passing the lease value
explicitly, so the check compares against the commit we actually fetched
rather than nothing. The protection stays real — it is what stopped the
malformed root commit from #311 reaching the branch.

title: chore: release
body:
## 🤖 New release * `trust-tasks-rs`: 0.14.0 -> 0.15.0 (✓ API compatible changes) * `trust-tasks-didcomm`: 0.15.0 -> 0.15.1 (✓ API compatible changes) * `trust-tasks-https`: 0.16.0 -> 0.16.1 (✓ API compatible changes) * `trust-tasks`: 0.2.0 -> 0.2.1 (✓ API compatible changes) * `trust-tasks-capability-client`: 0.14.0 -> 0.14.1 * `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1`: 0.14.0 -> 0.14.1 * `trust-tasks-proof`: 0.13.0 -> 0.13.1 * `trust-tasks-tsp`: 0.14.0 -> 0.14.1
Changelog

## `trust-tasks-rs`

## [0.15.0](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/compare/trust-tasks-rs-v0.14.0...trust-tasks-rs-v0.15.0) — 2026-08-26 ### Added - **specs**: Require issuedAt on every live consequential spec, and make the §7.3 item 17 floor fatal ([#302](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/302)) * spec: make the §7.3 item 17 freshness floor a hard failure - **rs**: Make SPEC §7.3 item 17's issuedAt MUST expressible ([#300](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/300)) Framework 0.5.0's §7.3 item 17 says a Trust Task specification defining a consequential Trust Task MUST require the `issuedAt` member, raising §4.2's SHOULD to a MUST for documents conforming to it. There was no way to declare that: the meta-schema had `proofRequirement` for the `proof` envelope member and nothing equivalent for `issuedAt`, so the MUST was unexpressible and none of the 209 consequential specs in the registry could comply. Adds `issuedAtRequirement` to the front-matter meta-schema, modelled on `proofRequirement` — same two forms (a single `requirement`, or a per-variant `request`/`response` pair), same enum, same `rationale`. It governs an envelope member, admits a per-variant reading because request and response are relied on differently, and reading one declaration now teaches the other. Declared rather than derived, with the derived floor checked and reported: * `sideEffects` and `exposure` are DESCRIPTIVE (§7.3 items 13/14). Deriving `issuedAt`-REQUIRED from them would mean that correcting `sideEffects.level` from `none` to `mutating` for accuracy silently changed which documents every consumer of that spec must reject. * §2 makes the *handler* authoritative for consequentiality, not the front matter — so a value computed from the front matter would enforce something the front matter does not authoritatively state. * A non-consequential spec may legitimately require `issuedAt` anyway; a derived-only mechanism cannot express that. * Deriving would flip 209 specs' wire behaviour in one commit, invisibly. So the build derives the floor instead of substituting for the declaration. `npm run validate` prints a `Freshness floor (§7.3 item 17)` line counting the consequential specs that have not declared it (currently 0/209), *fails* on a spec that declares something weaker than REQUIRED, and escalates the undeclared case to a hard error under `TT_STRICT_ISSUED_AT=1` — the ratchet that becomes the default once the registry has caught up. Enforcement reaches consumers the same way `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` does: * `Payload::IS_ISSUED_AT_REQUIRED` (Rust) and `SpecPolicy.isIssuedAtRequired` (TypeScript), emitted per variant by both generators from the front matter. * `TrustTask::enforce_spec_policy` / `enforceSpecPolicy` reject a document with no `issuedAt` as `malformedRequest`. Not `expired`: §8.3 defines no dedicated code, `expired` names a document that was once acceptable, and §7.2 item 13 already uses `malformedRequest` for the other freshness rejections. * The trait constant has a default of `false`, so hand-written impls — the crate's own `trust-task-error`, hand-modelled in `error.rs` because it is in the codegen's SKIP_SLUGS, and every downstream impl — keep compiling. * `check-bindings` compares the new key across front matter, Rust and TypeScript, so the two languages cannot drift on it. Distinct from `FreshnessPolicy::require_issued_at`, which is a *consumer's* own posture applied to every document it sees. This is the *specification's* requirement, published in the registry and not the consumer's to relax. No specification declares `issuedAtRequirement` yet — that is a follow-up, spec by spec. The generated Rust tree is therefore byte-identical (the const is emitted only on override) and the generated TypeScript gains one `isIssuedAtRequired: false` line per policy object. Nothing that was accepted before is rejected now. Also documents the declaration in CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md, and teaches `npm run new-spec` to emit it on a scaffold whose declared classes make the task consequential. ### Fixed - **rs**: Enforce both halves of the SPEC §6.1 slug reservation ([#293](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/293)) * fix(rs): enforce both halves of the SPEC 6.1 slug reservation TypeUri rejected a published framework specification and accepted a reserved one, in the same function pair: REJECTED trust-task-control published since 0.1; its Type URI would not parse PARSES trust-ceremony-evil reserved by 6.1, accepted from any party is_reserved_namespace checked only the trust-task half of ^trust-(task|ceremony)($|-|/), so the ceremony half of the reservation — which exists precisely so the ceremony layer has a namespace no other party can claim first — protected nothing. And is_allowed_framework_slug listed five slugs where specs/spec.meta.schema.json lists seven, so two published specs sat inside the reservation with no permission to be there. The allowlist is one of two hand-maintained copies. The new test reads the meta-schema's copy and fails naming the missing slug if they drift again; verified by removing trust-task-control and watching it fail. Found while retiring trust-task-ok ([#292](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/292)), which swept for references to the slug and noticed the two lists disagreed. ### Specifications - Bound the remaining free-text payload members and state who reads them ([#301](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/301)) SPEC.md §7.3 (framework 0.5.0) item 19 has three parts. PR #296 closed most of part 1 for eight member names (`reason`, `note`, `detail`, `description`, `message`, `text`, `label`, `comment`), 92 members in all. Sweeping the whole corpus rather than a name list finds **48 more** unbounded free-text members across 27 draft specifications and 10 shared schemas, under names the earlier sweep did not look for: `purpose`, `deviceLabel`, `displayName`, `explanation`, `summary`, `title`, `name`, `blurb`, `filename`, `trace`, `error`, `lastError`, `deniedReason`, `displayHint`, `consequences`, `rpName`, `userName`, `userDisplayName`. The one the earlier review named specifically is here: `task-consent`'s `Effect.summary` — the member its own schema calls "the ONLY member a consent surface is guaranteed to be able to render" — was unbounded on the surface a human reads to approve an action. It is now 500, the same figure as the `note` beside it. Bounds are drawn from the vocabulary the corpus already uses and sized per member, not applied uniformly: 64 WebAuthn entity names (`rp.name`, `user.name`, `user.displayName`, `rpName`, `userName`, `userDisplayName`) — the length WebAuthn tells authenticators to truncate to, so a longer value would be silently cut on the device rather than carried. 128 `purpose` where it names a decision slot or a declared intent. This is consistency repair, not a new judgement: policy/activate/0.1 and policy/active/0.1 already declared `maxLength: 128` on the request member while the response that echoes it declared none. 256 display labels and names — `deviceLabel`, `displayName`, `displayHint`, `label`, `title`, `name`, `blurb`, `filename`; matches #296's reasoning that a display name is not prose. 500 consent-surface prose a human reads while deciding — `Effect.summary`, `consequences[]`, credential-exchange `purpose`, `deniedReason`; matches task-consent/request/0.1 `note`. 1024 operator or service diagnostic prose — `explanation`, `trace[]`, `error`, `lastError`, and vta/credentials/issue `purpose`. **Part 3 of the MUST is the half nobody had done.** Item 19 also requires each specification to state who reads a free-text value, whether the recipient is expected to retain it, and whether it is trusted. Prose is added to the `## Security & Privacy` section of all **37** draft specifications that reach a newly bounded member — the 27 whose own payload schema moved, plus 10 that reach one through a shared `$def`. `vta/credentials/issue/0.{1,2}` had no such section at all and now carry one containing the item 19 statement; both remain on the Security & Privacy debt allowlist, because neither yet has the four sub-headings the repo lint wants. The other 35 sections were extended in place. Deliberately untouched, matching #296's own carve-outs: * `messaging/_shared/0.1` `AuditEntry.detail` and `did-management/_shared/0.1` `DomainEntry.label` — shared `$defs` reachable from a retired specification, so bounding them would move a frozen specification's wire contract. These are the only two shared schemas in this change's blast radius that a retired spec reaches; the ten this PR edits are draft-only. * Members item 19's own last paragraph excludes: identifiers, opaque handles, digests and references; and values carried verbatim from an external vocabulary — DNS domains, did:webvh agent-name local parts, DID logs, Rego source, RFC 6901 pointers, HTTP header and cookie names, APNs topics, IANA media types, BCP 47 language tags, and maintainer- or community-defined role and kind vocabularies. Two members were bounded where the schema's own description calls the value an undeclared closed set (`nature`, `wired` in vtc/ceremonies/list) — deliberately left alone, because the right fix there is the closed enumeration item 19 prefers, not a length. All 48 members sit in `status: draft` specifications and are amended in place per SPEC §5.2. `npm run validate` re-checks all 533 fenced example documents against the amended schemas; none is rejected by a new bound. **Still open, and deliberately not in this PR:** item 19's "SHOULD be OPTIONAL" half. 18 of the 48 members bounded here are REQUIRED — `CredentialCreationOptions` `rp.name`/`user.name`/`user.displayName`, credential-exchange `purpose` (both copies), `Effect.summary`, `ContextRecord.name` and vta/contexts/create `name`, the three `enroll-challenge` WebAuthn names, `CommunityProfile.name`, `CommunityProfileView.name`, `CommunityProfileSnapshot.name`, and the four decision-slot `purpose` members. Added to the 13 #296 found, that is 31. Making any of them optional is a wire-compatibility change and belongs in its own PR; several (purpose binding, `Effect.summary`) are required by design and the specification should say so rather than change. This is **breaking**, on the same terms #296 judged itself so: typify emits a bounded member as a validating newtype, so `Option` becomes `Option`, `Option`, `Option` and so on, and the newtype rejects in `Deserialize` a document the library previously accepted. `@openvtc/trust-tasks` generates unchanged *types* — TypeScript has no length refinement — but its embedded schemas now reject over-long values at runtime. No version is bumped and no changelog is written: release-plz computes both from this title. - Bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength (§7.3) ([#296](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/296)) * spec: bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength SPEC.md §7.3 (framework 0.5.0) requires that any member holding free text declare a `maxLength`. 92 free-text string members across 83 draft schemas carried none, leaving the wire contract unbounded and every consumer to invent its own ceiling — or none, which is what §10.3 (schema-validation DoS) exists to prevent. Bounds are chosen per member from the vocabulary the registry already uses rather than applied uniformly: 256 `label`, `comment` — a display name or an OpenSSH key comment; matches the existing 256 on provision/integration `label` and the `name` members alongside it. 500 requester-authored prose that a surface renders to a human who is deciding something; matches task-consent/request/0.1 `note`, the registry's considered consent-surface bound. 1024 `reason`, `description`, `message` — operator or service prose recorded for audit or returned as a diagnostic; matches the six existing `reason: 1024` and the `description: 1024` in policy/ and vtc/endorsement-type. 16384 chat/message `text` — the task's actual content rather than metadata about it; matches the corpus's long-form bound on vault `secureNotes`. All amended specifications are `status: draft`, so the change is made in place per SPEC §5.2. title: feat(vta)!: close the CI cache class, map the 0.5.0 lifecycle, cover more tasks (#1134)
body:
feat(vta)!: close the CI cache class, map the 0.5.0 lifecycle, cover more tasks (#1134)

Three things belonging to the same release.

CI. #1133 fixed the MSRV job after it failed on a commit a clean-room checkout
compiled fine. Six other jobs had the identical bug — Check, Test, Clippy,
Feature combos, Enclave build, Mobile build. Every crate here is a path
dependency, so a source-only change does not move Cargo.lock and therefore does
not move a key built from hashFiles of it; the job restores a `target/` built
from other source and reuses stale artifacts, and the failure names a field
that is plainly there in the diff. `target/` is dropped from all six; the
registry and git caches stay, being content-addressed by package version. The
risk direction is false red, not false green.

Lifecycle. 0.5.0 requires a transport binding to map its state table onto its
own protocol. Upstream dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#294 does that for the five binding
crates and does not reach this workspace, which uses one item from them and
dispatches through its own spine. The mapping is now documented against the
code: one state machine, three renderings. `suspended` and `cancelled` are
named as absent rather than left ambiguous — there is no `trust-task-control`
surface, and a policy refusal precedes acceptance so it is `errored`.

Coverage 62 to 64, and a fourth request-side divergence.
`auth/revoke-session/0.1` is `sessionId` XOR `all`; `RevokeSessionRequest`
required `sessionId`, so a conforming client sending `all: true` got
`malformedRequest` — telling it the shape is wrong when the shape was fine.
This VTA implements only the named-session arm, which is a legitimate limit,
but an unimplemented option deserves naming: `all` now parses and is refused
with `auth:revoke_all_unsupported`.

BREAKING CHANGE: `RevokeSessionRequest::session_id` is `Option<String>` and the
type gains `all`. `auth/revoke-session/0.1` with `all: true` is accepted as a
document and refused as unsupported, rather than rejected as malformed.

Refs #1059

title: ci: fix the release sign-off step — shallow fetch and missing push auth
body:
The sign-off step from #304 **ran and failed**. Two bugs, both mine.

## 1. `--depth=1` turned the amend into a new root commit

A parentless commit cannot be amended. `git commit --amend` on a shallow single-commit branch writes a **new root commit containing the entire tree as newly-added files** — the job log is full of `create mode 100644 …` for every file in the repo.

Reproduced locally both ways:

```
full history:   parent unchanged: YES   trailer added: yes   files in commit: 2
shallow clone:  has parent: NO — root commit
```

The job checkout already uses `fetch-depth: 0`, so the depth flag was never needed in the first place.

## 2. `persist-credentials: false` meant the push had no auth

The job checkout disables credential persistence, so a bare `git push` cannot authenticate. **That failure is the only reason the malformed commit never reached the branch** — `--force-with-lease` saved it, not my logic. Both release branches still show `chore: release` correctly parented on `adfa19e3`.

## Fix

- Drop `--depth=1`; fetch the ref normally.
- Push over an explicitly authenticated URL rather than re-persisting credentials for the whole job.
- **Two assertions before the push**, because this step edits the one commit that publishes and a wrong amend is worse than an unsigned one:
  - refuse if the amend changed the commit's parent;
  - refuse if it produced no `Signed-off-by` trailer.

The npm side needed none of this — `scripts/release-ts-pr.sh` commits with `git commit -s` directly rather than amending after the fact, which is why #303 was fine.

There was no way to declare that: the meta-schema had `proofRequirement` for the `proof` envelope member and nothing equivalent for `issuedAt`, so the MUST was unexpressible and none of the 209 consequential specs in the registry could comply. Adds `issuedAtRequirement` to the front-matter meta-schema, modelled on `proofRequirement` — same two forms (a single `requirement`, or a per-variant `request`/`response` pair), same enum, same `rationale`. It governs an envelope member, admits a per-variant reading because request and response are relied on differently, and reading one declaration now teaches the other. Declared rather than derived, with the derived floor checked and reported: * `sideEffects` and `exposure` are DESCRIPTIVE (§7.3 items 13/14). Deriving `issuedAt`-REQUIRED from them would mean that correcting `sideEffects.level` from `none` to `mutating` for accuracy silently changed which documents every consumer of that spec must reject. * §2 makes the *handler* authoritative for consequentiality, not the front matter — so a value computed from the front matter would enforce something the front matter does not authoritatively state. * A non-consequential spec may legitimately require `issuedAt` anyway; a derived-only mechanism cannot express that. * Deriving would flip 209 specs' wire behaviour in one commit, invisibly. So the build derives the floor instead of substituting for the declaration. `npm run validate` prints a `Freshness floor (§7.3 item 17)` line counting the consequential specs that have not declared it (currently 0/209), *fails* on a spec that declares something weaker than REQUIRED, and escalates the undeclared case to a hard error under `TT_STRICT_ISSUED_AT=1` — the ratchet that becomes the default once the registry has caught up. Enforcement reaches consumers the same way `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` does: * `Payload::IS_ISSUED_AT_REQUIRED` (Rust) and `SpecPolicy.isIssuedAtRequired` (TypeScript), emitted per variant by both generators from the front matter. * `TrustTask::enforce_spec_policy` / `enforceSpecPolicy` reject a document with no `issuedAt` as `malformedRequest`. Not `expired`: §8.3 defines no dedicated code, `expired` names a document that was once acceptable, and §7.2 item 13 already uses `malformedRequest` for the other freshness rejections. * The trait constant has a default of `false`, so hand-written impls — the crate's own `trust-task-error`, hand-modelled in `error.rs` because it is in the codegen's SKIP_SLUGS, and every downstream impl — keep compiling. * `check-bindings` compares the new key across front matter, Rust and TypeScript, so the two languages cannot drift on it. title: spec(bindings): target framework 0.5 in the five current bindings
body:
After #306, the eight binding specifications were the only **live** specifications not targeting framework 0.5 — and five of them were incoherent about it.

#294 gave `https/0.2`, `didcomm/0.2`, `didcomm-v1/0.2`, `tsp/0.1` and `push/0.1` the SPEC §4.12 document-lifecycle mapping, which framework 0.5.0 **requires** of a transport binding:

> A transport binding **MUST** map this table.

But they still declared `targetFrameworkVersion: 0.2` / `0.3` / `0.4`. They documented a framework they did not claim to conform to.

| binding | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `https/0.2` | 0.2 | **0.5** |
| `didcomm/0.2` | 0.3 | **0.5** |
| `didcomm-v1/0.2` | 0.4 | **0.5** |
| `tsp/0.1` | 0.2 | **0.5** |
| `push/0.1` | 0.2 | **0.5** |

## The three 0.1 bindings are deliberately left

`https/0.1`, `didcomm/0.1`, `didcomm-v1/0.1` keep 0.2/0.2/0.3. #294 skipped them for the lifecycle mapping because each is superseded in place by a `0.2` of the same slug and targets a framework predating the lifecycle table. Re-targeting them would claim a framework whose requirements they do not meet — the same incoherence, in the other direction.

The script guarding this change **asserts a lifecycle mapping is present before re-targeting**, so the pairing cannot come apart later.

## Verified

`npm run validate` exit 0 · `npm run build` exit 0 · `npm run check-bindings` — 349 specs vs 349 TypeScript and 344 Rust modules, all agree. Bindings are prose, so nothing regenerates.

Note CI has been creating no runs for this repo for some time; verified locally with the commands CI runs.

There was no way to declare that: the meta-schema had `proofRequirement` for the `proof` envelope member and nothing equivalent for `issuedAt`, so the MUST was unexpressible and none of the 209 consequential specs in the registry could comply. Adds `issuedAtRequirement` to the front-matter meta-schema, modelled on `proofRequirement` — same two forms (a single `requirement`, or a per-variant `request`/`response` pair), same enum, same `rationale`. It governs an envelope member, admits a per-variant reading because request and response are relied on differently, and reading one declaration now teaches the other. SPEC 4.12 document-lifecycle mapping that framework 0.5.0 requires of a

or 0.4. They documented a framework they did not claim to conform to.

that corpus and were the only live specifications left behind.

The three superseded 0.1 bindings are deliberately untouched. #294 skipped
them for the lifecycle mapping because each is superseded in place by a 0.2 of

title: feat(specs): re-target every live specification to framework 0.5
body:
Framework 0.5.0 has been merged canonically (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#2) and present in this repo (`SPEC.md` at 0.5, `specs/_framework/0.5/trust-task.schema.json`) — but until now **no specification targeted it**, so none of its requirements bound anything. This closes the 0.5 programme by making the registry actually conform to 0.5 rather than merely being able to.

## Before / after

`targetFrameworkVersion` across all 349 specifications:

| target | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `"0.1"` | 116 | 17 |
| `"0.2"` | 207 | 33 |
| `"0.3"` | 3 | 0 |
| `"0.4"` | 23 | 1 |
| `"0.5"` | **0** | **298** |

**298 live (`status: draft`) specifications re-targeted** — from 0.1 (99), 0.2 (174), 0.3 (3) and 0.4 (22).

**51 retired specifications deliberately skipped.** SPEC §5.3 freezes a specification at retirement, so re-targeting one edits a frozen spec. They keep their recorded target (0.1 × 17, 0.2 × 33, 0.4 × 1).

The diff is exactly one line per file — 298 files changed, 298 insertions, 298 deletions, and every changed line is the `targetFrameworkVersion` front-matter key. No prose, no schema, no `$ref` moved.

## Nothing becomes non-conforming

The two MUSTs 0.5.0 adds were closed **in advance**, deliberately, so that re-targeting does not make the corpus non-conforming the moment it claims conformance:

- **§7.3 item 17** — consequential specifications MUST require `issuedAt`. Closed by #300 and #302; the floor reads `177/177 live consequential spec(s) declare issuedAtRequirement: REQUIRED`.
- **§7.3 item 19** — free-text members MUST declare `maxLength`, and the specification MUST state who reads them and whether they are retained. Closed by #296 and #301.

The envelope itself is safe by construction. `specs/_framework/0.5/trust-task.schema.json` is **byte-identical to 0.4's apart from `$id`, `title` and descriptions**, and is a strict superset of 0.1–0.3: same `required` set (`id`, `type`, `payload`), `additionalProperties: true` throughout, adding only property schemas for `ceremony` and `parentThreadId` that the older envelopes left unconstrained. No document that conformed to its previous target stops conforming.

## The envelope actually resolves

SPEC §7.2 item 1 selects the framework schema by the specification's *declared target*, so this change re-points example validation for the whole corpus. `npm run validate` is what performs that, and it is the real test of this PR.

```
validated 533 example documents against the framework envelope schema
```

Identical before and after. To prove the routing is real rather than coincidentally unchanged output, the 0.5 envelope was temporarily withheld from disk and validation re-run:

```
warn: 466 example document(s) target framework 0.5, for which no envelope schema compiled ...
      These documents were NOT validated
validated 67 example documents against the framework envelope schema
```

**466 of the 533 examples now route through the 0.5 envelope** and all pass. The remaining 67 belong to retired specs, `SPEC.md` and `bindings/`, which resolve to their own targets or the build's `0.2` fallback.

## Floors: none regressed

Every floor line is **byte-identical** before and after (`diff` of the full `npm run validate` output exits 0):

```
Security & Privacy: 42/349 spec(s) carry the section and all four sub-headings; 307 allowlisted as pre-existing debt, 0 not allowlisted
Exposure floor: 0 spec(s) declare exposure.discloses: none while returning released material
Freshness floor (§7.3 item 17): 177/177 live consequential spec(s) declare issuedAtRequirement: REQUIRED; 32 frozen in retired spec(s) (§5.3 — exempt, not debt)
Error code casing: 602/650 extended code(s) are lowerCamelCase; 48 frozen in 15 retired spec(s), 0 non-conforming
Error code shadowing: 646/650 extended code(s) avoid the §8.3 standard vocabulary; 4 frozen in 4 retired spec(s), 0 shadowing
Standard error code casing: 1026 spec file(s) swept for §8.3 codes; 25 snake_case occurrence(s) frozen in 1 superseded/retired spec(s), 0 non-conforming
Validated 349 specs, indexed 66 shared schemas.
```

The Security & Privacy figure is repo policy, not a 0.5.0 requirement; 307 remains acknowledged pre-existing debt and no section was padded to move it.

## No generated drift

`targetFrameworkVersion` reaches no generator. Verified statically (neither `trust-tasks-codegen/src/main.rs`, `scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs` nor any generated source mentions it) **and empirically** — full regeneration of both bindings produces an empty diff:

```
cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen   # Generated 344 payload modules
cargo fmt --all
npm run build-ts-bindings          # Generated 410 TS modules
```

This was worth checking rather than assuming: `issuedAtRequirement` *does* reach the generators, via `IS_ISSUED_AT_REQUIRED`. `targetFrameworkVersion` does not.

## Two-part version, deliberately

This PR uses the **two-part `"0.5"`** form, and that is a choice worth stating rather than making silently.

`SPEC.md` §5.1 *in this repo* still describes two-part `MAJOR.MINOR` versions. The canonical spec repo moved to three-part `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` at 0.4.0 and this repo never received that change — a known, pre-existing divergence already flagged for its own ticket, and not one this PR should resolve by fiat across 298 files.

`specs/spec.meta.schema.json` accepts both forms, and `build-registry.mjs` truncates to the `MAJOR.MINOR` prefix when selecting the envelope, so either would validate and either would resolve to `specs/_framework/0.5/`. Two-part wins on consistency: all 349 published specs use it, and it matches this repo's own SPEC text.

Note that the meta-schema's own description says "Prefer the three-part form for new specs". These are not new specs, and re-versioning the entire corpus on an editorial point belongs in the divergence ticket, not here.

## Scope boundary

The eight draft specifications under `bindings/` are **not** re-targeted — they stay at 0.2 (×5), 0.3 (×2) and 0.4 (×1). They are transport bindings rather than Trust Task specifications, carry their own conformance check, and sit outside the `specs/` corpus this change scoped. Worth a follow-up ticket.

Shared-component `$ref` pins are untouched, as required: SPEC §6.6 makes a spec pin a shared component by version, and `_framework/0.5` deliberately publishes no `framework.schema.json`. The 18 schema files carrying 25 `$ref`s into `_framework/0.3/framework.schema.json` (23 × `DigestMultibase`, 2 × `Ext`) keep pointing there. No `_framework` path appears anywhere in this diff.

## Why `feat`, and why not `!`

`feat` rather than `spec`: release-plz scores `spec` as a patch, and this is not an editorial edit. A consumer reads `targetFrameworkVersion` to choose which envelope to validate against (§7.2 item 1) and which consumer requirements apply — after this, documents from these 298 specs newly fall under 0.5's §7.2 item 13 freshness bounds and §4.12 lifecycle. That is additive normative behaviour reaching consumers, which is a minor bump, and typing it `spec` would silently under-report the release.

Not breaking, so no `!`: the 0.5 envelope is a superset of every target it replaces, all 533 examples validate unchanged, and both generated libraries regenerate to a zero diff. Nothing that conformed stops conforming and nothing stops compiling.

No version or CHANGELOG edited — release-plz computes those.

## Verification

```
npm run validate            # 533 examples validated; output byte-identical to baseline
npm run build               # Done. — wrote no tracked artifact
npm run check-bindings      # 349 specifications vs 349 TS and 344 Rust modules — all agree
npm run validate-ceremonies # Validated 2 ceremony definition(s), 0 warning(s)
cargo test --workspace --all-features   # all suites ok, 0 failed (incl. 736-test registry suite)
npm test (trust-tasks-ts)   # tests 79, pass 79, fail 0
```

Commits are grouped by family and DCO-signed.
