title: feat(rs): a trust-tasks facade crate and a root GETTING-STARTED.md
body:
A newcomer now writes **one line**:

```toml
trust-tasks = { version = "0.1", features = ["https", "proof-affinidi"] }
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The first publish of `trust-tasks` must be done by hand.** Merging this PR
> does **not** release it. crates.io's Trusted Publishing tokens cannot *create*
> a crate, so `publish.yml` will report
> `::warning::trust-tasks is not on crates.io yet — needs a manual first publish`
> and the `publish-rust` job will end red on that one crate (every other crate
> still publishes normally — the 404 is collected up front, not hit mid-run).
> Someone with crates.io rights runs `cargo publish -p trust-tasks` once, adds a
> Trusted Publisher for it (this repo + `publish.yml`), and CI takes over from
> the next release.

---

## Problem 1 — eight crates, five version numbers

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.14.0 · `-https` 0.15.0 · `-didcomm` 0.15.0 · `-didcomm-v1`
0.14.0 · `-proof` 0.13.0 · `-tsp` 0.14.0 · `-capability-client` 0.14.0 ·
`-ceremony` 0.2.0. The split is right for dependency hygiene — each transport
drags in a different heavy Affinidi tree — and a tax at the front door.

### The new `trust-tasks` crate (0.1.0)

Pure `pub use`. **No wrapper types**: a wrapper would be a second API to keep in
step, which is the problem this crate exists to remove. `trust_tasks::TrustTask`
**is** `trust_tasks_rs::TrustTask`, and `trust_tasks::https::HttpsClient` **is**
`trust_tasks_https::HttpsClient`, so outgrowing the facade is a find-and-replace
rather than a migration. Core is flattened at the crate root by a glob (an item
added to `trust-tasks-rs` appears here without anyone remembering to add it);
each sibling is re-exported as a feature-gated module.

| feature | module | crate |
|---|---|---|
| *(always on)* | crate root — `TrustTask`, `consume_inbound`, `specs`, `RejectReason`, … | `trust-tasks-rs` |
| `https` | `trust_tasks::https` | `trust-tasks-https` |
| `didcomm` | `trust_tasks::didcomm` | `trust-tasks-didcomm` |
| `didcomm-v1` | `trust_tasks::didcomm_v1` | `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` |
| `tsp` | `trust_tasks::tsp` | `trust-tasks-tsp` |
| `proof-affinidi` | `trust_tasks::proof` | `trust-tasks-proof` |
| `ceremony` | `trust_tasks::ceremony` | `trust-tasks-ceremony` |
| `capability-client` | `trust_tasks::capability_client` | `trust-tasks-capability-client` |
| `validate` | `trust_tasks::validate`, `::schema_index` | `trust-tasks-rs` |
| `all-transports` | all four transport modules | — |
| `https-jwt` | `trust_tasks::https::JwtBearerAuth` | `trust-tasks-https` |
| `all-specs` **(default)** | every spec family | `trust-tasks-rs` |

Also `pub use trust_tasks_rs as rs;` for when you want to name the crate
explicitly.

**Version is `0.1.0`.** It is new; it does not inherit and does not chase anyone
else's number.

### The 26 spec-family features are deliberately NOT forwarded

`trust-tasks-rs` has 26 per-family features (`vault`, `acl`, `keys`, …, #283).
Only the `all-specs` umbrella is forwarded, and it is on by default — so
`default-features = false` still gets you a working core with no spec modules
(verified: `cargo build -p trust-tasks --no-default-features` passes). Enabling a
transport re-enables them, because the transport crates depend on
`trust-tasks-rs` with its own defaults — another reason the fine-grained trim
belongs on a direct dependency.

Two reasons, both stated in the crate's rustdoc and README:

1. Twenty-six more feature names in front of a newcomer is exactly the problem
   this crate exists to remove.
2. Cargo unifies features across the whole graph, so trimming spec families only
   pays off when nothing else in the graph asks for them — which the facade,
   sitting above every binding, makes less likely rather than more.

So the documented answer for a size-sensitive consumer is **depend on
`trust-tasks-rs` directly and skip the facade**. Same for *subtracting* a
transport crate's own defaults (`trust-tasks-https`'s `server`,
`trust-tasks-didcomm-v1`'s `legacy-basic-message`): Cargo features are additive,
so nothing here can turn those off. For the same reason `https-client` /
`https-server` are *not* offered — they would be names that do nothing.

### `publish.yml`

`trust-tasks` is appended **last** to `CRATES` — it depends on every other crate,
so its `cargo publish` can only resolve once they are all in the index.
`trust-tasks/**` joins the `paths:` trigger. See the manual-first-publish callout
at the top.

---

## Problem 2 — no path from zero to a working round-trip

New root **`GETTING-STARTED.md`** (linked from `README.md`, which addresses spec
*authors*):

1. **Crate matrix** — "I want to send over X / receive over Y → these features".
2. **A signed `acl/grant` round trip in Rust**, sender and receiver, built on the
   `trust-tasks-https` demos fixed in #284.
3. **The TypeScript equivalent** via `consumeInbound`, with the full outcome
   `switch` (including `suppressed` and `duplicate`).
4. **The four traps**, collected in one place for the first time:
   - party members and `issuedAt` must be set **before** signing — `HttpsClient::send`
     fills unset ones in, and a member added after signing is not covered by the
     proof, so you get `proofInvalid` that looks like a broken signature;
   - the server runs the SPEC §4.8.1 in-band-vs-transport cross-check, so signing
     one side alone yields `identityMismatch` (and §8.1 makes some of those
     *unanswerable*, so the client can see a hang rather than an error);
   - generated types are `#[non_exhaustive]` as of 0.14.0 — cross-crate
     construction goes through `X::builder()`, and struct literals still compile
     *inside* `trust-tasks-rs`, which is why this bites consumers only;
   - the eight crates version independently and the facade does not track them.

### How the Rust snippets are gated

**A compiled, runnable example plus a drift test — not doctests.**

Every Rust block in `GETTING-STARTED.md` is a marked region of
`trust-tasks/examples/acl_grant_roundtrip.rs`, and
`trust-tasks/tests/getting_started_snippets.rs` asserts the two are
byte-identical in both directions (a region added to the example and never
embedded also fails, so a rename cannot silently stop being checked).

Why not doctests: **`cargo test --workspace --all-targets` — what `rust.yml`
actually runs — excludes doctests.** A doctest gate would have looked like a gate
and checked nothing. The example, by contrast, is compiled by a check this repo
*already* runs (`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features`), and it
is executable end to end, which a doctest that needs a live TCP listener on both
ends is not.

`rust.yml` gains `trust-tasks/**` and `GETTING-STARTED.md` to its `paths:` so a
doc-only edit still runs `cargo test`.

### The round trip, actually run

```
$ cargo run -p trust-tasks --features https,proof-affinidi --example acl_grant_roundtrip
  [server] listening on http://127.0.0.1:3000/trust-tasks (vid did:web:maintainer.example)
  [client] POST /trust-tasks  id=urn:uuid:6363d554-429b-4d6e-a441-78a845571d28
  [server] acl/grant from did:key:z6MkvDqGT54cXesYGvABpF1UapVNwjCqRcafi4Px6Thv5T3Z → subject=did:web:carol.example role=moderator
  [client] ← https://trusttasks.org/spec/acl/grant/0.1#response
           threadId=urn:uuid:6363d554-429b-4d6e-a441-78a845571d28 entry: subject=did:web:carol.example role=moderator
```

---

## Verification

Real output, all on this branch:

```
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
(no output)                                                      exit 0

$ cargo build --workspace
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 1m 06s   exit 0

$ cargo test --workspace --all-targets
    test result: ok. 7 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
    ... (all suites ok)                                          exit 0

$ cargo test --workspace                    # includes doctests
    test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 12 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
    ... (all suites ok)                                          exit 0

$ cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 1m 32s   exit 0

$ RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps --all-features
    Documenting trust-tasks v0.1.0 (…/trust-tasks)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 1m 49s   exit 0

$ cargo test -p trust-tasks --test getting_started_snippets
    test getting_started_rust_snippets_match_the_example ... ok
    test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed                          exit 0
```

The workspace-wide clippy and the rustdoc build were run as written above, not
per-crate.

The facade also builds with `--no-default-features` and with **each transport
feature alone** — verified by building, not by reasoning:

```
$ cargo build -p trust-tasks --no-default-features                              exit 0
$ cargo build -p trust-tasks                                                    exit 0
$ cargo build -p trust-tasks --no-default-features --features https             exit 0
$ cargo build -p trust-tasks --no-default-features --features didcomm           exit 0
$ cargo build -p trust-tasks --no-default-features --features didcomm-v1        exit 0
$ cargo build -p trust-tasks --no-default-features --features tsp               exit 0
$ cargo build -p trust-tasks --no-default-features --features proof-affinidi    exit 0
$ cargo build -p trust-tasks --no-default-features --features ceremony          exit 0
$ cargo build -p trust-tasks --no-default-features --features capability-client exit 0
$ cargo build -p trust-tasks --no-default-features --features validate          exit 0
$ cargo build -p trust-tasks --all-features                                     exit 0
```

## Not changed

No existing crate's public API or version moved. The only edits outside the new
`trust-tasks/` crate are: workspace `members`, `Cargo.lock`, `publish.yml`
(`CRATES` + `paths`), `rust.yml` (`paths` only), one link line in `README.md`,
and the new `GETTING-STARTED.md`.

title: ci(ts): author the npm release commit as a CLA signatory
body:
The two Release PRs each had exactly the half the other was missing:

| PR | Author | DCO | EasyCLA |
|---|---|---|---|
| #299 crates | a signatory | ✗ no `Signed-off-by` | ✓ |
| #303 npm | `github-actions[bot]` | ✓ signed off | ✗ |

#304 fixed the first. This fixes the second.

EasyCLA authorises the commit **author**, and `github-actions[bot]` has signed no CLA — so a bot-authored release commit fails however well it is signed off. release-plz already authors its release commit as the `RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN` owner (that is what setting the token changed, and what turned #299 EasyCLA green); `scripts/release-ts-pr.sh` still hard-coded the bot.

The identity is resolved **from the token** rather than hard-coded — whoever the token belongs to is who the release is attributable to, and a hard-coded name would quietly misattribute the release the moment the token changed hands.

If `gh api user` fails — a GitHub App token has no user — the script **exits** rather than falling back to the bot. That fallback would reintroduce the silent EasyCLA failure this change exists to remove.

Not verifiable in a PR context; the proof is the next npm Release PR.

title: spec!: bound the remaining free-text payload members and state who reads them
body:
`SPEC.md` §7.3 item 19 has three parts. #296 closed most of part 1 across eight member names. This closes the rest of part 1 — **48 members** the name-based sweep did not reach — and does part 3, the half nobody had done.

## Part 1 — the remaining bounds

Sweeping every string subschema in `specs/**` that carries no `enum`, `const`, `pattern`, `format`, `$ref` or `contentEncoding`, then subtracting what item 19's own last paragraph excludes, leaves **48** unbounded free-text members across **27 draft specifications** and **10 shared schemas**.

The one the earlier review named specifically is here: `task-consent`'s `Effect.summary`, the member its own schema calls *"the ONLY member a consent surface is guaranteed to be able to render"*, was unbounded on the surface a human reads to approve an action. It is now 500 — the same figure as the `note` beside it.

| Bound | Members | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **64** | `webauthn` `rp.name`, `user.name`, `user.displayName`; `enroll-challenge` `rpName`, `userName`, `userDisplayName` | the length WebAuthn tells authenticators to truncate entity names to — a longer value is silently cut on the device rather than carried |
| **128** | `auth/challenge` `purpose`; `policy/activate` `Response.purpose`; `policy/active` `ActiveBinding.purpose`; `vtc/policies/test` `Response.purpose`; `vtc/ceremonies/list` `CeremonyManifest.purpose` | consistency repair, not a new judgement — `policy/activate` and `policy/active` already declared `maxLength: 128` on the **request** member while the response echoing it declared none |
| **256** | `deviceLabel` ×7, `Mention.displayName`, `AttachmentRef.filename`, `displayHint`, `CapabilityManifest.title`, `ContextRecord.name` + 3 context `name`s, `CommunityProfile{,View,Snapshot}.name` + `profile/update` `name`, `CeremonyManifest.blurb` | a display name, not prose — #296's own reasoning for `label`/`comment` |
| **500** | `Effect.summary`, `consequences[]`, `credential-exchange` `purpose` ×2, `deniedReason` ×2 | consent-surface prose a human reads while deciding — matches `task-consent/request/0.1` `note` |
| **1024** | `PolicyDecision.explanation` ×3, `Response.trace[]` ×3, `vtc` `error`/`lastError` ×3, `vta/credentials/issue` `purpose` ×2 | operator or service diagnostic prose |

Full list: 48 rows, `specs/**/payload.schema.json` and `specs/**/_shared/**`.

## Part 3 — who reads it, and whether it is retained

Item 19 also requires each specification to state **who reads** a free-text value, **whether it is retained**, and **whether it is trusted**. Prose is added to the `## Security & Privacy` section of all **37** draft specifications that reach a newly bounded member — the 27 whose own payload schema moved, plus 10 that reach one through a shared `$def`.

`task-consent/request/0.1` is the model, and its existing prose is extended rather than replaced. Elsewhere the paragraph says the same three things in the voice of the section it joins, e.g.:

> **Free text.** `deviceLabel` on each returned credential is free text, bounded at 256 characters. It was written at enrollment by whoever enrolled the credential — usually the subject, but an invited enrollment carries the *inviter's* suggestion — and nothing in the response attests to it. It is **untrusted** […] it is **retained** by the consumer for the life of the credential precisely so that this listing can show it.

**Remaining debt, stated plainly:** `vta/credentials/issue/0.1` and `0.2` had no `## Security & Privacy` section at all. They now carry one containing the item 19 statement, but **not** the four sub-headings the repo lint wants, so both stay on the Security & Privacy allowlist. The other 35 sections were extended in place; 5 of those (`chat/message`, both `credential-exchange`, `task-consent/request`, `vta/passkey-vms/enroll-challenge`) are full four-sub-heading sections from #295 and got their paragraph inside `### Data carried`.

## Deliberately untouched

Matching #296's own carve-outs, and item 19's last paragraph:

- **`messaging/_shared/0.1` `AuditEntry.detail`** and **`did-management/_shared/0.1` `DomainEntry.label`** — shared `$defs` reachable from a **retired** specification, so bounding them would move a frozen contract. Reachability was recomputed, not assumed: these are the only two shared schemas in this change's blast radius that a retired spec reaches. The ten this PR edits are draft-only.
- **All `retired` specs** (§5.3 freezes them) — 163 unbounded strings live there.
- **Not free text under item 19's own definition:** identifiers, opaque handles, digests, cursors and references; and values carried verbatim from an external vocabulary — DNS domains, `did:webvh` agent-name local parts, DID logs, Rego source, RFC 6901 pointers, HTTP header and cookie names, APNs topics, IANA media types, BCP 47 language tags, and maintainer- or community-defined `role`/`kind`/`provider`/`outcome` vocabularies.
- **`vtc/ceremonies/list` `nature` and `wired`** — the schema's own description names a closed set (`automatic | operator-driven | advisory`) that it never declares. A length is the wrong fix; the closed enumeration item 19 prefers is the right one, and that is a behaviour change for another PR.

## Still open — the "SHOULD be OPTIONAL" half

Not acted on here, as agreed: making a member optional is a wire-compatibility change.

**18 of the 48 bounded here are REQUIRED**, on top of the 13 #296 found — **31 in total**:

`CredentialCreationOptions` `rp.name` / `user.name` / `user.displayName` · `credential-exchange` `purpose` (query + deferred) · `Effect.summary` · `ContextRecord.name` + `vta/contexts/create` `name` · `enroll-challenge` `rpName` / `userName` / `userDisplayName` · `CommunityProfile.name` / `CommunityProfileView.name` / `CommunityProfileSnapshot.name` · `policy/activate` + `policy/active` + `vtc/policies/test` + `vtc/ceremonies/list` `purpose`

Several are required *by design* — purpose binding means a verifier cannot ask without saying why, and `Effect.summary` is the only member a consent surface is guaranteed to render — so the right outcome for those is for the specification to say so, not to change.

## Is item 19 closed?

**Part 1 and part 3 are closed for every `draft` specification.** What remains is: the two frozen `_shared` members above (reachable from retired specs — they close when those specs are superseded), the `retired` corpus itself (frozen by §5.3), the two `nature`/`wired` members that want an enumeration rather than a length, and the SHOULD-be-optional list.

## Breaking

Same terms #296 judged itself so. typify emits a bounded member as a validating newtype:

```diff
-    pub device_label: ::std::option::Option<::std::string::String>,
+    pub device_label: ::std::option::Option<PayloadDeviceLabel>,
```

```rust
if value.chars().count() > 500usize {
    return Err("longer than 500 characters".into());
}
```

Both halves break: the API a consumer compiles against moves, and a document the library previously accepted is now rejected. `@openvtc/trust-tasks` generates unchanged *types* — TypeScript has no length refinement — but its embedded schemas reject over-long values at runtime. Hence the `!`. **No version bumped, no changelog written** — release-plz computes both from the title.

## Verification

```
npm run validate     533 example documents re-checked; none rejected by a new bound
                     Security & Privacy: 42/349 full, 307 allowlisted, 0 not allowlisted
npm run build        Done.
npm run check-bindings  349 specifications vs 349 TS and 344 Rust modules — all agree
cargo build --workspace --all-targets   Finished (no call site broke)
cargo test --workspace --all-targets    39 suites, 0 failed
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings   Finished
cargo fmt --all --check    clean
```

There was no way to declare that: the meta-schema had `proofRequirement` for the `proof` envelope member and nothing equivalent for `issuedAt`, so the MUST was unexpressible and none of the 209 consequential specs in the registry could comply. Adds `issuedAtRequirement` to the front-matter meta-schema, modelled on `proofRequirement` — same two forms (a single `requirement`, or a per-variant `request`/`response` pair), same enum, same `rationale`. It governs an envelope member, admits a per-variant reading because request and response are relied on differently, and reading one declaration now teaches the other. Declared rather than derived, with the derived floor checked and reported: * `sideEffects` and `exposure` are DESCRIPTIVE (§7.3 items 13/14). Deriving `issuedAt`-REQUIRED from them would mean that correcting `sideEffects.level` from `none` to `mutating` for accuracy silently changed which documents every consumer of that spec must reject. * §2 makes the *handler* authoritative for consequentiality, not the front matter — so a value computed from the front matter would enforce something the front matter does not authoritatively state. * A non-consequential spec may legitimately require `issuedAt` anyway; a derived-only mechanism cannot express that. * Deriving would flip 209 specs' wire behaviour in one commit, invisibly. Distinct from `FreshnessPolicy::require_issued_at`, which is a *consumer's* own posture applied to every document it sees. This is the *specification's* requirement, published in the registry and not the consumer's to relax. No specification declares `issuedAtRequirement` yet — that is a follow-up, spec by spec. And is_allowed_framework_slug listed five slugs where specs/spec.meta.schema.json lists seven, so two published specs sat inside the reservation with no permission to be there. The allowlist is one of two hand-maintained copies. The new test reads the meta-schema's copy and fails naming the missing slug if they drift again; verified by removing trust-task-control and watching it fail. Found while retiring trust-task-ok ([#292](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/292)), which swept for references to the slug and noticed the two lists disagreed. ### Specifications - Bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength (§7.3) ([#296](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/296)) * spec: bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength SPEC.md §7.3 (framework 0.5.0) requires that any member holding free text declare a `maxLength`. 92 free-text string members across 83 draft schemas carried none, leaving the wire contract unbounded and every consumer to invent its own ceiling — or none, which is what §10.3 (schema-validation DoS) exists to prevent. All amended specifications are `status: draft`, so the change is made in place per SPEC §5.2. Deliberately untouched: * 17 members in `retired` specifications, frozen by SPEC §6.4. * messaging/_shared/0.1 `AuditEntry.detail` and did-management/ _shared/0.1 `DomainEntry.label` — shared $defs reachable from a retired specification, so bounding them would change a frozen specification's effective wire contract. * vault/_shared/{0.1,0.2,0.3} `TspMessageEnvelope.message` — opaque base64url TSP bytes, not free text. Reading a member still derefs to `&String`, so `label.as_deref().map(String::as_str)` recovers an `Option<&str>`. title: ci(ts): author the npm release commit as a CLA signatory (#305)
body:
ci(ts): author the npm release commit as a CLA signatory (#305)

The two Release PRs each had exactly the half the other was missing:

  #299 crates  authored by a signatory, no Signed-off-by   -> DCO failed
  #303 npm     signed off, authored by github-actions[bot] -> EasyCLA failed

#304 fixed the first. This fixes the second: EasyCLA authorises the commit
*author*, and github-actions[bot] has signed no CLA, so a bot-authored release
commit fails however well it is signed off.

release-plz already authors its release commit as the RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN owner
— that is what setting the token changed, and what turned #299's EasyCLA green.
This is the same fix for the npm side.

Resolved from the token rather than hard-coded: whoever the token belongs to is
who the release is attributable to, and a hard-coded name would quietly
misattribute the release the moment the token changed hands. If the lookup
fails — a GitHub App token has no user — the script exits rather than falling
back to the bot, because that fallback is exactly the silent EasyCLA failure
this change removes.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: ci: sign off the release commit so DCO passes on the Release PR
body:
PR #299 — the first Release PR — fails **DCO**. `EasyCLA` now passes (setting `RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN` made the commits authored by a CLA signatory rather than `github-actions[bot]`), so DCO is the last check standing between a Release PR and merging.

The commit carries no `Signed-off-by` trailer. `scripts/release-ts-pr.sh` already uses `git commit -s`, so the **npm** Release PR passes and only the **crates** one fails — an asymmetry with nothing behind it.

## Two mechanisms, deliberately

1. `git config --global format.signOff true` before the action — covers release-plz if it commits through the git CLI.
2. A verification step that reads the branch tip and amends a trailer on if the first did not take.

Belt and braces because the failure is silent: a Release PR that just sits red, on the one commit that publishes.

## A bug I caught in my own first attempt

I guarded the step on a `pr_head_branch` output. **That output does not exist** — `action.yml` for `release-plz/action@v0.5.131` declares exactly `pr`, `prs`, `prs_created`, `releases`, `releases_created`. The guard would have been permanently false and the step would never have run, silently reproducing the failure it exists to prevent. It now keys off `prs_created`, parses `head_branch` from the `pr` JSON, and errors loudly if that is absent.

Amending is safe on this branch specifically: it is release-plz's own, it force-pushes over it every run, and nothing branches from it. The amend preserves the original author and names them in the trailer — the DCO is a statement by whoever authored the commit, not by the workflow.

## On #299 itself

Not worth amending by hand. It is stale (`v0.14.1`, `CONFLICTING`, cut before #296, #301 and #302) and release-plz will force-push over it on its next run. Once this merges, the regenerated Release PR should be signed off and should read **0.15.0 with the six-crate cascade**.

Not verifiable here — no release runs in a PR context. The first real proof is the next Release PR.

    if the first did not take.

The step keys off the action's real outputs. My first attempt guarded on a
pr_head_branch output that does not exist — action.yml declares exactly
pr / prs / prs_created / releases / releases_created — which would have made
the guard permanently false and the step never run, reproducing the same
silent failure it exists to prevent. It now parses head_branch out of the pr
JSON and fails loudly if that is missing.

The amend preserves the original author and names them in the trailer: the DCO
is a statement by whoever authored the commit, not by the workflow.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: feat(vta): mint the consent ceremony's correlator instead of deriving it
body:
Framework **0.5.0**, *Identifier correlation and linkability* — the last
VTI-side item of the 0.5.0 set that is not upstream work.

`id`, `threadId` and `ceremony.enactment` are correlators. 0.5.0 makes them
normative: each **MUST** be freshly minted and unguessable, and **MUST NOT** be
derived from subject data, an account number, a session identifier or a
counter.

## What was wrong

The `task-consent/granted` notice threaded on `wire_digest`:

```rust
"threadId": wire_digest,
…
thread_id: Some(wire_digest.to_string()),
```

`wire_digest` is `SHA-256(type_uri ‖ JCS(payload) ‖ challenge)` — a function of
the task payload, and **the same string the document carries as
`payloadDigest`**.

## Why it matters, and why it is not merely cosmetic

I checked whether this was a real exposure before changing a consent ceremony.
The challenge is 256 bits of randomness, so the digest is *not* guessable from
the payload — it is not the "UUIDv5 over a subject identifier" case 0.5.0 names.

**The mediator is the exposure.** `threadId` is routing metadata: the mediator
reads it to route, and it forwards documents whose body carries `payloadDigest`.
With the same value in both, it can tie the routing it performs to the digest it
carries and link the refusal, the approval pushes and the notice into one
ceremony with named counterparties — which is exactly the linkage the rule
exists to remove.

## The change

`PendingTaskConsent` gains a minted `correlator` (a fresh UUID), created
alongside the challenge and stored with the pending request. The notice threads
on it; **the body still carries `payloadDigest` unchanged**, so a requester that
matches on the digest is unaffected.

The requester is told the correlator in the `auth:consent_required` refusal,
beside the digest it already receives, so it can still correlate the notice.

`#[serde(default)]` on the new field: a pending record written before this
change still loads, and correlates on an empty string — no worse than an
unthreaded notice, and it drains within the consent expiry.

## Scope checked before changing it

- The **request** push to approvers already threaded on the request document's
  own `id` — a fresh UUID per approver. Only the requester-facing notice was
  derived, so this is a smaller change than it first looked.
- The granted notice is **produced but never consumed in this workspace**, and
  is explicitly non-load-bearing: "the grant check at re-submit is the real
  gate". So the blast radius is an external client that filters on the envelope
  `threadId` — and the body member it would more naturally match on is
  unchanged.

## Test

`the_notice_threads_on_the_correlator_not_the_digest` asserts all three
properties together: the envelope threads on the correlator, the document's
`threadId` agrees, and `payload.payloadDigest` still carries the digest.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings`
- `./scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` — 28 suites, **0 violations**
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

Refs #1059

title: feat(specs): require issuedAt on every live consequential spec, and make the §7.3 item 17 floor fatal
body:
> **Follows #300**, which has now merged (`eb86d60e`). This branch was cut from
> `feat/issued-at-requirement` and has been **rebased onto `main`** — no stacking caveat
> remains, and it merges clean.

## What this does

SPEC §7.3 item 17 says a Trust Task specification defining a *consequential* Trust Task
**MUST** require the `issuedAt` member. #300 made that expressible and reported the gap.
This closes it and then locks it shut.

```
before   Freshness floor (§7.3 item 17): 0/209 consequential spec(s) declare issuedAtRequirement: REQUIRED
           — 209 undeclared, e.g. acl/change-role/0.1, acl/grant/0.1, acl/revoke/0.1
           (warning — set TT_STRICT_ISSUED_AT=1 to fail the build)

after    Freshness floor (§7.3 item 17): 177/177 live consequential spec(s) declare
         issuedAtRequirement: REQUIRED; 32 frozen in retired spec(s) (§5.3 — exempt, not debt)
```

## The count, re-derived

Re-derived from the front matter rather than taken from #300, since this number has been
wrong before. **209 confirmed**, exactly: 165 `mutating` + 34 `destructive` + 23
`discloses: secret` + 24 `actsAsSubject: true` → 209 distinct of 349 specs.

**32 of the 209 are `status: retired` and are excluded.** §5.3 freezes a retired
specification's schema and prose at the moment of retirement. Declaring `REQUIRED` on one
would change which documents every consumer must reject for a specification that is
terminal and so cannot take the `MAJOR` increment §5.2 would demand for that change. They
are reported separately as frozen, exactly as the error-code lints already report theirs.

That leaves **177 live consequential specs**, all `status: draft`, all amended in place per
§5.2. Not 209 — so the number to hold this work to is 177/177, and the check's denominator
now says `live` to make that legible.

## The variant form: single `requirement`, not per-variant

Considered `request: REQUIRED` alone, on the reasoning that §7.2 item 11 protects the
request — a response is not replayed into an effect the same way. **It is not expressible
as a distinct declaration**, and the mechanism in #300 is why:

- `resolveIssuedAtRequirement()` applies the "an omitted `response` takes the request's
  value" rule, so `request: REQUIRED` alone resolves to `response: REQUIRED` too. It is a
  longer spelling of the single form, not a weaker declaration.
- Writing `response` weaker *explicitly* fails `checkIssuedAtFloor`, which requires
  `REQUIRED` on every variant a consequential spec defines.

So the honest declaration is the single `requirement: REQUIRED`, applied consistently to
all 177. The per-variant form stays available for the case it was built for — a spec that
is not consequential but wants freshness on one variant.

## The rationales

Not one sentence pasted 177 times. Each says why *this* task needs a bounded acceptance
window — what a second execution or an undateable document actually does to it. The
recurring distinctions:

- **Replay into re-admission** — a grant, registration or enrolment replayed after a
  revocation re-admits what the revocation removed.
- **Overwrite ordering** — `set-wake`, `record/put`, `policy/upsert` and friends are
  overwrites, so a stale copy reverts to an earlier state rather than expressing an intent;
  `issuedAt` is what lets the maintainer refuse the older document.
- **Irreversibility landing on the wrong object** — a delete or revoke replayed after the
  name was reused destroys the replacement.
- **Extent decided by execution time** — `did/rollback`, `vtc/website/rollback`,
  `services/rollback`, `retire-orphan`: the payload names a target but never a moment, so
  an undateable document names a different destruction on each replay.
- **Secret released, unrecallable** — `vault/release`, `vtc/backup/export`, the invite
  specs: the window bounds how long a captured request stays a standing withdrawal.
- **A human's decision spent twice** — `auth/step-up/approve-response`,
  `consent/decision`, `task-consent/decision`: the case §7.2 item 11 exists for.

Text is shared only where the reason genuinely is: the same task at several versions
(`vault/upsert` 0.1/0.2/0.3, `provision/integration` 0.1/0.2/0.3, the paired 0.1/0.2
specs), never across unrelated families.

## The ratchet

`TT_STRICT_ISSUED_AT` is **gone**, and the undeclared case now fails the build
unconditionally — following `checkProofFloor`, which #300 modelled the floor on and which
takes no env var either. A floor with an escape hatch is a warning wearing a different hat.

Verified by removing one declaration:

```
Freshness floor (§7.3 item 17): 176/177 live consequential spec(s) declare
issuedAtRequirement: REQUIRED; 32 frozen in retired spec(s) — 1 undeclared,
e.g. acl/grant/0.1 (error)

Build failed with the following problems:
  - acl/grant/0.1/spec.md: consequential Trust Task with no issuedAtRequirement
    declaration. SPEC §7.3 item 17 makes issuedAt REQUIRED ...
```

## ⚠️ This drifts the bindings, and that is not avoidable

Worth flagging because the working assumption going in was that front matter does not reach
the generators. **For this member it does** — that is #300's whole point. Declaring it
flips `Payload::IS_ISSUED_AT_REQUIRED` / `isIssuedAtRequired`: **347 constants on each
side**, and `npm run check-bindings` reported 694 problems until both were regenerated.

- **TypeScript** is `npm run build-ts-bindings` output verbatim (177 files, 347 flips).
- **Rust** is the same 347 constants inserted in the exact position and form the emitter
  produces. A full `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` also rewrites ~44k lines of typify
  output unrelated to this change — **pre-existing drift that reproduces on a clean
  checkout of the base branch**, so it is deliberately not in this PR. Worth a separate
  look; it means local codegen and CI codegen currently disagree.
- `npm run check-bindings` verifies the result independently of the generator.

Six §7.2 pipeline tests also went red — they build an `acl/grant` document with no
`issuedAt` and assert it reaches the handler. That is the change working. Fixtures stamped
(`test(rs)` commit), including the eight that were still passing but would have gone on
passing for the wrong reason.

## Why `feat` and not `spec`

No schema moved and no wire format changed, but once consumers re-target, a conforming
pipeline rejects a document with no `issuedAt` as `malformedRequest` for 177 specs. CLAUDE.md
is explicit that behavioural breaks count and that the bump is judged by what a consumer
observes — so this sizes as a minor, not the patch `spec(...)` would score.

## Not in scope

- `targetFrameworkVersion` is untouched; a separate PR re-targets the corpus to 0.5.0.
- No versions or CHANGELOG entries hand-edited — release-plz computes those.
- No payload schemas, meta-schema, or `## Security & Privacy` prose touched (a sibling PR
  owns those). The acceptance window itself stays prose per item 17, not front matter.

## Verification

| | |
|---|---|
| `npm run validate` | 349 specs, floor line `177/177 ... 32 frozen` |
| `npm run build` | Done |
| `npm run check-bindings` | 349 specs vs 349 TS and 344 Rust modules — all agree |
| `cargo build --workspace --all-targets` | Finished |
| `cargo test --workspace` | 44 binaries, 0 failures |
| `cargo fmt --all -- --check` | clean |
| `trust-tasks-ts` `npm test` | 79 pass, 0 fail |
| strict-mode regression | removing one declaration fails the build |

title: feat(specs): require issuedAt on every live consequential spec, and make the §7.3 item 17 floor fatal (#302)
body:
feat(specs): require issuedAt on every live consequential spec, and make the §7.3 item 17 floor fatal (#302)

* spec: make the §7.3 item 17 freshness floor a hard failure

PR #300 made `issuedAtRequirement` expressible and reported the derived floor
as a count, because every one of the registry's consequential specs predated the
member and failing the build for all of them at once would only have taught
contributors to skip the message. The commits that follow take the live corpus
to 100%, so the report becomes a ratchet: an undeclared consequential spec now
fails the build the same way `checkProofFloor` fails one that declares proof too
weakly, and there is no `TT_STRICT_ISSUED_AT` opt-out — a floor with an escape
hatch is a warning wearing a different hat.

Also exempts `retired` specs from the undeclared case. §5.3 freezes a retired
specification's schema and prose at the moment of retirement, and adding a
declaration to one would change which documents every consumer must reject for a
specification that is terminal and so cannot take the MAJOR increment §5.2 would
demand for that change. 32 of the 209 consequential specs are retired; they are
counted and reported separately, exactly as the error-code lints already report
their frozen populations — exempt, not debt. A retired spec that *does* carry a
declaration is still held to it, since that can only arrive by an edit.

The reported line therefore moves from `0/209` to `177/177 live ... ; 32 frozen`.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec(acl): declare issuedAtRequirement REQUIRED

SPEC §7.3 item 17 makes `issuedAt` REQUIRED of a specification defining a
consequential Trust Task. All five live ACL specs are consequential and none
could say so until `issuedAtRequirement` existed.

Every rationale is written for the task it sits on rather than pasted. The
family shares a shape — the ACL entry is the record every later authorization
decision is read from — but the harm differs: `grant` and `revoke` are replayed
into a re-admission or a second removal, `change-role` and `update` are
overwrites whose stale copies revert an operator's newer edit rather than
express an intent, and `swap-key` displaces the previous key irreversibly, so a
replay re-arms a holder a later swap had already cut off.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec(auth): declare issuedAtRequirement REQUIRED on auth and consent specs

Session, enrolment, step-up and consent tasks are the ones for which a bounded
acceptance window is the primary defence rather than a secondary one: an
authentication or refresh request that cannot be placed in time is a credential
presentation with no expiry, which is the form a captured request is replayed in.

The step-up approvals and the two consent decision specs get the sharpest
rationales in the change, because they carry a human's answer to one specific
operation — the case §7.2 item 11 exists for, and one item 11 can only recognise
inside a window.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec(vault): declare issuedAtRequirement REQUIRED on vault and key specs

These two families share the property that makes freshness load-bearing: they
either release secret material that cannot be recalled once delivered, or act
with the subject's own authority to produce a signature that outlives the
exchange. A signing request that cannot be aged out is a signing oracle for as
long as it stays acceptable, and a captured `vault/release` is a standing
withdrawal against the entry — the entry's TTL bounds what the consumer should
keep, but only `issuedAt` bounds how long the request itself stays executable.

The three `vault/upsert` versions and the paired `proxy-login` / `release` /
`sign-trust-task` versions share their rationale text because they are the same
task at different versions, not different tasks with a copied sentence.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec(credential-exchange): declare issuedAtRequirement REQUIRED on exchange specs

Credential exchange is where the fire-and-forget variants concentrate: `issue`,
`present`, `query` and `request` define no response document, so a consumer has
no reply to correlate a duplicate against and depends entirely on the record of
§7.2 item 11 — which is bounded by this timestamp and nothing else. The
rationales say so where it is true and say something else where it is not.

`pending/approve` and `pending/deny` are the pair worth reading: an approval
replayed after the subject has moved on releases their credential material to a
request they never approved, and a denial replayed after a new request has taken
the same slot refuses the new one on a decision made about the old.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec(device): declare issuedAtRequirement REQUIRED on device, push and messaging specs

Registration and attachment tasks are replayed into re-admission — a device, a
push token or a mailbox the owner has since removed — and the removal is usually
the security action the replay undoes. The overwrite tasks (`set-wake`,
`account/update`, `access-list/update`) fail differently: a stale copy reverts to
an earlier state rather than expressing an intent, and ordering the two requires
a timestamp.

`device/wipe` and `chat/message` are the outliers and are written as such: a wipe
that cannot be placed in a window stays armed forever, and a fire-and-forget chat
message has nothing but its timestamp to stop a captured copy being re-delivered
later and read as newly said.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec(did-management): declare issuedAtRequirement REQUIRED on DID and registry specs

What these tasks write is resolved by third parties, so a stale document is not
merely an internal inconsistency — it is what other people read as current. The
rationales separate the three ways that happens: claims and registrations that a
replay re-asserts after a release, overwrites (`domain/update`, `record/put`,
`did/set-state`) whose out-of-order copies silently restore an earlier revision,
and irreversible removals (`domain/purge`, `did/delete`, `record/delete`) that
land on whatever has since taken the identifier.

`did/rollback` and `registry/did/rotate` are called out individually because what
they destroy is decided by *when* they run rather than by anything in the
payload, so an undateable document names a different destruction each replay.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec(policy): declare issuedAtRequirement REQUIRED on policy, config and control specs

Policy and configuration tasks are overwrites of things that gate other tasks, so
replaying a predecessor is a downgrade with nothing in the document recording it
as one — reinstating a step-up threshold an operator tightened, or a capability
disabled for cause. `config/restart` and the governance pair are timing
primitives outright: their value is entirely in when they arrive.

`audit/list` and the commit-signing pair are the two that are not about mutation
at all. A captured audit listing keeps yielding records as the log grows, so the
window limits how much one authorised request can eventually reveal; a
commit-signing grant is consulted long after issue by verifiers reading history,
so one that cannot be dated cannot be aged out.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec(vta): declare issuedAtRequirement REQUIRED on all 35 live consequential specs

The largest family, and the one where grouping the rationales genuinely pays: the
sub-families fail in different ways and are written accordingly.

  * `app-state` and `memory` are key-value overwrites, so two copies applied out
    of order leave the older value in place. `memory/put` is called out because
    the agent then *acts* on what it remembers, which makes a stale copy a
    superseded belief rather than merely an old value.
  * `contexts` is the isolation boundary other tasks are scoped by, so a replayed
    create leaves a second boundary the operator did not ask for, and a replayed
    delete destroys everything scoped inside a re-created one.
  * `webvh/*` writes to logs others resolve, and appended entries cannot be
    withdrawn — `dids/rotate-keys` is the sharpest case, since a replay retires
    the keys a later rotation installed and so restores the very material the
    operator was rotating away from.
  * `services/*` splits between availability effects (`enable`, `disable`) and
    operations whose extent is decided by when they run (`rollback`,
    `drain/cancel`).
  * `credentials/issue` acts with the subject's authority and returns material
    that leaves the agent's control, so a replay mints a second credential over
    the same claims and no holder can tell which the subject meant to exist.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec(vtc): declare issuedAtRequirement REQUIRED on all 37 live consequential specs

Community tasks are the ones whose duplicates are visible to third parties, so
the rationales say what an outsider sees rather than only what the maintainer
records.

  * `admin/bootstrap` gets the strongest statement in the change: it establishes
    the community's first administrator, the one moment at which the ordinary
    authorisation checks cannot apply, so a bootstrap document that stays
    executable is a standing route to a second administrator and the acceptance
    window carries weight there that policy cannot.
  * The invite and invitation specs return secret material that admits its
    bearer; a replay issues it again and it cannot be withdrawn once returned.
  * `backup/export` and `backup/import` are the bulk cases — an export request is
    the most valuable document in the family to replay, and an import rolls the
    community back to the archive's moment a second time.
  * `auth/recognise` and `members/rotate-challenge` are challenge-response, where
    a response accepted outside a window answers a challenge already answered.
  * The `members/*` removals and `endorsements/revoke` are written around the
    same failure: replayed after the member rejoined or was endorsed again, they
    remove the new thing on a decision made about the old.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* build: regenerate bindings for the 177 issuedAtRequirement declarations

`issuedAtRequirement` is not inert front matter: #300 wired it through both
generators, so declaring it flips `Payload::IS_ISSUED_AT_REQUIRED` in Rust and
`isIssuedAtRequired` in TypeScript. 177 specs × the variants they define is 347
constants on each side, and `npm run check-bindings` fails on every one of them
until the libraries are regenerated.

This is a **behavioural break for consumers**, in the sense CLAUDE.md describes
for `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED`: no schema moved and no wire format changed, but a
conforming consumer pipeline now rejects a document with no `issuedAt` as
`malformedRequest` for all 177 specs. Judged by what a consumer observes, that
sizes as a minor bump rather than a patch — hence `feat` on the PR title.

The TypeScript side is `npm run build-ts-bindings` output verbatim. The Rust side
is the same 347 constants inserted in the exact position and form the emitter
produces (after `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED`, before `IS_RECIPIENT_REQUIRED`), because a
full `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` on this machine also rewrites ~44k lines
of typify output unrelated to this change — pre-existing local drift that
reproduces on a clean checkout of the base branch and does not belong in this PR.
`npm run check-bindings` verifies the result independently of the generator: 349
specifications checked against 349 TypeScript and 344 Rust modules, all agree.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* test(rs): stamp issuedAt on the pipeline fixtures acl/grant now requires

Six §7.2 pipeline tests build an `acl/grant` document with no `issuedAt` and
assert it reaches the handler. Now that `acl/grant/0.1` declares
`issuedAtRequirement: REQUIRED`, the pipeline rejects them with
`malformedRequest` before the handler runs — which is the change working, not a
regression.

Stamped on all eleven fixtures in `consume.rs` rather than only the three that
turned red, and on the shared `inbound()` helper in `async_dispatch.rs` that
covers the other three. The eight that were still passing were passing because
they expect a rejection for some *other* named reason, and an unstamped document
now has a second, closer ground to be rejected on — so they would have gone on
passing while testing something they do not claim to test.

These fixtures are the smallest honest demonstration of what the declaration
costs a consumer: one line, at the producer, for a document that could not
otherwise be placed in an acceptance window.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: spec!: bound the remaining free-text payload members and state who reads them (#301)
body:
spec!: bound the remaining free-text payload members and state who reads them (#301)

SPEC.md §7.3 (framework 0.5.0) item 19 has three parts. PR #296 closed most
of part 1 for eight member names (`reason`, `note`, `detail`, `description`,
`message`, `text`, `label`, `comment`), 92 members in all. Sweeping the whole
corpus rather than a name list finds **48 more** unbounded free-text members
across 27 draft specifications and 10 shared schemas, under names the earlier
sweep did not look for: `purpose`, `deviceLabel`, `displayName`, `explanation`,
`summary`, `title`, `name`, `blurb`, `filename`, `trace`, `error`, `lastError`,
`deniedReason`, `displayHint`, `consequences`, `rpName`, `userName`,
`userDisplayName`.

The one the earlier review named specifically is here: `task-consent`'s
`Effect.summary` — the member its own schema calls "the ONLY member a consent
surface is guaranteed to be able to render" — was unbounded on the surface a
human reads to approve an action. It is now 500, the same figure as the `note`
beside it.

Bounds are drawn from the vocabulary the corpus already uses and sized per
member, not applied uniformly:

    64   WebAuthn entity names (`rp.name`, `user.name`, `user.displayName`,
         `rpName`, `userName`, `userDisplayName`) — the length WebAuthn tells
         authenticators to truncate to, so a longer value would be silently
         cut on the device rather than carried.
   128   `purpose` where it names a decision slot or a declared intent. This
         is consistency repair, not a new judgement: policy/activate/0.1 and
         policy/active/0.1 already declared `maxLength: 128` on the request
         member while the response that echoes it declared none.
   256   display labels and names — `deviceLabel`, `displayName`,
         `displayHint`, `label`, `title`, `name`, `blurb`, `filename`;
         matches #296's reasoning that a display name is not prose.
   500   consent-surface prose a human reads while deciding — `Effect.summary`,
         `consequences[]`, credential-exchange `purpose`, `deniedReason`;
         matches task-consent/request/0.1 `note`.
  1024   operator or service diagnostic prose — `explanation`, `trace[]`,
         `error`, `lastError`, and vta/credentials/issue `purpose`.

**Part 3 of the MUST is the half nobody had done.** Item 19 also requires each
specification to state who reads a free-text value, whether the recipient is
expected to retain it, and whether it is trusted. Prose is added to the
`## Security & Privacy` section of all **37** draft specifications that reach a
newly bounded member — the 27 whose own payload schema moved, plus 10 that
reach one through a shared `$def`. `vta/credentials/issue/0.{1,2}` had no such
section at all and now carry one containing the item 19 statement; both remain
on the Security & Privacy debt allowlist, because neither yet has the four
sub-headings the repo lint wants. The other 35 sections were extended in place.

Deliberately untouched, matching #296's own carve-outs:

  * `messaging/_shared/0.1` `AuditEntry.detail` and `did-management/_shared/0.1`
    `DomainEntry.label` — shared `$defs` reachable from a retired specification,
    so bounding them would move a frozen specification's wire contract. These
    are the only two shared schemas in this change's blast radius that a
    retired spec reaches; the ten this PR edits are draft-only.
  * Members item 19's own last paragraph excludes: identifiers, opaque handles,
    digests and references; and values carried verbatim from an external
    vocabulary — DNS domains, did:webvh agent-name local parts, DID logs, Rego
    source, RFC 6901 pointers, HTTP header and cookie names, APNs topics, IANA
    media types, BCP 47 language tags, and maintainer- or community-defined
    role and kind vocabularies.

Two members were bounded where the schema's own description calls the value an
undeclared closed set (`nature`, `wired` in vtc/ceremonies/list) — deliberately
left alone, because the right fix there is the closed enumeration item 19
prefers, not a length.

All 48 members sit in `status: draft` specifications and are amended in place
per SPEC §5.2. `npm run validate` re-checks all 533 fenced example documents
against the amended schemas; none is rejected by a new bound.

**Still open, and deliberately not in this PR:** item 19's "SHOULD be OPTIONAL"
half. 18 of the 48 members bounded here are REQUIRED — `CredentialCreationOptions`
`rp.name`/`user.name`/`user.displayName`, credential-exchange `purpose` (both
copies), `Effect.summary`, `ContextRecord.name` and vta/contexts/create `name`,
the three `enroll-challenge` WebAuthn names, `CommunityProfile.name`,
`CommunityProfileView.name`, `CommunityProfileSnapshot.name`, and the four
decision-slot `purpose` members. Added to the 13 #296 found, that is 31.
Making any of them optional is a wire-compatibility change and belongs in its
own PR; several (purpose binding, `Effect.summary`) are required by design and
the specification should say so rather than change.

This is **breaking**, on the same terms #296 judged itself so: typify emits a
bounded member as a validating newtype, so `Option<String>` becomes
`Option<PayloadDeviceLabel>`, `Option<PayloadDeniedReason>`,
`Option<AttachmentRefFilename>` and so on, and the newtype rejects in
`Deserialize` a document the library previously accepted. `@openvtc/trust-tasks`
generates unchanged *types* — TypeScript has no length refinement — but its
embedded schemas now reject over-long values at runtime. No version is bumped
and no changelog is written: release-plz computes both from this title.

title: feat(rs): make SPEC §7.3 item 17's issuedAt MUST expressible
body:
## The gap

`SPEC.md` §7.3 item 17 (framework 0.5.0, in this repo since #297):

> a *Trust Task specification* defining a *consequential Trust Task* **MUST** require the `issuedAt` member, raising the framework's **SHOULD** to a **MUST** for documents conforming to it.

**There was no way to declare that.** The meta-schema had `proofRequirement` for the `proof` envelope member and nothing equivalent for `issuedAt`. So the MUST was unexpressible, and the **209 consequential specs** in the registry could not comply with it even in principle.

This PR builds the mechanism. It declares it on **no spec** — that is a follow-up, spec by spec.

## What a spec will write

```yaml
proofRequirement:
  requirement: REQUIRED
  rationale: A one-sentence reason your threat model needs this strength.
issuedAtRequirement:                 # ← new
  requirement: REQUIRED              # OPTIONAL | RECOMMENDED | REQUIRED
  rationale: Why this task's documents must be placeable in time.
sideEffects:
  level: mutating
```

Or, where the two variants are relied on differently — the same per-variant form `proofRequirement` already has:

```yaml
issuedAtRequirement:
  request: REQUIRED
  response: RECOMMENDED
  rationale: The request causes the effect item 11 must not repeat; the acknowledgement does not.
```

`npm run new-spec` now emits the declaration on a scaffold whose classes make the task consequential, so a new spec is conformant as generated.

## Naming, and modelling it on `proofRequirement`

`issuedAtRequirement`, named for the envelope member it governs, exactly as `proofRequirement` is. Same two forms, same three-value enum, same required `rationale`, same "an omitted `response` takes the request's value" normalisation. `freshnessRequirement` was considered and rejected: item 17 is titled *Freshness* but also carries a **SHOULD** about the acceptance window and a **MAY** about `expiresAt`, and a name that promised those would be lying about what the field carries.

The window and the `expiresAt` **MAY** stay prose. A window is *consumer* policy; a duration in front matter would invite consumers to adopt one specification's guess as their own.

## Declared or derived?

Consequentiality is already computable — §2 spells it out as `sideEffects.level ∈ {mutating, destructive} ∨ exposure.discloses = secret ∨ exposure.actsAsSubject = true`, all of which every spec already declares. Deriving would have removed 209 hand-edits.

**Declared**, with the derived floor checked and reported. Four reasons:

1. **Items 13 and 14 are DESCRIPTIVE, and say so loudly.** Deriving would mean that correcting `sideEffects.level` from `none` to `mutating` *for accuracy* silently changed which documents every consumer of that spec is obliged to reject. That is precisely the coupling the descriptive/prescriptive split exists to prevent.
2. **§2 makes the handler authoritative for consequentiality, not the front matter.** A value computed from a declaration §2 explicitly says is not authoritative would be enforcing something the declaration does not authoritatively state.
3. **A non-consequential spec may legitimately require `issuedAt`** for its own reasons. A derived-only mechanism cannot express that. The derived value is a floor, not a ceiling.
4. **Deriving flips 209 specs' wire behaviour in one commit, invisibly**, shipped as a minor. Declaring keeps each flip a reviewed, per-spec, visible change — and keeps the requirement in the front matter a reader scans.

## …but the build derives it anyway, and says so

The drift argument for deriving is real, so the floor is derived — it just isn't *substituted for* the declaration:

```
Freshness floor (§7.3 item 17): 0/209 consequential spec(s) declare issuedAtRequirement: REQUIRED
  — 209 undeclared, e.g. acl/change-role/0.1, acl/grant/0.1, acl/revoke/0.1
  (warning — set TT_STRICT_ISSUED_AT=1 to fail the build)
```

- **Declared weaker than the floor → hard error, today.** A consequential spec declaring `RECOMMENDED` fails `npm run validate` with a message naming the triggering declarations. (Modelled on the existing `checkProofFloor`.)
- **Undeclared → counted and reported.** 209 specs predate the field; failing the build for all of them would only teach contributors to ignore the message. `TT_STRICT_ISSUED_AT=1` makes it fatal now, and becomes the default once the registry has caught up — the same ratchet `TT_STRICT_DISCLOSURE` / `TT_STRICT_SECURITY_PRIVACY` already use.

The number is the point: it is visibly a number that has to go to zero.

## Enforcement

The constant reaches consumers by the route `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` already takes:

| | |
|---|---|
| Rust | `Payload::IS_ISSUED_AT_REQUIRED`, **defaulted to `false`** |
| TypeScript | `SpecPolicy.isIssuedAtRequired`, **optional**, absence reads as false |
| Checked in | `TrustTask::enforce_spec_policy` / `enforceSpecPolicy` |
| Rejection | **`malformedRequest`** |

**Why `malformedRequest`.** §8.3 defines no dedicated code. `expired` names a document that was once acceptable — one that can never be placed in a window never was. And §7.2 item 13 already reports the other two freshness failures (future-dated `issuedAt`, `expiresAt ≤ issuedAt`) as `malformedRequest`, so this joins them rather than inventing a third treatment. It follows `IS_RECIPIENT_REQUIRED`, which is the closest existing case; `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` maps to `proofRequired` only because §8.3 gives it a code of its own.

**The default is load-bearing.** `trust-task-error` is in the codegen's `SKIP_SLUGS` and hand-modelled in `error.rs`; a defaultless trait constant would break it and every downstream hand-written impl. A test asserts a bare hand-written impl still compiles.

**Not the same thing as `FreshnessPolicy::require_issued_at`**, and the docs say so at both ends. That field is the *consumer's* posture, chosen at the call site. This constant is the *specification's* requirement, true of the type regardless of who holds it — a consumer on the permissive default policy still rejects, because the obligation is not the consumer's to relax.

**`check-bindings` compares the new key** across front matter, Rust and TypeScript, so the mechanism cannot exist in one language only. Verified by temporarily declaring `REQUIRED` on `acl/grant/0.1`, regenerating, reverting the front matter, and confirming all four drift errors fire.

## Generated output: unchanged (Rust) / additive-only (TypeScript)

No spec declares the field, so:

- **`trust-tasks-rs/src/specs/` — byte-identical.** The const is emitted only on override, exactly like `IS_BEARER` and `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED`. `git diff --stat` over the tree after `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` is empty.
- **`trust-tasks-ts/src/` — one line per policy object**, `isIssuedAtRequired: false`. 679 insertions, **0 deletions**, across 349 generated modules; TS emits its policy flags unconditionally, so this is the shape consistent with its siblings.

Nothing that was accepted before is rejected now.

## Gates

```
npm run validate      Validated 349 specs, indexed 66 shared schemas.
npm run build         Done.
npm run check-bindings 349 specifications checked against 349 TypeScript and 344 Rust modules — all agree.
cargo build --workspace                                          Finished
cargo test --workspace --all-targets                             0 failed
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -D warnings clean
cargo fmt --all --check                                          clean
RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps --all-features    clean
trust-tasks-ts: node --test                                      79 pass, 0 fail
```

New tests: `trust-tasks-rs/tests/issued_at_requirement.rs` (4) and three cases in `trust-tasks-ts/test/consume.test.ts` — the reject, the accept once `issuedAt` is present, and the additive guarantee that an undeclaring spec still accepts a document without one.

## Versioning

Additive to `trust-tasks-rs` (new trait constant with a default) and to `@openvtc/trust-tasks` (new optional `SpecPolicy` member). No version or CHANGELOG is hand-edited — release-plz sizes the bump from the `feat(rs):` title.

## Follow-up

Declaring `issuedAtRequirement: REQUIRED` on the 209 consequential specs, family by family, and then flipping `TT_STRICT_ISSUED_AT` on by default. Each of those *is* behavioural — a consumer starts rejecting documents it used to accept — which is exactly why this PR does not do it silently for all of them at once.

title: Framework 0.5.0: identifier correlation, one document lifecycle, freshness bounds, retention/ingest/identifier-scope declarations, and error-model hardening
body:
Framework version **0.5.0**. Additive, with one deprecation: the document wire format gains no member and loses none, every document conforming to 0.4.0 still conforms, and the three new front-matter declarations are **SHOULD** with a fail-safe reading of an absent value, so no already-published Trust Task specification becomes non-conforming for want of them.

Ten commits, one per change, each with the rationale in its message. `npm run render` succeeds with no Spec-Up-T warnings; all 82 internal anchors resolve against the rendered output and no `[[ref:]]` is left unresolved.

## What changed, and why

### 1. Identifier correlation and linkability (new normative subsection under Privacy Considerations)

The Security and Privacy sections have never mentioned correlation or linkability. A census of the registry says they should: **346 of 349** published specifications declare both `issuer` and `recipient` **REQUIRED**, and **210** declare `proof` **REQUIRED** — so the median Trust Task document is a signed, retainable record naming both parties in clear. Privacy Considerations item 2 already noted such a document is durable evidence of its *content*; nothing addressed what it is evidence of about the *parties*.

Four rules:

- `issuer`/`recipient` **SHOULD** be relationship-scoped (pairwise) VIDs unless the specification states why a public identifier is intrinsic to what the task asserts.
- `id`, `threadId` and `ceremony.enactment` are correlators: each **MUST** be freshly minted and unguessable, and **MUST NOT** be derived from subject data, an account number, a session identifier or a counter. A UUIDv5 over a subject identifier *is* the subject identifier under an encoding; a counter additionally discloses volume.
- `issuedAt` **MAY** be coarsened where the specification does not need sub-minute freshness — a full-precision timestamp is a fingerprint.
- A `ceremony.enactment` links every counterparty in a flow by default. The mitigation is the existing `enactmentPrivacy: blinded` declaration, not a receipt going undistributed — bearer governs audience, not distribution.

The subsection is normative inside an otherwise informative section; the section lead-in now reads "informative except where a subsection states otherwise".

### 2. One document lifecycle (new section at the end of Trust Task Documents)

The lifecycle was implied differently in five places — the acceptance bound of Consumer Requirements item 4, the duplicate record of item 11, the re-evaluation of item 12, Task Control, and Error Responses — and no section named the whole set, so implementations have inferred five overlapping lifecycles from one document.

A normative state table now names them once: `received` → `validated` → `accepted` → {`executing`, `suspended`} → {`responded`, `errored`, `cancelled`, `expired`}, with a column naming the reserved reply that carries each transition and an explicit **meaning-of-silence** column.

Silence had acquired four distinct meanings — success for fire-and-forget, nothing for `trust-task-ok`, "duplicate absorbed" under item 11, and nothing again for control notifications — and the document's own text already warned that item 11's silence "must not be reused to signify work half-done". The table settles on the only safe reading: **the absence of a reply distinguishes no two states**, and a producer MUST NOT infer any state from it.

A transport binding **MUST** map the table onto its own protocol; the requirement is also added as a **MUST** item in *What a Transport Binding Specifies*. This is what stops a `202` being read as acceptance, an acknowledged delivery as execution, or a dropped connection as cancellation.

### 3. Freshness (Consumer Requirements item 13, Specification Requirements item 17)

Item 11's duplicate-execution record is implementable only inside a bounded window, and nothing obliged a document to carry a timestamp that could place it in one. A document with no `expiresAt` and no usable `issuedAt` never leaves the set a consumer must recognize, so its record must be kept **forever**.

- A consumer **MUST** reject a document whose `issuedAt` is in its own future beyond its skew tolerance.
- A consumer **MUST** reject one whose `expiresAt` is at or before its `issuedAt`.

Both are `malformedRequest`, not `expired` — `expired` names a document that was once acceptable, and neither of these ever was; returning `expired` would tell the producer to wait when what it must do is reissue. No new error code is minted.

A Trust Task specification defining a **consequential** Trust Task **MUST** require `issuedAt`, putting the obligation on the party that can satisfy it for nothing.

### 4. Three new front-matter declarations (Specification Requirements items 5, 14, 18)

Each is **descriptive, not prescriptive**, on identical terms to the existing `sideEffects` and `exposure` items — the same "MUST NOT be read as obliging", the same "MUST treat an absent or unresolvable declaration as no weaker than…", the same prohibition on deriving a consent requirement.

- **`retention: { class: transient | exchange | durable, rationale }`** — what the recipient may keep and for how long. The framework has had no retention vocabulary at all, and the gap is not neutral: every rule in this document and in the corpus that uses the word *retain* mandates **more** retention (a proof so a document can be relied on later, a digest so a duplicate can be absorbed, an `inResponseTo` so an error can be evidence) and none bounds it — so the safe reading of every task has been to keep everything. Absent reads as `durable`. A `transient` declaration explicitly does **not** disapply item 11, whose record is a digest rather than the data.
- **`exposure.ingests: none | metadata | personal | secret`** — the existing `exposure.discloses` is response-only, so a task ingesting a full verifiable presentation or free-text personal data declares `none` today and is *correct*. Absent or unresolvable reads as no less sensitive than **`personal`**; the floor is `personal` rather than `secret` because assuming `secret` of every undeclared specification would make the class carry no information, whereas personal data in a request is the ordinary case.
- **`parties[].identifierScope: pairwise | public | any`** — makes change 1's first rule machine-readable, so a reviewer or the registry can see which specifications expect a public identifier without reading each one for the justification. Absent reads as no less correlatable than `public`.

### 5. Free-text members (Specification Requirements item 19)

A free-text member is the one place in a Trust Task document where the schema constrains the shape and nothing constrains the content — so it is where personal data arrives in a task declaring it ingests none, where a secret arrives pasted by someone asked for a reason, and where instructions addressed to a downstream reader arrive in a field the specification took for a comment. It is also unbounded wire cost: Parser Hardening puts the limit at the transport layer, which is the right defence and the wrong place to pick the number, since one figure there covers every task the consumer implements.

Any free-text member **MUST** declare a `maxLength`, **SHOULD** be **OPTIONAL**, and the specification **MUST** state who reads it, whether it is retained, and whether it is trusted. Prefer a closed enum plus one bounded optional note. `task-consent/request/0.1`'s `note` is cited as the model: 500 characters, optional, attributed to its author on every surface, explicitly untrusted, and forbidden from displacing the executor-authored effects it sits beside.

### 6. Fire-and-forget acknowledgement, and `trust-task-ok` deprecated

Today a fire-and-forget specification is forbidden from emitting `#response`, which is the *sole* reason the `trust-task-ok` slug exists — and that slug is defined so it cannot carry meaning (consumers MUST NOT require any member, producers MUST NOT rely on receiving one). A registry entry, a schema and a generated type per language, on a `type` bearing no relation to the one the producer sent, to convey "something arrived".

- A fire-and-forget specification's consumer **MAY** now return `<type>#response` with `payload` exactly `{}` as a courtesy acknowledgement; a producer still **MUST NOT** rely on it. The receiving party validates it against the framework schema alone and does not resolve a `response` anchor, which item 7.6 forbids the specification to declare.
- `trust-task-ok` is **deprecated**, not removed: consumers SHOULD NOT emit one from this version, producers **MUST** keep accepting one for as long as the specification is served, and the slug stays RESERVED permanently. Retiring the registry entry is a separate change in `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`.
- Request and Response Variants gains a table of the **three response dispositions** — success `#response`, failure `trust-task-error`, continuation `trust-task-next-step` — beside the fragment rule. "Is this a response?" was answerable in three separate places, so implementations hard-code a list of the slugs they happen to know, which the next reserved slug silently invalidates.

### 7. Discovery hardening

The discovery specification justifies its OPTIONAL `proof` requirement by saying the parties "have already authenticated through the transport". That is false over the HTTPS binding, whose own security profile states plainly that it provides no producer-to-consumer end-to-end guarantee — and *Permitting `proof` to Be Omitted* already refuses to let a guarantee be read off a transport's name.

- The applicable `proof` requirement rises to **RECOMMENDED**.
- A discoverer **MUST NOT** act on a discovery response whose origin it can authenticate neither in-band nor from the transport — mirroring the rule `trust-task-next-step` already imposes, for the same reason: an unauthenticated redirection is indistinguishable from an injected one.
- A responder's advertised requirements (e.g. a `requiredExt` namespace) are **untrusted input** and **MUST NOT** cause a producer to attach data it would not otherwise have sent. The contrary reading turns a discovery response into a data-collection instrument that costs an attacker one unauthenticated reply.
- A request's `patterns` list **SHOULD** be bounded — the matching work is paid by the party that did not choose it.

### 8. Error model

- **`message` disclosure is now normative for every code**, not just `identityMismatch`. An error response is emitted to a party the consumer has just failed to validate, usually before any authorization decision is reached, and it is retainable. A `message` **MUST NOT** reveal consumer-internal state, the contested value of a mismatched party, or resolver / verifier / key-status internals — otherwise each error response is an identity- and reachability-probing oracle that the consumer pays for and operates on the sender's behalf. Nothing bars logging any of it locally; the rule is about what is sent.
- **`details` gains a bound.** It was the one error-payload member with no size constraint, travelling in the direction no producer-side bound reaches, on the least-tested path. A specification defining a `details` shape MUST declare a bound; absent one, 4096 bytes of JCS or 16 immediate members. An oversized `details` is ignored — never grounds to discard the `code`, which is what the receiving party actually needs.
- **`cancelled` gains a defined `effects` shape**, reusing the same array-of-effects (`description`, `ref`, `reversible`) that `trust-task-control` already defines for a producer-requested stop. The two report the identical fact — what had already landed when the stop took hold — and differed only in that one was machine-readable and the other prose, according to which party decided. `effects: []` means nothing landed; an **absent** `effects` means the consumer did not report, and MUST NOT be read as "nothing landed".

### 9. Two digests, named

`taskDigest` excludes the top-level `proof` and asks *what the document says*; `stepDigest` includes it and asks *which serialization arrived*. Both have been carried in members called `digestMultibase`, so an implementation with a single function of that name has picked one answer and applies it to both questions — and whichever it picked is wrong for one of them. A short table now states the difference beside the citation rule that turns on it. Clarification only: neither is a document member, no computation changes, and every existing citation and step chain stays conforming.

### 10. Appendix B and header

New `0.5.0` changelog entry covering all of the above. `spec/header.md` bumped to `0.5.0`, with a `_Last Updated:_ 2026-08-26` line added — the header carried no date field before, so this introduces one rather than editing one.

## ⚠️ Two items need a companion change in `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`

1. **The three new front-matter declarations need meta-schema support.** `retention`, `exposure.ingests` and `parties[].identifierScope` are not yet expressible in `specs/spec.meta.schema.json`, so until that lands they are declarable in prose only. They are deliberately **SHOULD** with fail-safe defaults, so nothing is blocked in the meantime and no published specification becomes non-conforming.
2. **The `trust-task-ok` deprecation is a position, not a retirement.** This PR does not retire the registry entry — that follows Maturity Levels and belongs to the registry's own change process, on its own schedule, once consumers have moved. The slug remains reserved permanently either way, and producers must keep accepting the document while it is served.

Separately, the `trust-task-discovery` registry entry will want re-issuing to declare `proof` as RECOMMENDED. The framework default stated here governs in the meantime, and Specification Requirements item 8 already forbids a specification declaring a requirement weaker than the framework default.

## Not changed

- The three-part `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` framework version rule introduced by #1 is untouched, as the parallel registry-side meta-schema PR expects.
- `docs/` (rendered, gitignored) and `node_modules` are untouched.
- Appendix A's worked example is left as it stands. It already predates the 0.3 `sideEffects` / `exposure` declarations and does not show them; adding only the three new ones would have made it more inconsistent, not less. Refreshing that example in full is worth a separate PR.
