title: feat(rs): make SPEC §7.3 item 17's issuedAt MUST expressible (#300)
body:
feat(rs): make SPEC §7.3 item 17's issuedAt MUST expressible (#300)

Framework 0.5.0's §7.3 item 17 says a Trust Task specification defining a
consequential Trust Task MUST require the `issuedAt` member, raising §4.2's
SHOULD to a MUST for documents conforming to it. There was no way to declare
that: the meta-schema had `proofRequirement` for the `proof` envelope member
and nothing equivalent for `issuedAt`, so the MUST was unexpressible and none
of the 209 consequential specs in the registry could comply.

Adds `issuedAtRequirement` to the front-matter meta-schema, modelled on
`proofRequirement` — same two forms (a single `requirement`, or a per-variant
`request`/`response` pair), same enum, same `rationale`. It governs an envelope
member, admits a per-variant reading because request and response are relied on
differently, and reading one declaration now teaches the other.

Declared rather than derived, with the derived floor checked and reported:

  * `sideEffects` and `exposure` are DESCRIPTIVE (§7.3 items 13/14). Deriving
    `issuedAt`-REQUIRED from them would mean that correcting `sideEffects.level`
    from `none` to `mutating` for accuracy silently changed which documents
    every consumer of that spec must reject.
  * §2 makes the *handler* authoritative for consequentiality, not the front
    matter — so a value computed from the front matter would enforce something
    the front matter does not authoritatively state.
  * A non-consequential spec may legitimately require `issuedAt` anyway; a
    derived-only mechanism cannot express that.
  * Deriving would flip 209 specs' wire behaviour in one commit, invisibly.

So the build derives the floor instead of substituting for the declaration.
`npm run validate` prints a `Freshness floor (§7.3 item 17)` line counting the
consequential specs that have not declared it (currently 0/209), *fails* on a
spec that declares something weaker than REQUIRED, and escalates the undeclared
case to a hard error under `TT_STRICT_ISSUED_AT=1` — the ratchet that becomes
the default once the registry has caught up.

Enforcement reaches consumers the same way `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` does:

  * `Payload::IS_ISSUED_AT_REQUIRED` (Rust) and `SpecPolicy.isIssuedAtRequired`
    (TypeScript), emitted per variant by both generators from the front matter.
  * `TrustTask::enforce_spec_policy` / `enforceSpecPolicy` reject a document
    with no `issuedAt` as `malformedRequest`. Not `expired`: §8.3 defines no
    dedicated code, `expired` names a document that was once acceptable, and
    §7.2 item 13 already uses `malformedRequest` for the other freshness
    rejections.
  * The trait constant has a default of `false`, so hand-written impls — the
    crate's own `trust-task-error`, hand-modelled in `error.rs` because it is
    in the codegen's SKIP_SLUGS, and every downstream impl — keep compiling.
  * `check-bindings` compares the new key across front matter, Rust and
    TypeScript, so the two languages cannot drift on it.

Distinct from `FreshnessPolicy::require_issued_at`, which is a *consumer's*
own posture applied to every document it sees. This is the *specification's*
requirement, published in the registry and not the consumer's to relax.

No specification declares `issuedAtRequirement` yet — that is a follow-up,
spec by spec. The generated Rust tree is therefore byte-identical (the const is
emitted only on override) and the generated TypeScript gains one
`isIssuedAtRequired: false` line per policy object. Nothing that was accepted
before is rejected now.

Also documents the declaration in CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md, and teaches
`npm run new-spec` to emit it on a scaffold whose declared classes make the
task consequential.

title: feat(vta): mint the consent ceremony's correlator instead of deriving it (#1133)
body:
feat(vta): mint the consent ceremony's correlator instead of deriving it (#1133)

* feat(vta): mint the consent ceremony's correlator instead of deriving it

Framework 0.5.0, *Identifier correlation and linkability*: `id`, `threadId` and
`ceremony.enactment` MUST be freshly minted and unguessable, and MUST NOT be
derived from subject data.

The `task-consent/granted` notice threaded on `wire_digest` — a function of the
task payload, and the same string the document carries as `payloadDigest`.

The challenge is 256 bits of randomness, so the digest is not guessable from
the payload; this is not the "UUIDv5 over a subject identifier" case. The
mediator is the exposure. `threadId` is routing metadata, and the mediator also
forwards documents carrying `payloadDigest`; with the same value in both it can
tie the routing it performs to the digest it carries and link the refusal, the
approval pushes and the notice into one ceremony with named counterparties.

`PendingTaskConsent` gains a minted `correlator`, created alongside the
challenge. The notice threads on it and the body still carries `payloadDigest`
unchanged, so a requester matching on the digest is unaffected. The requester
is told the correlator in the `auth:consent_required` refusal beside the digest
it already receives.

Smaller than it first looked: the request push to approvers already threaded on
the request document's own id, so only the requester-facing notice was derived.
The notice is produced but never consumed in this workspace and is explicitly
non-load-bearing — the grant check at re-submit is the real gate.

Refs #1059

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* ci: stop caching `target/` in the MSRV job

The MSRV job cached `target/` keyed on `hashFiles('**/Cargo.lock')` with a
prefix `restore-keys` fallback. Every crate in this workspace is a path
dependency, so changing one member's source does not move `Cargo.lock` and
therefore does not move the key: a PR that edits `vta-policy` and nothing else
restores main's `target/` byte-for-byte, and `cargo check` reuses the stale
`vta-policy` artifact.

The build then fails on the new code with `no field `correlator` on type
`PendingTaskConsent``, naming a field that is right there in the source. That
is a false red that points at the author's own diff — it failed #1133 exactly
this way, on a commit a clean-room checkout compiled without complaint.

The registry and git caches stay: they are content-addressed by package
version, so a stale entry is impossible by construction. `cargo check` on a
warm registry is under two minutes, which is not worth a class of failure that
costs an afternoon to disbelieve.

title: feat(audit): bound the operator reason an audit row keeps
body:
Framework **0.5.0** requires every free-text member to carry a bound. Most of
that is upstream schema work — see the note at the end — but one free-text path
is this workspace's own and is bounded by nothing: the operator `reason` that
`record_with_detail` writes into the audit log.

## Why this one is worse than a wire bound

0.5.0 argues free text as unbounded **wire** cost. Here the cost is worse: the
row goes into a **hash-chained, append-only** log. An oversized `detail` is
permanent, and it cannot be trimmed later without breaking the chain that makes
the log evidence in the first place.

`vault.delete`, `vault.archive` and every other operator-reasoned action feed
this path. Nothing checked the length at any point between the CLI and the
chain.

## Truncated, not rejected

4096 characters — generous for a reason a human typed, small against the chain.

The choice of truncation over rejection is the substance. `record_with_detail`
runs **after** the operation it records has already happened, so refusing the
row would trade an over-long reason for **no audit record at all** — losing the
evidence to protect its formatting. Truncation keeps the row, the actor, the
action and the outcome, which is what the log is for.

The cut is marked (`… [truncated]`), because a silently shortened reason reads
as the operator's own words.

## Cut on a character boundary

Byte-slicing panics mid-codepoint, and it would do so on the first operator who
wrote a reason in a language this workspace did not anticipate. An audit path
is the worst place to discover that, so there is a test with a 4-byte-per-char
string.

## Note: the rest of the free-text rule is already in hand upstream

I measured the registry before writing this: **1013 of 1067 free-text string
members carry no `maxLength`.** That is not VTI's to fix, and it is already
being done —
[dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#296](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/296)
("bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength") is open across 275
files. Once it merges and publishes, the dispatch spine's `validate_payload`
enforces those bounds for free.

Worth stating for anyone sizing 0.5.0 readiness: **taking the latest
`trust-tasks-rs` today would not bound free text** — 0.14.0 predates #296.

Likewise
[#294](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/294) maps the
0.5.0 document lifecycle in the five binding crates. That does **not** reach
this workspace: VTI imports exactly one item from those crates
(`trust_tasks_https::status_for_code`), so a VTI-side lifecycle mapping remains
open and is not duplicated by it.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings`
- `./scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` — 28 suites, **0 violations**
- `cargo test -p vta-audit` — 6 passed
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

Refs #1059

title: spec(trust-task-ok): retire the registry entry, deprecated by framework 0.5.0
body:
> ## ✅ Cleared to merge — the gate this PR opened with is resolved
>
> It originally read *"do not merge until [trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#2](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec/pull/2) is merged"*, because this repo's `SPEC.md` was at framework `0.4` and contained no deprecation — retiring the registry entry first would have put the registry **ahead of the framework it conforms to**.
>
> **#297 removed that condition.** `SPEC.md` here is now at framework `0.5` and marks `trust-task-ok` deprecated in three places: §4.4.2, the §8.6 reserved-slug table (*"Deprecated at framework version 0.5"*), and §8.6 prose. The registry build validates against this copy, so the dependency is satisfied. spec#2 is the canonical repo's copy of the same text.
>
> Rebased onto `main` after #295, #297 and #294. The rebase conflicted in `SPEC.md` §8.6 — #297 rewrote the sections this PR edits. Resolved by keeping #297's canonical wording and carrying over only this PR's unique addition: the **Registry note** recording the retirement, marked *"not part of the canonical framework text; recorded in this copy because the registry serves it"*.

## Why

Framework `0.5.0` amends the request/response section so that a fire-and-forget specification's *consumer* **MAY** return that task's own `<type>#response` with `payload` exactly `{}` as a courtesy acknowledgement.

That removes the only reason `trust-task-ok` existed. The previous text forbade a response-less specification from emitting a `#response`, so "received and performed" needed a document of its own — and the document it got is defined so that it cannot carry meaning. Its own prose says the absence of one "carries no information", a *consumer* **MUST NOT** require any member, a *producer* **MUST NOT** rely on receiving one, and anything a *producer* actually needs "is using the wrong document". A registry entry, a schema, and a generated type in each supported language, on a `type` bearing no relation to the one the *producer* sent, to convey "something arrived".

`0.5.0` marks the slug **deprecated** and leaves retirement of the registry entry to the registry's own change process. This PR is that retirement.

In practice the mechanism that replaces it already shipped: `trust-tasks-https` 0.16.0 (#291) added `HttpsServer::on_ack`, which answers a fire-and-forget task with `204 No Content`.

## What changed

**`specs/trust-task-ok/0.1/spec.md`**

- `status: draft` → `status: retired` — SPEC §5.3 permitted transition 3 (`draft` → `retired`, abandoning a working draft). `retired` is terminal.
- `summary` now opens with "Retired." and names the replacement (still within the 280-character bound).
- New **Deprecation and retirement** section carrying the three normative consequences from framework 0.5.0 §8.6: a *consumer* **SHOULD NOT** emit one from 0.5.0 onward; a *producer* **MUST** continue to accept one for as long as the specification is served; and the slug and its *Type URI* remain **RESERVED permanently**.
- **Status of this Document** rewritten for retirement, stating that the schema and prose are frozen and that the entry continues to be served and generated.

**`SPEC.md`** — §6.1 reserved-slug table and §8.6, updated from the actual 0.5.0 text on `spec/framework-0.5-privacy-lifecycle-freshness` rather than paraphrased: the "**Deprecated at framework version 0.5.0**" table rows, the rewritten `trust-task-ok` paragraph, and the three-bullet consequences list. Anchors adapted to this copy's `§n.n` style.

The one deliberate addition beyond the canonical text is a **clearly marked registry note** recording that the entry is now retired. Canonical §8.6 says explicitly that retirement "is a matter for the registry, not for this document", so the note is fenced as *not part of the canonical framework text* to keep the sync rule in the SPEC.md preamble honest.

## `supersededBy`: deliberately absent

`supersededBy` is validated as retired-only (`build-registry.mjs` **fails** if it is set on a non-retired spec) and is **RECOMMENDED, not required** when retired — SPEC §7.3 item 11 and §5.3 both say **SHOULD**, and the build emits a warning rather than an error.

There is **no successor slug**. What replaces this document is a framework mechanism — the empty `#response` on the task's own *Type URI* — not another *Trust Task specification*. `supersededBy` resolves to a registry entry (it drives the bare-URL redirect and the website's successor link), so any value here would have to be invented, and an invented one would misdirect implementers. It is therefore omitted, and both the spec prose and the commit message say why.

The build reports this exactly as intended:

```
warn: trust-task-ok/0.1/spec.md: status is 'retired' but no supersededBy declared — SPEC §7.3 item 11 RECOMMENDS one
```

## The slug stays reserved

Retirement is a status, not a release of the name. Both hand-maintained allowlists are **untouched** and still contain `trust-task-ok`:

- `specs/spec.meta.schema.json` → `#/properties/slug/anyOf[1]/enum`
- `trust-tasks-rs/src/type_uri.rs` → `is_allowed_framework_slug()`

`SPEC.md` §6.1 and §8.6 both now say in terms that the slug remains reserved **permanently**.

## Bindings: no drift, no version bump

Regenerated both sides after the change:

```
$ cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all
Generated 344 payload modules into trust-tasks-rs/src/specs
Feature-gated 26 spec families (5 framework-reserved families are always compiled)

$ npm run build-ts-bindings
Generated 410 TS modules into trust-tasks-ts/src
```

The working tree afterwards showed **only `SPEC.md` and `specs/trust-task-ok/0.1/spec.md` modified.** Neither generator reads front-matter `status` — the Rust modules come from `payload.schema.json` via typify, and the TS modules from the same schema — so a status change is invisible to them. `trust-tasks-rs` and `@openvtc/trust-tasks` are therefore **not** bumped: there is nothing to republish.

This also confirms #283's decision empirically: `SKIP_SLUGS` is still just `["trust-task-error"]`, so `trust_task_ok::v0_1` is still emitted, still exported from `trust-tasks-ts/src/index.ts`, and still in `schema_index.rs`. A retired spec is still published and still generated.

## Verification

```
$ npm run validate
  Security & Privacy: 0/349 spec(s) carry the section and all four sub-headings; 349 allowlisted as pre-existing debt, 0 not allowlisted
  warn: trust-task-ok/0.1/spec.md: status is 'retired' but no supersededBy declared — SPEC §7.3 item 11 RECOMMENDS one
  Exposure floor: 0 spec(s) declare exposure.discloses: none while returning released material
  Error code casing: 602/650 extended code(s) are lowerCamelCase; 48 frozen in 15 retired spec(s) (§5.3 — exempt, not debt), 0 non-conforming
  Error code shadowing: 646/650 extended code(s) avoid the §8.3 standard vocabulary (14 code(s), derived from trust-task-error/0.5); 4 frozen in 4 retired spec(s) (§5.3 — exempt, not debt), 0 shadowing
  Standard error code casing: 1025 spec file(s) swept for §8.3 codes; 25 snake_case occurrence(s) frozen in 1 superseded/retired spec(s) (§5.2/§5.3 — exempt, not debt), 0 non-conforming
Validated 349 specs, indexed 65 shared schemas.

$ npm run build
… Validated 349 specs, indexed 65 shared schemas.
  wrote website/assets/tasks.generated.js
  wrote website/registry.json
  synced specs/ → website/specs/
  synced bindings/ → website/bindings/
  synced ceremonies/ → website/ceremonies/
  synced SPEC.md → website/SPEC.md
Done.

$ npm run check-bindings
Bindings conformance: 349 specifications checked against 349 TypeScript and 344 Rust modules — all agree.
```

**One expectation not met, reported rather than papered over.** The three "frozen in *N* retired spec(s)" counters did **not** move (15, 4 and 1, unchanged). They are not counts of retired specs — each counter only records a retired spec that *contributed an offending declaration* (`frozenSpecs.add(rel)` sits inside the offender branch in `error-code-casing.mjs` and in the shadowing lint). `trust-task-ok` declares `errorCodes: []`, so it has nothing to freeze and correctly does not appear in any of the three. The retirement is visible in the registry output and in the `supersededBy` warning instead.

No Rust source was touched (`cargo fmt --all` produced no diff over the committed tree), so the workspace build is unaffected.

## Reference sweep

Every mention of the slug in the repo, and what was done with it:

| Location | What it is | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `specs/trust-task-ok/0.1/spec.md` | the registry entry | **retired** (this PR) |
| `specs/trust-task-ok/0.1/payload.schema.json` | its payload schema | untouched — frozen at retirement |
| `SPEC.md` §6.1, §8.6 | framework copy | **updated** to the 0.5.0 wording |
| `specs/spec.meta.schema.json` | reserved-slug allowlist | **untouched — entry retained**, the slug stays reserved |
| `trust-tasks-rs/src/type_uri.rs` | second reserved-slug allowlist (`is_allowed_framework_slug`) | **untouched — entry retained** |
| `trust-tasks-codegen/src/main.rs` | `SKIP_SLUGS` is `["trust-task-error"]` only; a comment cites `trust-task-ok` as *not* the way to fill a missing response type | untouched — the module must keep being generated |
| `trust-tasks-rs/src/specs/trust_task_ok/v0_1.rs`, `schema_index.rs`, `trust-tasks-ts/src/trust-task-ok/0.1/payload.ts`, `trust-tasks-ts/src/index.ts` | generated bindings | untouched, regenerated identically |
| `trust-tasks-rs/src/payload.rs` | trait doc already says "framework 0.5.0 deprecates `trust-task-ok`" | already correct, no change needed |
| `specs/trust-task-discovery/0.1/spec.md` | names the slug when listing what §6.1 reserves | left as-is — the statement is about the **reservation**, which is unchanged and permanent |
| `.github/CODEOWNERS` | routes `/specs/trust-task-ok/` review | left — a retired spec still has an owner |
| `trust-tasks-rs/README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md` | list it among always-compiled framework families; historical entries | left — still accurate, and changelog history is not rewritten |
| `docs/adr/0001-…`, `docs/design-notes/trust-ceremonies.md`, `docs/design-notes/task-control-and-corrigibility.md` | dated design records describing the slug as "reserved, unspecified" | left — historical documents, correct as at their date |
| `CLAUDE.md` | says "`trust-task-ok` when it lands" in the reserved-slug callout | left — cosmetically stale (it landed), not worth a spec PR |
| `scripts/lib/security-privacy-allowlist.json` | lists `trust-task-ok/0.1` as pre-existing Security & Privacy debt | left — the concurrent Security & Privacy prose work owns that file |
| `website/` | no hand-maintained reference; the entry is generated into `tasks.generated.js` and `website/specs/` | **not removed from the website** — retirement is a status, not a deletion |

### One pre-existing inconsistency noticed, not fixed here

`is_allowed_framework_slug()` in `trust-tasks-rs/src/type_uri.rs` lists five slugs; `specs/spec.meta.schema.json` lists seven — the Rust copy is missing `trust-task-control` and `trust-ceremony-receipt`, and `is_reserved_namespace()` next to it checks only the `trust-task` half of SPEC §6.1's `^trust-(task|ceremony)($|-|/)`. Unrelated to this retirement and left alone; worth its own issue.

title: Trust Task Context Binding on published mechanisms, taskContext re-anchoring, and W3C proof/digest alignment
body:
Consolidated Working Draft 01 batch from the task force's working fork, superseding #15 by carrying it: the first commits are @bmiller59's #15 restructuring (authorship preserved), with three further changes built on top of it and the #15 first-pass review addressed. Closes #11. Resolves #17.

## What's inside, in order

**1. The #15 restructuring** (@bmiller59) — Trust Task Context Binding depends only on mechanisms already defined in the Trust Tasks core specification; the "qualifying specification" profile; outcome evidence travels with the presentation.

**2. `taskContext` re-anchoring and framework-0.4 alignment** — the outcome of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#173: `taskContext` carries the **`id` of the originating exchange's initiating document** (globally unique per the core specification's §4.3; the innermost exchange that attests the event, per §4.9.1), retiring the issuer-side uniqueness workaround. The qualifying profile is reworded against framework 0.4 (per-variant proof; the error variant honestly excluded — a task specification cannot strengthen `trust-task-error`'s own declaration; the no-`#response` escape hatch dropped). Outcome Interpretability cites the core specification's reply-disposition classification (§8.6) rather than hand-rolling the terminal/non-terminal split, and states the verifier's pairing checklist for retained evidence. A `trust-task-error` is failure evidence only, attributable to third parties when it carries `inResponseTo` (§8.2).

**3. W3C proof and digest alignment** (#17, all three items) — the VWC digest becomes `digestMultibase` (multibase multihash over the JCS canonical form the definition already named); multibase headers restricted to `z`/`u` per CID 1.0 §2.4 with alphabets enforced; proofs move from `Ed25519Signature2020` to the `DataIntegrityProof` envelope with `eddsa-jcs-2022` as the RECOMMENDED default suite (offline-verifiable; one canonicalization shared with `digestMultibase`) and `bbs-2023` named as the selective-disclosure path.

**4. The #15 first-pass review, addressed** — normative citations are commit-pinned permalinks (framework 0.4, `fbe196a`) so "pinned" is literally true; the stray subsection marking is removed; the per-issuer-uniqueness comment is mooted by the re-anchoring; and the term **"Trust Tasks core specification"** is now defined (`spec/terms-definitions/`), stating the core-vs-individual-specification architecture, explaining the upstream document's own "framework 0.4" version labels, and explicitly disclaiming the ToIP governance-framework sense.

## Evidence

The pairing checklist and the anchoring rule are executable: [`tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange`](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange) runs the witnessed exchange end-to-end — the VWC's `taskContext` lands on the ceremony's initiating document `id` structurally, and the retained `submit#response` passes exactly the checks the text states. The digest change is encoding-only for implementations already canonicalizing with JCS (verified against the Keyring witness implementation's own digest function).

Spec-Up-T render verified locally: every `[[ref:]]` resolves, no unresolved terms. Review history: Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#2, Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#3, Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#4.

title: spec: bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength (§7.3)
body:
Framework 0.5.0 §7.3 requires that any member holding free text declare a `maxLength`. This closes the schema half of that MUST across the registry.

## What the corpus actually held

The starting figure I was given was 68 unbounded free-text members. Re-measuring with a schema-aware walk rather than a regex — one that distinguishes a member *named* `description` from the JSON Schema `description` **keyword**, which is an annotation and must never be touched — the corpus held **114** unbounded string members under the eight free-text names, not 68:

| | count |
|---|---|
| in `payload.schema.json` of a **draft** spec | 70 |
| in a `_shared/**` schema component | 27 |
| in `payload.schema.json` of a **retired** spec | 17 |
| **total** | **114** |

The 68 figure is close to the draft-payload subset and misses the `_shared` tree entirely, which is where the highest-fan-out members live: one `AclEntry.label` is reached by seven specifications, one `KeyRecord.label` by four.

Two `detail` members matched by name are `type: "object"`, not strings (`audit` `AuditEnvelope.detail`, `task-consent` `Effect.detail`); they are correctly excluded. No schema `description` keyword was modified.

**92 members are bounded here. 22 are deliberately left alone** — see *Not touched* below.

## Bounds

Bounds are chosen per member and drawn from the vocabulary the registry already uses (`64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 4096, 16384`, plus the considered `500`), rather than one number applied everywhere.

| Class | Bound | Why this number |
|---|---|---|
| `label`, `comment` | **256** | A display name, not prose. Matches the existing `label: 256` on `provision/integration` and the `name: 256` members beside it. `comment` is an OpenSSH public-key comment (`user@host`) — an identifier line. |
| `reason` on a consent surface | **500** | Requester-authored prose that a surface renders to a human who is deciding something. This is exactly the class `task-consent/request/0.1` `note` sits in, and it is capped at 500 with the prose to explain why; the same reasoning gives the same number. A tighter bound here is a real property — an over-long string in an approval prompt is a way to obscure what is being approved. |
| `reason` elsewhere | **1024** | Operator- or service-authored rationale recorded for audit, or a refusal explanation returned to a caller. Matches the six existing `reason: 1024` in `vtc/*` written for exactly this purpose. |
| `description` | **1024** | A paragraph describing a record, template, community profile or capability manifest. Matches `policy/*` and `vtc/_shared/endorsement-type` `description: 1024`. |
| `message` | **1024** | An error, ack or status diagnostic for logs and operator UI. Bounds the §10.3 schema-validation-DoS surface without truncating a genuine diagnostic. |
| `text` | **16384** | The one member that is the task's *content* rather than metadata about it: a `chat/message` body. Sized against the corpus's long-form bound (`vault` `secureNotes: 16384`), not against the metadata ladder. |

The non-obvious ones, called out:

- **`trust-task-control` `effects[].description` → 1024, though it is a one-sentence effect statement.** Sized by class rather than by length so a control response and a `policy` description do not disagree on their ceiling.
- **`chat/message` `text` → 16384, 64× the next-largest bound.** Sizing it like a `reason` would cap a conversational message at a sentence, which is the member's whole purpose. It is the only member here where the free text *is* the payload.
- **`vault/_shared/*/vault-entry` `label`** carried the sentence *"Maintainers MAY enforce a maximum length; the wire spec does not."* The wire spec now does, so the annotation is corrected rather than left contradicting the schema it annotates.

## Not touched

| | count | why |
|---|---|---|
| members in `retired` specifications | 17 | SPEC §5.3 makes `retired` terminal and §6.4 freezes the schema at the moment of retirement. |
| `messaging/_shared/0.1` `AuditEntry.detail` | 1 | The only specification that reaches this `$def` is `messaging/admin/audit-log/0.1`, which is **retired**. Bounding it would change a frozen specification's effective wire contract through the back door of a shared component. |
| `did-management/_shared/0.1` `DomainEntry.label` | 1 | Same shape: reached by `domain/disable/0.1` and `domain/enable/0.1`, both retired, alongside six draft specs. §6.6 rule 3 means the component cannot move without moving them. |
| `vault/_shared/{0.1,0.2,0.3}` `TspMessageEnvelope.message` | 3 | A false positive on name. The value is base64url-encoded TSP message bytes — opaque binary, not free text. A length bound here would be a bound on ciphertext. |

All 92 amended members live in `status: draft` artifacts, so the change is made in place per SPEC §5.2 rather than minting new versions.

## The other two halves of the MUST

**"SHOULD be optional" — reported, not acted on.** Making a currently-required free-text member optional is a wire-compatibility change and belongs in its own PR with that as its subject. Thirteen of the bounded members are currently `required`:

| member | bound |
|---|---|
| `auth/step-up/approve-request/{0.1,0.2}` `/properties/reason` | 500 |
| `config/_shared/0.1` `RejectedKey.reason` | 1024 |
| `did-management/did/problem-report/0.1` `/properties/message` | 1024 |
| `trust-task-control/0.1` `Response.effects[].description` | 1024 |
| `vault/_shared/{0.1,0.2,0.3}` `VaultEntry.label` | 256 |
| `vault/upsert/{0.1,0.2,0.3}` `/properties/label` | 256 |
| `vtc/backup/import/0.1` `Response.message` | 1024 |
| `vtc/ceremonies/list/0.1` `CeremonyManifest.label` | 256 |

Not all of these should move — `CeremonyManifest.label` being required is what makes an operator UI renderable at all, and `approve-request.reason` being required is what stops a consent prompt from being blank. The SHOULD is rebuttable and each wants deciding on its own terms.

**"MUST state who reads it and whether it is retained" — prose, left for the Security & Privacy pass.** `npm run validate` reports 0/349 specs currently carry the section, all allowlisted as pre-existing debt. The bounded members touch **106 specification directories**, which is the priority subset for that pass. The list is in the review comment below.

## Also found, out of scope here

The eight names I was given are not the whole free-text surface. Sweeping for unbounded, unconstrained string members outside those names — no `enum`, no `pattern`, no `format` — turns up **68 more** across 51 files that are plainly free text: `name` (44), `purpose` (9), `deviceLabel` (8), `explanation` (3), `displayName` (2), `title`, `summary`. Notably `task-consent/request/0.1` `Effect.summary`, which the schema itself calls "the ONLY member a consent surface is guaranteed to be able to render", is unbounded. §7.3 covers those too; they want a follow-up on the same pattern.

## Version — breaking, and deliberately not bumped

Adding `maxLength` is **breaking** on both counts the versioning rules at the top of `trust-tasks-rs/CHANGELOG.md` name:

1. **API.** typify emits a free-text member with a `maxLength` as a validating newtype, so `Option<String>` becomes `Option<PayloadReason>` / `Option<AclEntryLabel>`. Reads through `Deref` survive; construction and assignment do not. Four in-repo call sites stopped compiling, which is the crate's only view of what a consumer sees.
2. **Behaviour against an unchanged wire format.** The newtype enforces its bound in `Deserialize`, so a document this library previously accepted is now rejected — the case the CHANGELOG calls out by name.

That means a leading-component bump on `trust-tasks-rs` and the six crates pinning it, released in `publish.yml`'s order. **I have not taken it.** Three specification PRs are in flight against the same registry and that cascade wants sequencing as one planned change rather than started from inside this one, so the migration is written up under `## [Unreleased]` in `trust-tasks-rs/CHANGELOG.md` and the number is left to whoever sequences the release. `@openvtc/trust-tasks` is unbumped for the same reason — its generated *types* are unchanged, since TypeScript has no length refinement, but its embedded schemas now reject over-long values at runtime.

**This PR should not merge to `main` before that decision is made**, because merging is what triggers `publish.yml`.

## Verification

```
npm run validate      Validated 349 specs, indexed 65 shared schemas.
                      533 example documents validated against the framework envelope schema
npm run build         Done.
npm run check-bindings  349 specifications checked against 349 TypeScript and 344 Rust
                        modules — all agree.
cargo build --workspace          Finished `dev` profile
cargo test --workspace --all-targets --all-features
                      40 test binaries, all `test result: ok` (0 failed)
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
                      Finished `dev` profile   (clean)
cargo fmt --all --check          clean
trust-tasks-ts: npm test         tests 76 / pass 76 / fail 0
```

Re-running both generators after committing produces an empty diff, so neither drift check will fire.

The `npm run validate` result is the load-bearing one: it re-checks every fenced example in all 349 `spec.md` files against the amended schemas. No bound rejects an example that exists in the corpus, which is the evidence that none of them is set too tight.

Commits are split so the schema change is reviewable on its own, with the regenerated tree behind it.

title: spec: bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength (§7.3) (#296)
body:
spec: bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength (§7.3) (#296)

* spec: bound every free-text payload member with a maxLength

SPEC.md §7.3 (framework 0.5.0) requires that any member holding free
text declare a `maxLength`. 92 free-text string members across 83 draft
schemas carried none, leaving the wire contract unbounded and every
consumer to invent its own ceiling — or none, which is what §10.3
(schema-validation DoS) exists to prevent.

Bounds are chosen per member from the vocabulary the registry already
uses rather than applied uniformly:

  256   `label`, `comment` — a display name or an OpenSSH key comment;
        matches the existing 256 on provision/integration `label` and
        the `name` members alongside it.
  500   requester-authored prose that a surface renders to a human who
        is deciding something; matches task-consent/request/0.1 `note`,
        the registry's considered consent-surface bound.
  1024  `reason`, `description`, `message` — operator or service prose
        recorded for audit or returned as a diagnostic; matches the six
        existing `reason: 1024` and the `description: 1024` in policy/
        and vtc/endorsement-type.
  16384 chat/message `text` — the task's actual content rather than
        metadata about it; matches the corpus's long-form bound on
        vault `secureNotes`.

All amended specifications are `status: draft`, so the change is made in
place per SPEC §5.2. Deliberately untouched:

  * 17 members in `retired` specifications, frozen by SPEC §6.4.
  * messaging/_shared/0.1 `AuditEntry.detail` and did-management/
    _shared/0.1 `DomainEntry.label` — shared $defs reachable from a
    retired specification, so bounding them would change a frozen
    specification's effective wire contract.
  * vault/_shared/{0.1,0.2,0.3} `TspMessageEnvelope.message` — opaque
    base64url TSP bytes, not free text.

The `label` description in vault/_shared/*/vault-entry.schema.json said
the wire spec enforced no maximum length. It now does, so the sentence
is corrected rather than left contradicting the schema it annotates.

`npm run validate` re-checks all 533 fenced example documents against
the amended schemas; none is rejected by a new bound.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore(bindings): regenerate for the free-text maxLength bounds

`cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` and
`npm run build-ts-bindings` over the bounded schemas.

The Rust side is a **breaking** regeneration and the diff shows why: a
free-text member that gains a `maxLength` is emitted by typify as a
validating newtype, so `Option<String>` becomes `Option<PayloadReason>`,
`Option<AclEntryLabel>` and so on, and the newtype enforces its bound in
`Deserialize`. Both halves are breaking under the rules at the top of
`trust-tasks-rs/CHANGELOG.md` — the API a consumer compiles against
moves, and a document the library previously accepted is now rejected.

**No version has been bumped.** Releasing this moves the leading
component of `trust-tasks-rs` and drags `-https`, `-didcomm`, `-proof`,
`-tsp`, `-capability-client` and `-didcomm-v1` with it, in
`publish.yml`'s order. That seven-crate cascade wants sequencing against
the other specification PRs in flight, not starting from inside this
one, so the migration is written up under `## [Unreleased]` and the
number is left for whoever sequences the release. `@openvtc/trust-tasks`
is unbumped for the same reason; its generated *types* are unchanged
(TypeScript has no length refinement) but its embedded schemas now
reject over-long values at runtime.

The four in-repo call sites that stopped compiling are migrated rather
than worked around — they are the crate's only view of what a consumer
sees, and they now demonstrate the newtype rather than hiding it:

  * trust-tasks/examples/acl_grant_roundtrip.rs
  * trust-tasks-https/examples/client_demo.rs
  * trust-tasks-didcomm/examples/local_roundtrip.rs
  * trust-tasks-rs/tests/generated_specs.rs

GETTING-STARTED.md carries the extracted copy of the first of those, and
`tests/getting_started_snippets.rs` fails when the two disagree, so the

title: feat(vta): bound the error `details` member
body:
Framework **0.5.0**, *Bounding `details`*. Continues #1130.

`details` was the one error-payload member with no size bound, and it travels in
the direction no producer-side bound reaches: a producer caps what it *sends*,
and nothing caps what comes back.

## This service had a live instance

A policy denial puts the Rego module's `explanation` on the wire:

```rust
details: Some(json!({ "explanation": why })),
```

`why` is authored by whoever wrote the policy. Nothing checked its length, so a
verbose — or hostile — policy put an arbitrary string into every denial that
module produced.

## The bound, and where it goes

4096 bytes of JCS or 16 immediate members, which is 0.5.0's default where a
specification declares none.

Applied in `reject_with`, the single funnel every rejection passes through,
rather than at the **thirty** `details: Some(...)` construction sites. A new
site cannot be added that skips it.

## An oversized `details` is ignored, never grounds to discard the `code`

Straight from the spec, and it is the part worth being deliberate about: the
`code` is what the receiving party actually needs. Dropping the whole rejection
because its annex was too long would turn a verbose policy into an unexplained
failure — strictly worse than the problem being fixed.

An *uncanonicalisable* `details` is also dropped: it cannot be measured, so it
does not go out.

## Tests

Three, covering the two halves of the bound and the case that must keep
working:

- oversized by bytes → dropped, `code` survives;
- too many members → dropped (sixteen short members are small by byte count,
  so this is not implied by the first);
- inside the bound → passes through untouched, so the bound cannot quietly
  become "nothing useful is ever returned".

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings`
- `./scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` — 28 suites, **0 violations**, coverage 62/109
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

Refs #1059

title: fix(rs): enforce both halves of the SPEC §6.1 slug reservation
body:
`trust-tasks-rs` 0.14.0 fails SPEC §6.1 in **both directions**, in the same pair of functions:

```
REJECTED  trust-task-control      a published registry spec whose Type URI will not parse
PARSES    trust-ceremony-evil     a slug §6.1 reserves for the framework, accepted from anyone
```

Reproduced against the published 0.14.0 crate, not just the working tree.

## Cause

`is_reserved_namespace()` checked only the `trust-task` half of `^trust-(task|ceremony)($|-|/)`. The `trust-ceremony` half is unused by published specs today and exists *precisely* so the ceremony layer has a namespace no other party can claim first — a check that omits it protects nothing.

Separately, `is_allowed_framework_slug()` listed **five** slugs where `specs/spec.meta.schema.json` lists **seven**, missing `trust-task-control` and `trust-ceremony-receipt`. So `trust-task-control/0.1` — published, with a spec, a schema and generated modules — had a Type URI this crate refused.

`trust-ceremony-receipt` escaped only by accident: the broken namespace check never classified it as reserved, so the allowlist was never consulted for it.

## The durable half

The allowlist is one of **two** hand-maintained copies; the registry build enforces the other. A new test reads `specs/spec.meta.schema.json` and fails naming the offending slug if they disagree. Verified by deleting `trust-task-control` again:

```
reserved_allowlist_matches_the_meta_schema ... FAILED
  trust-task-control is allowlisted by specs/spec.meta.schema.json but not by
  is_allowed_framework_slug — the two copies have drifted
```

It returns early when the registry is not vendored alongside the crate, so it does not break a published-crate build.

## Is this breaking?

No. A consumer relying on the accepting half — publishing under a `trust-ceremony-*` slug it does not own — was already non-conforming under §6.1. The rejecting half was a straightforward bug. **0.14.0 → 0.14.1**, no cascade.

## Verification

```
cargo test --workspace --all-targets    39 suites ok, 0 failed
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings   clean
cargo fmt --all --check                 clean
RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps --all-features   clean
```

Found while retiring `trust-task-ok` (#292) — that sweep noticed the two allowlists disagreed.

title: spec(bindings): map the framework 0.5.0 document lifecycle in all five current bindings
body:
Framework 0.5.0 adds a normative **Document Lifecycle** section — a single state table (`received → validated → accepted → {executing, suspended} → {responded, errored, cancelled, expired}`), each row naming the reserved reply that carries the transition and what silence in that state means. It closes with a rule that binds every transport binding:

> **A transport binding MUST map this table.** A transport binding **MUST** state, for its own protocol, which protocol event or status corresponds to each state above, or state explicitly that its protocol expresses no counterpart for a given state.

No binding did this. This PR adds the mapping to all five current bindings, one commit each.

Prose only — no schema, no front matter, no generated artifact touched. `git diff --stat` against `main` is five `spec.md` files, +136 lines, nothing else.

## The matrix

`document` means the state is observable, and observable **as a Trust Task document** in the binding's own carriage rather than as a transport event. Blank means the binding states explicitly that its protocol expresses no counterpart.

| State | `https/0.2` | `didcomm/0.2` | `didcomm-v1/0.2` | `tsp/0.1` | `push/0.1` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `received` | — | — | — | — | — |
| `validated` | — | — | — | — | — |
| `accepted` | — | — | — | — | — |
| `executing` | — | — | — | — | — |
| `suspended` | — | document | document | document | — |
| `responded` | `200` / `204` | document | document | document | — |
| `errored` | `400`/`403`/`409`/`422`/`500`/`503` + error body | document | document | document | — |
| `cancelled` | `422` `cancelled` | document | document | document | — |
| `expired` | `422` `expired` | document | document | document | — |

Three shapes fall out of it.

**HTTPS is synchronous and single-shot**, so the five non-terminal states are passed through inside one request and only a terminal state — or nothing — reaches the producer. Most of the terminal column was already written in §4's status table; what was missing was any statement of *which state each row reports*, which is precisely the gap the framework's rule names. `suspended` is blank here for a different reason from the rest: suspension is a separate `trust-task-control` POST, and the response to *that* request carries the transition, long after the original POST returned.

**The three asynchronous bindings agree exactly**, and that is the honest result rather than a copy-paste. One-way transports have no request/response pair to hang a state on, so only the four states with a reserved framework reply become observable — and each becomes observable as a document, never as a DIDComm decorator, an Aries `ack`, or a TSP hop.

**Push maps nothing at all.** It carries no Trust Task document and is never the transport a document arrives over; the document arrives when the consumer drains its mediator queue, and its lifecycle belongs to the DIDComm binding from that point. Explicit absence is a conforming answer under the rule, and here it is the only correct one.

## The confusions each binding now forecloses

The framework's rule exists because a transport fact gets read as a document state. Each binding names the ones reachable *in it*, rather than restating the framework's three examples:

- **`https/0.2`** — `202` is the framework's own worked example and this binding ships it. §4 gives `202` exactly one meaning: a **duplicate** whose *first* execution is still running. A first arrival is never answered `202`, so a `202` reports a state strictly **past** `accepted`, about a *different* request. Also: a closed connection is not `cancelled`; and `401`, a bodiless `500`, and a hung connection establish nothing.
- **`didcomm/0.2`** — a mediator's `messagepickup` acknowledgement or inbound `202` is the **mediator** speaking, and the mediator is not the consumer; a `problem-report` is about a message and carries no document state; the DIDComm `expires_time` header is a message lifetime, not the document's `expiresAt`.
- **`didcomm-v1/0.2`** — an RFC 0015 `ack` elicited by `~please_ack` is emitted by the agent framework, often before a handler has seen the attachment, and §2 already makes acknowledgement requests a decorator the consumer ignores. Plus the v1-specific one: an unaware peer — including a `0.1` consumer meeting a `0.2` `@type` — drops the message **silently**, which is indistinguishable from every non-terminal state.
- **`tsp/0.1`** — an intermediary accepting or forwarding a routed message is a transport actor that never opens the document (§5.2); in **nested** mode it provably cannot, since the envelope is sealed to the final recipient. And §6's fire-and-forget case means a terminal state can be correctly reached *and* correctly reported and still never observed.
- **`push/0.1`** — an APNs/FCM delivery receipt reports a doorbell reaching a device while the document is still sealed in a queue; a woken device connecting and draining is below the document layer; a push failure or dead token leaves the queued document deliverable (§4 item 4); an allowlist refusal goes to the trigger with no document involved.

## One state that is genuinely unmappable, and worth a reviewer's eye

`errored` over `tsp/0.1` is the only row where a binding both *has* a mapping and needs a caveat attached to it. §6 already says response and error delivery are best-effort where no return relationship exists. The lifecycle consequence: a document can reach `errored`, the consumer can emit the correct `trust-task-error/0.2`, and the producer can still hear nothing — a terminal state correctly reached, correctly reported, and unobservable. The same holds for `responded`, `cancelled` and `expired` on that binding. §4.1 states it rather than letting the mapping imply a delivery guarantee §6 does not make.

## Bindings not amended, and why

`https/0.1`, `didcomm/0.1`, `didcomm-v1/0.1` are **left alone**. All three are `status: draft`, so §5.3's retirement freeze does **not** apply and §5.2's in-place errata rule would permit amending them. The decision is deliberate rather than forced:

1. Each is superseded in place by a `0.2` of the same slug published in this repo, whose §7.1 / §2.3 records the migration. The `0.1` text exists to keep already-issued documents readable, not to be built against.
2. Each targets a framework version that predates the lifecycle table (`0.2`, `0.2`, `0.3`). Mapping it would mean citing a section its target framework does not contain.

The current five will re-target `0.5.0`; the superseded three never will, so a mapping added to them would document a rule that is never going to bind them. If a reviewer would rather have the mapping everywhere for uniformity, it is a small follow-up — say so and I will add it.

## Two things left for a follow-up, deliberately

- **`targetFrameworkVersion` is unchanged** on all five (`0.2`/`0.3`/`0.4`/`0.2`/`0.2`). Bumping it to `0.5.0` while this repo's `SPEC.md` is still at `0.4` would create a dangling reference. This PR adds the content so that the re-target, when the framework lands here, is a front-matter bump against no gap.
- **The `SPEC.md` anchor is a prediction.** Each mapping links `[SPEC §4.12 *Document Lifecycle*](.../SPEC.md#412-document-lifecycle)`, assuming the section lands after §4.11 (`The ceremony member`) and before §5, which is where it sits in the canonical repo. If it is numbered differently when `SPEC.md` is updated, five links need the number corrected — the section is named in full in the link text so it stays readable either way. Binding links are not link-checked by the build (only `specs/**` is), so nothing will catch this automatically.

## Placement

Each mapping is a **subsection of the binding's existing status/error mapping section** — `§4.1` in four bindings, `§7.1` in push — rather than a new top-level section. A new `##` would renumber every section after it and break the internal `[§5.1](#51-...)`-style anchors that these files use heavily. It also puts the mapping directly against the status table it interprets, which for `https/0.2` is where it does the most work.

## Verification

Baseline was captured before any edit and matched after each commit:

```
$ npm run validate
  validated 533 example documents against the framework envelope schema
Validated 349 specs, indexed 65 shared schemas.

$ npm run build
Validated 349 specs, indexed 65 shared schemas.
  wrote website/assets/tasks.generated.js
  wrote website/registry.json
  synced bindings/ → website/bindings/
Done.

$ npm run check-bindings
Bindings conformance: 349 specifications checked against 349 TypeScript and 344 Rust modules — all agree.
```

Unchanged from baseline in every count, warnings included. The `website/assets/bindings.js` cross-check is undisturbed: it matches on binding `id` and `prosePath` and never reads section structure, so adding a subsection cannot affect it. `check-bindings` walks `specs/**` only, and confirms the generated Rust and TypeScript libraries still agree with their specifications — no drift, as expected for a prose-only change.

title: spec(bindings): map the framework 0.5.0 document lifecycle in all five current bindings (#294)
body:
spec(bindings): map the framework 0.5.0 document lifecycle in all five current bindings (#294)

* bindings/https/0.2: map the framework document lifecycle

Framework 0.5.0 adds a normative Document Lifecycle table and makes
mapping it a MUST for every transport binding (SPEC 9.1): each state
must name the protocol event or status that carries it, or be declared
to have no counterpart.

Adds 4.1, hung off the existing status table because most of the
mapping was already written there without saying which state each row
reports. The gaps it fills are the synchronous ones: received,
validated, accepted, executing and suspended have no counterpart over a
single-shot request, and saying so is the conforming answer rather than
inventing a status for each.

Three substitutions are named explicitly, because this binding ships
the status the framework uses as its own worked example: 202 is a
statement about an earlier request's duplicate and reports a state past
accepted, never the acceptance of the request answered; a closed
connection terminates a delivery and is not semantic cancellation; and
an absent response - including 401 and a bodiless 500 - establishes no
state at all.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* bindings/didcomm/0.2: map the framework document lifecycle

Framework 0.5.0 adds a normative Document Lifecycle table and makes
mapping it a MUST for every transport binding (SPEC 9.1): each state
must name the protocol event or status that carries it, or be declared
to have no counterpart.

Adds 4.1. DIDComm is one-way and store-and-forward, so there is no
transport-level reply to map anything onto: every state that becomes
observable does so as a Trust Task document in a fresh envelope of 2's
type, correlated per 3.1, and only the four states carrying a reserved
framework reply become observable at all. received, validated, accepted
and executing have no counterpart.

Names the substitutions this transport invites: a mediator's
messagepickup acknowledgement or inbound 202 is the mediator speaking,
not the consumer, so it is neither received nor executing; a dropped
WebSocket is not cancellation; a DIDComm problem-report is about a
message and cannot carry a document state; and the DIDComm expires_time
header is a message lifetime, not the document's expiresAt.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* bindings/didcomm-v1/0.2: map the framework document lifecycle

Framework 0.5.0 adds a normative Document Lifecycle table and makes
mapping it a MUST for every transport binding (SPEC 9.1): each state
must name the protocol event or status that carries it, or be declared
to have no counterpart.

Adds 4.1. Same shape as the v2.1 binding - one-way and mediated, so
only the four states with a reserved framework reply become observable,
and each becomes observable as a document in this binding's own
carriage. received, validated, accepted and executing have no
counterpart.

Three of the named substitutions are v1-specific. An RFC 0015 ack,
elicited by ~please_ack, is emitted by the agent framework about a
message and often before a handler sees the attachment - 2 already
makes acknowledgement requests a decorator the consumer ignores, so it
establishes neither received nor accepted. A silently dropped message,
including a 0.1 consumer meeting a 0.2 @type, is indistinguishable from
every non-terminal state, which is why 2.2 negotiates before sending.
And ~timing expires_time is a message lifetime, not the document's
expiresAt.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* bindings/tsp/0.1: map the framework document lifecycle

Framework 0.5.0 adds a normative Document Lifecycle table and makes
mapping it a MUST for every transport binding (SPEC 9.1): each state
must name the protocol event or status that carries it, or be declared
to have no counterpart.

Adds 4.1. One-way substrate, so only the four states with a reserved
framework reply become observable, and each becomes observable as a
document packed per 2 and delivered per 6. received, validated,
accepted and executing have no counterpart.

Routing gives this binding two cases the others do not have. An
intermediary accepting or forwarding a routed message is a transport
actor that never opens the document (5.2), so a successful hop is not
received - in nested mode it provably cannot be, since intermediaries
cannot open the envelope. And 6's fire-and-forget case means a terminal
state can be correctly reached and correctly reported and still never
observed: with no return relationship the reply is undeliverable, so
the resulting silence must not be read as any state, success included.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* bindings/push/0.1: map the framework document lifecycle

Framework 0.5.0 adds a normative Document Lifecycle table and makes
mapping it a MUST for every transport binding (SPEC 9.1): each state
must name the protocol event or status that carries it, or state
explicitly that the protocol expresses no counterpart.

Adds 7.1, and the whole column is 'no counterpart'. That follows
directly from 2 and 5: a push carries no Trust Task document and is
never the transport a document arrives over. The document arrives when
the consumer drains its mediator queue, and its lifecycle belongs to
the DIDComm binding from that moment.

Stating the whole column is the point, because each candidate mapping
is wrong in a way worth naming: an APNs/FCM delivery receipt reports a
doorbell reaching a device while the document is still sealed in a
queue; a woken device connecting and draining is transport activity
below the document; a push failure or dead token is a gateway concern
that leaves the queued document deliverable, per 4 item 4; and an
allowlist refusal goes to the trigger with no document involved.

Also separates the one lifecycle this binding does have from the one it
does not: push/* and device/set-wake are Trust Task documents with
ordinary lifecycles, expressed by whichever binding carries them, not
by the push channel they cause.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: spec: bring framework 0.5.0 into the registry (SPEC.md + specs/_framework/0.5)
body:
Brings framework **0.5.0** into the registry, so specifications can target it. Two files: `specs/_framework/0.5/trust-task.schema.json` and `SPEC.md`.

## This is a port, not new drafting

Every normative sentence here is taken **verbatim** from `spec/*.md` at commit `ced9a3a` ("docs(spec): release framework version 0.5.0") of [trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec), PR #2 — approved, awaiting merge. Nothing was paraphrased and no MUST/SHOULD was reworded.

The two documents are structured differently, so the port is mechanical in two respects and only two:

* the canonical source is Spec-Up-T with **no manual numbering** — headings and slug anchors only — while `SPEC.md` is hand-numbered (`### 4.11 The ceremony member`, `#411-the-ceremony-member`). Every ported heading was renumbered and re-anchored into `SPEC.md`'s scheme, and every cross-reference rewritten to the `[§x.y](#xy-…)` form used here.
* `[[ref: term]]` term references were converted to the plain-italic convention `SPEC.md` already uses (`*Trust Task document*`). No `[[ref: …]]` survives; the `[[RFC3339]]`/`[[RFC8785]]` reference tokens used are the ones §13 already defines.

Out of scope, deliberately: the canonical spec's three-part `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` framework versioning (introduced there at 0.4.0 and never ported here) and its ToIP Governance / Internationalization / Accessibility boilerplate. Neither is part of the 0.4 → 0.5 delta, and `specs/spec.meta.schema.json` already accepts both the two- and three-part forms.

## No specification is re-targeted here

0.5 becomes **available**. Moving any specification onto it is an ordinary version bump of that specification, sequenced as in §5.4, and is a separate decision that belongs to the coordinator. Every one of the 349 published specifications still declares its existing target and validates against its existing envelope.

## The envelope really is unchanged

Verified against the source rather than assumed. The canonical 0.5.0 changelog states it outright — *"The document wire format gains no member and loses none; every document conforming to 0.4.0 still conforms"* — and a structural comparison confirms it: `specs/_framework/0.5/trust-task.schema.json` is byte-identical to 0.4's once `$id`, `title`, `description` and two `description` annotations are set aside.

0.5.0's changes land outside the envelope: consumer requirements (the §4.12 lifecycle table; freshness bounds on the existing `issuedAt`/`expiresAt`), specification requirements (`retention`, `exposure.ingests`, `parties[].identifierScope`, `maxLength` on free text), and prose.

A version with no member change still needs its own schema, and the schema's own description says why: §7.2 item 1 selects the envelope by the specification's **declared target version**, so a targetable version must exist on disk. Without `specs/_framework/0.5/`, `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.5"` compiles no validator and the build reports the spec's example documents as *NOT validated*.

Two `description` annotations — on `issuedAt` and `expiresAt` — gained pointers to §7.2 item 13 and §7.3 item 17. **No constraint changed**: item 13's bounds are relative to the consumer's clock and to a sibling member, so tightening them here would make a conforming 0.4 document invalid against 0.5.

### No `framework.schema.json` at 0.5

Deliberate, and it follows the 0.4 precedent exactly. The reusable `$defs` (`Ext`, `DigestMultibase`) were last published at 0.3; `_framework/0.4` publishes no copy, and 0.4-targeting specs `$ref` back two versions. 0.5.0 changes neither `$def`, so minting a third `$id` for identical definitions would give one contract two names, invite drift between them, and — because §6.6 requires a spec to pin a shared component by version — split the corpus across two pins for no gain. Specs targeting 0.5 keep `$ref`-ing the 0.3 file, as 0.4's do.

## Anchor diff — no existing link broke

`SPEC.md` is linked to **783 times** from `specs/` and `bindings/`, across **40 distinct anchors**, and the build's link check verifies only that `/SPEC.md` *exists* — a broken fragment would fail silently here and on the live site. So every heading and its GitHub-computed anchor was extracted before and after and diffed:

```
98 anchors before  →  106 after

> #442-acknowledging-a-fire-and-forget-task   4.4.2 Acknowledging a fire-and-forget task
> #412-document-lifecycle                     4.12 Document lifecycle
> #821-what-a-message-may-not-say             8.2.1 What a `message` may not say
> #822-bounding-details                       8.2.2 Bounding `details`
> #831-effects-reported-with-cancelled        8.3.1 Effects reported with `cancelled`
> #105-identifier-correlation-and-linkability 10.5 Identifier correlation and linkability
> #116-authenticity-of-a-discovery-response   11.6 Authenticity of a discovery response
> #05                                         0.5   (Appendix B changelog entry)
```

**Purely additive: 8 anchors added, 0 changed, 0 removed.** All 40 distinct anchors linked from `specs/` and `bindings/` still resolve, and every internal `(#…)` link inside `SPEC.md` resolves to a heading that exists.

That held because every addition appends or inserts at the end of its parent, never in the middle:

| New | Placed | Why there |
|---|---|---|
| §4.4.2 | after §4.4.1, before §4.5 | — |
| §4.12 | after §4.11.4, before `## 5.` | — |
| §7.2 item 13 | after item 12 | end of the list |
| §7.3 items 17, 18, 19 | after item 16 | end of the list |
| §8.2.1, §8.2.2 | after §8.2's example, before §8.3 | — |
| §8.3.1 | after §8.3's table, before §8.4 | — |
| §10.5 | after §10.4 | — |
| §11.6 | **after** §11.5 | "Authenticity" reads better before "Privacy considerations", but inserting it as 11.5 would renumber the existing §11.5 and break every link to `#115-privacy-considerations`. Appended instead. |
| Appendix B `0.5` | above `0.4` | changelog is newest-first |

In-place amendments that add no heading: §4.2's `issuedAt` row, §4.4.1 (the three-dispositions table), §4.9.3 (the `taskDigest`/`stepDigest` table), §7.2's stopping/duplicate prose, §7.3 items 5 and 14, §8.2's `message` and `details` rows, §8.6, §10's preamble, §10.4, §11.1.

## What 0.5.0 adds

* **§4.12 Document lifecycle.** One normative state table — `received`, `validated`, `accepted`, `executing`, `suspended`, `responded`, `errored`, `cancelled`, `expired` — replacing five overlapping lifecycles implementations had been inferring from one document, with the reserved reply that carries each transition. **Silence signifies no state**: the absence of a reply distinguishes no two states, and a producer MUST NOT infer any state from it. A transport binding MUST map the table onto its own protocol, so a `202` is not silently read as acceptance.
* **§10.5 Identifier correlation and linkability** (normative). The framework had said nothing about what its own identifiers disclose about the parties, and a registry census settles that this is not hypothetical: 346 of 349 specs declare both `issuer` and `recipient` REQUIRED and 210 declare `proof` REQUIRED. Four rules: pairwise identifiers by default; `id`/`threadId`/`ceremony.enactment` freshly minted, unguessable, never derived from subject data or a counter; `issuedAt` MAY be coarsened; `enactmentPrivacy: blinded` rather than relying on a receipt not being handed out.
* **Freshness** (§7.2 item 13, §7.3 item 17). Item 11's duplicate-execution record is implementable only inside a bounded window. A consumer MUST now reject a future-dated `issuedAt` and an `expiresAt` at or before its `issuedAt` — both `malformedRequest`, not `expired`, because `expired` names a document that was once acceptable.
* **Three new front-matter declarations** (§7.3 items 5, 14, 18): `retention`, `exposure.ingests`, `parties[].identifierScope` — each descriptive not prescriptive, each fail-safe when absent.
* **§7.3 item 19** — every free-text member MUST declare a `maxLength`.
* **§4.4.2 + §8.6** — a fire-and-forget consumer MAY return `<type>#response` with `payload` exactly `{}`; `trust-task-ok` is deprecated in its favour, and its slug stays RESERVED permanently.
* **§8.2.1, §8.2.2, §8.3.1** — the error model states what a `message` may not say (now normative for every code), bounds `details` (4096 bytes of JCS / 16 members by default), and gives `cancelled` a framework-defined `effects` array.
* **§11.6 + §11.1** — discovery hardening: the applicable `proof` requirement rises to RECOMMENDED, a discoverer MUST NOT act on a response it cannot authenticate, and a responder's advertised requirements are untrusted input.
* **§4.9.3** — `taskDigest` vs `stepDigest` named side by side. Clarification only; no computation changes.

## Still owed by this repository

Recorded in the Appendix B entry, not done here — both are other people's files:

* `retention`, `exposure.ingests` and `parties[].identifierScope` need support in `specs/spec.meta.schema.json` before a specification can declare them. Until then they are declarable in prose only.
* Retiring the `trust-task-ok` registry entry follows §5.3 and is the registry's own change process. This PR states the framework's position; it does not retire anything.

## Verification

```
npm run validate    → Validated 349 specs, indexed 66 shared schemas.       exit 0
                      validated 533 example documents against the framework envelope schema
npm run build       → Done.                                                 exit 0
npm run check-bindings
                    → Bindings conformance: 349 specifications checked
                      against 349 TypeScript and 344 Rust modules — all agree.  exit 0
```

The new schema compiles as JSON Schema 2020-12 and accepts a minimal 0.4-shaped document.

**No generated-library drift.** `_framework` is skipped by both generators — verified, not assumed: `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` and `npm run build-ts-bindings` were run before and after adding `specs/_framework/0.5/`, and both leave the tree clean (344 Rust and 410 TS modules, unchanged). The Rust codegen triggers only on `payload.schema.json`; the TS generator emits a `_framework` type only when a spec `$ref`s it, and nothing targets 0.5 yet.

title: spec: bring framework 0.5.0 into the registry (SPEC.md + specs/_framework/0.5) (#297)
body:
spec: bring framework 0.5.0 into the registry (SPEC.md + specs/_framework/0.5) (#297)

* spec: publish the framework 0.5 envelope schema

Adds specs/_framework/0.5/trust-task.schema.json so that a Trust Task
specification can declare targetFrameworkVersion: "0.5". Without it the
registry build has no envelope to compile for that target, and every
example document under a 0.5-targeting spec goes unvalidated.

Framework 0.5.0 adds no envelope member: its changes are consumer
requirements, specification requirements and prose. The schema is
therefore 0.4's carried forward with a new $id, and every document
conforming to 0.4 conforms to 0.5. Two description annotations gained
pointers to the new freshness bounds of SPEC §7.2 item 13 and §7.3
item 17; no constraint changed, which is what keeps a 0.4 document
valid against 0.5.

A version with no member change still needs its own schema because
§7.2 item 1 selects the schema by the specification's declared target
version, so a targetable version must exist on disk.

No framework.schema.json is published at 0.5: the reusable $defs (Ext,
DigestMultibase) were last published at 0.3, 0.5.0 changes neither, and
0.4 set the precedent of referring back rather than minting a duplicate
$id for identical definitions.

This publishes 0.5; it re-targets no specification.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec: port framework 0.5.0 §4 changes into SPEC.md

Ports the §4 half of the canonical 0.5.0 release (trustoverip/
dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec, PR #2, ced9a3a) into this copy, renumbered and
re-anchored into SPEC.md's hand-numbered scheme and with [[ref: …]]
term references converted to the plain-italic convention used here.

* §4.12 Document lifecycle (new, appended after §4.11.4). One normative
  state table naming the nine states the rest of the document already
  presupposed in five places, the reserved reply that carries each
  transition, and the settled reading of silence: the absence of a reply
  distinguishes no two states, and a producer MUST NOT infer any state
  from it. A transport binding MUST map the table onto its own protocol.
* §4.4.2 Acknowledging a fire-and-forget task (new, appended after
  §4.4.1). A fire-and-forget consumer MAY now return <type>#response
  with payload exactly {}; a producer still MUST NOT rely on it. This
  replaces §4.4.1's former MUST NOT-emit-a-#response rule and is what
  deprecates trust-task-ok.
* §4.4.1 gains the table of the three response dispositions — success
  #response, failure trust-task-error, continuation
  trust-task-next-step — so that "is this document a response?" is
  answered in one place rather than three.
* §4.9.3 gains the taskDigest/stepDigest table. Clarification only:
  neither is a document member and no computation changes.
* §4.2's issuedAt row points at the new freshness bounds.

Append-and-insert-at-end only: no pre-existing section number or anchor
changes. Two anchors are added, #442-acknowledging-a-fire-and-forget-task
and #412-document-lifecycle.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec: port framework 0.5.0 §7 changes into SPEC.md

* §7.2 item 13 (new, appended). A consumer MUST reject with
  malformedRequest a document whose issuedAt is in its own future beyond
  its skew tolerance, and one whose expiresAt is at or before its
  issuedAt. Both are malformed rather than expired, because expired
  names a document that was once acceptable and neither of these ever
  was. The accompanying prose says why: item 11's duplicate-execution
  record is implementable only inside a bounded window, and a document
  with no expiresAt and no usable issuedAt never leaves the set a
  consumer must recognize.
* §7.3 item 17 (new). A specification defining a consequential Trust
  Task MUST require issuedAt — the producer-side half of item 13, put on
  the party that can satisfy it for nothing.
* §7.3 item 18 (new). A retention class — transient / exchange /
  durable plus a rationale — giving the framework the retention
  vocabulary it has never had. Absent or unresolvable reads as durable.
* §7.3 item 19 (new). Every free-text payload member MUST declare a
  maxLength, SHOULD be OPTIONAL, and the specification MUST state who
  reads the value, whether it is retained, and whether it is trusted.
* §7.3 item 5 gains parties[].identifierScope, and item 14 gains
  exposure.ingests. Both are descriptive, not prescriptive, on the same
  terms as items 13 and 14, and both fail safe when absent.
* §7.2's stopping-and-duplicate prose now defers to §4.12 for what
  silence means, and records that a fire-and-forget duplicate may be
  answered with the §4.4.2 acknowledgement.

The three new front-matter declarations are declarable in prose only
until specs/spec.meta.schema.json supports them; that file is out of
scope for this PR.

Appended at the end of each list. No pre-existing section number,
list-item number, or anchor changes.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec: port framework 0.5.0 §8 changes into SPEC.md

* §8.2.1 What a `message` may not say (new). The message-sanitization
  rule was normative for identityMismatch alone and a SHOULD in an
  informative section for everything else — yet every rejection is
  emitted on the same path, to the same possibly-unauthenticated party,
  generally before any authorization decision has been reached. It is
  now normative for every code: consumer-internal state, the contested
  value of a mismatched party, and resolver/verifier/key-status
  internals MUST NOT appear.
* §8.2.2 Bounding `details` (new). details was the one error-payload
  member with no size bound, travelling in the direction no
  producer-side bound reaches. A specification defining a details shape
  MUST declare a bound; absent one, 4096 bytes of JCS or 16 immediate
  members apply. An oversized details is ignored, never grounds to
  discard the code.
* §8.3.1 Effects reported with `cancelled` (new). A framework-defined
  details shape for cancelled — the same array-of-effects
  trust-task-control already defines for a producer-requested stop.
  effects: [] means nothing landed; an absent effects means the consumer
  did not report, and MUST NOT be read as "nothing landed".
* §8.6 records the deprecation of trust-task-ok in favour of the §4.4.2
  empty #response. A consumer SHOULD NOT emit one from this version, a
  producer MUST continue to accept one for as long as the specification
  is served, and the slug stays RESERVED permanently. Retirement of the
  registry entry is the registry's own decision and is not effected
  here.
* §8.2's message and details rows, and §10.4, point at the new
  subsections.

Appended and inserted at the end of their parents. No pre-existing
section number or anchor changes; three anchors are added.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec: port framework 0.5.0 §10 and §11 changes into SPEC.md

* §10.5 Identifier correlation and linkability (new, appended after
  §10.4, and normative). The framework had said nothing about what its
  own identifiers disclose about the parties, and a census of the
  registry settles that this is not hypothetical: 346 of 349 published
  specifications declare both issuer and recipient REQUIRED, and 210
  declare proof REQUIRED, so the median document is a signed, retainable
  record naming both parties in clear. Four rules: issuer and recipient
  SHOULD be pairwise; id, threadId and ceremony.enactment MUST be
  freshly minted, unguessable, and never derived from subject data, an
  account number, a session identifier or a counter; issuedAt MAY be
  coarsened; and a ceremony whose participation must not be linkable
  declares enactmentPrivacy: blinded rather than relying on a receipt
  not being handed out.

  §10's preamble becomes non-normative *except where a subsection states
  otherwise*, which is what lets §10.5 be normative inside it.

* §11.6 Authenticity of a discovery response (new, appended after
  §11.5). The discovery specification rests its OPTIONAL proof
  requirement on the parties having authenticated through the transport;
  the HTTPS binding's own security profile says it provides no such
  guarantee, and §9.1.1 already refuses to let a guarantee be read off a
  transport's name. The applicable proof requirement rises to
  RECOMMENDED, a discoverer MUST NOT act on a response whose origin it
  can authenticate neither in-band nor from the transport, and a
  responder's advertised requirements are untrusted input that MUST NOT
  cause a producer to attach data it would not otherwise have sent.

  Appended as §11.6 rather than inserted before §11.5 Privacy
  considerations, so that no existing anchor moves.

* §11.1 records that a discovery request's patterns list SHOULD be
  bounded — matching work paid by the party that did not choose it.

No pre-existing section number or anchor changes; two anchors added.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec: mark SPEC.md as framework 0.5 and add the Appendix B entry

Bumps the document version header 0.4 -> 0.5 and the date to 2026-08-26,
matching the canonical 0.5.0 release (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec
ced9a3a), and ports that release's changelog entry as Appendix B `0.5`.

The entry records what this repository still owes: retention,
exposure.ingests and parties[].identifierScope need support in
specs/spec.meta.schema.json before a specification can declare them, and
retiring the trust-task-ok registry entry follows §5.3 and is the
registry's own decision. It also records that publishing
specs/_framework/0.5/ makes 0.5 an available target framework version
and re-targets no specification.

Appended above the `0.4` entry; the changelog reads newest-first, so no
existing entry moves and the added anchor is #05.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>
