title: feat(rs)!: generated types are #[non_exhaustive] with builders, and a request/response pairing (#287)
body:
feat(rs)!: generated types are #[non_exhaustive] with builders, and a request/response pairing (#287)

* feat(rs, codegen)!: non_exhaustive + builders on generated types, and RequestPayload

The largest consumer in the ecosystem — `vta-sdk` in
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure — bypasses these generated types
entirely in favour of 172 hand-maintained URI string constants and
`serde_json::Value`. The root cause is structural: the generated structs are
plain, public-field, builderless and exhaustive, so *every additive spec
change is a source break*. This CHANGELOG has recorded the tax repeatedly —
"consumers constructing `AclEntry` with a struct literal must add
`step_up: None`", "source-breaking for Rust consumers (the wire is
unchanged)". A minimal `acl/grant` request needed a struct literal spelling
thirteen members carrying no information: twelve `None`s and an empty `vec![]`.

This takes the break once so that no future additive spec change is one.

`trust-tasks-codegen` now runs typify with `with_struct_builder(true)` and
post-processes the emitted syn AST to mark every named-field struct and every
enum `#[non_exhaustive]`. Tuple/newtype wrappers (`Ext`, `ExtKey`) are
deliberately excluded: typify emits no builder for them, so the attribute
would remove the only construction path a consumer has and leave nothing in
its place. Their shape is fixed by the scalar or map they wrap, so there is no
additive change for it to absorb.

The builder is typify's, not ours. Construction becomes

    let entry: grant::AclEntry = grant::AclEntry::builder()
        .subject("did:web:alice.example")
        .role("admin")
        .try_into()?;

and a missing required member is a `Result`, not a panic. typify already emits
`impl Default` for a struct whose members are all optional (149 of them), so
`Default` needed no extra derive.

`ext` was left as `Option<Ext>`. Mapping it to `#[serde(default)] ext: Ext`
was considered and rejected: `Ext` carries `minProperties: 1`, so an empty
`Ext` would serialise as `{}` where the member is today simply absent. That
changes the wire, which an ergonomics release does not get to do — and the
builder removes the need anyway, since an unset `ext` is never spelled.

`RequestPayload` is added alongside `Payload`, pairing a request payload with
its response type (SPEC §4.4.1), and `HttpsClient::send` drops its second type
parameter to use it — `send::<grant::Payload, revoke::Response>(req)` used to
compile and fail against a live server. It is a separate trait rather than an
associated type on `Payload` because associated type defaults are still
unstable on stable Rust (rust-lang/rust#29661): a required `type Response`
would break every hand-written `Payload` impl, this crate's own hand-modelled
`trust-task-error` payload included.

A specification defining no `$defs.Response` gets no `RequestPayload` impl.
Neither stand-in was worth taking: `()` is not a `Payload` and would let
`send()` compile for an exchange that returns no document, and
`trust_task_ok::v0_1::Payload` is being retired by framework 0.5.0 in favour
of a specification declaring an empty `#response` of its own. When a spec
adopts that, the codegen sees the `$defs.Response` and emits the impl with no
change here.

`HttpsServer::on` keeps both type parameters for now. Constraining it is the
same win on the server side, but it also decides whether a server may register
a handler for a response-less specification, which is a separate question from
this one.

The break is a workspace event, so each dependent takes its own leading bump
and moves its requirement to `"0.14"`:

    trust-tasks-rs                 0.13.4 -> 0.14.0
    trust-tasks-https              0.14.1 -> 0.15.0
    trust-tasks-didcomm            0.14.0 -> 0.15.0
    trust-tasks-didcomm-v1         0.13.0 -> 0.14.0
    trust-tasks-proof              0.12.1 -> 0.13.0
    trust-tasks-tsp                0.13.0 -> 0.14.0
    trust-tasks-capability-client  0.13.0 -> 0.14.0

`@openvtc/trust-tasks` is unchanged: nothing here touches the TS bindings.

Call sites fixed in the binding crates and in `trust-tasks-rs`' integration
tests (separate crates, so they see what a consumer sees):
`trust-tasks-https/{tests/end_to_end.rs, examples/client_demo.rs,
examples/server_demo.rs}`, `trust-tasks-didcomm/examples/local_roundtrip.rs`,
`trust-tasks-didcomm-v1/src/pack.rs`, and
`trust-tasks-rs/tests/{audience_binding,generated_specs,replay_guard}.rs`.
The signing the demos gained in #284 is preserved. One `match` needed a
wildcard arm — `uri_of` over `discovery::ResponseSupportedTypesItem` — which
is the enum half of the trade doing exactly what it is there for.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore(rs): regenerate specs/ under the new codegen settings

`cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` — 344 modules.
Mechanical: each generated named-field struct and enum gains
`#[non_exhaustive]`, each struct gains `X::builder()` and a `builder`
module, and each request payload with a `$defs.Response` gains
`impl RequestPayload`.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* docs(changelog): the binding crates do not track trust-tasks-rs's MAJOR.MINOR

Four CHANGELOG headers claimed they did. It has not been true since the
0.7.0 alignment drifted apart — `trust-tasks-https` was 0.14.1 against
`trust-tasks-rs` 0.13.4 before this release — and this release makes it
plainly false, since each dependent takes its own leading bump. Say what
actually happens instead, so a reviewer approving a breaking release is not
reading a rule the version numbers contradict.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: feat(ts-bindings): hoist cross-file $defs into one generated module — 481 `Ext` declarations become 1
body:
## Before / after

| | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| `Ext` declarations | **481**, across 341 modules, as `Ext` / `Ext1` / `Ext2` / `Ext3` | **1** |
| top-level type declarations in `src/` | 2,646 | 1,510 |
| counter-suffixed declarations (`NameN` beside `Name`) | 206, in **133** files | 6, in **3** files |
| generated lines | 128,839 | 118,145 (−8.3%); **207 files shrank** |
| exported names removed | — | 200, **every one ending in a digit** |

`Ext` is the framework's extension object (SPEC §4.5.1). The generator emitted a
fresh copy of every `$ref`'d definition into each module that reached it, and
numbered the copies when two collided inside one file — so which of `Ext`,
`Ext1` or `Ext2` a consumer got depended on declaration order inside a generated
file, and there was no name you could write a signature over.

Every cross-file `$ref` is now rewritten to json-schema-to-typescript's `tsType`
escape hatch naming a type declared once in `src/_shared/components.ts`. Each
module imports it and **re-exports it under the name it used before**.

## Migration

Mechanical: drop the digit, same import path.

| before | after |
|---|---|
| `Ext1`, `Ext2`, `Ext3` | `Ext` |
| `Vid1`, `Vid2` | `Vid` |
| `DigestMultibase1` | `DigestMultibase` |
| `SecretKind1` | `SecretKind` |
| `AclEntry1`, `AccountType1`, `MediatorAcl1`, `QueueLimits1`, `KeyCustody1`, `KeyType1`, `KeyStatus1`, `SignAlgorithm1`, `WakeTriggerPolicy1`, `Namespace1`, `Version1`, `Version2`, `CredentialId1`, `ConsentSubject1`, `PersonhoodGovernance1` | the same name without the digit |

Nothing else moves. **Every unsuffixed name a module exported before it still
exports now** — verified by diffing the exported surface of all 411 modules
against `origin/main`; the 200 names that disappear all end in a digit.

The replacement is type-safe: the suffixed and unsuffixed forms were
structurally identical and TypeScript already treated them as mutually
assignable, so no value changes type.

`@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.14.2 → **0.15.0**. No Rust crate version is touched —
a sibling PR is running the seven-crate cascade and the two must not collide.
That deliberately breaks the CLAUDE.md "keep the two libraries in step"
convention for one release; the change is breaking on this side only.

## Grouping is by structure, not by name

#283 declined the Rust hoist for a reason that does not carry over — in Rust
`upsert::v0_3::VaultEntry` and `delete::v0_1::VaultEntry` are distinct *nominal*
types, so merging them is an E0119 coherence break for any consumer with a trait
impl on each. TypeScript is structurally typed and has no coherence rule, and I
checked that nothing generated here is branded, uses a `unique symbol`, or
relies on declaration merging — the three constructs that would make declaration
*identity* observable. So the merge changes names and nothing else.

**#283's other finding does carry over, and I confirmed it holds in TypeScript
too.** Of 113 distinct definition names reached by a cross-file `$ref`
(155 `file#def` components in all), **22 denote more than one shape**:

- `VaultEntry` — **three** shapes (`vault/_shared/0.1`, `0.2`, `0.3`)
- `PolicyDecision`, `PolicyInput` — three each (`policy/_shared/0.1`–`0.3`)
- `Scope` — two *unrelated* ones: `consent/_shared/0.1` and `vta/_shared/0.1`
- `Effect` — `consent` vs `task-consent`
- plus `SiteTarget`, `SecretKind`, `AttachmentRef`, `SealedEnvelope`,
  `TspMessageEnvelope`, `HpkeArmoredEnvelope`, `DidcommAuthcryptEnvelope`,
  `StepUpProof`, `ConsumerKind`, `Capability`, `DeviceAttestation`,
  `DeviceBinding`, `SyncEvent`, `PolicyChangedEvent`, `AclChangedEvent`,
  `VaultUpsertedEvent`, `VaultDeletedEvent`

Grouping is therefore by **fully-resolved schema**, not by name: each component
is expanded through every `$ref` (cross-file and internal), key-ordered, and
compared. A name covering more than one group is emitted once per group under a
family/version-qualified identifier — `VaultEntry_VaultV0_1`,
`VaultEntry_VaultV0_2`, `VaultEntry_VaultV0_3`, `Scope_ConsentV0_1`,
`Scope_VtaV0_1`. **Every** shape is qualified, including the oldest: leaving one
bare would imply there is a canonical `VaultEntry`, and there isn't.

Spec modules are unaffected by the qualification — `vault/get/0.3/payload.js`
still exports `VaultEntry`, bound to `VaultEntry_VaultV0_3`.

## Also fixed: the shared modules published nothing

`src/**/_shared/**.ts` and `src/_framework/**.ts` are generated from schemas
whose root declares no `type` and no `properties`. The compiler emitted a lone
`[k: string]: unknown` interface and dropped every `$def` as unreachable — so
`VaultEntryShared_v0_1.VaultEntry` in the barrel named nothing at all, while the
generator's own header comment claimed "a consumer wanting one canonical
`VaultEntry` can import it directly". Each now re-exports the definitions it
owns.

## `StandardCode`: keeping the closed union, deliberately

`StandardCode` stays `(typeof STANDARD_CODES)[number]`. Widening to
`StandardCode | (string & {})` was considered and rejected: it makes every
`StandardCode`-typed position accept any string, so a misspelled
`"proofRequred"` would compile everywhere the union is used — including
`RejectReason.code`, which decides what error document the runtime emits. That
cost is paid on every line of every consumer, forever, to soften a break that
arrives at most once per framework minor and arrives *as a compile error naming
the exact sites*.

The asymmetry with Rust is now written down in both places the next person will
look — a long doc comment on the type itself, and a standing note in
`CHANGELOG.md`:

> `trust-tasks-rs`'s `StandardCode` is `#[non_exhaustive]` (since 0.7.0), so a
> new SPEC §8.3 code is **additive** there and **breaking** here. Budget a
> **minor** bump on `@openvtc/trust-tasks` and a **patch** on the crate.

with the supported narrowing pattern (`isStandardCode` + a `default` arm)
documented as the way to be immune to it.

## New in this release

`src/_shared/components.ts`, exported from the barrel as `SharedComponents`:

```ts
import { SharedComponents } from "@openvtc/trust-tasks";
const namespaces = (ext: SharedComponents.Ext) => Object.keys(ext);
```

Plus `trust-tasks-ts/CHANGELOG.md` (the package had none) and
`test/shared-components.test.ts`, which asserts the invariant no existing check
could see: `tsc --noEmit` is happy with 481 identical `Ext`s, `bindings-drift`
compares the generator to itself, and `check-bindings` reads only the policy
constants and the response half.

## What I did not do

- **The 6 remaining counter-suffixed declarations.** `provision/integration`
  0.1/0.2/0.3 `$ref` their *own* `$defs.DidTemplateRef` from three sites with a
  different `description` at each, and the compiler emits a copy per
  description. That duplication is inside one schema rather than across files,
  so cross-file hoisting does not reach it. The new test names those three files
  explicitly so a fourth has to be looked at rather than absorbed.
- **59 `$defs` in shared schemas that no payload reaches** (most of
  `vault-secret.schema.json` and `session-blob.schema.json`) are not hoisted, so
  their modules still publish nothing. They are not duplicated anywhere either,
  so this is a gap rather than a defect; hoisting them could also force a rename
  on a *live* name if a dead one turned out to share it.
- **Anything outside `trust-tasks-ts/` and `scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs`** —
  no Rust crate, no `Cargo.toml`, no `specs/`, no `scripts/build-registry.mjs`.

## Checks

```
$ npm run build-ts-bindings && git status --porcelain trust-tasks-ts/src | wc -l
Generated 410 TS modules into trust-tasks-ts/src
       0                                    # bindings-drift clean; output is deterministic

$ npx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit         # (the repo has no lint script; this is the lint job)
                                            # clean

$ npm test
ℹ tests 76   ℹ pass 76   ℹ fail 0

$ npm run smoke
dist root import OK — 452 exports, pipeline reachable

$ npm run check-bindings
Bindings conformance: 349 specifications checked against 349 TypeScript
and 344 Rust modules — all agree.
```

title: test(vtc): expect the HTTPS binding's flat 422 for refused documents
body:
`main`'s `Test` job still fails after #1124, on two different tests:

```
rest_submit_rejects_a_foreign_recipient   join_requests.rs:400   left: 422  right: 403
rest_submit_rejects_an_expired_document   join_requests.rs:418   left: 422  right: 400
```

**These were already broken, not newly broken.** `cargo test --workspace` aborts at the first failing test binary; the `vta-sdk` webvh tests that #1124 fixed were failing ahead of these, so this binary never ran. Fixing webvh let the run reach the next failure — which is the argument for keeping `main` green: a red baseline hides whatever is behind it.

## Cause

`trust-tasks-https` aligned `status_for_code` to the binding spec's §4 status table, which maps `wrongRecipient`, `expired`, `proofRequired`, `proofInvalid`, `unsupportedType`/`unsupportedVersion`, `identityMismatch`, `cancelled` and `taskFailed` all to **422**. VTI picked that up in #1121's upgrade to `trust-tasks-https` 0.12. Both assertions here encoded the pre-alignment 403/400.

The library is right and the tests were stale. The flat bucket is deliberate: a finer split lets an unauthenticated prober distinguish `wrongRecipient` from `expired` from `proofInvalid` by status line alone, which is exactly the identity oracle the table closes. Both `vtc-service` and `vta-service` route their error responses through `status_for_code` (`helpers.rs:152` and `:188`), so adopting that helper means adopting the property.

The error **codes** in the response bodies are unchanged and still asserted — only the status line moved.

## Verification

`cargo test -p vtc-service --test join_requests` — **50 passed, 0 failed**.

I also swept both services' test suites for other assertions pairing a refused-document code with 403/400; these two were the only ones.

title: fix(specs): close two error-code declaration defects — §8.5 shadowing and the undeclared keys/* codes
body:
Two error-code declaration defects in the registry, both surfaced by earlier PRs that deliberately reported rather than fixed them, plus the lint that closes the first class for good.

## Defect 1 — extended codes that shadow a §8.3 standard code (a SPEC §8.5 **MUST** violation)

SPEC §8.5 closes its namespacing paragraph with: *"Extended codes **MUST NOT** shadow any code listed in §8.3."* **95 declarations across 93 specs** did exactly that:

| local part | count |
|---|---|
| `permissionDenied` | 90 |
| `expired` | 2 — `credential-exchange/pending/approve/0.1`, `task-consent/request/0.1` |
| `idConflict` | 2 — `vta/contexts/create/1.0`, `vta/webvh/servers/register/1.0` |
| `identityMismatch` | 1 — `vtc/backup/import/0.1` |

The namespaced duplicate is worse than nothing. A consumer switching on the standard `permissionDenied` never matches `audit/verify:permissionDenied`, and §8.5's fallback rule then tells it to degrade the unrecognized extended code to `taskFailed` — a strictly worse signal than the standard code being duplicated. So **the fix is deletion, not re-casing**: the standard code exists framework-wide and needs no declaration, and re-spelling the local part leaves the shadow under a tidier name. This is the same correction `vta/app-state:permissionDenied` already received in trust-tasks-rs 0.11.3, applied to the rest of the corpus.

**91 declarations across 89 `draft` specs are removed.** 24 of those specs are left with `errorCodes: []`, which the meta-schema permits (no `minItems`) and which 43 specs already declared. Eight prose sites that named the namespaced form now name the standard code and cite §8.3.

**The remaining 4 are in `retired` specs and are deliberately left alone** — `vtc/join-requests/approve/0.1`, `vtc/join-requests/reject/0.1`, `vtc/relationships/graph/0.1`, `vtc/relationships/list/0.1`. §5.3 freezes a retired spec at retirement, `retired` is terminal so there is no conforming version increment in which to correct one, and those specs exist to keep already-issued documents verifiable. The new lint counts them as exempt rather than as debt.

**Nothing consumed the namespaced form.** Re-verified across both SDKs: the only `<something>:permissionDenied` string literals anywhere are three unit-test assertions on the family-namespace *helper* (`trust-tasks-rs/src/payload.rs:279`, `:316`, `trust-tasks-ts/test/codes.test.ts:109`), all asserting `acl:permissionDenied` — a family namespace the helper under test builds, not a declaration read from any spec. The only other hit in the repo is the trust-tasks-rs CHANGELOG entry recording the 0.11.3 precedent.

### Closing the class

`checkErrorCodeNamespaces()` validated *where* an extended code may be rooted but never asked whether the local part was a name §8.3 had already taken — the other half of the same paragraph, and a MUST. That condition is added as a **hard failure**, on the same reasoning the two casing lints record: the corpus is at zero live offenders, so a failure costs nothing today and is the only thing that stops the drift returning.

The §8.3 vocabulary is **derived from the newest `trust-task-error` payload schema's `code` enum**, not hard-coded. That schema is the definition — a document carrying a code the declared version doesn't list will not validate — so it is the only copy that cannot rot, and a hard-coded list would fail *quietly*: adding a `trust-task-error/0.6` code would not break the lint, it would just stop catching one shadow. The derivation refuses to fail open: if no version yields an enum, the build fails saying so rather than checking nothing.

Verified by re-injecting `audit/verify:permissionDenied` into the cleaned tree — the build exits 1, names `audit/verify/0.1/spec.md`, and says to delete the declaration rather than re-case it.

## Defect 2 — the `keys/*` specs name codes that cannot exist on the wire (a §8.5 namespacing defect)

**Seven** specs declared `errorCodes: []` while their prose named codes as though declared — four distinct ones, in **normative** sentences ("Refuse with `not_found` where no record carries `keyId`"; "Failures (`permissionDenied`, `not_found`) use `trust-task-error`").

None is in §8.3, none was declared, and none could ever reach the wire: `trust-task-error`'s `code` member accepts a §8.3 standard value or a namespaced extended code, so a bare `not_found` fails payload validation. Seven specs told a conforming consumer to emit an error it could not emit.

Re-casing alone would not fix it — `notFound` is just as undeclared and unvalidatable as `not_found` — so declaration and §4.10 rule 4 re-casing land together:

| code | declared on |
|---|---|
| `keys:notFound` | `rename`, `revoke` |
| `keys:alreadyExists` | `create`, `import`, `rename` |
| `keys:invalidArgument` | `create`, `import`, `sign`, `derive-and-sign`, `derive-and-sign-document` |
| `keys/sign:failedPrecondition` | `sign` |

The first three take the `keys` **family namespace**, which §8.5 rule 2 permits for a code whose meaning is defined once for the whole family in a shared convention the family's specs reference. That convention is the new `specs/keys/_shared/0.1/CONVENTIONS.md`, on the `did-management/_shared/0.1/CONVENTIONS.md` model; each declaration's `meaning` links to it. The family form is also what makes the codes usable — a consumer recognises all three from the document's `type` alone.

`failed_precondition` does **not** get one: only `keys/sign` can reach it, and §8.5 rule 2 says a family namespace is "never to give a specification-specific code a broader name than it has earned".

### Two deliberate choices, both against the tidier-looking option

**`already_exists` is not folded into the standard `idConflict`.** §8.3 defines `idConflict` over the *Trust Task document's own* `id` — a document whose `id` matches one already accepted but whose content differs — and it exists to keep that case distinguishable from a retry (§7.2 item 11, §8.4). A `keyId` collision is a *domain*-identifier collision inside a well-formed, never-before-seen document; answering it with `idConflict` would send the producer to inspect its envelope instead of choosing a different key identifier.

**`not_found` becomes a family code, not anything standard.** §8.3 has no equivalent. `malformedRequest` — the nearest neighbour for `invalid_argument` — reports schema failure, whereas these payloads validate and fail on semantics the schema cannot express. Neither is promoted to §8.3: that vocabulary is the `code` enum in `trust-task-error`'s payload schema, so adding to it means minting a new version of that spec, which is out of scope here.

`keys/list/0.1` and `keys/show/0.1` were checked and need nothing — the only code either names is the standard `permissionDenied`, declared nowhere by design. Both keep `errorCodes: []`.

## Status handling

Every amended spec is `status: draft`, confirmed per file, where §5.2 requires the correction in place, errata-style, with no new version. The four `retired` specs listed above are excluded.

## Bindings

**No drift.** Neither `trust-tasks-codegen` nor `scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs` nor `scripts/check-bindings-conformance.mjs` reads `errorCodes` at all (zero references), and the generated `keys/*` modules carry no error-code surface. Nothing under `trust-tasks-*`, no `Cargo.toml` and no `CHANGELOG.md` is touched by this PR — any regeneration and version cascade is deliberately left to the sibling PR that owns those trees.

## Verification

```
$ npm run validate     # exit 0
  Error code casing: 602/650 extended code(s) are lowerCamelCase; 48 frozen in 15 retired spec(s) (§5.3 — exempt, not debt), 0 non-conforming
  Error code shadowing: 646/650 extended code(s) avoid the §8.3 standard vocabulary (14 code(s), derived from trust-task-error/0.5); 4 frozen in 4 retired spec(s) (§5.3 — exempt, not debt), 0 shadowing
  Standard error code casing: 1025 spec file(s) swept for §8.3 codes; 25 snake_case occurrence(s) frozen in 1 superseded/retired spec(s) (§5.2/§5.3 — exempt, not debt), 0 non-conforming
Validated 349 specs, indexed 65 shared schemas.

$ npm run build        # exit 0, Done.
$ npm run check-bindings  # exit 0
Bindings conformance: 349 specifications checked against 349 TypeScript and 344 Rust modules — all agree.
```

The declared-code total moves 730 → 639 (defect 1 removes 91) → 650 (defect 2 adds 11).

title: fix(specs): close two error-code declaration defects — §8.5 shadowing and the undeclared keys/* codes (#286)
body:
fix(specs): close two error-code declaration defects — §8.5 shadowing and the undeclared keys/* codes (#286)

* fix(specs): drop extended error codes that shadow a §8.3 standard code

SPEC §8.5 closes its namespacing paragraph with a MUST: "Extended codes
MUST NOT shadow any code listed in §8.3." 95 declarations across 93
specs did exactly that — 90 `permissionDenied`, 2 `expired`,
2 `idConflict`, 1 `identityMismatch` — each one a namespaced duplicate
of a name the framework had already taken.

The duplicate is not a harmless synonym. A consumer switching on the
standard `permissionDenied` never matches `audit/verify:permissionDenied`,
and §8.5's fallback rule tells it to degrade an unrecognized extended
code to `taskFailed` — a strictly worse signal than the standard code
being duplicated. The registry was therefore publishing, 95 times over,
a declaration that could only make a conforming consumer behave worse
than if it had never been declared.

So the fix is deletion, not re-casing: the standard code already exists
framework-wide and needs no declaration, and re-spelling the local part
would leave the shadow in place under a tidier name. This is the same
correction `vta/app-state:permissionDenied` received in trust-tasks-rs
0.11.3, applied to the rest of the corpus.

91 declarations across 89 draft specs are removed. 24 of those specs are
left with `errorCodes: []`, which the meta-schema permits and 43 specs
already declared before this change. Eight prose sites that named the
namespaced form now name the standard code and cite §8.3.

The remaining 4 declarations sit in 4 `retired` specs
(`vtc/join-requests/approve`, `vtc/join-requests/reject`,
`vtc/relationships/graph`, `vtc/relationships/list`) and are deliberately
left alone: §5.3 freezes a retired specification at the moment of
retirement, `retired` is terminal so there is no conforming version
increment in which to correct one, and those specs exist to keep
already-issued documents verifiable. The lint added in the next commit
counts them as exempt rather than as debt.

Nothing consumed the namespaced form. Across both SDKs the only
`<something>:permissionDenied` string literals are three unit-test
assertions on the family-namespace helper (`trust-tasks-rs/src/payload.rs`
:279 and :316, `trust-tasks-ts/test/codes.test.ts:109`), all of which
assert `acl:permissionDenied` — a family namespace built by the helper
under test, not a declaration read from any spec. Neither generator nor
`check-bindings-conformance.mjs` reads `errorCodes` at all, so the
generated bindings are unaffected.

No spec version is minted: every amended spec is `status: draft`, where
§5.2 requires the correction in place, errata-style.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore(scripts): fail the build on an extended code that shadows §8.3

`checkErrorCodeNamespaces()` validated where an extended code may be
rooted — the emitting slug or a family prefix of it — but never asked
whether the local part after the colon was a name §8.3 had already
taken. That is the other half of the same SPEC §8.5 paragraph, and it
is a MUST; nothing enforced it, which is how 95 shadowing declarations
accumulated across 93 specs.

The condition is added alongside the namespace check, as a hard failure
rather than a warning, on the same reasoning the two casing lints
record: the previous commit took the corpus to zero live offenders, so
a failure costs nothing today and is the only thing that stops the
drift returning.

The §8.3 vocabulary is derived from the newest `trust-task-error`
payload schema's `code` enum, not typed into this file. That schema is
the definition — a document carrying a code the declared version does
not list will not validate — so it is the only copy that cannot be
wrong, and a hard-coded list here would become a fourth hand-maintained
taxonomy of the kind the CLAUDE.md callouts exist to warn about. It
would also fail quietly: adding a `trust-task-error/0.6` code would not
break the lint, it would just stop catching one shadow. The derivation
refuses to fail open — if no published version yields an enum, the
build fails saying so rather than silently checking nothing.

`retired` specs are exempt, for the reason §5.3 gives and the casing
lints already encode: a retired spec is frozen at retirement to keep
already-issued documents verifiable, and `retired` is terminal, so
there is no conforming version increment in which to correct one. The
exemption is counted and printed on every build rather than hidden, so
a number that ever grows says something has re-published a frozen
artifact.

Reports as a third summary line beside the existing two:

  Error code shadowing: 635/639 extended code(s) avoid the §8.3
  standard vocabulary (14 code(s), derived from trust-task-error/0.5);
  4 frozen in 4 retired spec(s) (§5.3 — exempt, not debt), 0 shadowing

Verified by re-injecting `audit/verify:permissionDenied` into a clean
tree: the build exits 1, names `audit/verify/0.1/spec.md`, and says to
delete the declaration rather than re-case it.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* fix(specs): declare the keys/* error codes the prose already names

Seven `keys/*` specs declared `errorCodes: []` while their prose named
codes as though they had been declared — four distinct ones,
`already_exists`, `invalid_argument`, `not_found` and
`failed_precondition`, in sentences that are normative ("Refuse with
`not_found` where no record carries `keyId`"; "Failures
(`permissionDenied`, `not_found`) use `trust-task-error`").

None is in §8.3. None was declared. And none could ever have reached the
wire: `trust-task-error`'s `code` member accepts a §8.3 standard value or
a namespaced extended code, so a bare `not_found` fails payload
validation. Seven specs therefore instructed a conforming consumer to
emit an error it could not emit, and told a producer to expect a code no
document could carry.

Re-casing alone would not have fixed this — `notFound` is just as
undeclared and just as unvalidatable as `not_found` — so declaration and
lowerCamelCase re-casing (§4.10 rule 4) land together:

  keys:notFound          rename, revoke
  keys:alreadyExists     create, import, rename
  keys:invalidArgument   create, import, sign, derive-and-sign,
                         derive-and-sign-document

Those three take the `keys` **family namespace**, which §8.5 rule 2
permits for a code whose meaning is defined once for the whole family in
a shared convention the family's specs reference. That convention is the
new `specs/keys/_shared/0.1/CONVENTIONS.md`, on the
`did-management/_shared/0.1/CONVENTIONS.md` model, and each declaration's
`meaning` links to it. The family form is also what makes the codes
usable: a consumer recognises all three from the document's `type` alone,
without enumerating the specs that emit them.

`failed_precondition` does not get one. Only `keys/sign` can reach it, and
§8.5 rule 2 says a family namespace is "never to give a
specification-specific code a broader name than it has earned" — so it is
declared as `keys/sign:failedPrecondition`, under its own slug.

Two deliberate choices, both against the tidier-looking option:

`already_exists` is **not** folded into the standard `idConflict`. §8.3
defines `idConflict` over the Trust Task document's own `id` — a document
whose `id` matches one already accepted but whose content differs — and
it exists to keep that case distinguishable from a retry (§7.2 item 11,
§8.4). A `keyId` collision is a domain-identifier collision inside a
well-formed, never-before-seen document. Answering it with `idConflict`
would send the producer to inspect its envelope instead of choosing a
different key identifier.

`not_found` becomes a family code rather than anything standard, because
§8.3 has no equivalent, and `malformedRequest` — the nearest neighbour
for `invalid_argument` — reports schema failure, whereas these payloads
validate and fail on semantics the schema cannot express. Neither is
promoted to §8.3: the standard vocabulary is the `code` enum in
`trust-task-error`'s payload schema, so adding to it means minting a new
version of that spec, which is out of scope here.

`keys/list` and `keys/show` are checked and need nothing: the only code
either names is the standard `permissionDenied`, which is declared
nowhere by design, so both keep `errorCodes: []`.

All seven amended specs are `status: draft`, where §5.2 requires the
correction in place with no new version. Neither generator nor
`check-bindings-conformance.mjs` reads `errorCodes`, and the generated
`keys/*` modules carry no error-code surface at all, so the bindings do
not drift.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: feat(vta)!: adopt ReplayGuard and FreshnessPolicy, deleting the hand-rolled pair (#1126)
body:
feat(vta)!: adopt ReplayGuard and FreshnessPolicy, deleting the hand-rolled pair (#1126)

The last of the three stopgaps #1121 unblocked. Deletes trust_tasks/replay.rs
and the hand-rolled freshness bounds from #1117.

They land together because ConsumeChecks bundles them in one argument: SPEC
§7.2 makes the acceptance window and the replay record's retention the same
bound, and splitting them is how a deployment ends up with a ten-minute record
against an unbounded window believing it has a replay defence. This service had
exactly that.

The retired module keyed on (actor, id) and kept no digest, which cost two
things. It never produced idConflict — item 11 requires a different document
under an accepted id to be rejected, and with no digest that case was silently
absorbed as a retry, the one outcome §7.2 and §8.4 both rule out. And the key
was wrong: §7.2 fixes it as the document id alone, so actor-scoping let two
callers each spend the same id. A duplicate is also no longer answered with
taskFailed, which §7.2 forbids outright.

A failed outcome releases the claim, mirroring the idempotency layer beside it;
a successful one records its response so a retry is answered with the result.
The Err arm fails closed with a retryable unavailable, and the non_exhaustive
ReplayVerdict gets an arm that refuses rather than executes.

No acceptance window yet, and that was measured rather than assumed:
with_max_age(10 minutes) scoped to consequential tasks failed 41 assertions
across 10 suites with expired, because the suite is full of documents stamped
hours or days in the past. Fixing those alters what the service accepts and
belongs in a change whose subject is the window.

BREAKING CHANGE: a duplicate Trust Task document is answered with the prior
response (or 202 while the first execution is in flight) instead of a taskFailed
rejection. A different document under an already-accepted id is now rejected
with idConflict instead of being absorbed as a retry. The duplicate-execution
record keys on the document id alone, no longer scoped by caller.

Refs #1059

title: ci: watch every generated file in trust-tasks-rs, not just src/specs
body:
The `codegen-drift` job diffed only `trust-tasks-rs/src/specs`. The generator also owns:

- `trust-tasks-rs/src/schema_index.rs` — generated, and unwatched even before the recent feature work
- `trust-tasks-rs/Cargo.toml`'s `[features]` block — one feature per spec family, generated between TOML markers since #283

Neither was covered, so **a family added without its feature would have shipped a spec no consumer could enable**, with the drift gate green. #283's author flagged this rather than widening the path from inside their own PR, which was the right call — it belongs in a change whose subject is the gate.

`CLAUDE.md` documents three separate incidents of a hand-maintained list drifting from the tree (the category taxonomy, the reserved-slug allowlist, the binding registry), each of which shipped a real defect. This closes the fourth before it happens.

## Why widening is safe

`cargo fmt --all` runs immediately before the diff, and the hand-written sources are formatted (`cargo fmt --all --check` is its own green job), so they cannot drift here. Anything this diff reports was written by the generator.

## Verified both directions

```
$ cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all
Generated 344 payload modules
Feature-gated 26 spec families (5 framework-reserved families are always compiled)
$ git diff --stat trust-tasks-rs      # widened path, clean tree
                                       # (empty)

$ # inject a hand-edited feature the generator would not emit
$ git diff --quiet trust-tasks-rs  ->  CAUGHT
```

The old path saw nothing in the second case.

CI-only change: no crate touched, no version bump.

title: test(vta-sdk): mount dids/get responses in the post-fold shape
body:
`main` has been red since #1114. Two tests in `vta-sdk --test client_rest` fail with `missing field \`record\``:

```
get_did_webvh_returns_record   client_rest.rs:1348
get_did_webvh_log_returns_log  client_rest.rs:1364
test result: FAILED. 84 passed; 2 failed
```

**They are not caused by any open branch.** The same two fail identically on #1120 (test coverage for contexts/app-state/memory) and #1122 (error-code casing), neither of which touches the SDK or webvh. I also reproduced them on a detached `origin/main` with nothing applied.

## Cause

#1114 folded the dedicated get-log task into `dids/get` + `includeLog`. The response now carries the record under `record` with `log` beside it, and `get_did_webvh`/`get_did_webvh_log` correctly decode `GetDidWebvhResultBody { record, log }`. The two mocks still returned the pre-fold flattened record, so decoding failed.

The production code is right; only the fixtures were stale. Note `mount_json` ignores its `method`/`path` arguments and always mounts `POST /trust-tasks`, so the payload shape was the only thing to correct.

## Why it matters beyond two tests

Every VTI pull request currently shows a red `Test` check, so a genuine regression is indistinguishable from the inherited failure — reviewers have to know which reds to ignore.

## Verification

`cargo test -p vta-sdk --features client --test client_rest` — **86 passed, 0 failed** (was 84 passed, 2 failed). The suite is `#![cfg(feature = "client")]`, so a plain `cargo test -p vta-sdk` compiles none of it.

Scoped to the test file only.

title: docs(https): make the end-to-end demo actually sign
body:
`trust-tasks-https`'s documented end-to-end demo has never worked. `acl/grant/0.1` declares `proof` REQUIRED and the server enforces it, so `client_demo` was rejected:

```
→ POST http://localhost:3000/trust-tasks   type: .../acl/grant/0.1
← HTTP 422 trust-task-error: code=proofRequired retryable=false
```

This matters more than a broken example usually would: it is the first thing an implementer runs, and it taught them the pipeline was broken rather than that they had skipped a step. The earlier ergonomics review found the largest consumer in the ecosystem (`vta-sdk`) bypassing the typed API entirely — a demo that rejects itself is part of that story.

## Why three files, and why none works alone

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `Cargo.toml` | dev-deps gain `trust-tasks-proof` + `affinidi-secrets-resolver`. No cycle — `trust-tasks-proof` depends on `trust-tasks-rs`, not on this crate, and dev-deps are stripped at publish. |
| `client_demo.rs` | Derives a `did:key` from a fixed seed; sets `issuer`/`recipient`/`issuedAt` **before** signing; signs via `ProofExt` (#282). |
| `server_demo.rs` | Maps the `alice` bearer token to the **same** `did:key`; adds `Verifier::for_did_key()`. |

Two ordering traps are now documented in the code, because both produce a *different* failure rather than an obvious one:

- `HttpsClient::send` fills in any unset party member, and a member added after signing is one the proof does not cover — so setting `issuer`/`recipient` after signing yields `proofInvalid`, not success.
- The server runs the SPEC §4.8.1 in-band-vs-transport cross-check, so signing the client alone converts `proofRequired` into `identityMismatch`.

`did:key` from a fixed seed lets both binaries reach the same identity with no key exchange, and `Verifier::for_did_key()` resolves offline — so the demo verifies a real signature with no network and no DID document.

## Verified by running it

```
→ POST http://localhost:3000/trust-tasks
  type: https://trusttasks.org/spec/acl/grant/0.1
  signed by: did:key:z6MkvDqGT54cXesYGvABpF1UapVNwjCqRcafi4Px6Thv5T3Z
← https://trusttasks.org/spec/acl/grant/0.1#response (threadId matches the request id)
  entry: subject=did:web:carol.example role=moderator

# server:
acl/grant received from did:key:z6MkvDqGT54… for subject did:web:carol.example (role moderator)
```

`cargo clippy -p trust-tasks-https --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` clean; `cargo fmt --all --check` clean. Examples only — no library code, no version bump.

title: feat(rs): one Cargo feature per spec family — 22s to 4s for a single-family consumer
body:
## The number

Measured on one machine, dependencies cached, `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`, with
`cargo clean -p trust-tasks-rs` before each run.

| selection | before (`cd170a1`, 0.13.2) | this PR (0.13.4) |
|---|---|---|
| default features | 21.7 s | 22.4 s |
| `--features validate` | 21.3 s | 22.2 s |
| `--no-default-features --features vault` | n/a | **4.0 s** |
| `--no-default-features --features vault,validate` | n/a | **4.0 s** |
| `--no-default-features --features acl` | n/a | **1.2 s** |

`du -sh trust-tasks-rs/src/specs`: **15 M before, 15 M after** — 727 files,
263,514 lines, unchanged. This PR changes what a consumer *compiles*, not what
the crate ships.

The default column is flat on purpose: it compiles the same 344 modules it
always did, and the gap between the two figures is run-to-run variance (the
same command measured anywhere from 21.7 s to 28.0 s over the session). The
whole saving is in what a consumer can now decline: **5.5× for a one-family
selection, 18× for a small one.**

## What changed

`trust-tasks-rs/src/specs` is 344 generated modules and 15 MB, and every
consumer compiles all of it to use three tasks. That is an adoption barrier —
`vta-sdk`, the largest consumer in the ecosystem, keeps 172 hand-maintained URI
string constants and `serde_json::Value` rather than depend on these types, and
compile weight is part of why.

`trust-tasks-codegen` now emits, from what is on disk under `specs/`:

- `#[cfg(feature = "<family>")]` on each top-level `pub mod` in
  `src/specs/mod.rs` — one gate per first slug segment;
- the same gate on each `schema_for` match arm in `schema_index.rs`, so an
  unselected family answers `None`, which is what `None` already documents
  itself to mean ("this build knows no spec for it");
- the `[features]` table of `trust-tasks-rs/Cargo.toml`, between TOML markers,
  with `default = ["all-specs"]` and `all-specs` listing all 26 families.

Feature names are the family directory name verbatim. Cargo permits `-` in
feature names, so `credential-exchange` needs no mangling and the feature a
consumer types matches the path segment they see in the registry — verified by
building it.

## Non-breaking, with one caveat to note

`default = ["all-specs"]`, so a consumer who configures nothing compiles
exactly the module tree it compiled in 0.13.3. `cargo test --workspace`,
`clippy --all-features`, `cargo doc --all-features` and `cargo package` all
pass unchanged, and none of the six sibling crates needed an edit.

**The caveat:** a consumer that already wrote `default-features = false` — a
no-op against 0.13.3's empty `default` — now deselects every family and must
add `"all-specs"` (or the families it uses). No crate in this workspace does
this, and it is called out in the CHANGELOG. Treated as a patch under this
repo's rule that only a break in what a consumer compiles moves the leading
component; flagging it here so a reviewer can disagree.

Rebased over #282, which released 0.13.3, so this is **0.13.4**. No conflict
beyond the CHANGELOG heading and the version line; #282 touched only
hand-written code and this PR touches only the generator, the generated index
files and the manifest.

## Not a fourth drift incident

`CLAUDE.md` records three separate cases of a hand-maintained list quietly
falling out of step with the tree. A missing family feature would be the
quietest yet — the family would simply not be in the crate, and `codegen-drift`
would not see it because that job only diffs `trust-tasks-rs/src/specs`.

So the family set is enumerated from `specs/`, never listed, and the new
`trust-tasks-rs/tests/spec_feature_manifest.rs` **re-derives it from `specs/`
independently** and fails if the manifest table or the module gates disagree —
rather than checking the two generated artifacts against each other, which
would only assert that the generator agrees with itself. Verified by
introducing a bogus feature and watching it fail:

```
thread 'every_spec_family_has_a_cargo_feature' panicked at
trust-tasks-rs/tests/spec_feature_manifest.rs:141:5:
  a feature but not on disk: ["bogus-family"]
```

## Cross-family `$ref`s: no feature dependency was needed

`resolve_cross_file_refs` already inlines every `_shared` / `_framework` `$ref`
into each module *before* typify runs, so no generated module names another
module's types — `grep -r 'crate::specs::' trust-tasks-rs/src/specs/` returns
zero hits. Confirmed by building, not by reasoning: **all 26 single-family
selections compile individually**, plus `--no-default-features` with nothing at
all and `--no-default-features --features validate,vault`.

## The five framework-reserved families are not gated

SPEC §6.1's reserved slugs (`trust-task-control`, `trust-task-discovery`,
`trust-task-next-step`, `trust-task-ok`, `trust-ceremony-receipt`) stay
unconditional. `discovery.rs` does
`use crate::specs::trust_task_discovery::v0_1 as wire;` at module scope, so the
crate's own framework machinery needs them whatever a consumer selected, and
they are **1.4%** of the generated tree — gating them would cost every consumer
the framework surface and save nothing. The classification comes from the
reserved-slug pattern `^trust-(task|ceremony)($|-)`, not a hard-coded list, so
a new `trust-task-*` slug is handled without anyone remembering to.

## Two changes I did not make, and why

### Emitting each payload schema once per module — **declined, it buys nothing**

The premise does not hold: the request and response `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA` values are
**not** the same string in any of the 344 modules. The request schema is the
inlined root document; the response is `{"$defs": …, "$ref": "#/$defs/Response",
"$schema": …}`. Measured across the tree:

- request literals 1.87 MB, response literals 1.43 MB, 3.30 MB total of 12.91 MB
- byte-identical *req == resp*: **0 of 330**
- byte-identical shared prefix (the `$defs` block): 1.40 MB — the only thing
  a dedupe could remove, and it cannot be expressed as one `const` because
  `concat!` takes literals, not consts.

More to the point, the cost is not there. I blanked **every** `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA`
literal in the tree — all 3.3 MB, far more than any dedupe could remove — and
rebuilt:

| | with literals | all literals blanked |
|---|---|---|
| default features | 24.5 s | 27.2 s |
| `--no-default-features --features vault` | 4.0 s | 5.2 s |

Removing 3.3 MB of source made no measurable difference in either direction;
the effect is smaller than the noise. The cost is the typify structs and their
serde derives.

Against zero measured benefit, the change would have required weakening
`scripts/check-bindings-conformance.mjs`, which parses
`const PAYLOAD_SCHEMA: … = Some("…")` **literally out of the impl block** — the
strongest conformance check in the repo, and the one deliberately kept
independent of the generator. Not worth it.

### Hoisting `_shared` components — **declined, it would break consumers**

There is a real number here — **2.38 MB of byte-identical redundant top-level
type definitions** (1,896 items; `Ext` ×341, `ExtKey` ×341, `VaultEntry` ×8,
`DidRecord` ×16, …), 18% of the tree. But:

1. **It is a coherence break that no `pub use` can paper over.** Today
   `vault::upsert::v0_3::VaultEntry` and `vault::delete::v0_1::VaultEntry` are
   *distinct types*. Hoisting makes them one type behind two aliases, and a
   consumer with `impl From<upsert::v0_3::VaultEntry> for X` and
   `impl From<delete::v0_1::VaultEntry> for X` stops compiling with E0119. The
   brief says do it not at all if every existing path cannot be preserved: the
   paths can be preserved, the type *identities* cannot, and identity is what
   the coherence checker keys on.
2. **It would partly undo this PR.** `sync/event/0.1` (family `sync`) carries
   `VaultEntry` from `vault/_shared`. Hoisting to `specs::vault::shared` makes
   feature `sync` require feature `vault` — exactly the cross-family coupling
   the gating avoids today.
3. **The shapes are not unique.** `VaultEntry` appears in *two* distinct
   byte-shapes (×8 and ×5), so a single hoisted path would be wrong and a
   content-addressed one would become public API.

The gating stands on its own, and a silent coherence break would be worse than
the duplication.

## Verification (actual output)

```
cargo fmt --all --check                → OK: fmt clean
cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all
                                       → OK: no drift (working tree clean)
cargo test --workspace                 → exit=0, 0 failures
cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate
                                       → exit=0, failures=0, 13 test binaries ok
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
                                       → exit=0, 0 warning/error lines
RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --all-features
                                       → exit=0, 0 warning/error lines
cargo package -p trust-tasks-rs        → Packaged 766 files, 13.6MiB; verify build OK
cargo package -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate
                                       → verify build OK
npm run check-bindings                 → "349 specifications checked against 349
                                          TypeScript and 344 Rust modules — all agree."
```

Plus the 26 per-family builds and the guard-test negative case described above.

## One gap left for a reviewer

The `codegen-drift` job diffs only `trust-tasks-rs/src/specs`. Two things this
PR makes generated — `trust-tasks-rs/Cargo.toml`'s `[features]` block and
`src/schema_index.rs` (already generated before this PR, already unwatched) —
therefore sit outside it. `tests/spec_feature_manifest.rs` covers the feature
table from a different direction, and `src/specs/mod.rs` *is* inside the drift
path so the gates themselves are watched. Widening the job's diff path to
`trust-tasks-rs` would close the rest; I left `.github/workflows/rust.yml`
alone rather than touch a file outside this change's scope.

## Commits

1. `feat(codegen):` the generator change, the manifest markers and the guard
   test — isolated from its output.
2. `feat(rs):` the regenerated tree. Only `specs/mod.rs` and
   `schema_index.rs` move; the 344 payload modules are byte-identical, because
   gating happens at the family boundary and nothing below it changed.
3. `chore(rs):` 0.13.3 → 0.13.4, CHANGELOG, README, `Cargo.lock`.

title: feat(rs): one Cargo feature per spec family — 22s to 4s for a single-family consumer (#283)
body:
feat(rs): one Cargo feature per spec family — 22s to 4s for a single-family consumer (#283)

* feat(codegen): emit one Cargo feature per top-level spec family

`trust-tasks-rs/src/specs` is 344 generated modules, 15 MB and ~264k lines,
and every consumer compiles all of it to use three tasks. That is an adoption
barrier: the largest consumer in the ecosystem keeps 172 hand-maintained URI
string constants and `serde_json::Value` rather than depend on these types,
and compile weight is part of why.

The generator now writes:

* `#[cfg(feature = "<family>")]` on each top-level `pub mod` in
  `src/specs/mod.rs`, one gate per first slug segment;
* the same gate on each `schema_for` match arm in `schema_index.rs`, so a
  family that was not selected answers `None` — which is what `None` already
  documents itself to mean;
* the `[features]` table of `trust-tasks-rs/Cargo.toml`, between TOML
  markers, with `default = ["all-specs"]` and `all-specs` listing every
  family. An unconfigured consumer therefore compiles exactly what it
  compiled before.

The family set is enumerated from `specs/` rather than listed. `CLAUDE.md`
records three separate incidents of a hand-maintained list drifting from the
tree and a fourth would be the quietest yet: a family whose feature went
missing would simply not be in the crate, and `codegen-drift` would not see
it because that job only diffs `src/specs`. `tests/spec_feature_manifest.rs`
re-derives the family set from `specs/` and fails if the manifest or the
module gates disagree with it, rather than checking the two generated
artifacts against each other.

The five framework-reserved families of SPEC §6.1 are deliberately not gated.
`discovery.rs` does `use crate::specs::trust_task_discovery::v0_1` at module
scope, so the crate's own framework machinery needs them whatever a consumer
selected, and they are 1.4% of the generated tree.

No cross-family feature dependency is needed: `resolve_cross_file_refs`
already inlines every `_shared` / `_framework` `$ref` into each module before
typify runs, so no generated module names another module's types. All 26
single-family selections were built to confirm it.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(rs): regenerate the spec tree with per-family feature gates

Output of `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all`. Only the two
index files move: the per-module payload types are byte-identical, because
gating happens at the family boundary and nothing below it changed.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore(rs): release 0.13.4 — per-family Cargo features

Additive under `default`, so a patch per this repo's rule that only a break
in what a consumer compiles moves the leading component. The one caveat is
recorded in the CHANGELOG: a consumer who already wrote
`default-features = false` — a no-op against 0.13.3's empty `default` — now
deselects every family and needs `"all-specs"` or the families it uses.

README gains the measured numbers and a worked `default-features = false`
example, since the point of the change is that a consumer can act on it.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: fix(vta)!: take keyId from the wire instead of minting one
body:
First of the three stopgaps #1121 unblocked. `keys/create/0.1` publishes `keyId`
as of `trust-tasks-rs` 0.12.1
([dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#275](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/275)),
so the caller can name a key and the trust-task binding no longer has to invent
one.

## What is deleted

#1118 minted an id at the binding:

```rust
key_id: if req.internal.unwrap_or(false) {
    Some(format!("internal-{}", uuid::Uuid::new_v4()))
} else {
    None
},
```

That was a **deliberate deviation from a SHOULD in the specification** — one I
wrote in #275, which says a maintainer offering internal keys and receiving no
`keyId` SHOULD reject. It was taken because the alternative was a security
feature nobody could use: an internal key has no derivation path to be named
after, the operation layer refuses one without an id, and the wire had no
member to carry it.

The comment at that site said to delete it when the bump landed. It is deleted.

Now `key_id: req.key_id` — straight from the request. `None` stays correct for
a derived key, which the operation layer names after its derivation path.

## The client stops dropping it too

`VtaClient::create_key` never read `CreateKeyRequest::key_id`. That was the
third of the three fields #1118 found being dropped between the CLI and the
wire; the other two were fixed there, and this one had nowhere to go until now.

## The test asserts the caller's name survives

`an_internal_key_is_actually_internal` now supplies `keyId` and asserts it comes
back unchanged, alongside the existing `origin == "internal"` check. The two
answer different questions — *was the request honoured*, and *was the name I
chose the name I got* — and a maintainer that silently renamed a key would pass
the first.

## Still open, from the same unblock

- the hand-rolled freshness bounds from #1117, in favour of `FreshnessPolicy` /
  `TrustTask::validate_freshness`;
- `replay::check_and_record`, in favour of `ReplayGuard`.

Those two go together: `ConsumeChecks` bundles freshness and replay in one
argument on purpose, because SPEC §7.2 makes the acceptance window and the
replay record's retention *the same bound*, and splitting them is how a
deployment ends up with a five-minute record and an unbounded window believing
it has a replay defence.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings`
- `./scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` — 28 suites green, **0 violations**, coverage 48/109
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

BREAKING CHANGE: `CreateKeyBody` gains `key_id`. `keys/create/0.1` with
`internal: true` now requires the caller to supply `keyId`; the binding no
longer mints one.

Refs #1059

title: feat(rs, proof): typed signing (ProofExt) and async context-carrying dispatch (AsyncDispatcher)
body:
Two pieces of ceremony that stop implementers using the typed API. Both additive: every existing call site compiles unchanged. ## 1 — Signing was a five-step ritual (`trust-tasks-proof`) `affinidi::sign_trust_task` works on `serde_json::Value`, so a producer holding a `TrustTask

` had to serialise it, call the free function, check the result, deserialise back, and get the ordering right. `trust-tasks-capability-client` declines to sign for exactly this reason and tells consumers to do it themselves — and `trust-tasks-https/examples/client_demo.rs`, the documented end-to-end demo, contains no signing at all. That is not hypothetical. Running the two shipped demos against each other today: ``` → POST http://localhost:3000/trust-tasks type: https://trusttasks.org/spec/acl/grant/0.1 ← HTTP 422 trust-task-error: code=proofRequired retryable=false message=Some("proof required but not present") ``` ### Before ```rust let mut value = serde_json::to_value(&req)?; // 1. down to Value let signed = sign_trust_task(&value, &secret, SignOptions::new()) // 2. sign .await?; let req: TrustTask = serde_json::from_value(signed)?; // 3. back up // 4. and remember to do all of that *after* every other member is set, // 5. because `send()` fills issuer/recipient/issuedAt in if you didn't. ``` ### After ```rust use trust_tasks_proof::{affinidi::SignOptions, ProofExt}; req.issuer = Some(my_did.clone()); req.recipient = Some(server_did.clone()); req.sign(&secret, SignOptions::new()).await?; // one line, on the typed doc ``` **Where it lives and why.** `trust-tasks-rs` cannot depend on `trust-tasks-proof` — that is the dependency direction — so `TrustTask::sign` cannot be an inherent method. It is `trust_tasks_proof::ProofExt`, an extension trait implemented for `TrustTask

` for every `P: Serialize + Send + Sync`, carrying both `sign` and `verify` so the producer and consumer halves of the round-trip are one import. `sign` is gated on the `affinidi` feature (it needs that backend's `Signer`); `verify` is backend-agnostic and always available, which is why the trait sits at the crate root rather than inside `affinidi`. `ProofExt` is greppable and rustdoc-searchable from either end — "proof", "sign", "verify". **It is a wrapper, not a reimplementation.** `sign_trust_task` is called verbatim, so the canonicalisation contract, the deterministic `eddsa-jcs-2022` default, the replace-don't-nest rule for an existing proof, and the SPEC §4.7/§4.8 issuer pre-flight are all unchanged. A test asserts the two paths emit byte-identical documents. The free functions stay public and unchanged. One deliberate detail: `sign` lifts only the emitted `proof` member back onto the typed document rather than re-parsing the whole thing into `TrustTask

`. Every other member came from `self` unchanged, so the round-trip would add nothing — and a payload type whose serde round-trip is not exact would silently invalidate the proof it was just given. It also means `sign` needs no `DeserializeOwned` bound. A sign that fails leaves the document untouched. `SignError::ProofRoundTrip` is new; `SignError` is `#[non_exhaustive]`, so that is additive. ## 2 — No async, context-carrying dispatch (`trust-tasks-rs`) `Dispatcher::on` takes `Fn(TrustTask

) -> R`: synchronous, no context argument. A handler cannot `await` a database. So receivers hand-roll routers — `OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure` imports exactly one symbol from the binding crates (`status_for_code`) and builds its whole pipeline by hand, `vtc-service` routes with a string `match`, and the `affinidi-tdk-rs` mediator uses a 12-arm `if doc.type_uri == type_uri_of::

()` chain that re-parses `P::TYPE_URI` and re-serialises the document once per arm per message. **None of those three emits `unsupportedVersion` correctly** for a known slug at an unknown version. They answer `unsupportedType` — telling a producer its specification is unimplemented when the real fix is to downgrade. A `match` on the whole URI string cannot see that the slug was recognised, so the bug is structural. The library `Dispatcher` gets it right and nobody can use it. ### Before ```rust // once per spec, per message if doc.type_uri == type_uri_of::() { let typed: TrustTask = serde_json::from_value(serde_json::to_value(&doc)?)?; // re-serialise to downcast return handle_grant(typed, &state).await; } if doc.type_uri == type_uri_of::() { /* … × 12 */ } Err(problem_report("unsupportedType")) // …even when the slug *was* known ``` ### After ```rust use trust_tasks_rs::{specs::acl, AsyncDispatcher}; let dispatcher = AsyncDispatcher::, Outcome>::new() .on_async::(|req, ctx| async move { ctx.db.record_grant(&req.payload.entry).await; // a real await Outcome::Granted }) .on_async::(|req, ctx| async move { ctx.db.revoke(&req.payload.subject).await; Outcome::Revoked }); match dispatcher.dispatch_or_reject(inbound, state.clone(), new_id()).await { Ok(outcome) => emit(outcome), Err(error) => emit(error), // §8.1-routed trust-task-error } ``` What falls out by construction: - **One downcast per message**, synchronously, before any future is created — not once per arm. - **`unsupportedType` vs `unsupportedVersion`.** Registration records the Type URI *and* its slug, so a known slug at an unregistered `MAJOR.MINOR` is `unsupportedVersion` (SPEC §5.2 / §8.3) and only an unknown slug is `unsupportedType`. Tested both ways, and through `dispatch_or_reject` so the distinction is asserted on the wire form a binding actually emits. - **The typed §7.2 checks.** Right after the downcast — the first point at which the codegen-emitted `Payload` flags are reachable — a request-variant document is checked with `TrustTask::enforce_spec_policy` (items 5b `recipient` REQUIRED, 7A `proof` REQUIRED, 8 audience binding). That is the same method `consume_inbound` and the HTTPS server call, so the three cannot drift apart. `#response`-variant URIs route straight through, since those items govern what a consumer demands of a *request*. The checks that do not need the payload type stay in `consume_inbound`. `AsyncDispatcher` is `Send + Sync` for any `Ctx`/`R`, so it lives in an `Arc` on shared state and dispatches from any tokio task (asserted by a `tokio::spawn` test). **`Dispatcher` is untouched** — three of its helpers became `pub(crate)` so the routing, downcast and §8.1 error-response logic is shared rather than duplicated; nothing else changed. ## The demo still needs a coordinator fix `client_demo.rs` is outside this PR's ownership and the fix is **not** confined to that file, so it is reported rather than made. It needs, together: 1. `trust-tasks-https/Cargo.toml` `[dev-dependencies]`: `trust-tasks-proof = { path = "../trust-tasks-proof" }` and `affinidi-secrets-resolver = "0.5"`. No cycle — `trust-tasks-proof` does not depend on `trust-tasks-https` — and dev-dependencies are stripped at publish time. 2. `client_demo.rs`: mint a deterministic `did:key` secret, set `issuer` / `recipient` / `issuedAt` **explicitly before signing** (`HttpsClient::send` fills those three in when unset, which would invalidate a proof minted earlier), then `request.sign(&secret, SignOptions::new()).await?`. `my_vid` must become that `did:key` too, because the client checks the response's `recipient` against it. 3. `server_demo.rs`: `BearerAuth::from_pairs` must map the `alice` token to the same `did:key`. The server runs the §4.8.1 cross-check, so an in-band `did:key` issuer against a transport-authenticated `did:web:alice.example` is `identityMismatch` — swapping one side alone moves the failure rather than fixing it. Optionally `.with_verifier(trust_tasks_proof::affinidi::Verifier::for_did_key())` on the server builder, so the demo exercises verification and not just presence. ## Versions Additive only, so patch bumps of the two crates touched (the leading non-zero component is what signals a break below 1.0): - `trust-tasks-rs` `0.13.2` → `0.13.3` - `trust-tasks-proof` `0.12.0` → `0.12.1` Nothing here is breaking: two new public items, one new variant on an already-`#[non_exhaustive]` enum, no signature changed, no behaviour changed on an existing path. ## Verification All run at the workspace level from a clean tree on this branch: ``` cargo build --workspace Finished `dev` profile ... in 28.52s cargo test --workspace all suites ok; 0 failed (483 in the trust-tasks-rs lib, incl. 8 new async_dispatch tests; 5 new proof_ext tests) cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings Finished `dev` profile ... in 49.65s (no diagnostics) cargo fmt --all --check clean RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps --all-features Documenting all 9 crates; Finished ... in 30.62s ``` The rustdoc build caught one real failure during development — `private-intra-doc-links` on a `[module documentation](self)` link from a public trait in a private module — exactly as warned. Fixed by moving the rationale onto the trait itself. New tests: - `trust-tasks-proof/tests/proof_ext.rs` — signed typed round-trip verifies; payload mutated after signing fails with `SignatureInvalid` and re-signing recovers; typed sign is byte-identical to the free function; a failed sign leaves the document untouched; verifying a proofless document fails cleanly. - `trust-tasks-rs/src/async_dispatch.rs` — a handler that actually awaits and returns a response document with the context threaded through; unknown slug → `unsupportedType`; known slug at unknown version → `unsupportedVersion`; the same distinction through `dispatch_or_reject` with §8.1 routing asserted; `proofRequired` raised before the handler runs; mismatched payload → `malformedRequest`; bare and `#request` URIs route together; dispatch from a spawned tokio task.

title: test(vtc): expect the HTTPS binding's flat 422 for refused documents (#1125)
body:
test(vtc): expect the HTTPS binding's flat 422 for refused documents (#1125)

trust-tasks-https aligned status_for_code to the binding spec's §4 table,
which puts every "understood, well-formed, and refused" code in one 422
bucket. VTI took that mapping in #1121 with the 0.12 dependency upgrade; both
assertions here still encoded the pre-alignment 403 and 400.

The flat bucket is deliberate. A finer split lets an unauthenticated prober
distinguish wrongRecipient from expired from proofInvalid by status line
alone, which is the identity oracle the table exists to close. Both services
map through status_for_code, so adopting it means adopting that property.

These were masked until now: cargo test --workspace aborts at the first
failing test binary, and the vta-sdk webvh tests fixed in #1124 were failing
ahead of them, so this binary never ran.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: fix(vta)!: re-case the extended error codes the Trust Tasks registry moved
body:
`trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#279` re-cased 200 extended error-code local
parts to lowerCamelCase per SPEC §4.10 rule 4 — `vault/upsert:version_conflict`
→ `vault/upsert:versionConflict`. Only the part after the `:` moved; the
namespace is unchanged. This repo still produced (and in one place read) the old
spelling for **32** of them.

Verified against `trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf@main` (543 declared codes
from `grep -rhoE 'code: …' specs --include=spec.md`). Every code below is
declared by the registry in the new spelling; only `did-management:unknownDomain`
is *also* still declared in the old one, and only by retired specs.

## Emitter vs matcher

The distinction governs every edit:

- **Emitter** — this repo decides what to send, and the registry decides what is
  correct to send. Moves to the new spelling, no compatibility arm.
- **Matcher** — this repo reads a code a peer produced, and cannot control that
  peer's deploy order. Accepts **both** spellings, with a `TODO` naming when the
  old arm can go.

**31 emitter codes, 1 matcher.** Commits are split so the two are reviewable
apart: `fix(vta)!` is the emitter side, `fix(vta-sdk)` is the matcher.

### Emitters (31 codes)

| Namespace | Local parts moved to camelCase |
|---|---|
| `auth/step-up/approve-response` | `acrUnsatisfied`, `approverUnauthorized`, `assertionInvalid`, `challengeExpired`, `challengeUnknown`, `noGate`, `subjectMismatch` |
| `device/heartbeat` | `notRegistered` |
| `device/register` | `alreadyRegistered`, `noPendingEnrolment` |
| `device/set-wake` | `notRegistered` |
| `did-management` | `unknownDomain` (prose only — see below) |
| `provision/integration` | `contextRequired` (`PROVISION_CONTEXT_REQUIRED`) |
| `task-consent/decision` | `noPending` |
| `vault/get` | `notFound` |
| `vault/proxy-login` | `credentialRejected`, `notFound`, `notProxyable`, `targetUnreachable` |
| `vault/release` | `notFound` |
| `vault/sign-trust-task` | `envelopeAlreadyProofed`, `envelopeExpired`, `envelopeInvalid`, `envelopeIssuerMismatch`, `notFound`, `notSignable` |
| `vault/upsert` | `contextChangeForbidden`, `envelopeUnsupported`, `notFound`, `sealedSecretInvalid`, `secretRequired`, `versionConflict` |

### Matcher (1)

`vta_sdk::agent_session::is_already_registered` reads
`device/register:alreadyRegistered` off whatever VTA the agent enrolled
against, so it now accepts both spellings. It matters more than its size
suggests: a missed match does not crash, it **falls open into a hard error** on
re-enrolment, and a smoke test that enrols once against a clean VTA never takes
the branch. `already_registered_accepts_both_registry_spellings` pins the
dual-accept as a property rather than trusting the comment beside it.

## ⚠️ Deploy order: the plugin PR must ship before this service

`PROVISION_CONTEXT_REQUIRED` now makes this service emit
`provision/integration:contextRequired`. `OpenVTC/vta-browser-plugin` matches
only the old spelling in users' browsers today — `onboard-view.tsx:307` gates
the onboarding context picker on an **exact equality**, so the picker would
silently stop appearing. A sibling change makes the plugin dual-accept.

**Ship the plugin PR, and let it reach users, before deploying this service.**

## Corrections to the code census

Two findings beyond the original list:

- **Three vault emitters build their namespace by interpolation**, so their
  codes appear as a literal nowhere and a flat grep misses them:
  `vault/{verb}:not_found` and `vault/{verb}:version_conflict`
  (`vault_not_found`, `check_expected_version`) and `vault/{op}:not_found`
  (`refuse_if_not_active`). Those helpers are what actually emit
  `vault/delete:notFound` and **`vault/delete:versionConflict`** — the code the
  census placed in the browser-plugin's set. It is emitted here too, and is
  fixed here.
- **`did-management:unknownDomain` splits 18 draft / 8 retired**, not 21/5. All
  eight snake_case declarations are `status: retired`; all eighteen camelCase
  ones are `status: draft`.

## How `did-management:unknown_domain` was handled

Both spellings are legitimately live, so the deciding question is which side
each site describes — and in this repo the answer is easy, because **there is no
emitter and no matcher for it here**. All eleven occurrences are prose.

- Ten describe register / publish / delete against a live hosting backplane.
  Their specs (`did-management/did/register`, `domain/assign`, and
  `did/publish`, which is retired and `supersededBy: did-management/did/register`)
  are draft and declare `unknownDomain`. Those move.
- The `CHANGELOG.md` entry is history and is left as written.

No dual-accept is needed for a code this repo neither sends nor reads.

## Deliberately not touched

Reported rather than changed:

- **`vault/credentials/*`** and the `LifecycleError::code()` tokens
  (`not_active`, `not_archived`, `already_deleted`, `not_deleted`,
  `grace_expired`) — the registry declares neither namespace in either casing.
  Re-casing them would invent a spelling rather than follow one.
- **Codes emitted into a registry namespace the registry does not declare them
  in** — `auth/step-up/approve-response:proof_invalid` (`step_up.rs:142`),
  `vault/proxy-login:{invalid_login_url,not_implemented,no_audience}`
  (`vault.rs:1671,1692,1959,1962`). A conforming consumer cannot branch on any
  of these. This is a spec gap, not a casing bug.
- **`vault/get` emits a bare `AppError::NotFound("vault entry {id} not found")`**
  (`vault.rs:706`) carrying no code at all, though the registry declares
  `vault/get:notFound`. Also a gap, and also out of scope here.
- **`password_post.rs:94-100`** writes `vault/proxy-login: credential_rejected`
  — namespace, *space*, token. Not a `ns:localPart` code, and the real emitter
  for that path is `password_post_error_to_reject` in `vault.rs`, which is
  fixed.
- **This repo's own vocabularies**: `auth:step_up_required`,
  `auth:consent_required`, `denied:no_pending`, `bbs:*`, `bootstrap:*`,
  `webauthn-vti-v1:*`, and the `not_registered` / `step_up_required` REST
  `error` fields on mediator drain-cancel (`protocol.rs:1218`,
  `api_integration.rs:3794`) and in `vtc-service`.

## Verification

Run with `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` inside the worktree, on the CI command set from
`.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
- `cargo build --workspace` — `Finished dev profile`, no warnings
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace` — passing, **except two failures that predate this
  branch**: `vta-sdk --test client_rest` `get_did_webvh_returns_record` and
  `get_did_webvh_log_returns_log`, both `missing field \`record\``, fallout from
  the #1114 `dids/get` response fold. Reproduced identically on a detached
  `origin/main` with no changes applied.

Refs #1059

title: test(vta-sdk): mount dids/get responses in the post-fold shape (#1124)

test(vta-sdk): mount dids/get responses in the post-fold shape (#1124)

#1114 folded the dedicated get-log task into `dids/get` + `includeLog`, so
the response carries the record under `record` with `log` beside it. Both
webvh get tests still mounted the flattened record, and the SDK — which
correctly decodes `GetDidWebvhResultBody` — failed them with
`missing field \`record\``.

They have been failing on main since #1114, not on any one branch: the same
two tests fail identically on #1120 and #1122, which touch neither the SDK nor
webvh. Every VTI pull request has shown a red Test check as a result, which
hides a real regression behind an expected one.

`mount_json` ignores its method and path arguments and always mounts
