title: chore(specs): re-case extended error code local parts to lowerCamelCase, and lint it
body:
## This changes values on the wire

An error `code` is a string consumers match on. This PR re-cases **200 extended error codes across 80 draft specs**, and the running VTA emits many of them today. **Downstream consumers must be updated in lockstep with deploying this.** The inventory of every real call site is below.

SPEC §4.10 rule 4 requires string values from a closed set that a Trust Task specification defines — extended error `code` identifiers named explicitly — to be lowerCamelCase. The registry did not comply: **275 snake_case local parts across 95 `spec.md` files**, out of 730 declarations. The meta-schema's `code` pattern accepts both casings by design, so nothing was forcing the issue.

Only the **local part** changes. The namespace keeps its slug spelling — lowercase-hyphenated by §6.1 and put out of §4.10's scope by rule 6. `git-trust/grant:already_granted` → `git-trust/grant:alreadyGranted`.

## Two commits

1. **The mechanical rename** — 112 files, 452 replacements, no net line change.
2. **The regression lint** — the durable half; without it the drift returns.

## What is renamed, and what is deliberately not

**80 draft specs are amended in place.** §5.2's within-draft rule is not merely permissive here, it is mandatory:

> an **editorial or normalization change** to a `draft` artifact — re-casing an enumerated value or member name into conformance with §4.10 (…) — **MUST** be made in place, errata-style, within the existing version, and **MUST NOT** mint a new version.

**15 retired specs keep their 48 snake_case codes.** This is the one place the change stops, and the SPEC is explicit. §5.3 freezes a retired specification's schema and prose "at the moment of retirement". §5.2 applies the strict classification from `candidate` onward, under which a re-cased value is a breaking change requiring a MAJOR increment — and `retired` is **terminal**, so there is no conforming way to mint that increment. Retired specs also exist "to keep already-issued documents verifiable", which re-casing would defeat. All 15 already declare a `supersededBy` successor that is lowerCamelCase.

<details><summary>The 15 frozen specs and their successors</summary>

| Spec | Codes | supersededBy |
|---|---|---|
| `confirm/request/0.1` | 2 | `task-consent/request` |
| `confirm/response/0.1` | 3 | `task-consent/decision` |
| `did-management/agent-name/disable/0.1` | 7 | `did-management/agent-name/update` |
| `did-management/agent-name/enable/0.1` | 6 | `did-management/agent-name/update` |
| `did-management/agent-name/set/0.1` | 6 | `did-management/agent-name/update` |
| `did-management/did/disable/0.1` | 3 | `did-management/did/set-state` |
| `did-management/did/enable/0.1` | 3 | `did-management/did/set-state` |
| `did-management/did/publish/0.1` | 4 | `did-management/did/register` |
| `did-management/domain/disable/0.1` | 3 | `did-management/domain/set-state` |
| `did-management/domain/enable/0.1` | 2 | `did-management/domain/set-state` |
| `push/provision/0.1` | 2 | `push/provision/0.2` |
| `push/register/0.1` | 2 | `push/register/0.2` |
| `push/wake/0.1` | 3 | `push/wake/0.2` |
| `registry/record/create/0.1` | 1 | `registry/record/put` |
| `registry/record/update/0.1` | 1 | `registry/record/put` |

</details>

**One consequence worth stating plainly.** `did-management:unknown_domain` is a family-namespaced code shared by 26 specs — 21 draft, 5 retired. The draft ones become `did-management:unknownDomain`; the retired ones cannot. **Both spellings are live in the registry** until those specs age out. A `did-management` consumer must accept both. SPEC §8.5's own non-normative example already names this code as `did-management:unknownDomain`, so the draft spelling is the one the framework text assumes.

**`details.reason` enum values are untouched.** `vault/list` declares a code `cursor_invalid` *and* a `details.reason` enum member spelled `"cursor_invalid"`. They are different closed sets; only the code is re-cased. Those enums are their own §4.10 rule 4 drift (see "Not in this PR").

---

## Migration inventory

Raw grep counts badly overstate this. `not_found` matches **43 files** in `verifiable-trust-infrastructure`; only **2** of them contain a namespaced Trust Task `not_found` code. The other 41 are HTTP 404 helpers, JSON problem-details titles, and enclave-proxy protocol functions. Every site below was opened and read.

**74 genuine references to a renamed code, across 27 files in 2 repos: 1 matcher, 49 emitters, 24 doc comments.**

### Breaks behaviour — matchers (must change before deploy)

These read an incoming code. After the rename the comparison silently stops matching; nothing errors, the branch just never fires.

| Repo / file | Line | Code | What breaks |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pnm-browser-plugin` `packages/extension/src/onboard-view.tsx` | **307** | `provision/integration:context_required` | `res.code === "…:context_required"` gates the context-candidate picker. After the rename the operator is bounced back into a re-prepare cycle instead of being shown the picker. **Production path, highest severity.** |
| `verifiable-trust-infrastructure` `vta-sdk/src/agent_session.rs` | **320** | `device/register:already_registered` | `is_already_registered()` does `e.to_string().contains("already_registered")` on the DIDComm reject. After the rename a re-enrolment stops being treated as "already enrolled" and surfaces as a hard error. **Production path.** |
| `verifiable-trust-infrastructure` `vta-service/src/trust_tasks/credentials.rs` | **241** | `vta/credentials/issue:step_up_required` | Test asserts `body.contains("step_up_required")` on the step-up gate rejection. **Test goes red.** |

Also stale, though not a live break: `vta-sdk/src/client/mod.rs:2485,2489` builds its own fixture reject carrying `"vault/get:not_found"` and asserts on `not_found`. Self-contained, so it keeps passing — but it encodes the old spelling and should be updated for accuracy.

### Emits the renamed codes — 49 sites (all `verifiable-trust-infrastructure`)

These write the code onto the wire. They keep compiling and keep emitting the **old** spelling, so consumers matching the new one see nothing. Not a crash — a silent protocol mismatch.

| File | Sites | Codes |
|---|---|---|
| `vta-service/src/trust_tasks/vault.rs` | 29 | `vault/upsert:{not_found, context_change_forbidden, version_conflict, sealed_secret_invalid, envelope_unsupported, secret_required}`, `vault/release:not_found`, `vault/proxy-login:{not_found, not_proxyable, credential_rejected, target_unreachable}`, `vault/sign-trust-task:{not_found, not_signable, envelope_invalid, envelope_already_proofed, envelope_issuer_mismatch, envelope_expired}` |
| `vta-service/src/trust_tasks/step_up.rs` | 9 | `auth/step-up/approve-response:{no_gate, subject_mismatch, assertion_invalid, challenge_unknown, challenge_expired, acr_unsatisfied}` |
| `vta-service/src/operations/device.rs` | 6 | `device/register:{no_pending_enrolment, already_registered}`, `device/heartbeat:not_registered`, `device/set-wake:not_registered` |
| `vta-service/src/trust_tasks/task_consent.rs` | 2 | `task-consent/decision:no_pending` |
| `vta-sdk/src/agent_session.rs` | 1 | `device/register:already_registered` |
| `vta-sdk/src/protocols/mod.rs` | 1 | `provision/integration:context_required` |
| `vta-sdk/src/client/mod.rs` | 1 | `vault/get:not_found` |

Note `step_up.rs:141` emits `auth/step-up/approve-response:proof_invalid` — a *framework standard* code (`proofInvalid`, §8.3) wrongly namespaced under a slug. Pre-existing and outside this PR, but worth a look while that file is open.

### Documentation only — 24 sites, no behaviour

Doc comments and prose in `vta-webvh/src/webvh_client.rs`, `vta-service/src/webvh_didcomm.rs`, `vta-service/src/routes/bootstrap.rs`, `vta-service/src/operations/{vault/upsert.rs, provision_integration/preconditions.rs, did_webvh/mod.rs}`, `vta-sdk/src/protocols/did_management/{create.rs, servers.rs}`, `vta-sdk/src/provision_integration/http.rs`, `pnm-cli/src/{cli.rs, commands/webvh.rs}`, `docs/02-vta/runtime-service-management.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and in `pnm-browser-plugin` `packages/core/src/{vta/protocol.ts, vault/delete.ts, vault/sign-trust-task.ts, provision/send.ts}` and `packages/extension/src/{bridge-protocol.ts, onboard-view.tsx:84}`. Worth updating for accuracy; nothing fails if they lag.

### Verified as NOT affected

- **`permission_denied`** — 11 downstream files use it, **none** as a namespaced `<slug>:permission_denied`. Every one is the *framework standard* code, un-namespaced (and mis-cased downstream — see below). The 16 declarations this PR re-cases have **zero** downstream call sites.
- **`auth:consent_required`** (`pnm-browser-plugin` `packages/core/src/vta/request-task.ts:81`, matched at :176) — not a registry code at all. The registry declares `credential-exchange/query:consentRequired`, already camelCase and untouched here.
- **`vti-common/src/vault/mod.rs:268`** `LifecycleError::code()` returns bare `already_deleted` — a vault-local token, not the `did-management/did/delete:already_deleted` code. Coincidental string match.

### Prior art: PR #272 covers two codes in one consumer

`trust-tasks-capability-client` declares both spellings and matches all four in `is_idempotent_code()` (`src/lib.rs:85-100, 436-444`):

```rust
GIT_TRUST_ALREADY_GRANTED_CODE       // "git-trust/grant:already_granted"
GIT_TRUST_NOT_GRANTED_CODE           // "git-trust/revoke:not_granted"
GIT_TRUST_ALREADY_GRANTED_CODE_CAMEL // "git-trust/grant:alreadyGranted"
GIT_TRUST_NOT_GRANTED_CODE_CAMEL     // "git-trust/revoke:notGranted"
```

**That dual-accept covers only these 2 codes, in only this one consumer.** It is not a general safety net: the other 198 renamed codes have no dual-accept anywhere, and no other consumer implements one. The three matchers listed above are unprotected.

---

## The lint

`scripts/lib/error-code-casing.mjs`, wired into `build-registry.mjs` beside the existing `checkErrorCodeNamespaces` — one covers the namespace against §8.5, the other the local part against §4.10, and between them a whole code.

The rule is `/^[a-z][a-zA-Z0-9]*$/` on the local part, which rejects snake_case, kebab-case, SCREAMING_CASE and PascalCase in one test. As of this PR snake_case is the only form that occurred.

**It ships as a hard failure, not a warning.** The Security & Privacy lint (#273) is a warning behind a shrinking allowlist because all 349 specs fail it. This is the opposite case — the corpus is at zero offenders in the same PR, so a failure costs nothing and is the only thing that holds the line.

**There is no allowlist file.** The single exception is the 48 codes frozen in 15 retired specs, and it is derived from `status` in front matter rather than hand-maintained, so it cannot rot. It is counted on every build:

```
Error code casing: 682/730 extended code(s) are lowerCamelCase; 48 frozen in 15 retired spec(s) (§5.3 — exempt, not debt), 0 non-conforming
```

That frozen count can only shrink — `retired` is terminal and frozen, so nothing can join it. If it ever rises, something has re-published a frozen artifact and the build log says so.

Verified by injecting `vault/list:cursor_invalid` back into a draft spec: build exits 1 and names the offending code, the reason, and the conforming spelling.

## Generated bindings: two drift checks are red, deliberately

**`build-ts-bindings drift` and `trust-tasks-codegen drift` fail on this branch, and this PR does not fix them.** Read this before re-running CI.

The important part first: **`errorCodes` is not consumed by any code generator.** It is read only by `scripts/build-registry.mjs` — for `$ref` resolution of `detailsSchema`, for the §8.5 namespace check, and to emit into `website/registry.json`. Neither `trust-tasks-codegen` nor `build-ts-bindings.mjs` nor `check-bindings-conformance.mjs` reads it, and **no enum, type or constant is generated from an error code**. `check-bindings` passes: 349 specs vs 349 TypeScript and 344 Rust modules, all agree.

The drift comes from somewhere else. The generators embed each `payload.schema.json` **verbatim**, `description` strings included — as a JSDoc comment and as the `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA` string constant. This PR edited code references *inside 21 schema descriptions* (a description saying "reject with `vault/upsert:envelope_unsupported`" had to be updated, or it would name a code that no longer exists), so the embedded copies are now stale.

Running the generators locally produces exactly **21 files, 118 insertions, 118 deletions — every single line inside a `description` or the JSDoc rendered from one.** No type, identifier, enum, or validation-relevant value moves. Example, the whole shape of it:

```
-  * … consumers reject `tspMessage` envelopes explicitly (`envelope_unsupported`) …
+  * … consumers reject `tspMessage` envelopes explicitly (`envelopeUnsupported`) …
```

**Why it is not fixed here.** A concurrent PR is editing `exposure:` and `proofRequirement:` front matter, and `proofRequirement` *does* feed the generated output (`IS_PROOF_REQUIRED`). Regenerating in both branches would collide in the same generated files. The regeneration is mechanical and deterministic, so it is cleaner to run it once, after both land, than to merge two generated diffs.

The two branches do not overlap today — none of the 21 binding files this PR would touch belong to the two specs the other PR also edits (`vta/credentials/issue/0.2`, `vta/memory/list/0.1`) — but the ordering still matters.

**To land:** merge this and the `exposure:`/`proofRequirement:` PR, then run `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` and `npm run build-ts-bindings` in one follow-up commit. Or, if this merges first, regenerate here — the diff is 118 lines of prose and needs no review beyond confirming it is prose.

## Checks

```
npm run validate     ✅ exit 0 — Validated 349 specs, indexed 65 shared schemas
npm run build        ✅ exit 0
npm run check-bindings ✅ 349 specs vs 349 TypeScript and 344 Rust modules — all agree

build-ts-bindings drift    ❌ expected — see "Generated bindings" above
trust-tasks-codegen drift  ❌ expected — see "Generated bindings" above
(all other CI checks pass: build, cargo test, clippy, fmt, deny, package,
 tsc --noEmit, node --test, bindings match specs, DCO, EasyCLA)
```

Sweep: `grep -rE 'code: [a-z0-9/-]+:[a-z0-9]+_' specs --include=spec.md` returns only the 48 intentionally-frozen retired declarations; **0** remain in any draft, candidate or standard spec.

## Not in this PR — three findings that each deserve their own

1. **~90 specs re-declare `permissionDenied` under their own namespace** when §8.3 already defines it as a standard code (16 of them were the `permission_denied` this PR re-cased). Re-casing preserves them exactly as they were; **nothing was deleted**. But the downstream evidence above is telling: every implementation uses the *standard* un-namespaced code and not one uses the namespaced form, which suggests the local declarations are redundant. Removing a declared code is a bigger change than re-casing one and wants its own PR.

2. **42 references to framework standard codes are mis-cased**, across 19 files — `permission_denied`, `malformed_request`, `proof_invalid`, `task_failed`, `unsupported_type`, `wrong_recipient`, `identity_mismatch`, `internal_error`. This is §4.10 **rule 2**, a **MUST**, and stricter than the rule 4 SHOULD fixed here. `specs/trust-task-error/0.1/spec.md:79-90` restates the whole §8.3 table in snake_case. Left alone to keep this diff to one rule.

3. **Un-namespaced, undeclared codes in `specs/keys/*`.** Eight `keys/*` specs have `errorCodes: []` yet their prose names `not_found`, `already_exists`, `invalid_argument`, `failed_precondition` as codes, several citing §8.3 — but none of those four is in §8.3. §8.5 requires extended codes to be namespaced. Re-casing them would paper over the real defect, so they are untouched.

Also unaddressed: `details.reason` enum values are snake_case corpus-wide, the same §4.10 rule 4 drift on a different closed set.

title: chore(specs): re-case extended error code local parts to lowerCamelCase, and lint it (#279)
body:
chore(specs): re-case extended error code local parts to lowerCamelCase, and lint it (#279)

* chore(specs): re-case extended error code local parts to lowerCamelCase per SPEC §4.10

SPEC §4.10 rule 4 requires string values from a closed set that a Trust Task
specification defines — extended error `code` identifiers among them — to be
lowerCamelCase. The registry did not comply: 275 snake_case local parts across
95 spec.md files, out of 717 declarations.

This re-cases the local part only. The namespace keeps its slug spelling, which
is lowercase-hyphenated by §6.1 and explicitly out of §4.10's scope (rule 6).

Scope, and what is deliberately left alone:

* 80 draft specs are amended in place. §5.2's narrower within-draft rule is not
  merely permissive here, it is mandatory: "an editorial or normalization change
  to a draft artifact — re-casing an enumerated value or member name into
  conformance with §4.10 — MUST be made in place, errata-style, within the
  existing version, and MUST NOT mint a new version."

* 15 retired specs keep their 48 snake_case codes. §5.3 freezes a retired
  specification's schema and prose at the moment of retirement, and §5.2 applies
  the strict classification from candidate onward, under which a re-cased value
  is a breaking change requiring a MAJOR increment. Retired is terminal, so
  there is no conforming way to mint that increment — and retired specs exist
  "to keep already-issued documents verifiable", which re-casing would defeat.
  Every one of the 15 declares a supersededBy successor that is already
  lowerCamelCase.

* details.reason enum values are untouched. vault/list declares a code named
  cursor_invalid and also a details.reason enum member spelled "cursor_invalid";
  they are different closed sets and only the code is re-cased here. The enums
  are their own §4.10 rule 4 drift and want their own change.

* Bare, un-namespaced code references in prose are re-cased only where the same
  specification declares that code. References to framework standard codes and
  to codes declared nowhere are left as they are; both are separate defects.

One consequence worth stating: did-management:unknown_domain is a family
namespaced code shared by 26 specs, 21 draft and 5 retired. The draft ones
become did-management:unknownDomain and the retired ones do not, so both
spellings are live in the registry until the retired specs age out. SPEC §8.5's
own non-normative example already names this code as did-management:unknownDomain.

112 files changed: 90 spec.md, 21 payload/shared schema JSON, 1 CONVENTIONS.md.
452 string replacements, no net line change. Generated bindings are unaffected —
no codegen path reads errorCodes.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore(specs): fail the build on an error code local part that is not lowerCamelCase

The rename in the previous commit is only half the work. Nothing forced §4.10
rule 4 on extended error codes — the meta-schema's `code` pattern accepts both
casings deliberately — which is how 275 snake_case local parts accumulated
across 95 specs without a red build. This is the part that keeps them from
coming back.

The rule checks the local part only, strictly as /^[a-z][a-zA-Z0-9]*$/, which
rejects snake_case, kebab-case, SCREAMING_CASE and PascalCase together. The
namespace is not checked: it is a slug, lowercase-hyphenated by §6.1 and put
out of §4.10's scope by rule 6. checkErrorCodeNamespaces already covers the
namespace against §8.5, so the two sit next to each other in the loop and
between them cover both halves of a code.

Unlike the Security & Privacy lint, this one ships as a hard failure rather
than a warning behind an allowlist. That lint is a warning because all 349
specs fail it, so an error would mean a permanently red build. Here the corpus
was taken to zero offenders in the commit before this one, so a failure costs
nothing today and is the only thing that actually holds the line.

There is no allowlist file. The single exception — the 48 codes frozen in 15
retired specs by §5.3 — is derived from `status` in front matter rather than
enumerated by hand, so it cannot rot into a list of things nobody rechecks, and
it is counted on every build:

  Error code casing: 682/730 extended code(s) are lowerCamelCase;
  48 frozen in 15 retired spec(s) (§5.3 — exempt, not debt), 0 non-conforming

That frozen count can only shrink. `retired` is terminal and its prose is
frozen, so nothing can join it; an entry leaves only when a spec is deleted. If
the number ever rises, something has re-published a frozen artifact and the
build log says so.

Verified by injecting `vault/list:cursor_invalid` back into a draft spec: the
build fails with exit 1 and names the offending code, the reason, and the
conforming spelling to use.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore(release): regenerate bindings after the error-code re-casing

The generators embed payload.schema.json verbatim, so re-casing a code named
inside 21 schema descriptions drifts the generated modules. The movement is
confined to description text: no generated type, constant or behaviour changes,
because descriptions do not participate in validation. Patch bump on both
libraries accordingly.

Deliberately deferred until #278 had merged, so that PR and this one did not
each regenerate the same files and collide.

  trust-tasks-rs        0.13.0 -> 0.13.1
  @openvtc/trust-tasks  0.14.0 -> 0.14.1

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: fix(specs): correct eleven exposure declarations and harden trust-task-discovery
body:
Eleven specs declared an `exposure` value their own response schema contradicts, and `trust-task-discovery/0.1` justified an OPTIONAL proof with a claim about the transport that is false over the HTTPS binding. Both feed decisions consumers make automatically, so both under-gate something real.

## Why `exposure.discloses` is not decoration

SPEC §7.3 item 14 defines `discloses` as "the sensitivity of data the task returns to the caller", with `secret` meaning confidential material the caller retains — "released credential material" is item 14's own example. §2 then folds `exposure.discloses === 'secret'` into the definition of a *consequential Trust Task*, which is the predicate a delegated-execution consumer gates human approval on, and `checkProofFloor` in `scripts/build-registry.mjs` derives the response's proof floor from the same value. A wrong `discloses` is therefore wrong in three places at once, none of which read the prose.

## Task 1 — ten mis-declared `exposure` values

Every value below was checked against the spec's `$defs.Response`, not against its prose. All ten are `status: draft`, so per SPEC §5.2 they are amended in place; no schema moves, so no new version folder is warranted.

| Spec | Old | New | Response member that proves it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vta/credentials/issue/0.1` | `none` | `secret` | `credential` — REQUIRED, "the issued Verifiable Credential (W3C VC Data Model 2.0), signed by the issuing context's key" |
| `vta/credentials/issue/0.2` | `none` | `secret` | `credential` — REQUIRED via `credentials/_shared/0.2#/$defs/IssuedCredentialBase` |
| `vtc/endorsements/issue/0.1` | `none` | `secret` | `credential` — REQUIRED, "the signed VEC just minted. Present only here" |
| `vtc/relationships/request/0.1` | `none` | `secret` | `vrc` — REQUIRED, "a signed W3C Verifiable Relationship Credential" |
| `vtc/relationships/request/0.2` | `none` | `secret` | `vrc` — REQUIRED, same |
| `vta/memory/list/0.1` | `metadata` | `secret` | `items[].value` — REQUIRED, every free-text memory item in the context |
| `device/register/0.2` | `none` | `metadata` | `binding` — REQUIRED, the whole `DeviceBinding` (deviceId, consumerDid, attestation, keyCustody, capabilities) |
| `device/heartbeat/0.2` | `none` | `metadata` | `queuedOperations[].task` — full Trust Task documents, including a `device/wipe` carrying its operator `reason`; plus `syncHint` |
| `device/set-wake/0.2` | `none` | `metadata` | `triggerPolicy.allowedTriggers` — the DID allowlist permitted to wake the device |
| `push/provision/0.2` | `none` | `metadata` | `policy.allowedTriggers` — the effective DID allowlist the gateway recorded |

Nothing on the list was already correct. The four credential specs are the sharpest case: `vtc/invitations/issue/0.1` already declares `secret` for a response of the same shape (`vic`, a signed Invitation Credential), so the corpus disagreed with itself about identical material.

Each corrected declaration carries the `rationale` item 14 requires, naming the released member rather than restating the value. `actsAsSubject` was left alone everywhere — the two credential-issue specs already declared it `true`.

### One coupled change: `vta/memory/list/0.1` proof requirement

`proofRequirement` moves from a single `OPTIONAL` to `request: OPTIONAL` / `response: REQUIRED`. This is not discretionary. `checkProofFloor` enforces SPEC §7.3 item 8's derived floor — a `discloses: secret` response must declare a REQUIRED proof — and `npm run validate` fails without it. It is also right on the merits: a bulk export of a context's memory should stay attributable to the VTA that released it. The other five `secret` specs already declared REQUIRED on both variants and needed no change.

## Task 2 — `trust-task-discovery/0.1`

The old `proofRequirement: OPTIONAL` was justified by asserting that a discovery exchange happens "between parties that have already authenticated through the transport". `bindings/https/0.2/spec.md` §5 says otherwise about its own binding, in its own words: no end-to-end integrity, re-origination by any TLS-terminating intermediary "possible and undetectable", and a bearer token that authenticates whoever presented it to the terminator rather than whoever composed the document. A discovery response over that binding may have been rewritten in flight.

That matters more than "advisory" suggests, because the response steers everything the discoverer does next — which task it issues, to which party, with which `ext` namespaces attached. It is a redirection primitive in the sense `trust-task-next-step` describes: a refusal that cannot be trusted is ignored, a redirection that cannot be trusted is followed.

- **`proofRequirement` OPTIONAL → RECOMMENDED**, with the false justification replaced. RECOMMENDED rather than REQUIRED because the exchange is consumed in-band and retained by nobody, so the SPEC §4.7.1 condition that makes a proof mandatory does not arise.
- **New discoverer rule:** MUST NOT act on a discovery response whose origin it can authenticate neither in-band (via `proof`) nor from the transport — mirroring `trust-task-next-step` consumer rule 3, for the same reason it exists there.
- **`requiredExt` is stated to be untrusted.** It lets a responder tell producers to attach a vendor `ext` namespace to every document of a type, carried on a message that may be unproven. It now MUST NOT cause a producer to send data it would not otherwise send; a producer that cannot populate the namespace under its own policy declines rather than gathers.
- **`patterns` gains `maxItems: 16`.** It was unbounded, and every entry is matched against every published slug on an unauthenticated request. Parser hardening in the manner of SPEC §10.2, not a capability limit — `*` already returns everything, so a discoverer wanting more asks for that and filters locally.
- **`exposure.discloses` `none` → `metadata`**, the eleventh mis-declaration: the response enumerates every spec the responder implements, which the spec's own Privacy considerations already call "useful for an attacker fingerprinting deployments".

## New lint

`scripts/lib/disclosure-floor.mjs`, hooked into `scripts/build-registry.mjs`: a response schema that reaches a member named `credential`, `vc`, `vp`, `vrc` or `value` — through its own `properties` or through any `$ref`, including one into a shared schema in another directory — cannot declare `discloses: none`.

The `$ref` following is the load-bearing part. `vta/credentials/issue/0.2` reaches `credential` only through `credentials/_shared/0.2#/$defs/IssuedCredentialBase`, so a lint reading the response schema literally would have missed the case that motivated it.

Shipped as a warning with a `TT_STRICT_DISCLOSURE=1` switch, in the same shape as the Security & Privacy lint of #273 — **but the allowlist is empty**. Against the pre-fix tree it reports exactly the five specs this PR corrects and nothing else; against the corrected tree it reports zero across all 349. There is no debt to carry, so flipping the default from `warn` to `fail` is a one-line change whenever the maintainers want it, with no spec rewrites first. It deliberately does not guess between `metadata` and `secret` — `value` alone covers both a free-text memory item and a config echo, and that judgement belongs to the author; what the lint can tell is that neither is `none`.

## Generated bindings — NOT regenerated here

Left deliberately, per the scope of this change. Two things in this PR move generated output, and `codegen-drift` in `rust.yml` will be red until `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` and `npm run build-ts-bindings` are re-run and committed:

1. **`vta/memory/list/0.1` response `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` flips `false` → `true`.** `read_proof_required_flag` in `trust-tasks-codegen/src/main.rs` tests `s == "REQUIRED"` per variant, so only the `Response` impl is affected — the request impl keeps the trait default. Per `CLAUDE.md`, a consumer that starts rejecting proofless documents it used to accept is a **breaking** change to the library, so this wants the leading-component bump and the six-crate `trust-tasks-rs` requirement update described there, not a patch.
2. **`trust-task-discovery/0.1` `maxItems: 16`.** The generated Rust embeds each payload schema verbatim in doc comments, so any schema edit produces drift regardless of whether the emitted types change.

Everything else in this PR is inert to codegen: `exposure` is not read by `trust-tasks-codegen` at all (no `discloses` / `actsAsSubject` reference anywhere in it), and `trust-task-discovery`'s OPTIONAL → RECOMMENDED does **not** move a constant, since `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` is only overridden on `REQUIRED` and both OPTIONAL and RECOMMENDED leave the trait default `false` in place. Verified by reading `read_proof_required_flag` and the const-emission site rather than by regenerating.

No ceremony references any of these eleven specs, so no `ceremonies/*/ceremony.json` aggregate `exposure` declaration needs revisiting.

## Verification

```
$ npm run validate
Trust Tasks build (validate-only)
  Security & Privacy: 0/349 spec(s) carry the section and all four sub-headings; 349 allowlisted as pre-existing debt, 0 not allowlisted
  Exposure floor: 0 spec(s) declare exposure.discloses: none while returning released material
Validated 349 specs, indexed 65 shared schemas.

$ npm run build
Validated 349 specs, indexed 65 shared schemas.
  wrote website/assets/tasks.generated.js
  wrote website/registry.json
  ...
Done.
```

Both pass. The remaining warnings are the pre-existing set present on `main` at `8fe33cd` — the two nested-slug layout notes, the unparseable illustrative JSON block, the Security & Privacy backlog, and the eight `$defs.Response` closure warnings — byte-identical before and after this branch. No `errorCodes:` block, `trust-tasks-*` crate, or `SPEC.md` was touched.

title: fix(specs): correct eleven exposure declarations and harden trust-task-discovery (#278)
body:
fix(specs): correct eleven exposure declarations and harden trust-task-discovery (#278)

* fix(specs): declare the credentials and data ten tasks actually return

SPEC §7.3 item 14 defines `exposure.discloses` as the sensitivity of data a
task returns to the caller, and §2 folds `discloses: secret` into the
definition of a *consequential Trust Task* — the predicate a delegated-execution
consumer gates human approval on. Ten specs declared a value their own response
schema contradicts, so each under-gated a disclosure that really happens.

Verified against each spec's `$defs.Response`, not against its prose:

  vta/credentials/issue/0.1   none     -> secret    response requires `credential`
  vta/credentials/issue/0.2   none     -> secret    IssuedCredentialBase requires `credential`
  vtc/endorsements/issue/0.1  none     -> secret    response requires `credential` (the VEC)
  vtc/relationships/request/0.1 none   -> secret    response requires `vrc`
  vtc/relationships/request/0.2 none   -> secret    response requires `vrc`
  vta/memory/list/0.1         metadata -> secret    response requires `items[].value`
  device/register/0.2         none     -> metadata  response requires `binding` (DeviceBinding)
  device/heartbeat/0.2        none     -> metadata  `queuedOperations[].task`, `syncHint`
  device/set-wake/0.2         none     -> metadata  `triggerPolicy.allowedTriggers`
  push/provision/0.2          none     -> metadata  `policy.allowedTriggers`

The four credential specs are the sharpest case: `vtc/invitations/issue/0.1`
already declares `secret` for a response of the same shape, so the corpus
disagreed with itself about identical material.

Each corrected declaration carries the `rationale` item 14 requires, naming the
member that is released rather than restating the value.

vta/memory/list/0.1 additionally moves `proofRequirement` from a single
`OPTIONAL` to `request: OPTIONAL` / `response: REQUIRED`. That is not a
discretionary change: SPEC §7.3 item 8's derived floor, enforced by
checkProofFloor in scripts/build-registry.mjs, requires a REQUIRED response
proof wherever `discloses: secret`, and the reasoning holds on its own — a bulk
export of a context's memory should stay attributable to the VTA that released
it. The other five `secret` specs already declared REQUIRED on both variants.

No wire format moves and no schema changes, so per SPEC §5.2 these are amended
in place; all ten are `status: draft`.

`npm run validate` and `npm run build` pass with no new warnings.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec(discovery): raise proof to RECOMMENDED and stop treating the response as trusted

`trust-task-discovery/0.1` declared `proofRequirement: OPTIONAL` on the
justification that a discovery exchange happens "between parties that have
already authenticated through the transport". That is false over the HTTPS
binding, whose own §5 security profile records that it provides no end-to-end
integrity, that re-origination by any TLS-terminating intermediary is "possible
and undetectable", and that a bearer token authenticates whoever presented it to
the terminator rather than whoever composed the document. A discovery response
arriving over that binding may have been rewritten in flight with nothing
in-band to show it.

That matters more here than the "advisory" framing suggests. The response steers
everything the discoverer does next — which task it issues, to which party, with
which `ext` namespaces attached — so it is a redirection primitive of exactly the
kind `trust-task-next-step` describes, where a refusal that cannot be trusted is
ignored but a redirection that cannot be trusted is followed.

  * `proofRequirement` OPTIONAL -> RECOMMENDED, with the false transport claim
    replaced. RECOMMENDED rather than REQUIRED because the exchange is consumed
    in-band and retained by nobody, so the SPEC §4.7.1 condition that makes a
    proof mandatory does not arise. This does not move any generated constant:
    read_proof_required_flag in trust-tasks-codegen tests `s == "REQUIRED"`, so
    OPTIONAL and RECOMMENDED both leave Payload::IS_PROOF_REQUIRED at its `false`
    trait default.

  * A discoverer **MUST NOT** act on a response whose origin it can authenticate
    neither in-band nor from the transport — mirroring trust-task-next-step
    consumer rule 3, for the same reason it exists there.

  * `requiredExt` is stated to be untrusted. It lets a responder tell producers to
    attach a vendor `ext` namespace to every document of a type, on a message that
    may be unproven; it now MUST NOT cause a producer to send data it would not
    otherwise send. A producer that cannot populate the namespace under its own
    policy declines rather than gathers.

  * `patterns` gains `maxItems: 16`. It was unbounded, and every entry is matched
    against every published slug on an unauthenticated request. Parser hardening
    in the manner of SPEC §10.2, not a capability limit: `*` already returns
    everything, so a discoverer wanting more asks for that and filters locally.

  * `exposure.discloses` none -> metadata. The response enumerates every spec the
    responder implements, which the spec's own Privacy considerations already call
    "useful for an attacker fingerprinting deployments" — a capability enumeration
    is what `metadata` names.

`status: draft`, so amended in place per SPEC §5.2.

NOTE: `maxItems` is a payload.schema.json change and the Rust bindings embed each
payload schema in doc comments, so `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` and
`npm run build-ts-bindings` must be re-run before this merges. Left unregenerated
here deliberately; see the PR body.

`npm run validate` and `npm run build` pass with no new warnings.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* build(specs): lint a discloses:none declaration against the response it describes

The exposure corrections in this branch were all found by hand, and the sibling
inconsistency that gave them away — `vtc/invitations/issue/0.1` declaring
`secret` while `vtc/endorsements/issue/0.1` declared `none` for a response of the
same shape — is exactly the kind a machine finds better than a reviewer.

Adds scripts/lib/disclosure-floor.mjs: a response schema that reaches a member
named `credential`, `vc`, `vp`, `vrc` or `value`, through its own `properties` or
through any `$ref` including one into a shared schema in another directory,
cannot declare `exposure.discloses: none`. SPEC §7.3 item 14 reserves `none` for
"an acknowledgement or a determination only", which no such response is.

The `$ref` following is the load-bearing part: `vta/credentials/issue/0.2` reaches
`credential` only through `credentials/_shared/0.2#/$defs/IssuedCredentialBase`,
so a lint that read the response schema literally would have missed the case that
motivated it.

Shipped as a warning with a `TT_STRICT_DISCLOSURE=1` switch, in the same shape as
the Security & Privacy lint of #273 — but the allowlist is EMPTY. Run against the
pre-fix tree it reports exactly the five specs this branch corrected and nothing
else; run against the corrected tree it reports zero across all 349. There is no
debt to carry, so a maintainer wanting CI to hold the line can flip the default
from `warn` to `fail` without rewriting a single spec first.

It deliberately does not guess between `metadata` and `secret`. `value` alone
covers both a free-text memory item and a config echo, and that judgement belongs
to the spec author; what the lint can tell is that neither of them is `none`.

`npm run validate` and `npm run build` pass; the new summary line reports
"Exposure floor: 0 spec(s)".

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore(release): regenerate bindings and cut 0.13.0 for the proof-requirement flip

Correcting vta/memory/list/0.1's exposure.discloses from metadata to secret
engages the registry's proof floor: a response that releases secret material
must be attributable. The generated Response impl's IS_PROOF_REQUIRED flips to
true, so a consumer now rejects an unproofed response it previously accepted.
Behaviour changed against an unchanged wire format, which under the rules at
the top of trust-tasks-rs/CHANGELOG.md the library version has to say so.

Only that one declaration moves a constant. The other ten exposure corrections
and the trust-task-discovery hardening are declaration-and-prose only; the
discovery patterns bound at 16 items is reflected in the regenerated modules
but flips nothing.

Moving the leading component carries the six dependent crates, as in #274:

  trust-tasks-rs                0.12.1 -> 0.13.0
  trust-tasks-https             0.13.0 -> 0.14.0
  trust-tasks-didcomm           0.13.0 -> 0.14.0
  trust-tasks-didcomm-v1        0.12.0 -> 0.13.0
  trust-tasks-proof             0.11.0 -> 0.12.0
  trust-tasks-tsp               0.12.0 -> 0.13.0
  trust-tasks-capability-client 0.12.0 -> 0.13.0
  @openvtc/trust-tasks          0.13.1 -> 0.14.0

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: feat(https): keep the SPEC §7.2 item 11 duplicate-execution record, on by default (#277)
body:
feat(https): keep the SPEC §7.2 item 11 duplicate-execution record, on by default (#277)

The HTTPS server runs its own §7.2 pipeline and never reaches
consume_inbound, so trust-tasks-rs 0.12.0's ReplayGuard and freshness bound
never applied to it: an HTTPS deployment executed a captured — or merely
re-delivered — request body as many times as it arrived, and a different
document under a reused id was executed rather than refused with idConflict.
The binding spec said 'Freshness / replay: None' and left the obligation
unnamed.

The claim now sits at the validated -> accepted transition: after validation,
attribution, the DID-method pre-screen and proof verification, immediately
before dispatch. Claiming earlier would burn the id of every document the
server then refuses. Verdicts are disposed of per §7.2: a recorded response is
returned to a duplicate, an in-flight duplicate gets 202, a duplicate with
nothing recorded gets 204, a conflict gets idConflict, and a guard error fails
closed to unavailable/retryable without executing. A refusal or panic
downstream of the claim releases it.

FreshnessPolicy::consequential is the default and its record_expiry supplies
retain_until, because §7.2 makes the acceptance window and the record's
retention one bound.

Also replaces the two format!("{e}") renderings of serde_json errors with
RejectReason::malformed_from_serde, which 0.12.0 exported for this: the
deserializer's Display spells the member path and byte offset onto the wire.

Breaking (0.13.0): both defaults change what a consumer observes.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: feat(didcomm,didcomm-v1,tsp): absorb a mediator redelivery instead of executing the task twice (#276)
body:
feat(didcomm,didcomm-v1,tsp): absorb a mediator redelivery instead of executing the task twice (#276)

* feat(didcomm): absorb a mediator redelivery instead of executing the task twice

SPEC §7.2 item 11 is unconditional for a consequential Trust Task, and
binding didcomm/0.2 §6 records that this transport guarantees nothing about
freshness and that a mediator may re-deliver at will. trust-tasks-rs 0.12.0
shipped the record and wired it into consume_inbound; this binding stopped at
unpack_trust_task and left every consumer to assemble the rest, so no
deployment over DIDComm enforced item 11.

DidcommConsumer is that path with the record and the freshness bound already
on. receive/receive_from unpack and run the guarded pipeline; consume applies
it to a document opened by an agent this crate does not drive. Every verdict
of the Disposition of a duplicate paragraph is honoured: the prior response is
returned without re-dispatching, an in-flight duplicate reports the running
execution rather than starting another, a differing document under a reused id
is idConflict, and a guard that cannot answer fails closed as unavailable with
retryable true.

The record is keyed on the document id, never on the DIDComm @id, thid or
pthid. §7.2 forbids the substitution and this transport is why: a redelivery
is a fresh DIDComm message carrying the same document, so it arrives with a
new @id. tests/replay.rs asserts the two envelopes' @ids differ before feeding
both through the path, then asserts the handler ran once.

Defaulting the record on changes what a consumer observes — an undated
document, and a second copy of one already executed, are now refused — so the
leading component moves. without_replay_record is the documented opt-out.

Binding didcomm/0.2 §6.1 names the mechanism the section previously left as an
unattributed consumer obligation.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(didcomm-v1): absorb a mediator redelivery instead of executing the task twice

Binding didcomm-v1/0.2 §6 records this transport's freshness guarantee as
None, and Aries store-and-forward mediation may hold a message and re-deliver
it at any later time. SPEC §7.2 item 11 is therefore the only thing standing
between a queued redelivery and a second grant, and 0.11.0 shipped a CHANGELOG
saying a ReplayGuard remained to be wired rather than wiring one.

DidcommV1Consumer is the inbound path with the record and the freshness bound
already on. receive takes an UnpackResult, applies the authenticated-sender
gate, the §2/§2.3 carriage gate, the attachment lookup and the ~thread
cross-check exactly as unpack_trust_task does, then runs consume_inbound over
the document; consume applies the same pipeline to a document an Aries
framework's own delivery loop extracted. Every verdict of the Disposition of a
duplicate paragraph is honoured, including the fail-closed unavailable on a
guard that cannot answer.

The record is keyed on the document id, never on the v1 message @id or the
~thread decorator. MessageV1's own documentation makes the point — the @id is
the transport identifier, with a different lifetime — and MessageV1::new mints
a fresh UUID for every message, which is exactly what a mediator forwarding a
queued message emits. ~thread cannot substitute either: the §3.1 omit rule
means a document whose correlator is not RFC 0008-shaped travels with no thid
at all.

Defaulting the record on changes what a consumer observes, so the leading
component moves. without_replay_record is the documented opt-out.

Binding didcomm-v1/0.2 §6.1 names the mechanism the section previously left as
an unattributed consumer obligation.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(tsp): absorb a re-forwarded message instead of executing the task twice

Binding tsp/0.1 §7 records that TSP data messages do not inherently prevent
replay, and §5.2's routed and nested carriage puts intermediaries on the path,
each free to hold and re-forward the sealed inner message. SPEC §7.2 item 11
is therefore the only thing standing between a re-forward and a second grant,
and 0.11.0 shipped a CHANGELOG saying a ReplayGuard remained to be wired
rather than wiring one.

TspConsumer is the inbound path with the record and the freshness bound
already on. receive opens the seal under every rule unpack_trust_task applies
and then runs consume_inbound over the document; consume applies the same
pipeline to a document another TSP stack unsealed. Every verdict of the
Disposition of a duplicate paragraph is honoured, including the fail-closed
unavailable on a guard that cannot answer, and including the fire-and-forget
case §6 describes, where silence is the correct disposition rather than an
error.

The record is keyed on the document id and not on the envelope. On this
transport the point is stark: sealing the same document again yields an
envelope sharing no bytes with the first, because TSP derives fresh ephemeral
material per message. There is nothing about the envelope a record could key
on and still absorb a re-send, and tests/replay.rs asserts exactly that before
feeding both envelopes through the path and asserting the handler ran once.

Defaulting the record on changes what a consumer observes, so the leading
component moves. without_replay_record is the documented opt-out.

Binding tsp/0.1 §7.1 names the mechanism the freshness bullet previously left
as an unattributed SHOULD.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(capability-client): make a changed request mint a fresh id instead of reusing one

This crate is a producer, and the producer half of SPEC §7.2 item 11 is §8.4:
a retry is a bit-for-bit identical resend. As of trust-tasks-rs 0.12.0 there
is a consumer that enforces it, and as of this release the DIDComm and TSP
bindings keep that record on by default — so the two ways of sending a request
again are now genuinely different operations, and getting them confused is an
idConflict from every consumer this client reaches.

The audit found the builders already correct: build_document, and therefore
every family builder over it, mints a fresh urn:uuid id and stamps issuedAt on
every call, so a caller that rebuilds has always been making a new attempt.
The gap was the other intent — re-sending a document already built and
possibly signed — for which the crate offered nothing, leaving a caller to
re-stamp and re-sign under the old id, which is exactly the document item 11
now refuses.

new_attempt closes that: same addressing, type and payload under a fresh id
and a fresh issuedAt, with the proof dropped because it committed to the old
id. Its documentation states the correlation consequence — where the previous
request opened its own exchange, §4.9 names that exchange by the document id,
so a new attempt opens a new one and the caller must hold the new correlation
thread.

A test drives all three cases (identical resend, reused id with altered
content, new_attempt) through the real InMemoryReplayGuard rather than
restating the rule in prose.

The leading component moves to keep the crate in step with the behavioural
break its siblings ship in the same release: the API addition is additive, but
a producer built against 0.11 will start meeting idConflict, and issuedAt is
now required by the bindings' default freshness policy.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* docs(bindings): make the inbound module docs reachable under a warnings-denying rustdoc

RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc failed on all three binding crates: the
module-level explanation of why the record is keyed on the document id was
linked with [module documentation](self) from a public type, and in the
DIDComm and TSP crates the inbound module was private, so rustdoc refused a
public item linking to a private one. It was also the wrong outcome
editorially - the reasoning was written and then rendered nowhere.

The inbound module is now public in all three crates (the re-exports at the
crate root are unchanged), and the redundant explicit link targets rustdoc
flagged alongside it are removed.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: fix(vta)!: --internal creates an internal key
body:
`pnm keys create --internal` printed a full non-recoverable-key warning, made
the operator type `i understand this key cannot be recovered`, and then
**created an ordinary seed-derived key** — one that *is* recoverable from the
mnemonic, *is* included in backups, and *is* exportable. The operator was told
the opposite of what happened.

## Three fields, dropped in the middle

`CreateKeyRequest` carries `internal`, `key_id` and `derivation_path`. The CLI
sets them. `VtaClient::create_key` built its wire body like this:

```rust
let body = CreateKeyBody {
    internal: None,                                       // hardcoded
    derivation_path: req.derivation_path.clone().unwrap_or_default(),  // "" for absent
    …                                                     // key_id never read
};
```

`req.internal` and `req.key_id` were never read. The operation layer was always
correct — `CreateKeyParams::derivation_path` is an `Option` that auto-derives,
and `internal` short-circuits to a CSPRNG key that records no path. Only the
wire types disagreed.

## And it could not have worked anyway

Even with the flag forwarded, it failed twice more:

1. **The spine rejected it.** `keys/create/0.1` was `additionalProperties:
   false` with no `internal` member, so the document never reached a handler.
   Fixed upstream in
   [#269](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/269), which
   also added `internal` to `KeyOrigin` — the value that makes the outcome
   *checkable*.
2. **An internal key needs an explicit `key_id`**, having no derivation path to
   be named after, and neither the wire type nor the specification had one.
   Fixed upstream in
   [#275](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/275).

So the capability existed at both ends and was unreachable by three
independent routes.

## What this PR does

- Forwards `internal` and `derivation_path` from the request instead of
  dropping them.
- Makes `CreateKeyBody::derivation_path` an `Option<String>`, matching both the
  specification ("omitting it leaves the choice to the custodian") and the
  operation layer. The old `unwrap_or_default()` sent `""`, which worked only
  because the op reads `""` as absent — a workaround that hid the type error.
- Mints a `key_id` for an internal key **at the trust-task binding**, since
  that binding has no `keyId` member to carry one yet.

### The minted id is a deliberate, temporary deviation

`keyId` is published as of `trust-tasks-rs` **0.12.1**, and this workspace
cannot move to 0.12: `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.19.12 pins `trust-tasks-rs
^0.11` and `vta_sdk::acl_setup` hands it a generated `MediatorAcl`, so two
nodes in one graph fail to compile. The specification says a maintainer that
offers internal keys and receives no `keyId` **SHOULD** reject — I wrote that
text, and this deviates from it, because the alternative is a security feature
that cannot be used at all until an external crate publishes.

The consumer is not left guessing: the id comes back on the response record,
the CLI prints it, and `keys/rename/0.1` can change it. **When the 0.12 bump
lands, take `key_id` from the request and delete the branch** — the comment
says so at the site.

## Tests

`an_internal_key_is_actually_internal` asserts `origin == "internal"`. That is
the check the CLI already made and that always silently failed, and it is the
only reliable signal: a maintainer that ignored the member returns `derived`,
and the two records are otherwise identical.

`a_create_without_a_derivation_path_succeeds` covers the other half, and
creating its context also covers `vta/contexts/create/1.0` — coverage 33 → 34.

## Found on the way, not fixed here

An internal key's record carries `derivationPath: "internal"`. The shared
`KeyRecord` component says that member is the path "the key was derived at,
when `origin` is `derived`", absent otherwise — so a sentinel there claims a
derivation that does not exist. The comment justifying it predates `origin`
gaining an `internal` value, which now carries the fact properly.

Not fixed here because making `derivation_path` an `Option` touches **84
construction sites**. Worth noting that the response-conformance gate *cannot*
catch this: the schema types the member `string`, so a sentinel validates
cleanly. It is a semantic divergence, and only a reader notices — a useful
reminder of where that gate's evidence stops.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings`
- `./scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` — 28 suites green, 0 violations, coverage **34/109**
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

BREAKING CHANGE: `CreateKeyBody::derivation_path` is `Option<String>` and is
omitted when unset instead of sent as `""`. `keys/create/0.1` requests now
carry `internal` when the caller set it.

title: vtc-client-v0.4.0
body:
### Fixed

- **common**: Send the pagination wrapper in camelCase, as the schemas always said ([#1078](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1078))

`Paginated<T>` carried no `rename_all`, so every list task sent `next_cursor`
  and `total_estimate` against published schemas that say `nextCursor` and
  `totalEstimate`. A direct R3.1 violation, and the same casing-drift class as
  #656/#658 — where an empty `allowed_contexts` silently minted a super-admin.

  Nothing caught it because nothing compared the two. The service sent one
  spelling, `vtc-client` mirrored the service rather than the schema, and the
  admin SPA typed its fields from the service too. All three agreed with each
  other and none agreed with the contract. The conformance witness added in
  #1076 is what finally put them side by side.

  Four consumers move together: the wrapper in `vti-common`, `vtc-client`'s
  `Page<T>`, and the `joinRequests` and `members` admin plugins. `audit.tsx`
  reads a `cursor` member of a different shape and is untouched.

title: vta-service-v0.21.0
body:
### Added

- **vta**: Framework 0.5.0 freshness bounds at the dispatch spine ([#1117](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1117))

Framework 0.5.0 Consumer Requirements item 13. A consumer MUST reject a
  document whose `issuedAt` is ahead of its own clock beyond its skew tolerance,
  and one whose `expiresAt` is at or before its `issuedAt`.

  Both are `malformedRequest`, never `expired`, and that distinction is the
  substance of the rule: `expired` names a document that was once acceptable and
  no longer is, so it tells the producer to wait when what it must do is reissue.
  Neither of these was acceptable at any instant.

  The rule makes the duplicate-execution record of item 11 implementable. That
  record is bounded only if every accepted document can be placed in a window,
  and both shapes escape every window while still looking acceptable: a future
  `issuedAt` sits in a window that has not opened and re-enters it as the clock
  advances, and an `expiresAt` at or before issuance describes an interval that
  never contained an instant.

  This is a stand-in and says so. `trust-tasks-rs` 0.12.0
  (dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#274) ships `FreshnessPolicy` and
  `TrustTask::validate_freshness`, which implement these two rules identically —
  same 60s skew — and add the `max_age` window and the `ReplayGuard` item 11
  needs. The 0.12 bump is blocked on an external crate: `affinidi-messaging-sdk`
  0.19.12 pins `trust-tasks-rs ^0.11` and `vta_sdk::acl_setup` hands it a
  generated `MediatorAcl`, so two nodes in one graph fail to compile with
  `expected MediatorAcl, found a different MediatorAcl`. The four sibling
  trust-tasks crates have published 0.12-compatible releases; the messaging SDK
  has not.

  The module doc names the blocker and the replacement call, and the tests are
  written against behaviour rather than this implementation, so they survive the
  swap unchanged and are the check that it was faithful.

- **app-state**: A third store for versioned, namespaced application state ([#1051](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1051))

Applications built on a VTA have had nowhere to keep versioned metadata.
  Adds `vta/app-state/{get,put,list,delete,get-many,put-many}/1.0` — a store
  beside the secrets vault and the credential vault, for JSON an application
  owns and the VTA does not interpret.

  Records are addressed `(contextId, namespace, key)`. The namespace scopes one
  application so several tools can share a context without colliding, and is the
  seam a per-namespace grant would later use — which is why it is part of the
  address rather than a prefix convention on the key. In 1.0 a namespace is
  collision avoidance and NOT a trust boundary: an application with write access
  to a context reaches every namespace in it, and the `put` and `delete` specs
  say so normatively. Isolation means separate contexts.

  Deliberately not built on `vta/memory/*`. `MemoryItem` is `{key, value}` with
  nothing to hang a precondition on, and its `list` returns the whole context —
  but the argument that settles it is that "forget everything" has to stay a safe
  thing to ask an agent, which it cannot be if account state lives there.

  Three properties are why this is a store rather than a field on an existing one.

  **One counter per `(contextId, namespace)`, not per record.** A record's
  `version` is the counter value its most recent write took, so one number is
  simultaneously the optimistic-concurrency token `expectedVersion` compares
  against and the watermark `sinceVersion` compares against. A per-record counter
  serves the first but cannot serve the second — two records' counters are not
  comparable, so no single number means "everything after this point" — and would
  have forced a second sequence kept consistent by hand. The cost is that a
  record's version jumps by whatever its neighbours consumed, which the wire
  contract states: versions are opaque and monotonic, never an edit count.

  **A failed precondition returns the current version AND value.** A bare
  rejection obliges a re-read, and the re-read races the next write; the pattern
  has no fixed point under contention. Returning the winner's view removes the
  race rather than narrowing it, and the spec makes it normative.

  **Delete leaves a versioned tombstone, and the tombstones are reaped.** Without
  one, a consumer pulling from a watermark learns of every create and update and
  never of a deletion, so deleted records resurrect on its next rebuild.
  Retention is `app_state.tombstone_retention_days` (default 30, matching the
  vault's `grace_days`) — a destructive window is an operator's choice, not a
  constant — and `list` advertises the configured value, since a consumer
  schedules against that number. The sweeper runs from the storage thread beside
  the ACL/consent/vault sweepers.

  The sweeper reaps a *prefix*, not a set: each namespace walks its tombstones in
  version order and stops at the first still inside the window. Reaping a later
  tombstone while leaving an earlier one would make the reap watermark
  unstateable — no single number would describe what survives, which is precisely
  what `watermarkTooOld` has to be able to say. `0` days disables reaping, and
  that is enforced at the call site rather than as a zero cutoff, which would mean
  the opposite.

  Version reservation is fsynced and re-seals the TEE integrity manifest, for the
  reason `vti_common::store::counter` gives for BIP-32 counters: a counter
  surviving only in the journal buffer can be re-derived after a crash and reissue
  a used value. Here a reused version means two records collide on one `appv:`
  index key, so one disappears from the change feed and every incremental consumer
  misses that change permanently, silently. A batch reserves a block and pays one
  fsync rather than N; writes that then fail leave gaps, which are safe and
  tested.

  Retry safety: reads are `ReadOnly`, `delete` is `RetrySafe` (a second delete
  finds a tombstone and deliberately takes no new version, so a watcher sees
  nothing), and `put`/`put-many` are `Keyed` — a `put` without `expectedVersion`
  does not converge, and the class is per URI, not per payload.

  Blobs are deliberately out of scope in 1.0; adding a `blobRef` is additive.

  Concurrency is a process-local lock per namespace, not a store-layer
  compare-and-swap. fjall takes an exclusive database lock so two processes cannot
  share a store, and the vsock protocol has no atomic opcode — its
  `insert_if_absent`/`swap` are already non-atomic fallbacks. A CAS today would be
  atomic exactly where the lock suffices and a warn-and-fallback exactly where it
  would need to be real. Recorded in the design note with what would change that.

  Schemas published upstream as trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#252 and #253;
  this depends on the released trust-tasks-rs 0.11.2, pinned to a minimum patch so
  an older resolve fails as a stale dependency rather than as unspecced URIs.
  Conformance witnesses cover all six URIs, so nothing enters
  `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`.

- **audit**: Make the audit destination a deployment choice, not a protocol one ([#1049](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1049))

`AuditLogEntry` is `{id, timestamp, action, actor, resource, outcome, channel,
  contextId, detail}` — no signature, no hash chain. The log corroborates what
  happened; it cannot prove it, and a compromised VTA can rewrite its own history.
  The canonical `AuditEnvelope` already names the members that would change that
  (`prevHash`, `entryHash`, `schemaVersion`) and records why this maintainer omits
  them: its log is flat and unchained.

  This does not add tamper-evidence, deliberately. It adds the seam, so an
  operator who needs a stronger guarantee implements one — an append-only file, a
  transparency log, a blockchain anchor, a hash chain filling in those three
  members — without the VTA committing to any scheme. Closes #1031.

title: fix(vta)!: --internal creates an internal key (#1118)
body:
fix(vta)!: --internal creates an internal key (#1118)

`pnm keys create --internal` printed a non-recoverable-key warning, required
the operator to type "i understand this key cannot be recovered", and then
created an ordinary seed-derived key — recoverable from the mnemonic, included
in backups, exportable. The operator was told the opposite of what happened.

`CreateKeyRequest` carries `internal`, `key_id` and `derivation_path`; the CLI
set them and `VtaClient::create_key` built its wire body with `internal: None`
hardcoded, `key_id` never read, and `derivation_path` as `unwrap_or_default()`
— `""` for absent, which worked only because the operation layer reads `""` as
absent. The operation layer was always right: `derivation_path` is an `Option`
there that auto-derives, and `internal` short-circuits to a CSPRNG key.

It could not have worked even with the flag forwarded. The spine rejected the
document, because `keys/create/0.1` was `additionalProperties: false` with no
`internal` member (fixed upstream in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#269, which also added
`internal` to `KeyOrigin` — the value that makes the outcome checkable); and an
internal key needs an explicit `key_id`, which neither the wire type nor the
specification had (dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#275).

Forwards `internal` and `derivation_path`, makes `CreateKeyBody`'s
`derivation_path` optional to match the specification and the operation layer,
and mints a `key_id` for an internal key at the trust-task binding, which has
no `keyId` member to carry one yet.

That minting is a deliberate, temporary deviation from a SHOULD in the
specification, taken because `keyId` needs trust-tasks-rs 0.12.1 and this
workspace cannot move to 0.12: `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.19.12 pins
`trust-tasks-rs ^0.11` and `vta_sdk::acl_setup` hands it a generated
`MediatorAcl`, so two nodes in one graph fail to compile. The id is returned on
the record and `keys/rename/0.1` can change it; the site says to delete the
branch when the bump lands.

`an_internal_key_is_actually_internal` asserts `origin == "internal"` — the
check the CLI already made and that always silently failed.

BREAKING CHANGE: `CreateKeyBody::derivation_path` is `Option<String>` and is
omitted when unset instead of sent as `""`. `keys/create/0.1` requests now
carry `internal` when the caller set it.

Refs #1059

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: vti-webauthn-v0.2.0
body:
### Chore

- **deps**: Bring every dependency to latest, collapsing two duplicates ([#1055](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1055))

`cargo outdated` reported 13 direct dependencies behind and `cargo update`
  had 36 compatible updates waiting. Both are now clear: `cargo outdated`
  reports "All dependencies are up to date".

  Two of these were not cosmetic.

  **p256 was duplicated in the build.** Our crates declared `0.13` while
  `affinidi-crypto` — reached through `affinidi-data-integrity` and the TDK —
  already pulled `0.14`, so the graph carried two copies of a curve
  implementation. The lock now holds a single `p256 0.14.0`. The bump brings
  `elliptic-curve` 0.14 and `ecdsa` 0.17, which rename the SEC1 family:
  `EncodedPoint` -> `Sec1Point`, `From/ToEncodedPoint` -> `From/ToSec1Point`.
  Renamed across `vta-keys`, `vta-service` and `vti-webauthn`.

  **tokio-tungstenite was load-bearing, not incidental.** `vta-mobile-core`
  depends on it solely as a feature enabler: iOS has no native trust store, so
  `rustls-tls-webpki-roots` has to be on graph-wide or the mediator WebSocket
  fails with "no native root CA certificates found". Features unify per major
  version, so the declaration only works while it matches the version
  `affinidi-messaging-sdk` pulls — and the SDK moved to 0.30 in this refresh.
  Updating everything *except* this one would have stranded the enabler and
  broken iOS `wss://` silently.

  The rest:

  - `rcgen` 0.13 -> 0.14 (dev). `signed_by` takes an `Issuer` rather than a
    `(certificate, key)` pair, and `self_signed` borrows instead of consuming.
    The mdoc IACA test helper builds its issuer with `Issuer::from_params`,
    which is also a more direct statement of what it wanted.
  - `syn` 2 -> 3 (dev). No source change; syn 3 was already in the graph via
    `trust-tasks-rs`.
  - `rmcp` 1.7 -> 3.1.4. Two majors, one rename: `Content` -> `ContentBlock`.
    The `#[tool_router]` / `#[tool_handler]` macro surface the crate is built
    on is unchanged.
  - 36 lockfile updates, including `trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.3 (the corrected
    `vta/app-state` error taxonomy from dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#253) and the AWS
    SDK set. `rustls-pemfile`, one of the unmaintained crates `cargo audit`
    flags, drops out of the graph entirely.

  Two deliberate choices where the shortest path was worse:

  `vti-webauthn` keeps parse-then-validate rather than collapsing to the
  one-shot `PublicKey::from_sec1_bytes`. That call merges "malformed SEC1
  encoding" and "valid encoding, point not on the curve" into one error, and
  those say different things to whoever reads the log — a broken client versus
  a point somebody chose.

  BIP-32 P-256 derivation replaces the now-deprecated `FieldBytes::from_slice`
  with `TryFrom` and a real error arm. The input is a fixed 32-byte window of a
  SHA-512 HMAC so it cannot fail, but the length check is now explicit rather
  than resting on a panic inside a deprecated helper.

  Unchanged and still suppressed: the four `cargo audit` advisories ignored in
  `deny.toml`, all transitive through the AWS SDK's hyper 0.14 / rustls 0.21
  path. `cargo deny check advisories` passes.

title: vta-backup-v0.2.0
body:
### Added

- **app-state**: A third store for versioned, namespaced application state ([#1051](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1051))

Applications built on a VTA have had nowhere to keep versioned metadata.
  Adds `vta/app-state/{get,put,list,delete,get-many,put-many}/1.0` — a store
  beside the secrets vault and the credential vault, for JSON an application
  owns and the VTA does not interpret.

  Records are addressed `(contextId, namespace, key)`. The namespace scopes one
  application so several tools can share a context without colliding, and is the
  seam a per-namespace grant would later use — which is why it is part of the
  address rather than a prefix convention on the key. In 1.0 a namespace is
  collision avoidance and NOT a trust boundary: an application with write access
  to a context reaches every namespace in it, and the `put` and `delete` specs
  say so normatively. Isolation means separate contexts.

  Deliberately not built on `vta/memory/*`. `MemoryItem` is `{key, value}` with
  nothing to hang a precondition on, and its `list` returns the whole context —
  but the argument that settles it is that "forget everything" has to stay a safe
  thing to ask an agent, which it cannot be if account state lives there.

  Three properties are why this is a store rather than a field on an existing one.

  **One counter per `(contextId, namespace)`, not per record.** A record's
  `version` is the counter value its most recent write took, so one number is
  simultaneously the optimistic-concurrency token `expectedVersion` compares
  against and the watermark `sinceVersion` compares against. A per-record counter
  serves the first but cannot serve the second — two records' counters are not
  comparable, so no single number means "everything after this point" — and would
  have forced a second sequence kept consistent by hand. The cost is that a
  record's version jumps by whatever its neighbours consumed, which the wire
  contract states: versions are opaque and monotonic, never an edit count.

  **A failed precondition returns the current version AND value.** A bare
  rejection obliges a re-read, and the re-read races the next write; the pattern
  has no fixed point under contention. Returning the winner's view removes the
  race rather than narrowing it, and the spec makes it normative.

  **Delete leaves a versioned tombstone, and the tombstones are reaped.** Without
  one, a consumer pulling from a watermark learns of every create and update and
  never of a deletion, so deleted records resurrect on its next rebuild.
  Retention is `app_state.tombstone_retention_days` (default 30, matching the
  vault's `grace_days`) — a destructive window is an operator's choice, not a
  constant — and `list` advertises the configured value, since a consumer
  schedules against that number. The sweeper runs from the storage thread beside
  the ACL/consent/vault sweepers.

  The sweeper reaps a *prefix*, not a set: each namespace walks its tombstones in
  version order and stops at the first still inside the window. Reaping a later
  tombstone while leaving an earlier one would make the reap watermark
  unstateable — no single number would describe what survives, which is precisely
  what `watermarkTooOld` has to be able to say. `0` days disables reaping, and
  that is enforced at the call site rather than as a zero cutoff, which would mean
  the opposite.

  Version reservation is fsynced and re-seals the TEE integrity manifest, for the
  reason `vti_common::store::counter` gives for BIP-32 counters: a counter
  surviving only in the journal buffer can be re-derived after a crash and reissue
  a used value. Here a reused version means two records collide on one `appv:`
  index key, so one disappears from the change feed and every incremental consumer
  misses that change permanently, silently. A batch reserves a block and pays one
  fsync rather than N; writes that then fail leave gaps, which are safe and
  tested.

  Retry safety: reads are `ReadOnly`, `delete` is `RetrySafe` (a second delete
  finds a tombstone and deliberately takes no new version, so a watcher sees
  nothing), and `put`/`put-many` are `Keyed` — a `put` without `expectedVersion`
  does not converge, and the class is per URI, not per payload.

  Blobs are deliberately out of scope in 1.0; adding a `blobRef` is additive.

  Concurrency is a process-local lock per namespace, not a store-layer
  compare-and-swap. fjall takes an exclusive database lock so two processes cannot
  share a store, and the vsock protocol has no atomic opcode — its
  `insert_if_absent`/`swap` are already non-atomic fallbacks. A CAS today would be
  atomic exactly where the lock suffices and a warn-and-fallback exactly where it
  would need to be real. Recorded in the design note with what would change that.

  Schemas published upstream as trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#252 and #253;
  this depends on the released trust-tasks-rs 0.11.2, pinned to a minimum patch so
  an older resolve fails as a stale dependency rather than as unspecced URIs.
  Conformance witnesses cover all six URIs, so nothing enters
  `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`.



### Fixed

- **vtc**: Follow the spec on every auth response, and close the conformance gate ([#1112](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1112))

* test(vtc)!: make response conformance fail the build

  Until now the layer reported and a green suite was not evidence of
  conformance — #1107's own memory note said to grep the run rather than trust
  the exit code, which is a signal nobody has to obey.

  A violation outside the allowlist now returns 500 with the schema error, so the
  test that provoked it fails on its own status assertion and prints the reason.
  Chosen over panicking in middleware, which surfaces at the call site as a
  transport error and says nothing about which task or why.

  The allowlist is eight `auth/*` tasks with ALLOWED_COUNT asserted beside them —
  the same discipline as KNOWN_DRIFT_COUNT, because the cheapest way to make a
  failing check pass is to add a line to a list nobody watches. An allowlisted
  violation is still reported, pinned by a test: a list that suppressed the
  evidence would mean rediscovering each entry before it could be closed.

  Two existing guards caught mistakes of mine on the first run. The allowlist
  named login/{start,finish}/0.1 where the service binds 0.2 — built from the
  violation output rather than the route mounts — and the manifest guard flagged a
  fake `trusttasks.org/spec/` URI in a new unit test, correctly, since binding
  such a URI asserts the registry serves it.

  Also retargets relationships/{list,graph} to the 0.2s from
  trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#266, and fixes a seeder that wrote
  `seed-{uuid}` into `vrcDigestMultibase` — unique per row, and so a suite
  structurally blind to digest format.

  The VTC family is now clean; every remaining violation is `auth/*`.
