title: feat: rotate the enrolment identity, and stop writing keys to the config
body:
Two corrections, both to things I had built by hand that the stack already solved.

## 1. The grant commands were wrong

`pnm contexts create` takes **`--id` and `--name`**; the printed line had only `--name`. Anybody following it got a clap error — in a ticket, with no way to tell whether the tool or the instruction was broken. Now two correct commands.

## 2. Enrolment minted a *permanent* key

The DID it asked you to paste into a ticket or a chat message stayed a live authenticator forever. That quietly makes the copy-paste channel part of the trust boundary. The config also held that key in plain JSON.

`vti_secrets::IntegrationOnboarding` already packages the right flow — **ephemeral `did:key` → ACL grant → auto-rotate on first connect** — and is what the mediator, PNM and DID-hosting use. Enrolment now drives it rather than re-deriving it:

- **`init`** parks a throwaway key in the session store and prints the grant. The private half never returns into this process, so it cannot reach a log, a config file, or an error message.
- **`connect`** authenticates, and the session store atomically swaps the throwaway for a fresh key, mirrors the ACL entry onto the new DID, and drops the temp one.
- **The config holds no key material** — only which session to open. There is a test asserting that, because it is exactly the kind of thing that regresses quietly.

`setup` routes through the same onboarding, so the same-machine convenience path gets the same rotation rather than being the weaker one. `Identity` collapses to a single session-backed shape and the raw-`did:key` variant is gone.

## Live

```console
$ vta-agent-memory init --vta-did did:webvh:QmWoJD…:webvh.storm.ws:glenn-vta --context agent-memory

This machine minted a temporary identity and needs it authorized.

  temp DID    did:key:z6Mkoqb2y3jbu6zoPDBoYGzA4j34JwsnToSUNqBgh9W7VebT
  vta         did:webvh:QmWoJD…:webvh.storm.ws:glenn-vta
  context     agent-memory

Run these wherever you hold VTA admin — it does not have to be this machine:

  pnm contexts create --id agent-memory --name agent-memory    # skip if it exists
  pnm acl create --did did:key:z6Mkoqb… --role application --contexts agent-memory --label vta-agent-memory

Then, back here:

  vta-agent-memory connect

The temporary DID above is rotated away on that first connect, so it stops
being an authenticator once it has done its job.
```

and the pending file, in full:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "ephemeralDid": "did:key:z6Mkoqb…",
  "vtaDid": "did:webvh:QmWoJD…:webvh.storm.ws:glenn-vta",
  "contextId": "agent-memory",
  "sessionKey": "agent:agent-memory",
  "sessionsDir": "/Users/…/Library/Application Support/vta-agent-memory"
}
```

No key, anywhere.

## Breaking

The config shape changes again. Anyone enrolled before this needs to re-run `init`/`connect` — and should, since their key is sitting in a JSON file.

## Testing

`cargo test` — 85 pass. New coverage: the grant commands match the real `pnm` flags, the grant is never `admin`, session keys are per-context and never collide with `pnm`'s, and neither the pending file nor the config contains key material. Clippy clean.

title: The publish authorization's specified binding is unimplementable on the REST binding
body:
## Summary

`trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#259` (merged) specifies the publish
authorization as bound to **the enclosing Trust Task document's `id`**. The
VTC's REST binding does not carry one, so the merged specification is currently
unimplementable on the route it governs.

This is my own doing and worth stating plainly: I argued for that binding on
the grounds that "every document carries a unique `id` (SPEC §4.3)". That is
true of Trust Task *documents*. It is not true of what this route actually
receives.

## What the route receives

`POST /v1/relationships` takes `PublishBody` — `{vrc, pop}`, a bare payload
(`vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs`). The task URI arrives in a header,
extracted as `TrustTaskHeader(TrustTask)`
(`vti-common/src/trust_task/extractor.rs:34`), where `TrustTask` is a newtype
over a `String` URI (`vti-common/src/trust_task/mod.rs:58`). There is no
document envelope, and therefore no `id`, `issuer`, `recipient` or `issuedAt`.

## What ships today, and how it diverges

The implementation (#1061) binds its authorization to `{type, vrc, aud,
sessionId, issuedAt}`:

- `sessionId` — the authenticated REST session, which is what makes the
  authorization unreplayable by another member
- `aud` — the VTC's own DID
- `issuedAt` — with a freshness window

The merged specification asks for `{type, documentId, vrcDigestMultibase,
proof}`, dropping `aud` and `issuedAt` as duplicative of framework members the
document already carries — members this binding also does not carry.

So the divergence is not one field. A client written to the published schema
cannot publish an edge to this service, and this service's authorization cannot
be described by the published schema.

## Options

1. **Accept a Trust Task document on this route.** The VTC already
   content-negotiates full documents on the auth routes — `/auth/challenge`,
   `/auth/`, `/auth/refresh` each accept a Trust Task document *or* flat JSON
   and respond in kind. Extending that to `relationships/publish` gives the
   route an `id`, `issuer`, `recipient` and `issuedAt`, and the specification
   becomes implementable as written. This is the option that makes the REST
   binding a real Trust Task binding rather than a payload transport, and it
   generalises past this one route.

2. **Bind to something the header binding already has.** There is nothing with
   the right property: the task URI is constant per route, and the session id
   is precisely what the specification declined to standardise.

3. **Revise the specification.** Possible, but it would mean standardising a
   transport-specific binding after the working group accepted a
   transport-neutral one, and I do not think the argument has changed.

I would take option 1, and I would not close this by weakening the schema.

## Note on scope

This is not only about `pop`. If the REST binding never carries a document,
then no VTC route can implement a payload member that references framework
members — and #1059's witness compares payloads against schemas that assume a
document context. Worth deciding once rather than per-task.

Raised from the conformance work in #1059; the `relationships/publish` drift
entry stays recorded until this is resolved.

title: feat(vtc)!: authenticate publishing by the document's own proof (#1088)
body:
feat(vtc)!: authenticate publishing by the document's own proof (#1088)

`POST /v1/relationships` took a bearer token and a bare `{vrc, pop}` body. It
now takes a signed Trust Task document and no token at all.

## Why the bearer went

The specification for the publish authorization binds it to the enclosing
document's `id` (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#259). This route received no
document, so the merged schema was unimplementable on the surface it governed
— #1084. Accepting a document fixes that and supplies the members the schema
assumes: `id` for the binding, `recipient` for the audience, `issuedAt` for
freshness.

Once the document carries a proof, the token answers a question already
answered, and better: a proof is transport-independent and cannot be used by
whoever captured it. Two of the three reasons to keep it dissolved — audience
binding is the document's `recipient`, and rate limiting had no business being
tied to a session in the first place.

What a session gave that a proof cannot is **immediate revocation**. A
signed-out session stops working on the next request; a proof has no such
handle. Publishing is therefore governed by ACL membership rather than session
state, and that is deliberate: a member who has signed out but not been removed
is still a member, and it is not obvious they should be barred from publishing
an edge they hold the key for. Removing them from the community still stops
them immediately, because `is_current_member` reads the ACL live.

## Rate limiting moved to the member

Keyed on an HMAC of the signer, not the address they arrived from — one member
moving between addresses evaded the per-IP governor, while a community behind
one NAT was throttled as a single caller. Hashed for the same reason the audit
writer hashes actors: a counter keyed on raw DIDs is a live register of who is
active here.

It runs after proof verification, so it cannot bound the cost of verification
itself. That stays the governor's job, and the route has moved onto the
governed chain to keep it — the same reason `auth/recognise` lives there, since
both run DID resolution and signature checks on attacker-supplied JSON before
they know who is calling.

The window is per process: N replicas enforce it N times. A sizing property,
stated in the module rather than discovered later.

## One digest, the one the specification names

Every hash in this path was a bare lowercase-hex SHA-256 over a recursive key
sort. That form hard-codes an algorithm into the wire contract, names no base
encoding, and — worse — names no canonicalization a second implementation could
reproduce, so two conforming services could digest the same credential
differently and neither be wrong.

All of them are now RFC 8785 + multihash + base58btc: the stored row, the
idempotency key, the publish authorization, and the VPC authorization.
`canonicalise()` is deleted. Its doc comment argued "we only need a
deterministic form, not a standard one", which was true while the value was
internal and stopped being true when it went into a response.

That in turn made `relationships/publish/0.2` the right version to bind: 0.1
asks for a bare-hex `vrcSha256` this service no longer computes.

## Tests

Both responses are `#response` documents, so the suite asserts the envelope as
well: `threadId` correlation, and issuer/recipient swapping.

Three tests pinned properties that no longer exist and were rewritten one layer
up, where the property moved — replay into another document, a document
addressed to another community, an expired document. The last two are the only
things in the suite that prove `validate_basic` is wired in at all.

Three more were retired with their reasons recorded in place, not deleted
silently: they asserted a session DID differing from the VRC issuer, a
malformed VRC now covered more thoroughly by the catalog-backed shape tests,
and an ordering this change deliberately reverses.

Mutation-tested rather than assumed: neutering the `documentId` binding fails
`rejects_an_authorization_replayed_in_another_document`; accepting an unsigned
document fails `rejects_a_document_with_no_proof`. Both reverted.

BREAKING CHANGE: `POST /v1/relationships` takes a signed Trust Task document
and returns one. It no longer accepts a bearer token, and the task URI it
serves is `relationships/publish/0.2`. Nothing calls this endpoint — verified
across this workspace, `vta-sdk`, `vtc-client` and `openvtc` — so no client
breaks today, but openvtc must sign documents when it starts publishing.

Closes #1084. Refs #1054, #1059, trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#259

title: test(vtc)!: check ingressed credentials against the catalog, and test validators against it too
body:
Closes #1064 (F2) and #1066 (F4) **together**, because either alone reopens the
trap: a shared ingress validator whose tests hand-roll their input validates
the implementation against itself, which is the exact condition that let the
recognition path match `"VerifiableEndorsementCredential"` for its entire life
while nothing has ever issued that type.

## One place decides what a DTG credential is

`credentials::ingress` checks §Common Structure — both required `@context`
entries, `VerifiableCredential` + `DTGCredential`, exactly one concrete subtype
— and classifies through `dtg_credentials::DTGCredentialType`, the same catalog
the issuing side mints from.

- `check_vrc_shape` becomes a call to it.
- **The recognition path gains the check it never had.** It classified on
  `type` alone, so a document carrying the right subtype tag and neither
  `@context` entry was routed as though it were a VEC.

## The tests assert against catalog output, not literals

This is the half that matters. A literal in a test can agree with a literal in
a validator while both disagree with what any client sends — that is not a
hypothetical, it is #1062.

So the guards mint through `new_vrc` / `new_vmc` / `new_vec` and require the
validator to accept the result. **Change the catalog's wire form and they fail;
change a validator away from the catalog and they fail; no literal in the file
can make them pass.**

`test_support::dtg_json` is the sanctioned way for a test to obtain a DTG
credential. Hand-rolled JSON stays correct for malformed-input cases — the
catalog cannot produce a credential missing its own `@context`.

## Each guard was mutation-tested, not assumed

A guard that cannot fail is worth nothing, so I broke each invariant and
confirmed the guard caught it:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| `check_vrc_shape` accepted subtype `Relationship` → `Membership` | round-trip test fails |
| legacy tag re-added to `classify` | refusal test fails |
| DTG context dropped from the recognition fixture | end-to-end holder test fails — with the same 400 #1062 produced |

## Also pinned by name

`VerifiableRecognitionCredential` and the `Verifiable`-prefixed membership and
endorsement tags are refused explicitly. All three were invented in this repo,
none is a DTG type, and each has already cost a bug.

## Breaking

A credential presented to `/v1/auth/recognise` that does not carry the DTG
common structure is now skipped rather than routed to its slot. Credentials
minted through `dtg-credentials` — every credential this stack issues — are
unaffected.

Full suite green: 53 suites, 0 failures, clippy clean.

## Scope note

35 hand-rolled credential fixtures remain across 16 files. I did not migrate
them: most are malformed-input cases or non-DTG credentials (status lists,
schema validation) where hand-rolling is correct, and a 35-file mechanical diff
would bury the part of this that matters. The guards above pin the invariant
those fixtures could violate, which is the durable fix — a fixture that drifts
from the catalog now fails a test that mints from it.

title: chore: repin vta-sdk to #1087, and pin the invariant that made us immune
body:
[VTI #1087](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1087) fixed `agent_connect::default_sessions_dir`, which returned `~/.config/pnm` where `pnm` uses `dirs::config_dir()` — wrong on macOS and Windows.

**This crate was never affected.** It resolves the directory itself (`PnmConfig::default_dir`) and passes `sessions_dir` explicitly on every session-mode path.

That is luck worth converting into a guarantee. A test now asserts `to_agent_connect()` leaves the field `Some` for a `pnmSession` identity:

```rust
let dir = connect.sessions_dir.expect("session mode must resolve the directory itself");
assert_eq!(dir.parent().unwrap(), dirs::config_dir().unwrap());
```

Without it, a future session-mode path that omits the field would find no session on two platforms and report an authentication failure to somebody who *is* authenticated — a failure indistinguishable from an expired login, and the exact shape of the bug that has now been fixed twice upstream.

Patch rev moves `e296dca` → `061300a`. Still comes out entirely once a released `vta-sdk` carries `agent_connect`.

## Testing

`cargo test` — 82 pass. Clippy clean.

title: fix(sdk): look for pnm sessions where pnm actually writes them
body:
`agent_connect::default_sessions_dir` returned `~/.config/pnm`. `pnm` uses `dirs::config_dir()` (see `config_dir` in `pnm-cli/src/config.rs`), which is:

| Platform | Actual path |
|---|---|
| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/pnm` |
| Windows | `%APPDATA%\pnm` |
| Linux | `~/.config/pnm` |

So on macOS and Windows a bridge in session mode finds **no session** — and reports an *authentication* failure to an operator who is authenticated. That is indistinguishable, from their side, from an expired login: they run `pnm auth status`, are told they are fine, and are none the wiser.

This is the second half of the same defect as [#1083](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1083), which fixed the keyring *key* (`vta:<slug>`) and left the *directory*. Both halves were in the original `vta-mcp` code and were carried into the SDK unchanged when #1081 extracted the ladder — so **`vta-mcp --vta <slug>`, the invocation its own README documents, has never worked on macOS.**

## How it surfaced

Running a downstream consumer of `agent_connect` on a real macOS machine. It reported "no VTA is configured" against a `pnm` install that was working perfectly, with the config sitting in `~/Library/Application Support/pnm` the entire time.

That is also why the new test asserts against `dirs::config_dir()` rather than a literal path — the whole bug was a literal path that looked right.

## Scope

`dirs` is **optional**, pulled only by the `session` feature, so nothing that does not already speak to a session store gains a dependency.

`vta-mcp`'s README is corrected; it documented the wrong default too.

## Testing

`cargo test -p vta-sdk --lib agent_connect` — 12 pass, one new. `cargo test -p vta-mcp` — 5 pass. `cargo check -p pnm-cli -p cnm-cli` clean. Clippy clean.

title: feat: enrol without an operator credential, and find pnm where it actually lives
body:
Two problems, both found by running this on a real machine rather than against fixtures.

## 1. `setup` could not see a working `pnm`

`pnm` uses `dirs::config_dir()` — `~/Library/Application Support/pnm` on macOS, `%APPDATA%\pnm` on Windows. This hardcoded `~/.config/pnm`.

A macOS user with a perfectly good login was told *"no VTA is configured on this machine"*, by an error naming neither the directory searched nor the possibility that it was the wrong one.

Now uses `dirs::config_dir()`, `$PNM_CONFIG_DIR` overrides, and the error names the path it looked in. Verified against a real install:

```console
$ vta-agent-memory setup --vta nope
Error: no `pnm` VTA named `nope`.

Configured:
  Glenn (glenn) — did:webvh:QmWoJD…:webvh.storm.ws:glenn-vta
```

> **`vta-sdk`'s `agent_connect::default_sessions_dir` has the same bug** — inherited from the original `vta-mcp` code. That needs its own PR upstream.

## 2. `setup` should not have needed `pnm` at all

It required the machine holding the memories to *also* hold an operator credential with admin over the context — far more power than a memory service should sit next to, on a laptop that may be nobody's admin workstation. It also made enrolment simply impossible on a machine where the operator never logs in.

`init` + `connect` is now the primary path, and is the shape the rest of the stack already uses: *"VTC deliberately never holds a VTA admin credential (no self-grant), same as mediator / did-hosting."*

```console
$ vta-agent-memory init --vta-did did:webvh:… --context agent-memory

This machine's memory agent is ready to be granted access.

  agent DID   did:key:z6MkqVfVXEHNu2TZDZX4nV3oGxsZGMAMYhWKNryGVKWniCDA
  vta         did:webvh:QmWoJD…:webvh.storm.ws:glenn-vta
  context     agent-memory
  mediator    did:webvh:QmTS3a…:webvh.storm.ws:mediator

Run this wherever you hold VTA admin — it does not have to be this machine:

  pnm acl create --did did:key:z6Mkq… --role application --contexts agent-memory --label vta-agent-memory

Then, back here:

  vta-agent-memory connect
```

- **`init` makes no authenticated call.** It mints a key locally and resolves the mediator from the VTA's DID document, which is a public read — so it works before anybody has granted this machine anything.
- **The grant runs anywhere.** Another laptop, CI, a colleague reading it off a ticket. That is the whole point.

title: feat: enrol without an operator credential, and find pnm where it actually lives
body:
feat: enrol without an operator credential, and find pnm where it actually lives

Two problems, both found by running this on a real machine.

**setup could not see a working pnm.** `pnm` uses `dirs::config_dir()`,
which is ~/Library/Application Support/pnm on macOS and %APPDATA%\\pnm on
Windows — not ~/.config/pnm, which this hardcoded. A macOS user with a
perfectly good login was told no VTA was configured, by an error that
named neither the directory searched nor the fact that it was the wrong
one. Now uses dirs::config_dir(), $PNM_CONFIG_DIR overrides, and the
error names the path. vta-sdk's agent_connect::default_sessions_dir has
the same bug and needs its own fix.

**And setup should not have needed pnm at all.** It required the machine
holding the memories to also hold an operator credential with admin over
the context — far more power than a memory service should sit next to,
on a laptop that may be nobody's admin workstation. It also made
enrolment impossible on a machine where the operator does not log in.

`init` + `connect` is now the primary path, and is the shape the rest of
the stack already uses: 'VTC deliberately never holds a VTA admin
credential (no self-grant), same as mediator / did-hosting.'

  init     mints an agent did:key here, resolves the mediator from the
           VTA's DID document, persists 0600, and prints the exact
           `pnm acl create` needed. No credential, no authenticated call —
           a DID document is a public read — so it runs before anyone has
           granted this machine anything.
  (grant)  run by whoever holds admin, on ANY machine. That is the point.
  connect  authenticates as the granted key, proves it can read the
           context with a real memory/list/0.1, writes the config, and
           deletes the pending file so the key lives in one place.

The two halves are joined by a file, not a session: nothing assumes phase
2 happens soon, or with the same person watching.

`setup` remains, doing both phases at once through a local pnm login, and
is now documented as the convenience it is.

Verified live against a real VTA: init resolved a did:webvh VTA's document
over the network and returned its actual mediator DID.

title: feat: assert personhood to a community over Trust Tasks
body:
The member side of the VTC's personhood ceremony. Pairs with **OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1085** (merged) and its follow-up, which routes the two verbs over messaging — before that they were REST-only, so a client that talks to communities over DIDComm and TSP and holds no bearer token could not reach them at all. Personhood appeared in this repo only as README prose.

## What lands

`openvtc-core::personhood` — `request_challenge`, `build_presentation`, `assert_personhood`, and parsers for both replies.

Both verbs ride the same Trust Task document path as the join ceremony: DIDComm wraps the document in an authcrypt envelope, TSP carries it bare, and the sender is cryptographically proven either way. Routing needed no change — `OPENVTC_CATCH_ALL_PATTERN` already admits `https://trusttasks.org/spec/vtc/.*`.

`Route` groups the transport plumbing both verbs need. Six same-typed DID strings passed loose is one transposed pair away from addressing the wrong party.

## The spoken match code

`challengeId` is a UUID: fine on a wire, hopeless read aloud. `match_code` derives eight Crockford base32 characters from it — no `I`/`L`/`O`/`U`, so nothing in one is confusable when spoken. This is what two people in a room actually say to each other.

It is **derived, never transferred**: anyone holding the challenge id computes the same characters, anyone who does not cannot. Nothing on the VTC checks it, because it proves nothing `proof.challenge` does not already prove. It exists so a human can tell that the ceremony their client is answering is the one the administrator in front of them just started — a Bluetooth pairing code, not a password.

`match_code_agrees_with_the_vtc` pins the vector `5CY1-GZEE`; the VTC pins the same one. Nothing else would catch the two derivations drifting — a changed domain tag or alphabet on either side still yields eight plausible characters that simply never match, which reads to the people in the room as "wrong ceremony" rather than "your software disagrees with itself". `parse_challenge_reply` turns a live disagreement into an error for the same reason.

## The challenge is written twice, deliberately

`assert/0.1` says `proof.challenge` must be the paired `challengeId`, and that this is what "stops one captured and replayed into another". In W3C Data Integrity that holds because the proof options are canonicalised with the document, so `challenge` is signed.

`affinidi_data_integrity` has no `challenge` proof option, and the VTC verifies over the presentation with the whole `proof` block removed. A value written only there is **not covered by the signature** — swapping it on a captured presentation would go unnoticed.

So `build_presentation` writes the challenge to `proof.challenge` (what the spec names) **and** to top-level `nonce` (what the signature covers), and the VTC requires both to agree. `the_signed_nonce_is_covered_by_the_proof` pins that tampering with `nonce` breaks verification — which is the whole reason it carries the challenge, and why neither copy can be dropped as redundant.

## Not in this PR

No CLI or TUI command yet — this is the library surface the command will call. `cargo test -p openvtc-core --lib` is green (437 tests, 9 of them new); clippy and fmt clean.

tampering with `nonce` breaks verification — which is the whole reason it
carries the challenge, and the reason neither copy can be dropped as
redundant.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat: read the community's personhood replies, and refuse a match-code disagreement

The two verbs could be sent but not understood: replies arrived as
`#response` documents that nothing parsed, so a member never learned the
challenge id to sign against.

`parse_challenge_reply` and `parse_assert_reply` normalise both reply
shapes the VTC produces — the dispatcher's `#response` document with members
under `payload`, and a hand-built bare body — the same way `messaging`
already does, which also makes them transport-agnostic: a TSP frame carries
the response document raw.

Routing needed no change; `OPENVTC_CATCH_ALL_PATTERN` already admits
`https://trusttasks.org/spec/vtc/.*`.

The challenge parser compares the community's own copy of the match code
against the one derived locally and treats a disagreement as an error. The
two are computed by different implementations, and a drift is otherwise
invisible: both sides still show eight plausible characters, so the people in
the room conclude they have the wrong ceremony rather than that the software
disagrees with itself. A community that sends no copy at all is fine — the
code is derived locally, so an older VTC costs nothing.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat: drive the personhood ceremony from the communities panel

The library surface had no way in. `p` on an Active membership asks the
community for a challenge; the reply lands as the panel's live challenge and
shows the match code; `P` answers it.

The match code gets its own line in the panel's emphasis colour rather than
being folded into the status text — it is the thing a member reads aloud, and
a code that has to be picked out of a sentence is a code that gets misread.

An expired challenge renders as expired rather than disappearing. A member
who has just been read a code, looking at a panel that never mentions one,
cannot tell "it lapsed" from "it never arrived".

Key hints are gated exactly as the handler gates the keys, which is this
file's existing discipline: `p` on Active rows only, `P` only while a live
challenge is in hand. Both would otherwise be dead keys — the defect that
gating was written to remove.

The assertion targets the membership the *challenge* names, not the
highlighted row. Answering against whichever row happens to be selected is
exactly the confusion the stored `vtc_did` exists to prevent. It presents
that membership's own credentials and lets the community's policy choose:
a client-side filter would have to guess at a policy it cannot read, and
guessing wrong withholds the very credential that would have satisfied it.
Scoping to the one membership also keeps one community's credentials from
being disclosed to another.

Two supporting changes:

- `Verb` gained the two personhood sends, so `CommunityOutcome`'s
  `leaving: bool` became a `Performed` enum. A boolean cannot say which of
  four things happened, and the arms that got it wrong would have told the
  member the wrong thing went wrong rather than failed.
- The three out-params of `process_inbound_message` became `InboundEffects`.
  The live challenge belongs to `State`, not the account, so it is reported
  up rather than persisted — a single-use nonce with a ten-minute life has no
  business surviving a restart.

title: feat(vtc)!: reach personhood over messaging, and bind its challenge to something signed
body:
Follow-up to #1085. Companion client PR: **OpenVTC/openvtc#257**.

Personhood was REST-only. `openvtc` — which talks to communities over DIDComm and TSP and holds no bearer token — could not run the ceremony at all, so the member half of the feature had no client that could reach it.

## Reachable over messaging

`members/personhood/{challenge,assert}` now route through the messaging Trust Task dispatcher alongside the join verbs, which also makes them reachable over TSP (the TSP inbound path hands every frame to the same dispatcher).

The route handlers keep their bodies in `challenge_inner` / `assert_inner`, which both transports call. Two implementations of one ceremony is a security difference nothing tests.

Each verb carries its own caller gate, because "an authenticated session" — what the REST routes rest on — has no equivalent on a transport that only proves who sent the bytes:

| Verb | Gate | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `challenge` | caller must be a member | Otherwise anyone who can reach the mediator could mint challenges against this community's members. The *subject* may be another member — that is the in-person ceremony. |
| `assert` | sender must **be** the subject | `assert/0.1` declares `exposure.actsAsSubject: true` — "the asserting member is the subject … exercising their own authority over their own personhood state". |

Minting a challenge for someone else confers nothing: the nonce is bound to the subject, and only a presentation signed by that subject's key can spend it.

## The challenge was not bound to anything

`assert/0.1` §Authorization says the challenge binding "establishes that this presentation was made for this exchange, and is what stops one captured and replayed into another". In W3C Data Integrity that holds because the proof options are canonicalised with the document, so `challenge` is signed.

`affinidi_data_integrity`'s `DataIntegrityProof` **has no `challenge` field**, and `verify_vp_proof` verifies over the presentation with the whole `proof` block removed. So `proof.challenge` was **unsigned**.

Anyone holding a captured presentation — a relaying mediator, anyone with log access — could mint a fresh challenge for that member, swap the one unsigned field, and replay it. The signature still verified, because it had never covered the challenge. For a flag whose revocation is an administrative act, that means a revoked assertion could be restored without the member's participation.

The challenge must now also appear at top-level `nonce`, which is outside the proof block and therefore covered by the holder's signature, and the two copies must agree. This is what the published task already says the binding does; it just did not do it.

Two tests pin it from both sides: a presentation with no signed `nonce` is refused, and one whose unsigned `proof.challenge` has been swapped away from its signed `nonce` is refused.

> [!WARNING]
> **BREAKING CHANGE**: a personhood presentation without a top-level `nonce` equal to `proof.challenge` is refused. No client produced one — `openvtc` had no personhood support and `vtc-client` only reads the flag — so nothing in the ecosystem is affected, and OpenVTC/openvtc#257 emits both copies.

## Match-code vector

Pins `5CY1-GZEE`, which `openvtc-core` pins too. The two derivations agree only because they compute the same digest over the same bytes, and nothing else would catch them drifting: a changed domain tag or alphabet on either side still yields eight plausible characters that simply never match, which reads to the two people in the room as "wrong ceremony" rather than "your software disagrees with itself".

## Verification

Rebased onto merged `main` (so it includes #1082's response-shape changes) and re-run there:

- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — 40 test binaries, 0 failures
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --check` — clean

Three new dispatcher tests cover the messaging path: a member mints a challenge and gets the match code back, a non-member is refused, and one member cannot assert for another.

title: feat(vtc): let a community vet a member in person and have it count as personhood evidence
body:
Personhood already shipped, and it already matches DTG Credentials: a PHC is a VMC, and `new_vmc(personhood: true)` appends `PersonhoodCredential` exactly as the spec's worked example shows. What was missing was the ceremony an operator actually performs — meeting someone, satisfying themselves the DID in front of them is theirs, and having that count.

The default `personhood.rego` accepted one evidence shape: a `WitnessCredential` from some third party. An administrator who did the verifying themselves had nowhere to put it.

## The community's own vetting becomes evidence

DTG Credentials §Identity Verification Credentials defines an IDVC as "any W3C VC satisfying a VTC/VTN's identity-proofing requirements" and explicitly *not* a `DTGCredential` subtype, so a community acting as its own identity-verification provider needs no new credential type. Registering `IdentityVerification` as an endorsement type and issuing it per member reuses `vtc/endorsement-types/register/0.1` and `vtc/endorsements/issue/0.1` verbatim — **no new Trust Task family**, and revocation comes free via the community's existing status list.

`vtc/members/personhood/assert/0.1` is untouched, which was the constraint worth respecting: its Authorization section is explicit that holder-equality and challenge-binding are both load-bearing and neither substitutes for the other. An admin-asserts-directly path would have had to bypass the presentation the task requires, so the vetting is evidence the member presents rather than a gate the admin steps around.

## Three bindings, each with a test that breaks exactly one

| Binding | Why |
|---|---|
| `issuer == community_did` | An endorsement type is a *name*, not an authority. Without this, any issuer anywhere could mint a credential typed `IdentityVerification` and unlock personhood here. This is why `community_did` is now in the policy input at all. |
| `credentialSubject.id == applicant_did` | The route's holder-match binds the presenter; this binds the credential, so a member cannot present a vetting record issued about somebody else. |
| the endorsement type | A role VEC is community-issued and names the member too, so without the type check every member holding a role credential satisfies the policy — which is every member. |

Two further tests run a credential from the **real builder** through the **real extractor** into the **real policy**. Every other test in that file hand-writes `vp_claims`, so they all agree about a shape none of them obtained from the code that produces it; if `build_custom_endorsement` moved `endorsement` out of `credentialSubject`, they would all keep passing while every vetting in production was denied.

## The spoken match code

`challengeId` is a UUID — fine on a wire, hopeless read aloud — so the challenge response now carries eight Crockford base32 characters derived from it (no `I`/`L`/`O`/`U`, nothing mishearable).

It is **derived**, never transmitted as an independent secret and never accepted as one: both parties compute it from the id they already hold and say it to each other. Nothing checks it server-side, because there is nothing it could prove that `proof.challenge` does not already prove. It is a Bluetooth pairing code, not a password.

It rides in `ext` because the response schema is `additionalProperties: false`. A conformance witness now pins that, and the assertion was checked for vacuity — moving the field to the top level does fail the test.

## What this deliberately does not do

**Enforce uniqueness.** DTG Credentials requires governance enforcing both real human personhood *and* exactly one membership per person; this is evidence for the first only. Nothing stops one human joining twice under two DIDs and being vetted twice.

The spec also locates PHC status in **governance and trust registries rather than credential structure** — the `PersonhoodCredential` type is described there as a *non-authoritative hint*, so a verifier following the spec reads the community's governance, not the type array. The VTC publishes no governance statement today.

Both limits are stated in the policy module and in the operator guide rather than left for someone to discover.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — 30 test binaries, 0 failures
- `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --check` — clean

title: chore: fill in the plugin manifest metadata
body:
Nothing had run `claude plugin validate` against this repo. It flags two omissions, both of which are what a person sees *before* deciding whether to install:

- the marketplace has no `description`
- `plugin.json` has no `author`

Both filled in. Marketplace validation is now clean:

```console
$ claude plugin validate .
Validating marketplace manifest: .claude-plugin/marketplace.json
✔ Validation passed
```

## The one remaining warning is intended

```
⚠ root: CLAUDE.md at the plugin root is not loaded as project context.
  To ship context with your plugin, use a skill instead.
```

Correct, and correct to ignore here. That `CLAUDE.md` is guidance for people working on *this repo*; what users of the plugin need is `skills/agent-memory/SKILL.md`, which is loaded. A note at the top of the file says so, since the warning will recur for anyone else who validates.

No author email — this is a public manifest, and the org is the right attribution.

## Testing

`claude plugin validate .` clean; `claude plugin validate .claude-plugin/plugin.json` passes with the one intended warning. `cargo test` unaffected — 69 pass.

title: fix: start the MCP server even when the VTA is unreachable
body:
`serve` connected *before* it served. Anything that stopped the connection — an unreachable VTA, a laptop on a train, a revoked ACL grant, a machine where `setup` was never run — ended the process with a message on stderr.

Claude Code launches this server at session start and takes what it gets. **A process that exits before speaking MCP does not appear as a broken memory service; it appears as no memory tools at all** — and the model then cannot tell anyone what is wrong, because the tool it would say it with is the thing that is missing.

Verified before the fix: exit 1, nothing written to stdout, never spoke MCP.

## After

```console
$ printf '<initialize>\n<tools/list>\n' | VTA_AGENT_MEMORY_CONFIG=/nonexistent ./vta-agent-memory serve
initialize -> {'name': 'vta-agent-memory', 'version': '0.1.0'}
tools      -> ['memory_context', 'memory_forget', 'memory_get',
               'memory_list', 'memory_recall', 'memory_save']
```

and a call comes back as something worth relaying:

```json
"error": { "message": "no memory configuration at /nonexistent …\n\nRun:\n  vta-agent-memory setup" }
```

## What that buys

- **`memory_context` answers without connecting.** It is what somebody reaches for *because* memory is failing, so needing a working connection to explain a broken one would make it useless exactly when wanted.
- **Failures are not latched.** `OnceCell::get_or_try_init` caches successes only, so a VTA that comes back is picked up on the next call, and `setup` run mid-session takes effect with no restart.
- **A session that never touches memory never opens a mediator socket.**

## One implementation note

The connect future is **not `Send`** — the session rung boxes an error across an await inside `SessionStore::connect_with_transport` — so awaiting it in an MCP tool handler does not compile. It is driven on the blocking pool via `Handle::block_on`: the future never migrates between threads, so `Send` is not required, and the `VtaClient` it yields *is* `Send + Sync` (`vta-mcp` already shares one across an rmcp handler). Making that future `Send` is a worthwhile SDK change, but a larger and less certain one than this.

## Testing

`tests/mcp_starts_without_a_vta.rs` drives the real binary over stdio with no config: handshake completes, all six tools offered, tool call returns an actionable error, and stdout carries only JSON-RPC. It is a property about process lifetime, so running the thing is the only way to observe it.

`cargo test` — 69 pass across six suites (up from 63). Clippy clean.

title: chore: delegate the pnm session-key rule to the SDK
body:
**No behaviour change** — this crate always resolved the session key correctly. It is about where the rule lives.

`ResolvedVta::session_key` was formatting `vta:<slug>` itself. That is a second copy of a rule that belongs to `pnm`, and the *first* copy of it being wrong is what left `vta-mcp` unable to find a session at all ([VTI #1083](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1083)) — precisely the failure a duplicated rule produces once the two drift.

It now calls `vta_sdk::agent_connect::pnm_session_key`, which #1083 added beside the connect ladder both agent-side bridges already share. One definition, owned by the crate closest to `pnm`.

The local test stays rather than deferring to the SDK's. The SDK owning the rule does not help if this module stops *asking* it, so the assertion that matters is at the call site:

```rust
let r = two_vtas().resolve(Some("personal")).unwrap();
assert_eq!(r.session_key(), "vta:personal");
```

The `[patch.crates-io]` rev moves from `8bd8d98` (#1081's merge) to `e296dca` (#1083's) to pick the helper up. That pin still comes out entirely once a released `vta-sdk` carries `agent_connect`.

## Testing

`cargo test` — 63 pass across all five suites. Clippy clean.

title: fix: restore visibility: public to probablistic-sampling-for-connection-vcs
body:
[#22](https://github.com/OpenVTC/governance/pull/22) inserted the `vta-agent-memory` entry immediately above the `visibility: public` line that belonged to the entry *before* it. The new repo ended up with its own visibility line, but the displaced one never got its back:

```yaml
  - name: probablistic-sampling-for-connection-vcs
    teams:
      openvtc-admins: admin
      openvtc-maintainers: maintain
      probablistic-sampling-members: write
                                        # <- visibility: public was here
  - name: vta-agent-memory
    ...
    visibility: public
```

Confirmed against the pre-merge file: that entry declared `visibility: public` before #22 and does not after. It is currently the **only** one of the 14 repositories in this file without the key.

It also had nothing to do with #22 — this is collateral from where the block landed in the diff.

Whether an absent `visibility` means "leave it alone", "default to private", or "fail the run" is the reconciler's business. None of those is what was intended, and one of them quietly makes a public repo private, which is the kind of change that gets noticed weeks later as "who did that?".

One line restored. All 14 entries now declare visibility.

title: spec(vtc): let a member prove they issued the edge they are publishing
body:
Stacks on #258 — please merge that first; the version bumps are sequential.

An edge may be published under a **relationship DID**: an identifier scoped to
one counterparty, which names no member. The community still has to know that a
member published it, and the document's own `proof` says only that a member
*sent* it, not that they control the credential's issuing key.

Without something to close that gap, **any member who was ever handed a VRC
could publish another party's edge.** Issuing a credential and publishing it to
a community's trust graph are different disclosures, and the second is the
issuer's to make.

`pop` is a data-integrity proof by a verification method the VRC's `issuer`
controls, bound to the enclosing document's `id` and to the credential's digest.
Omitted when the VRC's `issuer` *is* the document's issuer, where the document's
own proof already establishes control. Added to both `0.1` and `0.2` so the two
stay aligned; the implementation still binds `0.1`.

## The binding is the document, not a session — and this diverges from the implementation on purpose

The implementation this comes from
(OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1061, mine) binds its authorization to
a **REST session id**, plus an audience and a timestamp.

None of the three belongs in a transport-neutral specification, and two are
already framework members: a document carries its own `recipient` and
`issuedAt`, and a session exists only on one binding.

What the authorization actually needs is to be unreplayable into a *different
document*, and every document carries a unique `id` (SPEC §4.3). Binding to that
is **stricter** than binding to a session — a session covers many documents —
and it is available on every transport.

So this PR publishes what the implementation *should* do rather than what it
does. That leaves the implementation diverging from this schema until it
follows, and I would rather have that written down than standardise a REST
detail into a transport-neutral spec. If the WG disagrees and would rather the
schema describe what ships today, say so and I will change it — but I think
that would be the wrong way round.

## One consumer requirement the schema cannot carry

**A consumer MUST NOT retain the authorization after verifying it.**

It answers one question at one moment. Storing it accumulates a durable link
between the publishing member and a relationship DID that names nobody —
precisely the correlation that publishing under a relationship DID exists to
avoid. No schema can express "do not keep this", so the prose does.

## Not breaking

An optional member on a payload that previously forbade it. Every document that
validated before still validates.

## Verified

- `npm run validate` — 344 specs, 64 shared schemas
- `npm run check-bindings` — 344 specs against 344 TS and 339 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo build`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — clean

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.6 → 0.11.7, `trust-tasks-ts` 0.12.6 → 0.12.7, with the
changelog entry.

title: feat(sdk): extract the agent-side connect ladder into vta_sdk::agent_connect
body:
Every tool that runs *beside* a user and talks to their VTA on their behalf needs the same four ways in — did:webvh bundle, scoped did:key, bearer token, existing `pnm` session — in the same order, with the same fail-fast rules. That ladder existed only inside `vta-mcp`'s `main.rs`, so the next bridge had to copy 110 lines or invent a fifth way in.

`vta_sdk::agent_connect::AgentConnect` is that ladder as SDK surface.

- `mode()` resolves the rung with **no I/O**, so a bridge can log it — and refuse a rung it does not support — before connecting. `ConnectMode::is_dedicated_agent()` makes the operator-vs-agent distinction available to callers deciding whether to enroll as a managed device.
- `connect()` returns the authenticated `VtaClient`.
- Session mode keeps `TransportChoice::Auto`, so it inherits the workspace preference order (TSP > DIDComm > REST) from what both DID documents advertise.

Two rules are **enforced rather than documented**, both carried over from the `vta-mcp` original:

1. The two DIDComm identity modes are mutually exclusive — a bundle *and* a did:key is an error, not a silent precedence win.
2. A half-configured rung errors naming the missing fields instead of falling through to session mode. A bridge silently authenticating as the operator rather than as its scoped agent identity is the failure this exists to prevent, and there is a test asserting the error mentions the gap and *not* the session.

`vta-mcp` is refactored onto it, which is what proves the extraction: `build_client` is now a pure args → `AgentConnect` mapping plus a connect, and its tests assert which rung a set of flags selects — something the old inline ladder had no way to test.

## Motivation

The first consumer beyond `vta-mcp` is an agent-memory service (a Claude Code plugin over `vta/memory/*`), which needs exactly these four rungs and nothing else. It currently pulls `vta-sdk` from this branch via `[patch.crates-io]`.

## Testing

- 10 new unit tests on `agent_connect` covering rung selection, precedence, mutual exclusion, half-configuration, empty-token fall-through, and bundle loading from a path or inline JSON.
- 4 new tests in `vta-mcp` mapping CLI flags to rungs.
- `cargo clippy` clean on both crates.

title: spec(vtc): publish the refusal an applicant is entitled to, and let them ask without an id
body:
A community can refuse a join request for a stated reason and then have no way
to tell the applicant what it was. Three tasks send the refusal detail today
and none of their schemas define it.

Second batch from the conformance witness in
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1076.

## `JoinRequest.decision`

`code`, optional `reason`, `decidedAt`.

Deliberately **distinct from `policyDecision`**: that one records the
community's internal verdict, while this is written by *both* rejection paths —
a policy auto-deny at submit and an admin's later refusal — so a client reads
one shape instead of reconciling two.

`code` is stable and safe to branch on. `decidedAt` is when the decision was
taken, **not** when the poll answering it was produced; on an admin refusal the
two diverge by however long the applicant takes to ask.

## `JoinRequest.vpClaims`

The canonical projection of the applicant's presentation, extracted at submit
and used as the input the community's join policy reads. Opaque here — its
members are whatever that policy asks for.

Because the component carries `additionalProperties: false`, those two absent
properties put **three** tasks off their own schemas at once:
`join-requests/list`, `join-requests/show`, `join-requests/status`.

## `status/0.1`: the refusal members, and an optional `requestId`

The poll is the request an applicant actually makes, so it gains the three
refusal members directly.

`requestId` becomes **optional**. An applicant whose first reply was lost never
received an id; a poll resolved from their own authenticated DID is the only
form available to them, and *a refusal they cannot ask about is a refusal they
cannot act on*. A consumer given the id MUST prefer it over inferring the
request from the caller.

## One consumer requirement, stated rather than implied

The refusal members MUST NOT be returned for any status other than `rejected`.
They assert that a decision was taken, and emitting them beside a `pending`
status would tell an applicant they had been refused when they had not. That is
in the prose, not just the schema.

## Not breaking

Two optional members added to schemas that previously forbade them, and one
required member relaxed — every document that validated before still validates.
A consumer that assumed `requestId` was always present now has a case to
handle, which is the point of the change.

## How this one hid

Worth recording: only a **rejected** request carries these members. A witness
built from a pending poll conforms, and would have passed green over the whole
divergence. The drift is conditional, which is why it survived a suite that
otherwise checks this task.

## Verified

- `npm run validate` — 344 specs, 64 shared schemas
- `npm run check-bindings` — 344 specs against 344 TS and 339 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo build`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — clean
- 9 files changed, no codegen churn: regeneration is diff-stable when
  `cargo fmt` follows it, as #257 established

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.5 → 0.11.6, `trust-tasks-ts` 0.12.5 → 0.12.6, with the
changelog entry.

As with #257, I cannot verify this end to end from the implementation side:
`verifiable-trust-infrastructure` pins `trust-tasks-rs` from crates.io, so
those drift entries stay recorded there until a release carries this.

* fix: retire the invalid-example that pinned `requestId` as required

`payload.invalid-examples.json` carried `{}` with the note "`requestId` is
required", and the generated `rejects_invalid_examples` test asserts every such
fixture is refused by serde or by JSON Schema. Making `requestId` optional made

pins that instead — the constraint that survives the change.

feature and I ran `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` without it. `cargo test

title: fix(mcp): look the pnm session up under the key pnm actually writes
body:
`vta-mcp --vta <slug>` — the invocation its own README documents — could never find a session.

`pnm` stores every login under the keyring key **`vta:<slug>`** (`vta_keyring_key` in `pnm-cli/src/config.rs`); `cnm` uses `community:<slug>` for the same reason. Neither session backend adds a prefix on the way in or out — `keyring.rs` passes the key straight to `Entry::new`, `file.rs` uses it verbatim as a map key. `vta-mcp` passed the **bare slug**, so the lookup missed.

**The operator sees an authentication failure.** That is the part worth fixing rather than documenting around: it is indistinguishable, from their side, from an expired login. They run `pnm auth status`, are told they are fine, and are none the wiser.

## The fix

One definition of the rule — `vta_sdk::agent_connect::pnm_session_key` — placed next to the connect ladder both agent-side bridges already share. It is idempotent, so an operator who worked the bug out for themselves and passes `vta:mine` keeps working.

## How it surfaced

Building a second consumer of `agent_connect` (an agent-memory service) hit exactly this, which is also why the helper belongs in the SDK rather than in either bridge: there are now two callers and the rule is `pnm`'s, not theirs.

## Testing

`cargo test -p vta-sdk --lib agent_connect` — 11 pass, one new covering the prefix, idempotency, and that a `community:` key is not mistaken for an already-prefixed VTA key. `cargo test -p vta-mcp` — 5 pass; the session-mode test now pins `vta:my-vta`. Clippy clean on both. README corrected.

title: fix: identify the VTA by DID, and look its session up where pnm puts it
body:
Two problems, one of which meant `setup` did not work at all.

## The session key was wrong

`pnm` stores sessions under the keyring key **`vta:<slug>`** — see `vta_keyring_key` in `pnm-cli/src/config.rs` — and neither session backend (keyring or file) prefixes anything. Setup passed the **bare slug**, so it found no session and reported *"Not authenticated"* to somebody who was authenticated.

Inherited from `vta-mcp`, whose README documents the same bare-slug invocation. Worth a look there too.

## And the slug was the wrong thing to ask for

A `pnm` name is a nickname chosen on one machine at `pnm setup --name`. It means nothing anywhere else, so a setup instruction written in terms of one cannot be copied to another machine, into a runbook, or to a colleague. The identifier that travels is the VTA's **DID**.

`--vta` now accepts either, told apart by the `did:` prefix, and is optional:

```bash
vta-agent-memory setup                                        # pnm's default VTA
vta-agent-memory setup --vta did:webvh:abc:vta.example.com:me  # by DID (preferred)
vta-agent-memory setup --vta work                             # by local pnm name
```

Errors list the configured VTAs with their DIDs, since the usual failure is guessing at a nickname chosen months ago. `setup` and `doctor` both print the DID now, so the value worth reusing is on screen:

```
config      ~/.config/vta-agent-memory/config.json
vta         did:webvh:abc:vta.example.com:mine
context     my-project
identity    dedicated agent did:key
transport   Didcomm
memories    12
```

## Bonus: airgapped and did:key VTAs now work

`~/.config/pnm/config.toml` carries `mediator_did` / `url` for VTAs that **cannot** advertise a service endpoint. Setup previously went straight to `resolve_vta_endpoint`, which by definition cannot find those, so such a VTA hit the "no DIDComm mediator" bail and got pushed at `--use-session` for no good reason. Configured endpoints now win over discovery.

## Notes

Resolution reads `~/.config/pnm/config.toml` directly because `pnm-cli` is a binary crate with no library target — there is nothing to depend on. The shape read is narrow (`default_vta`, per-VTA `vta_did`/`url`/`mediator_did`) and unknown keys are ignored, so `pnm` gaining fields does not break it.

`Identity::PnmSession` now stores the resolved keyring key whole, plus the VTA DID, so nothing downstream has to remember the prefix rule. **This changes the config shape** — anyone with a `pnmSession` config from before will need to re-run `setup`. Nobody does yet.

## Testing

`cargo test` — 63 pass (up from 51), including 12 new in `src/pnm.rs` covering DID lookup, name lookup, default fallback, the `vta:` prefix, pending-setup detection, carried-through endpoints, and unknown-key tolerance. Clippy clean.

title: fix(vtc)!: return the response shapes the specs publish
body:
Third batch of the 33, applying the standing direction — **build to spec, not
to what has been built.** Drift **31 → 27**.

Five handlers, all the same kind of defect: each had every value its schema
asks for and replied with something narrower.

| Task | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `backup/export` | bare `BackupEnvelope` | `{envelope: …}` |
| `members/removed` | top-level array | `{removed: […]}` |
| `website/files/delete` | 200, zero bytes | `{path, deleted}` |
| `website/rollback` | 200, zero bytes | `{generation, current, noop}` |
| `endorsements/revoke` | `{id}` | `{endorsementId, revocation: {credentialId, revokedAt}, statusListIndex}` |

`endorsements/revoke` is the one worth looking at: all four members were in
hand. The handler bound `updated` and threw it away with `let _ = updated;`
one line before replying. The idempotent no-op path now answers with the same
shape, reading the timestamp already on the row rather than inventing one.

## Two things the witness taught me that reading would not have

**`website/rollback` types `current` as a boolean and `generation` as a
string.** `current` answers *"did the rollback take"*, not *"which generation is
live"* — I wrote it as the generation number, twice, and the sweep rejected
both. The string typing matches the path segment the spec declares. I would
have shipped an integer called `current` and been confident about it.

**`website/generations/list` is not envelope-only, and its own entry said it
was.** The missing wrapper is fixed here, but the rows diverge too: the spec's
row carries `generation` and `current`, while the service sends `isCurrent` and
adds `deployedAt` and `sizeBytes`. It stays a drift entry with the diagnosis
corrected — one rename belongs here, and two members worth having belong
upstream rather than being dropped.

So one of the 33 notes was wrong about its own shape. Worth knowing when
reading the rest of the table.

## A limit worth restating

The witness compares a **hand-transcribed fixture** with its schema. It proves
the fixture conforms; it does not prove the handler emits the fixture. That is
the transcription gap #1076 documented as its own mutation #6.

The integration tests are the other half, and they did their job — `members_crud`
read the removed list as a bare array in two places and failed until updated.

## Verified

- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — 53 suites, 0 failures
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean

## Breaking

`POST /v1/backup/export`, `GET /v1/members/removed`,
`DELETE /v1/website/files/{path}`, `POST /v1/website/rollback/{gen}` and
`DELETE /v1/credentials/endorsements/{id}` return the shapes their published
schemas declare. Every one was previously returning something the schema did
not describe.

## What is left

**27.** The remaining `HERE` entry is `auth/admin_session`, which returns 204
and puts its result in two `Set-Cookie` headers where the spec requires
`{sessionId, expiresAt}` — a real behaviour change for the admin SPA, so it
wants its own PR rather than riding along here.

After that the set is 9 upstream (spec should change), 6 mixed, 2 design
questions on the install-claim flow, and 6 I have not classified yet.

title: spec(vtc): publish the community's relationship-identifier default, and what an update changed
body:
Three VTC tasks send members these schemas do not define, and two of them are
one missing property.

Found by the conformance witness in
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1076 — the first thing on either side
of the boundary to compare a response with the schema its URI publishes. It
recorded 33 divergences; these are three of them, and the only three whose root
cause is a single absent property.

## `relationshipIdentifierDefault`

Declares which identifier form a community expects members to issue
relationship credentials under:

- **`attributed`** — the member's membership DID, so an edge names them. What a
  public community (an open-source project, say) reasonably wants.
- **`pairwise`** — a relationship DID unique to each counterparty. What DTG
  Credentials recommends.

It is a **declaration, not an enforcement**. The member still chooses per
relationship, and a community that wants to *require* one form does so in its
own policy. The value exists so a client can read what the community expects
**before** minting, rather than discovering it from a rejection.

It was added to the implementation in
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1061 and never brought here. That is the
whole defect — this PR is me closing my own gap.

Because `CommunityProfile` and `CommunityProfileSnapshot` both carry
`additionalProperties: false`, one absent property drifted three tasks:
`community/profile/update`, `config/export`, and `config/import` — the last
because an import replays the document an export produced.

## `fieldsChanged`

On the update response: names the members the patch actually changed, in their
wire spelling, empty when the submitted values matched what was stored. It lets
a caller tell a no-op from an applied change without diffing the returned
profile against the one it sent.

## Not breaking, and edited in place

Both are `status: draft` edits made in place, per CONTRIBUTING-SPECS §Version
rules. Each **adds** an optional member to a schema that previously forbade it,
so any document that validated before still validates.

## One consumer requirement worth stating rather than implying

Reject a `relationshipIdentifierDefault` outside the two defined values instead
of storing it. The value is published to clients, and one they cannot interpret
is worse than no declaration at all. That is in the prose, not just the `enum`.

## On the generated-bindings diff

Regenerated for the four affected specs only — `community/profile/show`,
`community/profile/update`, `config/export`, `config/import`.

A full `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` also **reformats all 339 Rust
modules**: my local formatter wraps differently from whichever produced the
committed ones. The 335 files whose only change was that reformatting are
reverted, so this diff is not 343 files of churn.

The four kept files still carry some of that reformatting mixed with the real
change. They are generated artifacts, and hand-editing them to shrink the diff
would make them disagree with what the codegen emits — which is a worse problem
than a noisy diff. Flagging it so a reviewer knows why ~870 lines moved for two
new properties.

If the project would rather pin the formatter so regeneration is diff-stable,
that seems worth doing on its own — it will hit every contributor who
regenerates, not just this PR.

## Verified

- `npm run validate` — 344 specs validated, 64 shared schemas indexed
- `npm run check-bindings` — 344 specs against 344 TS and 339 Rust modules, all agree
- `npm run build-ts-bindings`, `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen`
- `cargo build -p trust-tasks-rs`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — clean

One thing I could **not** verify end to end: `verifiable-trust-infrastructure`
pins `trust-tasks-rs` from crates.io, so the three drift entries stay recorded
there until a release carries this. I have not claimed them closed on that side.

* fix: regenerate with cargo fmt, and bump the versions the bindings ship under

Four gates failed on the first push, and three of them share a cause I got
wrong in that commit's own message.

I claimed the codegen reformats all 339 Rust modules because my local formatter
wraps differently from whichever produced the committed ones, and reverted the
335 files whose only change was that reformatting. That diagnosis was wrong.
The codegen emits unformatted output and the workflow is codegen **then**

So the revert was not a tidy-up, it was drift: `trust-tasks-codegen drift`

fixed by regenerating everything and formatting, which also shrinks the real

The remaining two failures were plain omissions: a spec change ships new

title: feat(sdk): extract the agent-side connect ladder into vta_sdk::agent_connect (#1081)
body:
feat(sdk): extract the agent-side connect ladder into vta_sdk::agent_connect (#1081)

* feat(sdk): extract the agent-side connect ladder into vta_sdk::agent_connect

Every tool that runs beside a user and talks to their VTA on their behalf
needs the same four ways in — did:webvh bundle, scoped did:key, bearer
token, existing pnm session — in the same order, with the same fail-fast
rules. That ladder existed only inside vta-mcp's main.rs, so the next
bridge had to copy 110 lines or invent a fifth way in.

`AgentConnect` is that ladder as SDK surface. `mode()` resolves the rung
with no I/O, so a bridge can log it (and refuse a rung it does not
support) before connecting; `connect()` returns the authenticated
VtaClient. Session mode keeps TransportChoice::Auto, so it inherits the
workspace preference order (TSP > DIDComm > REST) from what both DID
documents advertise.

Two rules are enforced rather than documented, both carried over from the
vta-mcp original: the two DIDComm identity modes are mutually exclusive,
and a half-configured rung errors naming the missing fields instead of
falling through to session mode — a bridge silently authenticating as the
operator rather than as its scoped agent identity is the failure that
matters here. ConnectMode::is_dedicated_agent() makes the same
distinction available to callers deciding whether to enroll as a device.

vta-mcp is refactored onto it, which is what proves the extraction: its
build_client is now a pure args -> AgentConnect mapping plus a connect,
and its tests assert which rung a set of flags selects.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(vta): document agent memory in the personal-AI-agents guide

The guide walks an operator from transports through identity, ACL, wake,
step-up and credentials, and never mentions the store that is the reason
most agents want a VTA in the first place. `vta/memory/{put,list,delete}/0.1`
has shipped, is context-gated and audited, and appears in no operator doc.

Adds a step covering it, and states the two boundaries up front because
both are easy to get wrong and expensive to unwind: memory is not the
secrets/credential vault (those are capability-gated), and memory is not
application state (no version, no cursor — and 'forget everything' has to
stay safe to ask). Also records the retrieval consequence of the task's
whole-context list, since that is the client's problem and the design note
for it lives elsewhere.

Also notes agent_connect in the vta-mcp README, so the four auth modes it
documents are attributed to the SDK rather than read as its own.

title: fix: decode memory responses into the published Trust Task types
body:
fix: decode memory responses into the published Trust Task types

The three tasks were always real Trust Tasks — dispatch_trust_task builds
the document, validates the payload against the published schema in
trust_tasks_rs::schema_index, and rides TSP/DIDComm/REST. The gap was on
the way back: Store walked serde_json::Value by hand and skipped anything
that did not look right.

That turns a renamed or re-cased response field into an EMPTY LIST. The
user is told they have no memories, which is both wrong and completely
believable — and casing drift on wire types is the recurring defect class
in this stack, not a hypothetical. Responses now deserialize into
MemoryListResponse / MemoryPutResponse / MemoryDeleteResponse, so a shape
that does not match vta/memory/*/0.1 is a loud error naming the task.

The tolerance that was actually wanted survives one level down: an entry
whose *key* is not <type>/<slug> belongs to another writer sharing the
context and is still skipped. A malformed envelope is a bug; an
unfamiliar neighbour is not.

put and delete now also check the key the VTA echoes. A put that landed
under a different key is worse than a failure: recall would never find it
and the user would believe it saved.

Both mutating methods run under VtaClient::idempotent — the SDK's owner
of operation-completion retry — since both tasks are classified RetrySafe
in vta_sdk::retry_safety. A websocket blip should not silently lose
something the user asked to be remembered.

title: feat: make the session-start hook a good citizen
body:
feat: make the session-start hook a good citizen

`recall --format json` runs on every session start, which gives it a
different contract from a command a person typed:

- It must never fail the session. An unreachable VTA, an expired ACL
  grant, or a machine that was never set up are not reasons to put an
  error in front of someone who just opened a terminal. It now reports to
  stderr and exits 0 with no context injected.
- It must say nothing when there is nothing. Injecting 'no memories
  stored' into every session is noise that never becomes signal.

The text path is unchanged — someone who typed `recall` wants to know it
failed and wants to be told the fix.

Both properties are the kind that get regressed by tidying up error
handling, so tests/hook_contract.rs pins them by running the real binary,

title: feat: agent memory for Claude Code, backed by a Verifiable Trust Agent
body:
feat: agent memory for Claude Code, backed by a Verifiable Trust Agent

A Claude Code plugin that makes a user's own VTA their memory service:
six MCP tools, a skill that says when to use them, four slash commands,
and a SessionStart hook that loads memories before the user types.

The VTA side already existed — vta/memory/{put,list,delete}/0.1 are
context-gated, audited Trust Tasks, and VtaClient::memory_* already
drives them through the generic dispatcher. So nothing here is transport
aware: TSP > DIDComm > REST is chosen from what both DID documents
advertise, and `doctor` is the only place that even names one.

What the raw Trust Tasks do not have is retrieval. memory/list/0.1
returns every entry in the context, ascending key order, with no prefix,
no cursor and no search, so:

- keys are <type>/<slug>, letting a type filter run on the raw key before
  any record is decoded;
- records carry a one-line description, and recall ranks and returns
  descriptions, never bodies — bodies come only from memory_get, because
  a memory service that pastes every body into the context window has
  made the session worse;
- ranking is weighted token containment, chosen over embeddings because
  the VTA offers no vector index and an unpredictable scoring function is
  worse than a crude predictable one.

Setup is online only and rides existing flows end to end: the pnm keyring
session authenticates, contexts/list finds the context, EphemeralSetupKey
mints the agent did:key, acl/create scopes it to that one context with
role application (never admin — an empty context list means unrestricted
there), and resolve_vta_endpoint reads the mediator out of the VTA's DID
document. Nothing lands on disk until a real memory/list/0.1 succeeds as
the new identity.

Tests drive the real client bodies through the SDK's test-loopback
transport into a fake keyspace implementing the VTA's own storage
semantics, so payload shape and store behaviour are covered without a
VTA, a mediator, or a socket.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>
author: stormer78

title: fix(vtc)!: accept the install flow's own field names
body:
Second batch of the 33. Closes one more entry, but the reason it matters is a
live bug rather than a conformance count.

## The install flow disagreed with itself

`claim/finish` derives `ClaimFinishResponse` **with** `rename_all`, so it
returns `setupSessionToken`. `admin/bootstrap` derived `BootstrapRequest`
**without** one, so it demanded `setup_session_token`.

The service handed a caller one spelling and required the other back.

Only the admin SPA survived it, because `Install.tsx:217` re-keyed the value by
hand between the two calls:

```ts
{ setup_session_token: finishBody.setupSessionToken }
```

**A client written from the published schema could not complete an install at
all** — its body deserialised as a missing required field. The schema has said
`setupSessionToken` all along.

`ClaimStartRequest` and `ClaimFinishRequest` had the same gap, so
`install_token`, `claim_secret`, `registration_id` and `webauthn_response` were
snake_case against schemas naming them in camelCase.

## What changed

All three request structs gain `rename_all = "camelCase"`, and the SPA now
passes the token straight through instead of translating it.

Drift count **32 → 31**. `admin/bootstrap` is promoted to `checked!`. The two
install/claim entries stay, rewritten to describe only what is left of them:
`claimSecret` is a real member the spec does not define, and the response omits
`didBindingChallenge`, which the spec requires because this service binds the
admin DID at `claim/finish` instead. Those are a spec-and-flow reconciliation,
not a casing fix, and they are not attempted here.

## One thing I got wrong and reverted

A first pass swept `RegisterFinishRequest` (`routes/admin/passkeys.rs`) up with
the rest — it is also snake_case. The tests caught it: `register/finish` started
returning 422.

Reverted. It is a different endpoint with its own drift entry, and widening
this change to cover it would have buried a decision inside a mechanical fix.
`install_flow.rs` exercises both flows and now shows the two casings side by
side, with a comment saying why.

## The pattern, third time today

R3.1 casing, after the `Verifiable`-prefixed credential tags (#1071) and the
`Paginated<T>` wrapper (#1078). The common thread is not carelessness about
casing — it is that **a request struct's serde attributes were never compared
to the schema its URI publishes**. The witness from #1076 is the first thing in
this repo that does that, and it has now found three.

## Verified

- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — 53 suites, 0 failures
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `tsc -b --noEmit` in `admin-ui` — clean

## Breaking

`POST /v1/install/claim/start`, `/v1/install/claim/finish` and
`/v1/admin/bootstrap` accept camelCase request members and reject the
snake_case names they previously required. Any caller that worked before did so
by disagreeing with the published schema.
