title: Cross-artifact lifecycle precedence: suspension, supersession, restoration
body:
## Summary

#1075 fixed an instance: an expired VRC became a permanent edge because the
relationship route read neither `validFrom` nor `validUntil`. It did not fix the
class. Nothing in this workspace establishes **precedence between a
cryptographically valid but stale artifact and a later lifecycle event**, and
several credential types have no lifecycle vocabulary at all beyond "exists" and
"deleted".

Filing the general problem so the instance fix does not stand in for it.

## Why the instance was reachable

Two defensible decisions composed into an unreachable state:

1. The relationship graph is read **without re-checking dates**. Reasonable on
   its own — the edge was validated at ingress.
2. A VRC carries **no `credentialStatus`**, per planning-review D7. Also
   reasonable, and deliberately so: a status-list host learns which verifier
   checked which credential and when, which is the correlation the pairwise work
   exists to remove.

Neither is wrong. Together they leave `DELETE /v1/relationships/{id}` as the only
removal path, so a valid-forever artifact has no lifecycle at all.

**The deliberate absence of revocation is what makes precedence load-bearing.**
Where a credential type omits status for privacy reasons — which we think is
usually the right call — precedence and effective-time rules become the only
remaining lifecycle mechanism, not a refinement on top of revocation.

## What is missing

No shared vocabulary or precedence rule for:

- **suspension** — temporarily ineffective, not withdrawn
- **supersession** — a later artifact displacing an earlier one
- **restoration** — and its boundary against replacement or fresh grant
- **effective time and event precedence** across composed artifacts
- **transaction-time state discovery**, including what a verifier does when
  discovery is deliberately unavailable because the presentation must carry what
  it needs
- **approval freshness after an authority change** — we re-evaluate approver-set
  membership at execution (`policy_gate.rs`), but nothing re-evaluates an
  approval against a *credential* whose authority has since changed

## Where it already bites

- **VRC** — no status, no suspension; #1075 gated ingress only, and the VIC and
  recognition paths deliberately keep their own window semantics rather than
  sharing the gate. Three paths, three answers.
- **Relationship graph** — since #1073 an edge is complete or half-complete, but
  neither state has a notion of *suspended*. A half-edge whose reciprocal has
  expired is indistinguishable from one that never arrived.
- **VPC** (#1074) — a persona annotation has no lifecycle of its own. Detaching
  is the only reversal, and there is no record that a correlation once existed
  and was withdrawn.
- **VDC**, when it lands — this is where it gets expensive. A delegation that can
  be suspended and restored is the whole point of a bounded appointment, and the
  design note already commits us to freshness-by-re-issuance rather than live
  lookup, which puts the entire weight on precedence rules we have not written.

## Proposed shape

1. A common lifecycle vocabulary across credential types, rather than per-type
   ad-hoc handling.
2. Effective-time and precedence rules for composed artifacts — which state
   controls at decision time when two valid artifacts disagree.
3. One transaction-time evaluation gate that every ingress path calls, extending
   `credentials::ingress` where #1075 put the window check, with any deviation
   documented at the call site rather than implied.
4. Explicit restoration-versus-replacement semantics.
5. A statement of what a verifier may conclude when authoritative current state
   is deliberately undiscoverable.

## Provenance

The instance is ours (#1075, conformance-review finding F9). The generalisation
is external: it matches RAHP finding **F-003** in
`sankarshanmukhopadhyay/rahp-toolkit#66`, which arrived at the same residual from
a guardianship/fiduciary pressure test rather than from our code. Evidence from
our instance is posted there.

Note the numbering collision: RAHP's **F-003** and our conformance review's
**F3** are unrelated. This issue is the general form of our **F9**.

title: fix(common)!: send the pagination wrapper in camelCase, as the schemas always said
body:
First of the 33 divergences #1076 recorded, and the one with the widest blast
radius per line changed.

## The bug

`Paginated<T>` (`vti-common/src/pagination/mod.rs`) carried no `rename_all`, so
every list task sent `next_cursor` and `total_estimate` against published
schemas that say `nextCursor` and `totalEstimate`.

A direct **R3.1** violation, and the same casing-drift class as #656/#658 —
which your own workspace guidance cites as how an empty `allowed_contexts`
silently minted a super-admin.

## Why nothing caught it

Three parties agreed with each other and none agreed with the contract:

- the service sent `next_cursor`
- `vtc-client`'s `Page<T>` mirrored **the service**, not the schema
- the admin SPA typed its fields from the service too

The module's own doc even documented `"next_cursor"` as the intended wire form.
The conformance witness from #1076 is what finally put implementation and
schema side by side.

Four consumers move together here. `audit.tsx` reads a `cursor` member of a
different shape and is deliberately untouched.

## The count goes 33 → 32, not 33 → 28

This is the part worth reading, and it corrects #1076's own module doc, which
claimed "5 entries, one fix".

Five entries cited the wrapper. **Only `relationships/list` becomes fully
conforming** — it was the only one whose drift was the wrapper *alone*, because
its spec types `items` as free objects. The other four also diverge at row
level (`createdByDid`, `vpClaims`, `MemberResponse` members), so they keep their
entries, rewritten to describe only what is left instead of restating a casing
bug that is now fixed.

**Closing a shared root cause moves four entries without closing them.** A count
that fell by five would have implied more progress than happened.

I did not work that out by reading — I tried 28, and
`known_drift_entries_still_diverge_where_they_say_they_do` refused it and named
the entries that still diverge. The guard earning its keep on its first real use
is a good sign for the remaining 32.

## Verified

- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vti-common -p vtc-client` — 59 suites, 0 failures
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `tsc -b --noEmit` in `admin-ui` — clean
- All three conformance tests pass at the corrected count

Branched from the #1077 hotfix and rebased onto merged main — deliberately not
cut from a main that would not compile.

## Breaking

`Paginated<T>` now serialises `nextCursor` / `totalEstimate`. `vti-common` is
published, so an external consumer reading the snake_case names breaks — though
what it was reading never matched the published schema. Every in-repo consumer
is updated in this PR.

## What is left, and the decision it needs

31 of the remaining 32 fall into two shapes. The larger is **no response
envelope** (12 entries): the spec wraps the payload and the handler returns the
bare object or array. Unlike this fix, that is twelve separate judgements about
whether the service or the spec is right, and it wants a stated default before
anyone starts — change the service to match the spec, or take the divergence
upstream where the service's shape is the better design.

title: fix(vtc): thread `now` into the VPC shape check, unbreaking main
body:
**`main` at `397d087c` does not compile.** This unbreaks it.

```
error[E0061]: this function takes 4 arguments but 3 arguments were supplied
   --> vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:994
```

## How three green PRs produced a red main

#1074 added `check_vpc_shape`, which calls `credentials::ingress::require_dtg_type`.
#1075 gave that function a `now` parameter.

Neither diff touched the other's lines, so git merged both cleanly and **both were green on CI** — each having been tested against a `main` that did not yet contain the other. A textual merge and a semantic conflict.

Nothing in the repo would have caught it. CI green on a pull request proves the branch works against the main it was *cut from*, not the main it will *land on*.

## The fix, and the decision inside it

`check_vpc_shape` now takes `now` and threads it through, matching `check_vrc_shape` beside it.

That is not only what the compiler wanted. It answers a question neither PR was positioned to ask: **should a VPC's validity window be checked when it is attached?** It should, for the same reason the window is checked on the publish path — an annotation that outlived its own credential would go on asserting a persona the issuer had stopped standing behind. `now` is read once per request and passed in, so every check in the request evaluates at one instant.

Had this been resolved as a pure compiler fixup, the obvious move would have been to pass a `now` that skips the check. That would have compiled and been wrong.

## Verified

Cut from `397d087c`, so this is against **all three** of #1074, #1075 and #1076 together.

- `cargo check -p vtc-service` — compiles
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- #1076's conformance witness passes on the fixed tree, including `known_drift_entries_still_diverge_where_they_say_they_do`

The full `cargo test -p vtc-service` run was at 51 suites / 0 failures when this PR was opened, and was not waited out — main being red is the more urgent fact, and a full re-test is planned once this lands.

## Worth acting on separately

Two changes to one function signature need one rebased onto the other before either merges, however disjoint their diffs look. A merge queue, or requiring branches to be current before merge, would enforce that mechanically. This PR does not add either — flagging it rather than bundling it.

title: test(vtc): witness that every bound Trust Task speaks its published schema
body:
Closes #1059.

The VTC binds 58 published `spec/vtc/*` Trust Task URIs and nothing checked
that any of them speaks its URI's wire shape. The two parity checks in
`vtc-service/tests/trust_task_manifest.rs` are about identity — the URI
resolves in `trust_tasks_rs::schema_index` — not shape, and there is no
runtime validation on this side either: the document dispatcher's
`parse_payload` (`vtc-service/src/trust_tasks/helpers.rs:59`) is a bare
`serde_json::from_value`, and the REST layer's gate checks the `Trust-Task`
header, not the body. So a response could diverge arbitrarily from the schema
its URI names and every gate stayed green.

This ports `vta-service/src/trust_tasks/conformance.rs` (#857), following its
shape rather than inventing a second idiom for the same job: a derived census,
a witness table, mechanical non-vacuity.

## What it does

`vtc-service/src/trust_tasks/conformance.rs`, a `#[cfg(test)]` module in `src`
because its census needs `DISPATCHED_URIS`, which no integration test can see.

- The census is derived from both places this service binds a task: the REST
  tower layers in `routes/mod.rs`, read as source text because a built axum
  `Router` cannot be enumerated for them (the technique
  `tests/trust_task_manifest.rs` already uses), and `DISPATCHED_URIS`, the
  document dispatcher's own list. Union, filtered to what `schema_for`
  resolves.
- Every URI in it must have a `checked!` witness or an annotated `drift!`
  entry, asserted in both directions — a URI with no witness and a witness for
  a URI nothing binds both fail.
- Both sides of each witness are parsed as the generated `Payload` /
  `Response` and validated against the embedded schema. Schema validation is
  not redundant with parsing: serde ignores `const`, `enum`, `pattern` and
  `minLength` entirely, and `submit/0.1`'s response `status` is a
  `const: "pending"` that no generated struct enforces. It caught two of my
  own fixtures during development — a truncated `vrcSha256` that serde
  accepted and `^[0-9a-f]{64}$` did not.
- Response-side validation is where this can be stricter than the VTA's
  sweep, which validates the request only. The VTA's note ("the codegen emits
  `ValidatedPayload` for `Payload` but not for `Response`") was true of the
  0.4/0.5 codegen and is stale at the 0.11 series this workspace pins.
- The table is keyed by generated type, not by URI literal, for two reasons:
  a literal can be paired with the wrong type and the sweep would then
  validate one task's response against another's schema, and the census scans
  this crate for `spec/vtc/` literals — a table full of them would find itself
  and the stale-witness direction would be vacuous.
- `Conformance::KnownDrift` carries the fixtures and the side that diverges,
  and the sweep asserts the named side fails and the other passes. The VTA's
  arm is `KnownDrift(&'static str)` and has never held an entry; this one
  holds 33 on day one, and a prose-only note could not tell you a drift was
  fixed upstream or that it was mis-diagnosed. The count is asserted so the
  debt can shrink but not grow unnoticed.

## What it found

**33 of 58, where #1059 named two.** The issue said it had not audited the
other 59; they are worse than the two it named. Both named divergences are
confirmed, with one correction and two additions:

- `join-requests/submit/0.1` — confirmed. The dispatcher returns
  `VerdictResponse` (`{requestId, verdict}`) where the spec requires
  `{requestId, status}` with `status` a `const: "pending"`. Also request-side:
  `JoinRequestSubmitBody.extensions` is `#[serde(default)]` with no
  `skip_serializing_if`, so an unset `extensions` serialises as `null` against
  a schema that types it `object` — the same null-into-`Option` class that
  shipped `keys/create/0.1` broken.
- `join-requests/status/0.1` — confirmed, with a correction: the drift is
  **conditional**. `code` / `reason` / `decidedAt` are only populated on a
  *rejected* request, so a pending-status witness conforms and would have
  passed green over it. The request also diverges: the spec requires
  `requestId` and this service deliberately makes it optional, because an
  applicant whose first reply was lost holds no id.

The other 31 fall into three recurring shapes: no response envelope (the spec
wraps, the handler returns the bare object or a bare array — 12); `Paginated<T>`
in `vti-common` has no `rename_all`, so every list task sends `next_cursor`
where the spec says `nextCursor` — 5 tasks, one fix, and a direct R3.1
violation; and unspecced members on `additionalProperties: false` responses.
Two responses have no body at all (`auth/admin-session/0.1` returns 204 and
puts its result in cookies, which no non-browser transport can read;
`website/rollback/0.1` computes `noop` and discards it).

Nothing is fixed here. That is #1059's own sequencing — land the ledger, then
"decide, separately and with the list in hand, which drifts get fixed by
correcting the service and which by taking the shape upstream" — and with 33
entries it is also the only way to keep either change reviewable. Each entry
names its recommended disposition.

## Mutation-tested

A guard that cannot fail is worth nothing, so each assertion was made to fail
deliberately and then reverted:

1. extra member on a conforming response (`members/renew`) — caught,
   "unknown field `renewedAt`".
2. required member removed (`members/purge`) — caught, "missing field
   `removed`".
3. a `KnownDrift` response made to conform (`join-requests/submit`) — caught,
   "the recorded drift says the response diverges, but it actually conforms".
4. a witness deleted (`members/purge`) — caught by the coverage assertion.
5. a witness added for a bound-nowhere URI (`join-requests/approve`) — caught
   by the stale direction.
6. **`RemoveResponse.removed` renamed to `wasRemoved` in the handler — NOT
   caught.** The witness for that task is a transcription, so it keeps
   asserting the old spelling while the service breaks.
7. `MemberVmcReceiptBody.status` renamed in `vta-sdk` — caught, because that
   witness is built from the real type.

6 and 7 are the honest limit of this change. Most `routes/` modules are
`mod x;`, private to `routes`, so a typed fixture would mean widening a dozen
production modules to `pub(crate)` to satisfy a test — a real change with its
own argument, and mixing it in here would make both harder to review. Every
transcribed fixture cites the `file:line` of the type it transcribes, and the

place, so widening it later is a one-line change plus the witnesses.

array) — `backup/export`, `ceremonies/list`, `community/profile/show`,
`endorsement-types/register`, `endorsements/show`, `join-requests/show`,
`members/removed`, `members/show`, `members/update`, `website/generations/list`.

`join-requests/list`, `relationships/list`, `endorsements/list`,
`endorsement-types/list`.

`website/files/delete`, `website/rollback`.

`install/claim/start`, `install/claim/finish` (all snake_case, R3.1),

gives it), `endorsements/revoke`, `website/files/list` (`sizeBytes` for `size`,

title: No conformance witness for VTC Trust Task responses, and two already diverge
body:
Surfaced while fixing #1052. The VTC binds 61 published `spec/vtc/*` Trust Task
URIs and **nothing checks that any of them speaks its URI's wire shape.** Two
of them provably do not.

## What is checked, and what is not

`vtc-service/tests/trust_task_manifest.rs` runs two parity checks, and both are
about *identity*, not *shape*:

- `every_bound_task_is_published_or_excepted` — coverage
- `every_bound_canonical_task_exists_in_the_registry` — the URI resolves in
  `trust_tasks_rs::schema_index`

Neither looks at a payload. There is no runtime validation either — a grep for
`validate_payload` / `schema_for` across `vtc-service/src` returns nothing but a
single unrelated comment. So a VTC response can diverge arbitrarily from the
schema its URI names and every gate in the repo stays green.

This is exactly the gap `vta-service` closed in #857 with
`vta-service/src/trust_tasks/conformance.rs`, whose own module docs name the
defect class: *"Nothing checked **correctness**: that a task bound to a
published URI actually speaks that URI's schema."* The VTC never got the
equivalent.

## Two confirmed divergences

Both in the `join-requests` family, both against
`additionalProperties: false` response schemas.

**1. `vtc/join-requests/submit/0.1`** — the published Response is:

```json
{ "requestId": "…", "status": "pending" }
```

`required: [requestId, status]`, `additionalProperties: false`.

The service returns `VerdictResponse`:

```json
{ "requestId": "…", "verdict": { "effect": "…", "with": { … } } }
```

No `status` field at all (a *missing required* member), plus an unspecced
`verdict`. The ceremony verdict envelope
(`docs/05-design-notes/vtc-ceremony-protocol.md` §3) superseded the published
response shape and was never taken upstream.

**2. `vtc/join-requests/status/0.1`** — the published Response allows
`requestId`, `status`, `needs`, `presentationDefinition`, `ext`. #1058 added
`code`, `reason` and `decidedAt` on top. That was flagged in the PR under R3.*
and merged deliberately, on the grounds that the family already diverged — but
it widens the gap rather than closing it, and nothing will notice if it widens
again.

I have not audited the other 59. The point of the issue is that no one can say
whether they conform, because nothing asks.

## Why it matters

The VTC's whole claim in binding `https://trusttasks.org/spec/vtc/<slug>` is
that the registry serves that slug and this is what it looks like on the wire.
A consumer generating types from the published schema — which is the entire
reason to publish one — gets a struct that will not deserialize what the VTC
sends. `deny_unknown_fields` on a generated `Response` turns the `status`
poll's three new members into a hard parse failure, and the missing `status` on
`submit` fails a *required*-member check even without strictness.

That is the same failure mode as [wire-casing version skew] and the
`trust-task-error/0.3` silent-success defect: a mismatch that compiles on both
sides and only appears as a decode error, or worse, a silently mis-read
message, against a peer nobody tested with.

## Proposed change

Port the `vta-service` harness. It already has the shape this needs:

1. A witness table keyed by dispatched-and-published URI, carrying a
   representative request **and response**. The generated `specs::…::Payload` /
   `::Response` types carry `deny_unknown_fields` plus the spec's required set,
   so parsing them is the assertion.
2. Validate the request against the embedded `payload.schema.json` too —
   parsing alone is strictly weaker (serde accepts `null` into `Option<T>`
   where the schema demands a string; that is how `keys/create/0.1` shipped
   broken).
3. Non-vacuity enforced mechanically: drift each witness with an unknown member
   after the good case passes and require rejection, so a schema that accepts
   anything cannot produce a green row.
4. A `Conformance::KnownDrift` arm for annotated debt. `submit/0.1` and
   `status/0.1` go in as the first two entries with the reasoning above, so the
   divergence is *counted* rather than invisible — same discipline as
   `UNPUBLISHED_CANONICAL_OK`, where the number can shrink but not grow
   unnoticed.

Then decide, separately and with the list in hand, which drifts get fixed by
correcting the service and which by taking the shape upstream to
`trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`. For the two above I would expect upstream:
the verdict envelope is the better design and the published response schema is
simply behind it.

## Acceptance

- Every dispatched `spec/vtc/*` URI that the registry publishes has a witness
  or an annotated `KnownDrift` entry.
- A new response member on a conforming task fails the suite.
- `submit/0.1` and `status/0.1` are recorded as known drift with their
  rationale, and the drift count is asserted so it cannot grow silently.

title: test(vtc): witness that every bound Trust Task speaks its published schema (#1076)
body:
test(vtc): witness that every bound Trust Task speaks its published schema (#1076)

Closes #1059.

The VTC binds 58 published `spec/vtc/*` Trust Task URIs and nothing checked
that any of them speaks its URI's wire shape. The two parity checks in
`vtc-service/tests/trust_task_manifest.rs` are about identity — the URI
resolves in `trust_tasks_rs::schema_index` — not shape, and there is no
runtime validation on this side either: the document dispatcher's
`parse_payload` (`vtc-service/src/trust_tasks/helpers.rs:59`) is a bare
`serde_json::from_value`, and the REST layer's gate checks the `Trust-Task`
header, not the body. So a response could diverge arbitrarily from the schema
its URI names and every gate stayed green.

This ports `vta-service/src/trust_tasks/conformance.rs` (#857), following its
shape rather than inventing a second idiom for the same job: a derived census,
a witness table, mechanical non-vacuity.

## What it does

`vtc-service/src/trust_tasks/conformance.rs`, a `#[cfg(test)]` module in `src`
because its census needs `DISPATCHED_URIS`, which no integration test can see.

- The census is derived from both places this service binds a task: the REST
  tower layers in `routes/mod.rs`, read as source text because a built axum
  `Router` cannot be enumerated for them (the technique
  `tests/trust_task_manifest.rs` already uses), and `DISPATCHED_URIS`, the
  document dispatcher's own list. Union, filtered to what `schema_for`
  resolves.
- Every URI in it must have a `checked!` witness or an annotated `drift!`
  entry, asserted in both directions — a URI with no witness and a witness for
  a URI nothing binds both fail.
- Both sides of each witness are parsed as the generated `Payload` /
  `Response` and validated against the embedded schema. Schema validation is
  not redundant with parsing: serde ignores `const`, `enum`, `pattern` and
  `minLength` entirely, and `submit/0.1`'s response `status` is a
  `const: "pending"` that no generated struct enforces. It caught two of my
  own fixtures during development — a truncated `vrcSha256` that serde
  accepted and `^[0-9a-f]{64}$` did not.
- Response-side validation is where this can be stricter than the VTA's
  sweep, which validates the request only. The VTA's note ("the codegen emits
  `ValidatedPayload` for `Payload` but not for `Response`") was true of the
  0.4/0.5 codegen and is stale at the 0.11 series this workspace pins.
- The table is keyed by generated type, not by URI literal, for two reasons:
  a literal can be paired with the wrong type and the sweep would then
  validate one task's response against another's schema, and the census scans
  this crate for `spec/vtc/` literals — a table full of them would find itself
  and the stale-witness direction would be vacuous.
- `Conformance::KnownDrift` carries the fixtures and the side that diverges,
  and the sweep asserts the named side fails and the other passes. The VTA's
  arm is `KnownDrift(&'static str)` and has never held an entry; this one
  holds 33 on day one, and a prose-only note could not tell you a drift was
  fixed upstream or that it was mis-diagnosed. The count is asserted so the
  debt can shrink but not grow unnoticed.

## What it found

**33 of 58, where #1059 named two.** The issue said it had not audited the
other 59; they are worse than the two it named. Both named divergences are
confirmed, with one correction and two additions:

- `join-requests/submit/0.1` — confirmed. The dispatcher returns
  `VerdictResponse` (`{requestId, verdict}`) where the spec requires
  `{requestId, status}` with `status` a `const: "pending"`. Also request-side:
  `JoinRequestSubmitBody.extensions` is `#[serde(default)]` with no
  `skip_serializing_if`, so an unset `extensions` serialises as `null` against
  a schema that types it `object` — the same null-into-`Option` class that
  shipped `keys/create/0.1` broken.
- `join-requests/status/0.1` — confirmed, with a correction: the drift is
  **conditional**. `code` / `reason` / `decidedAt` are only populated on a
  *rejected* request, so a pending-status witness conforms and would have
  passed green over it. The request also diverges: the spec requires
  `requestId` and this service deliberately makes it optional, because an
  applicant whose first reply was lost holds no id.

The other 31 fall into three recurring shapes: no response envelope (the spec
wraps, the handler returns the bare object or a bare array — 12); `Paginated<T>`
in `vti-common` has no `rename_all`, so every list task sends `next_cursor`
where the spec says `nextCursor` — 5 tasks, one fix, and a direct R3.1
violation; and unspecced members on `additionalProperties: false` responses.
Two responses have no body at all (`auth/admin-session/0.1` returns 204 and
puts its result in cookies, which no non-browser transport can read;
`website/rollback/0.1` computes `noop` and discards it).

Nothing is fixed here. That is #1059's own sequencing — land the ledger, then
"decide, separately and with the list in hand, which drifts get fixed by
correcting the service and which by taking the shape upstream" — and with 33
entries it is also the only way to keep either change reviewable. Each entry
names its recommended disposition.

## Mutation-tested

A guard that cannot fail is worth nothing, so each assertion was made to fail
deliberately and then reverted:

1. extra member on a conforming response (`members/renew`) — caught,
   "unknown field `renewedAt`".
2. required member removed (`members/purge`) — caught, "missing field
   `removed`".
3. a `KnownDrift` response made to conform (`join-requests/submit`) — caught,
   "the recorded drift says the response diverges, but it actually conforms".
4. a witness deleted (`members/purge`) — caught by the coverage assertion.
5. a witness added for a bound-nowhere URI (`join-requests/approve`) — caught
   by the stale direction.
6. **`RemoveResponse.removed` renamed to `wasRemoved` in the handler — NOT
   caught.** The witness for that task is a transcription, so it keeps
   asserting the old spelling while the service breaks.
7. `MemberVmcReceiptBody.status` renamed in `vta-sdk` — caught, because that
   witness is built from the real type.

6 and 7 are the honest limit of this change. Most `routes/` modules are
`mod x;`, private to `routes`, so a typed fixture would mean widening a dozen
production modules to `pub(crate)` to satisfy a test — a real change with its
own argument, and mixing it in here would make both harder to review. Every
transcribed fixture cites the `file:line` of the type it transcribes, and the
module docs record the measured difference between the two forms.

## Scope

`spec/vtc/*` only. The VTC also binds 36 URIs in the shared
`spec/{acl,audit,auth,config,policy}/*` families; those are served by both
daemons, so witnessing them belongs with a decision about which service's
response shape is canonical. The mechanism is prefix-parameterised at one
place, so widening it later is a one-line change plus the witnesses.

title: fix(vtc): reject a credential whose validity window has passed at ingress
body:
Closes #1069 (conformance audit F9).

`routes/relationships.rs` read neither `validFrom` nor `validUntil`, so a VRC
that had already expired became a permanent edge in the community trust graph.
Permanent because the graph is read back without re-checking dates, and because
per planning-review D7 a VRC carries no `credentialStatus` — the only removal is
the issuer or an admin calling `DELETE /v1/relationships/{id}`.

## What changed

`credentials::ingress` — the module that already owns the DTG common-structure
check — gains `check_validity_window`, and `require_dtg_type` now runs it. The
VRC publish path calls `require_dtg_type` (via `check_vrc_shape`), so it picks
the check up from there rather than growing a third bespoke copy. A future
ingress point that calls the same gate gets it for free.

`vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:146-154` now reads `now` once per
request and passes it in, so a test can choose the instant.

## How strong a claim this is

The requirement sits in DTG Credentials §Security Considerations 2, which is
marked *informative*. So this is a conformance expectation, not a normative
MUST. It is still worth closing: the VRC is the longest-lived credential in the
graph and it was the one path that never looked.

## What I deliberately left alone

- **`classify_dtg` stays structure-only.** `routes/recognise.rs:329` uses it as
  a *filter* over a presentation's `verifiableCredential` array, skipping
  entries that are not DTG credentials, since a VP may legitimately carry
  others. Folding the window check in would turn an expired VEC into a silently
  skipped entry and downgrade the error from `recognition::verify`'s "VEC
  validUntil … is in the past" to "presentation has no EndorsementCredential".

- **The VIC path** (`credentials/invitation_verify.rs:361-373`) **and the
  recognition path** (`recognition/verify.rs:198-228`) **are untouched.** Both
  already implement the same half-open window, and each carries semantics the
  shared check does not: recognition additionally *clamps* the minted session
  TTL to the earliest `validUntil` across the VEC/VMC pair
  (`routes/recognise.rs:408-417`), and both *require* `validUntil` to be
  present at all. Routing them through the shared check would either duplicate
  their logic or weaken it. Three implementations was the problem; replacing
  two working ones with a weaker one is not the fix.

- **VRCs still carry no `credentialStatus`.** That is D7, not an oversight.
  Stated explicitly in the `check_validity_window` doc comment so a reader
  comparing this code against the specification does not log it as a second
  finding.

## Judgement calls

**Absent bounds are not enforced.** Both properties are optional in W3C VC 2.0,
and this checks only the bounds a credential actually states. Most VRC fixtures
in this repo (including `tests/relationships.rs::fake_vrc`) carry no
`validUntil` at all. Whether an open-ended edge is acceptable is a community
policy question and belongs in `relationships.rego`, not in a type check.

**No clock-skew tolerance.** These windows are days to years, so a grace period
of any plausible size changes nothing operationally while making "expired" a
fuzzy predicate that disagreed with the two paths this is meant to align with —
both compare exactly. Contrast `PUBLISH_AUTHORIZATION_MAX_AGE_SECS` in the same
route file, which *does* allow skew: it bounds a five-minute freshness window,
where skew is a real fraction of the budget. Justified in a doc comment either
way, as asked.

**Both VC 2.0 and VC 1.1 property names are read.** I checked before deciding:
nothing in this stack *emits* `issuanceDate`/`expirationDate` — the catalog
always serializes the 2.0 names — but `DTGCommon` declares
`#[serde(alias = "issuanceDate")]` / `alias = "expirationDate"`, so a foreign
credential using them still parses, and `policy/extract.rs:104` surfaces
`issuanceDate` to operator policies. Reading only `validUntil` would leave a
1.1-named credential unchecked while every other layer accepted it. A document
stating *both* spellings of one bound is rejected rather than resolved: serde
treats an alias as the same field, so the catalog parser rejects it as a
duplicate field, and ingress must not admit what the catalog cannot parse. A
test asserts that agreement in both directions.

## Tests

Six new tests in `credentials/ingress.rs` plus one in `routes/relationships.rs`,
all minting through the catalog constructors (`DTGCredential::new_vrc`) via
`test_support::dtg_json` — no hand-rolled JSON. Unit tests rather than
integration tests because `dtg-credentials` is a normal dependency of
`vtc-service` and so is not reachable from `tests/`; a `tests/` version would
have to hand-roll fixtures, which is the thing the convention forbids.

`cargo test -p vtc-service` passes; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --
-D warnings` is clean.

## Mutation test

The guard fails when broken, in both directions:

- `valid_until <= now` → `valid_until <= DateTime::<Utc>::MIN_UTC` fails four
  tests: `rejects_a_credential_whose_window_has_passed`,
  `window_boundaries_are_valid_from_inclusive_and_valid_until_exclusive`,
  `enforces_the_window_under_the_vc_1_1_property_names`, and
  `refuses_a_vrc_whose_validity_window_has_passed`.
- `valid_from > now` → `valid_from > DateTime::<Utc>::MAX_UTC` fails
  `rejects_a_credential_not_yet_valid`.

Both reverted; the committed tree is the unmutated one.

---

Based on `main`, not on `test/catalog-validator-roundtrip`: #1072 merged as edec8277 before this branch was cut, so `credentials/ingress.rs` is already on main and no stacking is needed.

title: Credential validity windows are enforced unevenly across ingress paths
body:
## Summary

Some paths enforce `validFrom`/`validUntil`, others accept a credential whose
window has passed.

## Detail

Enforced:

- **VIC** — `credentials/invitation_verify.rs` checks `validFrom <= now <
  validUntil` and returns a specific "invitation expired at …" error.
- **Recognition** — clamps the minted session TTL to
  `min(jwt_default, vec.validUntil - now, vmc.validUntil - now)`, so an expired
  credential cannot mint a live session.

Not enforced:

- **VRC publish** (`routes/relationships.rs`) — reads neither field. An expired
  relationship credential becomes a permanent graph edge.

## Why it matters

Security Considerations 2: "Verifiers must reject credentials outside their
`validFrom`/`validUntil` window (or v1.1 equivalents) and should check
applicable revocation status via the governing trust registry."

Ranked below the other findings because that section is marked *informative*,
so this is a conformance expectation rather than a normative MUST. It is still
a real gap: the VRC is the credential with the longest practical lifetime in
the graph, and it is the one path that never checks.

Note the revocation half is a deliberate divergence rather than an oversight —
planning-review D7 gives VRCs no `credentialStatus`, revocation being row
deletion. Worth stating explicitly somewhere, since a reader comparing against
the specification will otherwise read it as a second gap.

## Suggested fix

Apply the window check in the shared ingress validator proposed in #1064,
rather than adding a third bespoke implementation.

Conformance audit finding **F9**.

title: The persona credential (VPC) has no implementation
body:
## Summary

`PersonaCredential` appears nowhere in this repo, and `DTGCredential::new_vpc`
is never called. The P-DID is consequently unimplemented across the whole
stack.

## Detail

DTG Credentials defines the VPC as a **DTG annotation credential** through
which a party asserts a persona to a counterparty:

- issuer: the P-DID of the persona
- `credentialSubject.id`: the counterparty's DID, typically the R-DID or M-DID
  used in the relationship

Its purpose is explicit — "Persona DIDs enable individuals to control
intentional correlation separately from their M-DIDs" — and §Privacy
Considerations 3 makes it one of only two sanctioned routes to correlation:
"Correlation across relationships should occur only through the holder's
deliberate assertion of a persona (via a VPC) or an M-DID — never as a side
effect of credential structure."

## Why it matters

Three things fall out of its absence:

1. **The vocabulary collapsed.** With no VPC, "persona" in this stack came to
   mean the membership DID — `openvtc`'s `persona_did` is the DID a member
   joins with. #1054 was largely spent establishing that, and the confusion is
   a direct consequence of the concept having no implementation to anchor it.
2. **Deliberate correlation has no mechanism.** A member who wants to be
   recognised across relationships can currently only do so by reusing their
   membership DID — the blunt instrument — because the precise one does not
   exist.
3. **It bounds the ZKP work.** The Pairwise Zero-Knowledge Proof discloses
   P-DIDs while hiding R-DIDs. Without the VPC there is nothing to disclose.

## Suggested fix

Implement the VPC as the deliberate-correlation mechanism it is meant to be,
and reserve the word "persona" for it — renaming `persona_did` in `openvtc` to
name what it actually is.

Sequencing note: trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#9 asks how a VPC binds to a
specific relationship or edge, which is unresolved upstream. The credential can
be implemented before that settles; the ZKP construction on top of it cannot.

Conformance audit finding **F7**. Relates to #1054 and
trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#22.

title: feat(vtc): implement the VPC as the deliberate-correlation mechanism on an edge (#1074)
body:
feat(vtc): implement the VPC as the deliberate-correlation mechanism on an edge (#1074)

* feat(vtc): implement the VPC as the deliberate-correlation mechanism on an edge

`PersonaCredential` appeared nowhere in this repo and
`DTGCredential::new_vpc` was never called, so the P-DID had no
implementation and the word "persona" drifted onto the membership DID for
want of anything to anchor it (#1067).

What the absence cost, concretely. After the publish proof-of-possession
change (#1054) a member had exactly two settings: publish under a pairwise
relationship DID and correlate with nothing, or publish under the
membership DID and correlate with everything, permanently, for anyone who
retains the credential. DTG Credentials §Privacy Considerations 3 says
correlation "should occur only through the holder's deliberate assertion of
a persona (via a VPC) or an M-DID". The precise instrument was missing, so
members had only the blunt one.

This adds the VTC half of it: `POST` / `DELETE
/v1/relationships/{id}/persona` (`vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs`).
A VPC is an *annotation* credential — it creates no graph structure, it
attaches to structure that already exists — so there is no "publish a VPC",
only "attach this persona to that edge", and the annotation is stored on the
edge row (`vtc-service/src/relationships/mod.rs`) rather than in a keyspace
of its own. The P-DID surfaces on `GET /v1/relationships/graph` as
`personaDid`, which is where the correlation becomes visible; an annotation
nothing reads would leave #1067 in the state it describes.

trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#9 asks how a VPC binds to a specific
relationship and is open. Nothing here answers it. A VPC names its persona
(`issuer`) and the counterparty (`credentialSubject.id`) and not the
relationship DID the persona used, so it does not identify an edge on its
own.

Rather than add a field to the credential and present that as the
resolution, the binding is made at the request level:

1. the caller names the edge by id in the URL;
2. the caller proves control of that edge's `issuerDid`, with the same
   proof-of-possession construction publishing the edge required;
3. the VPC's `credentialSubject.id` must equal the edge's `subjectDid`.

(2) is what makes it safe — the only party who could have published this
edge is the only party who can annotate it, so no new trust is extended.
(3) is a consistency check, not a binding. If #9 lands an in-credential
binding (a `digest` over the VRC, as the VWC already has), the endpoint can
require it as well without changing the stored shape.

Stated limitation: the spec says a VPC's subject is "typically the R-DID or
M-DID used in the relationship". A VPC naming the counterparty's M-DID, on
an edge whose `subjectDid` is their R-DID, fails check (3) and is rejected.
That case is real and needs the same #9 answer; guessing would mean
accepting a VPC naming a party the VTC cannot tie to the edge, which is the
problem restated.

- **No uniqueness check on the P-DID**, in direct contrast to the R-DID rule
  the publish path enforces unconditionally. A relationship DID that recurs
  across counterparties is a defect; a persona DID that recurs is the entire
  purpose of the credential.
- **Detach is in scope.** A privacy mechanism that cannot be reversed is
  worse than none, so withdrawing a persona is as available as asserting one
  — and gated identically, or anyone could strip another member's persona.
  The two authorization `type` values are distinct so neither can stand in
  for the other.
- **No `persona.rego`.** Attach is gated on a live member session plus proof
  of control of the edge's issuer. A community that already decides whether
  an edge may be published has not obviously earned a second say over what
  its issuer calls themselves. Additive if that is wrong.
- **No P-DID secondary index.** "List every edge of persona P" is answerable
  from the admin graph; an enumeration surface deserves its own design
  rather than falling out of an index write.
- **`new_vpc` is used in a wire-shape test, not a mint path**
  (`vtc-service/src/credentials/dtg.rs`). The VTC has no key that may
  legitimately sign a VPC — it is self-issued by a person — so there is no
  `issue_persona`. Pinning the catalog's VPC shape matters more here than
  for the credentials the VTC does mint: drift changes what we *accept*, and
  the failure mode is every conformant VPC in the ecosystem being rejected
  by a VTC that still compiles and still passes its own tests.
- **Audit** (`VpcAttached` / `VpcDetached`, `vti-common/src/audit/event.rs`)
  records the P-DID with the authenticated member as actor — the same
  attribution decision, and the same accepted residual, as VRC publish. The
  `info!` on both paths carries the persona and not the member.

`vtc/relationships/persona/0.1` is bound ahead of its publication in the
upstream Trust Task registry and recorded in `UNPUBLISHED_CANONICAL_OK`
(`vtc-service/tests/trust_task_manifest.rs`) — the first entry the
`spec/vtc/` family has had. Deliberate: a payload schema authored now would
encode this request-level binding as if #9 were closed.

Design note: `docs/05-design-notes/vpc-persona-annotation.md`.

Closes #1067

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vtc): let the issuer of a pairwise edge retract it

`revoke` kept the identity equality `publish` replaced in #1054/#1061 —
`auth.did == rel.issuer_did` — sitting one function below where it was
fixed, in the same file. For an edge published under a pairwise
relationship DID that compares a membership DID against an R-DID and is
false by construction, so since #1061 a member could lodge an edge and
then never take it back. Only an admin could. The publish path grew a
proof-of-possession precisely because the identifier had stopped being the
member's own; revocation needed the same thing and did not get it.

`revoke_issuer_can_retract_own` (`vtc-service/tests/relationships.rs`)
seeds `ISSUER_DID` as the session DID — the attributed form, where the
equality still holds. That is why this shipped green, and it is the whole
reason the new test suite is written against the pairwise form.

`DELETE /v1/relationships/{id}` now takes an optional body carrying a
`VrcRevokeAuthorization`: `check_authorization_envelope` (`type`, `aud`,
`sessionId`, `issuedAt` — shared with the publish and persona objects) plus
the row `id`, then the same data-integrity check against the row's
`issuerDid`. Bound to the row rather than to a credential digest because
the request names a row and carries no credential.

Three routes to authorization, and the first two are exactly as before:
attributed (`auth.did == rel.issuer_did`, no proof needed — the session
already demonstrates control of that key), admin moderation (keys on row
id, untouched), and pairwise (the new proof). Every client sending this
request today sends no body at all and keeps working: `Option<Json<_>>`
yields `None` without a JSON content-type, and still rejects a malformed
body when one is present.

The authorization is verified and discarded — never stored, logged or
audited. It carries `sessionId`, which is attributable to a membership DID,
and this handler writes to the audit store, so it is the one place on the
pairwise path where that linkage could plausibly become durable. Proving
control of the issuing key is recorded as `revoked_by: "issuer"`, not
"admin": it *is* being the issuer, and the trail is what an operator reads
to answer who did what.

## Mutation testing, and the two tests it added

The suite was written first and confirmed failing against the unfixed
handler (403 `only the issuer or an admin can revoke a VRC`). Four
mutations were then applied to the new check:

- type guard neutered — **survived**. `rejects_a_publish_authorization_
  replayed_as_a_revoke` was being caught by the *edge* binding, because a
  publish authorization has no `relationship` field, so `type` was never
  exercised. Added `rejects_an_authorization_of_the_wrong_type`, valid in
  every respect except the field under test. Mutant now killed.
- edge binding removed — killed by `rejects_an_authorization_bound_to_a_
  different_edge`.
- signature check removed — killed by `rejects_an_authorization_signed_by_
  another_key`.
- session binding neutered — **survived**. Every test presented its
  authorization in the session it was minted for, so nothing exercised the
  binding the publish design note calls load-bearing. Added
  `rejects_an_authorization_replayed_in_another_members_session`: a second
  member replays a captured object whose signature is still the issuer's
  and still verifies, so `sessionId` is the only thing standing between
  them and an edge they do not control. Mutant now killed.

Both survivors were tests that passed for the wrong reason. Neither would
have been found by reading the diff.

`docs/05-design-notes/vrc-publish-proof-of-possession.md` said "admin
revocation is unaffected — it keys on row id, not issuer identity", which
is true and was the wrong half to reassure the reader about. It now states
what happens to both halves, and records the general lesson: replacing an
identity equality is not done until every sibling operation on the same
resource has been checked for the same equality.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* test(vtc): read the persona off the half, not the edge

The graph became pair-grouped in #1073 — an edge carries `halves`, and the
per-VRC fields moved onto them. The persona is asserted per VRC, so it moved
too. These assertions were written against the flat shape on a branch cut
before that landed.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(vtc)!: distinguish half-edges from complete edges in the relationships graph
body:
Closes the remaining graph work on #1054. One of the two open items is built,
one is deliberately not, and the reasoning for the second is the part worth
reading.

## Built: half-edges vs complete edges

DTG Credentials defines a DTG edge as **two** VRCs, one in each direction.
`GET /v1/relationships/graph` returned one entry per stored VRC, so a mutual
relationship and a unilateral claim rendered identically — two members who had
each vouched for the other looked the same as one member asserting an edge the
other has never acknowledged.

That distinction is what the dropped subject-membership check was replaced
*with*. #1061 stopped requiring the subject to be a current member, on the DTG
rule that "community membership is not a precondition for issuing, holding, or
presenting a VRC", and on the reasoning that the subject's consent to an edge is
their publication of the reciprocal VRC. An operator who cannot see whether that
reciprocal VRC arrived cannot see the consent signal at all.

The response now groups by unordered pair (`build_graph`,
`vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:817`). Each edge carries:

- `endpoints` — the two DIDs, sorted, so a pair has one identity whichever half
  was published first
- `halves` — every VRC published between them, oldest first, each with the row
  id that `DELETE /v1/relationships/{id}` takes
- `complete` — a VRC exists in **both** directions

Two cases that are easy to get wrong, both pinned by tests:

- **Several VRCs in one direction do not complete an edge.** Idempotency is
  keyed on the credential hash, not on direction
  (`vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:322`), so a member can publish three
  A→B VRCs. `complete` checks for a VRC in each direction, not for two rows.
- **A self-issued VRC (`issuer == subject`) is never complete.** No counterparty
  can reciprocate, and the naive both-directions test matches the same row
  twice. Nothing on the publish path rejects a self-issued VRC, so this is
  reachable.

Admin UI (`vtc-service/admin-ui/src/plugins/relationshipsGraph.tsx`): complete
edges draw solid and double-headed, half-edges dashed and single-headed pointing
at the party who has not answered; the overview counts the two separately and a
selected node's edge list reads "mutual with" vs "not reciprocated".

**Breaking:** `edges[]` was `{id, issuerDid, subjectDid, createdAt}` per VRC and
is now `{endpoints, halves, complete}` per pair, with the old fields moved onto
`halves[]`. The only consumer is the in-repo admin UI, updated here.

## Not built: making the graph derived rather than stored

Item 3 of the proposal on #1054 was "make the graph derived rather than
stored… without persisting an M-DID adjacency list." I did not build it. Three
reasons, recorded in full in
`docs/05-design-notes/vrc-publish-proof-of-possession.md`.

**The motivation was removed by #1061, not deferred.** The concern was a durable
*membership-DID* adjacency list. Since #1061 the stored DIDs are whichever
identifier the member chose to publish under: under the pairwise form an R-DID,
which names nobody and correlates nothing beyond the one relationship it was
minted for; under the attributed form a membership DID the member has
deliberately asserted, which DTG Credentials permits directly. Neither is what
item 3 was written against.

**"Derived" has no source to derive from.** The relationships keyspace is the
only place a published VRC exists on the VTC side — `Relationship.vrc_jsonld`
holds the credential verbatim, and `issuer_did`/`subject_did` are projections of
fields inside it (`vtc-service/src/relationships/mod.rs:62-85`). Deriving the
graph from something else means not storing published VRCs at all, which deletes
`POST /v1/relationships` and both read endpoints with it. The change that *is*
available is narrower — drop the two projected DID columns and re-read them from
the stored credential on each scan — and it removes no information, because the
credential containing them is still the row.

**Nothing publishes.** I checked the claim rather than taking it: `POST
/v1/relationships` is the only production writer to the keyspace and it has no
caller. Not in this workspace (only `vtc-service/tests/relationships.rs`), not
in `vta-sdk` (no relationship protocol module at all), not in `vtc-client`, and
not in `openvtc`. OpenVTC mints VRCs through `DTGCredential::new_vrc` and
exchanges them peer-to-peer over DIDComm
(`openvtc/src/state_handler/inbox_actions.rs:745`,
`openvtc/src/state_handler/main_page/mod.rs:2096`), then retains them locally;
it speaks the VTC's join, ACL, credential-exchange and self-remove Trust Tasks
but never `relationships/publish`. So the graph is empty in every deployment
that exists.

None of that makes the question wrong — a community that gets real publish
traffic under the attributed form does accumulate a correlatable edge set, by
design and with the members' assertion, and one that gets pairwise traffic
accumulates a set correlatable only to an operator holding the audit trail,
which #1061 already recorded as an accepted residual. It makes it premature.
The point to revisit is when something publishes, and the decision then is
whether to keep the two DID columns or read them out of the credential — not
whether to hold the credentials.

## Uncertainty worth flagging

The half-edge/complete rule assumes the two directions are linkable by DID
equality: A's VRC names B's identifier as subject and B's names A's as issuer.
Under pairwise identifiers that holds only because each party publishes the R-DID
its counterparty already knows. If a future flow has a party rotate its R-DID
mid-relationship, the two halves stop pairing and a complete edge silently
becomes two half-edges. Nothing in the stack does that today and the R-DID
uniqueness check would reject the rotated DID's second counterparty anyway, but
it is the assumption the grouping rests on.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — 30 test binaries, 0 failures
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt`
- `npm run lint` in `vtc-service/admin-ui` (tsc, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` on)

New coverage: 6 unit tests on `build_graph` (minted through
`DTGCredential::new_vrc`, not hand-rolled JSON) and 2 integration tests on the
endpoint (`graph_separates_complete_edges_from_half_edges` pins the wire shape,
`graph_is_admin_only` the gate — the endpoint had no test before).

Refs #1054

title: Pairwise relationship identifiers vs. the relationships ACL policy
body:
Raised from OpenVTC/openvtc#241, which proposes defaulting relationship
communication to pairwise Relationship DIDs (R-DIDs) rather than the persona
DID. That issue originates in an external RAHP/DRARM assessment finding
(`OVTC-RAHP-04`) scoring persona-DID relationship communication as stable-
identifier correlation.

The client-side half of that change is straightforward. But it collides with a
VTC policy, and the protocol question belongs here.

## The collision

`vtc-service/policies/default/relationships.rego` is the whole policy:

```rego
default allow := false
allow if {
	input.action == "publish"
	input.issuer_member.is_current
	input.subject_member.is_current
}
```

Both parties must be current, ACL-listed, non-tombstoned community members
(`vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:122-134`, `:349-356`). And the issuer
is pinned to the authenticated session DID:

`vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:97-107`
```rust
let issuer_did = extract_did_field(vrc, "issuer")?;
let subject_did = extract_subject_id(vrc)?;
if auth.did != issuer_did {
    return Err(AppError::Forbidden(format!(
        "session DID ({}) does not match VRC issuer ({issuer_did}) — \
         VRCs are self-issued; the VTC never mints them on a member's behalf", auth.did)));
}
```

A pairwise R-DID has no ACL row, so a VRC issued under one is rejected — 422
"subject DID … is not a current community member", or 403
`RelationshipPolicyDenied`. **The only enforcement that exists on this path
forbids pairwise identifiers rather than requiring them.**

`GET /v1/relationships/graph` (`routes/relationships.rs:446`) then deliberately
exposes the full correlatable member-to-member edge set to admins.

This is not a bug report — the ACL check is doing what it was designed to do.
It is a design question that the client cannot resolve on its own.

## The question

Should relationship communication use pairwise identifiers, and if so, how does
that reconcile with a trust graph whose entries are required to be attributable
to current members?

Some shapes worth weighing:

1. **Separate the two.** Pairwise identifiers govern the *communication channel*;
   the published VRC stays persona-attributed. This is roughly what OpenVTC does
   today — the R-DID carries post-handshake messages, the VRC `issuer` is the
   persona DID. It bounds the exposure to the graph, but the graph is exactly
   where the correlation the assessment describes lives.
2. **Pairwise in the graph, with a membership proof.** Let a VRC be issued under
   an R-DID accompanied by evidence that the R-DID belongs to a current member,
   without naming which. Costs a proof mechanism the stack does not have.
3. **Accept persona attribution as intended.** The trust graph's value may
   depend on edges being attributable; if so, say that explicitly so clients
   stop treating pairwise as an unrealised goal.

## What is currently true, for the record

The pairwise concept is absent from this repo and from `vta-sdk`. `pairwise`,
`R-DID` and `P-DID` do not appear as concepts; the word `pairwise` occurs once,
in an unrelated comment at `vtc-service/src/config.rs:764`. There is no
relationship protocol module in `vta-sdk` — the wire surface is four Trust Tasks
(`relationships/{list,graph,publish,revoke}/0.1`, `vtc-service/src/routes/mod.rs:631-644`),
and `PublishBody` is a single `vrc` field (`routes/relationships.rs:57`).
`vta-sdk` 0.27.0 → 0.28.0 changes nothing here.

Related prior decision: TSP relationship formation (the RFI/RFA invite→accept
FSM, and TSP's nested/pairwise VID APIs) was evaluated and dropped in favour of
relationship-free routed send —
`docs/05-design-notes/tsp-outbound-send.md:79-85`. Neither `form_relationship`
nor any nested-VID API is called anywhere in the repo.

The one "default to pairwise" statement in the design docs is
`design-docs/trust-task-delegation-architecture.md:278-285`, and it is scoped to
SIOPv2 / proxy-login subject DIDs against relying parties — not to relationship
edges.

## Why it matters more here than the generic pattern

The stable identifier in question is a published, resolvable `did:webvh` that
frequently carries a verified agent name. Two counterparties do not need traffic
analysis to correlate a persona across contexts — they compare a string and then
resolve it to a named identity. The linkage is a lookup, not an inference.

title: Tests hand-roll DTG credentials instead of minting them through the catalog
body:
## Summary

Where a test builds credential JSON by hand, it encodes the *implementation's
belief* about the wire form rather than the catalog's definition of it. The
test and the bug then agree with each other and with nothing that exists, and
the suite stays green through arbitrary drift.

This is the systemic cause behind #1062 and behind the VRC type error corrected
in #1061 — not a defect in itself, which is why it is worth fixing as its own
piece of work.

## Detail

The confirmed instance: `tests/recognise.rs` built its VEC as

```rust
let vec = sign_vc(issuer_seed, "VerifiableEndorsementCredential", &subject_did).await;
```

while `issue_endorsement` mints `EndorsementCredential` through
`DTGCredential::new_vec`. The handler matched the same fictional string, so
every recognition test passed and cross-community recognition was broken
against every genuinely-issued VEC. Changing only the fixture to the real wire
form — handler untouched — produced

```
400 presentation has no VerifiableEndorsementCredential
```

Both are fixed. The pattern is not: `sign_vc`-style hand-rolled builders remain
in `credentials/exchange/tests.rs` and elsewhere, and nothing prevents the next
one.

## Why it matters

A test suite that mints through the same catalog as production cannot disagree
with production about the wire form. One that hand-rolls can, silently, and the
green suite is then evidence of nothing.

## Suggested fix

1. Make `dtg_credentials` constructors the sanctioned way to build a DTG
   credential in a test. A helper crate-side (`test_support`) that wraps
   `new_vmc` / `new_vec` / `new_vrc` / `new_vic` + signing would cover most
   call sites.
2. Hand-rolled credential JSON becomes a deliberate, commented exception —
   legitimate for malformed-input cases, which genuinely need shapes the
   catalog cannot produce.
3. Consider a census test over the test tree for literal `"*Credential"` type
   strings, in the spirit of the existing `catalog_wire_shape` guard.

Conformance audit finding **F4**.

title: No shared ingress validator: DTG credentials are accepted without checking the common structure
body:
## Summary

DTG Credentials §Common Structure is normative and applies to every credential
type: `@context` MUST include both the W3C v2 and DTG contexts, and `type` MUST
include `VerifiableCredential`, `DTGCredential`, and exactly one concrete
subtype.

The stack asserts this on **everything it mints** and on almost nothing it
**accepts**.

## Detail

Issuance is in good shape. `credentials/dtg.rs` builds every VTC-minted
credential through the `dtg-credentials` catalog, and `catalog_wire_shape`
pins each one's exact `@context` and `type` arrays, in order, with a comment
explaining why order matters in JSON-LD. That is the pattern a reference
implementation should have.

Ingress has no equivalent. Until #1061 the VRC publish path never read `type`
at all, so any signed JSON with an `issuer` and a `credentialSubject.id` became
an edge in the community trust graph. #1063 fixes the same class in the
recognition path. Neither is a general solution — each closed one boundary by
hand.

Remaining boundaries that accept a DTG credential without validating the
common structure:

- `routes/recognise.rs` — validates type *classification* after #1063 but not
  `@context` or the `DTGCredential` base type
- `ceremony/verify.rs` / `ceremony/facts.rs` — credentials enter the decision
  pipeline as facts
- the join path — VIC handling validates temporal and single-use properties
  thoroughly, but not the common structure

## Why it matters

A credential that does not carry the DTG context is not a DTG credential, and
an edge is only interpretable if it says what it is. More practically: the two
bugs found so far (#1062 and the VRC type in #1061) were both invisible
*because* nothing validated the field they were wrong about.

## Suggested fix

One shared validator — `@context` entries, `DTGCredential`, exactly one
concrete subtype, classified through `dtg_credentials::DTGCredentialType` —
applied at every boundary that accepts a DTG credential. `check_vrc_shape` in
`routes/relationships.rs` (added in #1061) is the shape to generalise; it
should move out of that module rather than be copied.

Found in a conformance audit of the stack against DTG Credentials, prompted by
#1054. This is finding **F2**; the systemic reason it survived is F4.

title: test(vtc)!: check ingressed credentials against the catalog, and test validators against it too (#1072)
body:
test(vtc)!: check ingressed credentials against the catalog, and test validators against it too (#1072)

* test(vtc)!: check ingressed credentials against the catalog, and test validators against it too

Audit findings F2 and F4, together — because either alone reopens the trap. A
shared ingress validator whose tests hand-roll their input validates the
implementation against itself, which is the exact condition that let a handler
match `"VerifiableEndorsementCredential"` for its entire life while nothing has
ever issued that type.

**One place decides what a DTG credential is.** `credentials::ingress` checks
§Common Structure — both required `@context` entries, `VerifiableCredential` +
`DTGCredential`, exactly one concrete subtype — and classifies through
`dtg_credentials::DTGCredentialType`, the same catalog the issuing side mints
from. `check_vrc_shape` becomes a call to it. The recognition path gains the
check it never had: it classified on `type` alone, so a document carrying the
right subtype tag and neither `@context` entry was routed as though it were a
VEC.

**The tests assert against catalog output, not literals.** A literal in a test
can agree with a literal in a validator while both disagree with what any
client sends. So the guards mint through `new_vrc` / `new_vmc` / `new_vec` and
require the validator to accept the result. Change the catalog's wire form and
they fail; change a validator away from the catalog and they fail; no literal
in the file can make them pass.

`test_support::dtg_json` is the sanctioned way for a test to obtain a DTG
credential. Hand-rolled JSON stays correct for malformed-input cases — the
catalog cannot produce a credential missing its own `@context`.

Each guard was mutation-tested rather than assumed:

- accepted subtype in `check_vrc_shape` Relationship → Membership: the
  round-trip test fails
- the legacy tag re-added to `classify`: the refusal test fails
- the DTG context dropped from the recognition fixture: the end-to-end holder
  test fails, with the same 400 that #1062 produced

A guard that cannot fail is worth nothing, and three of these now demonstrably
can.

Also pinned: `VerifiableRecognitionCredential` and the `Verifiable`-prefixed
membership and endorsement tags are refused by name. All three were invented
here, none is a DTG type, and each has already cost a bug.

BREAKING CHANGE: a credential presented to `/v1/auth/recognise` that does not
carry the DTG common structure is now skipped rather than routed to its slot.
Credentials minted through `dtg-credentials` — which is every credential this
stack issues — are unaffected.

Refs #1054, #1062, closes #1064, closes #1066

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vtc): drop a duplicated #[test] attribute

An edit inserted a test function between `#[test]` and the function it
belonged to, leaving the new test with two attributes. Clippy's
`duplicate-macro-attributes` catches it under `-D warnings`, which is what
CI runs.

Harmless in effect — the affected test ran twice and passed twice, and the
displaced attribute was replaced — but the doubled name in the test output was
a signal, and it was there to be read before CI found it.

title: fix(join)!: require the DTG common structure on an ingested invitation (#256)
body:
fix(join)!: require the DTG common structure on an ingested invitation (#256)

`validate_invitation_credential` is careful and well-documented — it checks the
W3C VC Data Model 2.0 mandatory properties and the VIC profile the receiving
VTC enforces. It checked neither half of DTG Credentials §Common Structure,
which is normative for every DTG credential:

- `@context` MUST include `https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1`
- `type` MUST include `DTGCredential`

That string appears nowhere else in this repo. It is never required and never
checked, because everything openvtc *mints* goes through `dtg-credentials`,
which supplies it — so the one place a credential arrives from outside was also
the one place nothing verified it was a DTG credential at all. A document with
the right subtype tag and neither common-structure element passed as a VIC.

The fixtures agreed, which is why nothing noticed. `complete_vic` and
`pasteable_vic` both called themselves complete while carrying only the W3C
half, and the validator checked only the same half — so the test encoded the
implementation's belief about the wire form rather than the specification's
definition of it. Both now use the form `new_vic` actually emits, which is what
makes the new checks a regression test rather than a restatement: revert the
validator and nothing fails; revert the fixtures and the validator catches them.

Real VICs are unaffected. The VTC mints them through `DTGCredential::new_vic`
and its wire-shape guard pins both contexts and all three type entries, so a
credential any community actually issued already satisfies this.

The three constants are named in `openvtc-core` rather than spelled inline.
`dtg-credentials` builds all of them into what it mints but exports none of
them; removing the duplication needs a public constant upstream, requested in
OpenVTC/dtg-credentials#10.

BREAKING CHANGE: a pasted invitation lacking the DTG context or the
`DTGCredential` type is now refused at ingest with a message naming what is
missing, rather than accepted and submitted.

Refs OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1064

title: Audit events record credential type names that nothing issues
body:
## Summary

Emitted audit envelopes carry `credential_type: "VerifiableMembershipCredential"`
and `"VerifiableEndorsementCredential"`. Neither is a DTG credential type, and
nothing in the stack mints either.

## Detail

- `vti-common/src/audit/event.rs:901-902` documents the field as the "wire-form
  credential type", naming both.
- `vti-common/src/audit/event.rs:1593,1612` write them.
- `vtc-service/src/routes/endorsements.rs:226` sets
  `credential_type: "VerifiableEndorsementCredential"`.

What is actually issued is `MembershipCredential` and `EndorsementCredential`
— pinned by `catalog_wire_shape` in `credentials/dtg.rs`, and by
`DTGCredentialType`'s `Display`.

## Why it matters

No protocol behaviour depends on these strings, so the impact is low. But the
audit trail is the record intended to be authoritative after the fact, and it
currently names credential types that do not exist — which is misleading in
precisely the artifact an operator reaches for when reconstructing what
happened.

It is also the same root cause as #1062: a `Verifiable`-prefixed literal that
was never a wire tag, surviving because nothing compared it to what the catalog
emits.

## Suggested fix

Record `DTGCredentialType`'s `Display` value rather than a literal. Since these
strings are persisted, decide explicitly whether to migrate existing rows or
leave historical entries as-is and note the changeover — the field is inside
the envelope's chained content, so rewriting rows is not free.

Conformance audit finding **F10**.

title: refactor!: delete the Verifiable-prefixed credential tags that were never DTG types (#1071)
body:
refactor!: delete the Verifiable-prefixed credential tags that were never DTG types (#1071)

`VerifiableMembershipCredential` and `VerifiableEndorsementCredential` are not
DTG credential types and never were. The specification defines seven concrete
subtypes; neither is among them, and nothing in this stack has ever issued
either. They survived as a name, a pair of literals and a compatibility shim,
and between them they broke cross-community recognition for every real
presentation (#1062).

Four places, one cause.

**The SDK constant.** `VERIFIABLE_MEMBERSHIP_CREDENTIAL_TYPE` held the value
`"MembershipCredential"`, with a doc comment explaining that the prefix in the
name was historical and the tag did not have it. A constant whose name
disagrees with its value is an invitation, and it was taken: someone reading
the name hand-rolled `"VerifiableEndorsementCredential"` into the recognition
path, where it matched nothing. Renamed to `MEMBERSHIP_CREDENTIAL_TYPE`, and
`ENDORSEMENT_CREDENTIAL_TYPE` added beside it so the VEC tag has a home rather
than being a literal at the point of use.

**The compatibility shim.** #1063 added `LEGACY_TYPE_TAGS`, accepting both
prefixed tags from peers predating the catalog adoption. Nothing is published,
so no such peer exists — and a reference implementation that accepts a type the
specification does not define reintroduces exactly the drift the function it
sits in was written to prevent. Removed; the test that pinned the behaviour now
pins its refusal.

**The audit trail.** Emitted envelopes recorded `credential_type:
"VerifiableMembershipCredential"` / `"VerifiableEndorsementCredential"` — tags
no credential ever carried, in the one record meant to be authoritative after
the fact. They now record what was issued.

**The policy input.** `issuer_member` / `subject_member` were carried alongside
`issuer` / `subject` for operator policies written against the pre-#1061 shape.
There are no deployed operator policies to preserve, and two spellings of one
concept is how the concept drifts. The duplicates are gone and the surviving
fields carry `is_current`.

Docs: the `relationships` rows in the MVP spec described the old input shape and
the old default-policy rule. The retired `publish/1.0` trust-task doc called a
VRC a "Verifiable Recognition Credential" — wrong in every version, so corrected
in place rather than left as a retired-doc excuse.

Deliberately untouched: `subject_member` in `removal.rego` and the ceremony
documents is an unrelated input shape that happens to share a name.

BREAKING CHANGE: `vta_sdk::protocols::members::VERIFIABLE_MEMBERSHIP_CREDENTIAL_TYPE`
is renamed to `MEMBERSHIP_CREDENTIAL_TYPE` (value unchanged). The
`relationships.rego` input drops `issuer_member` / `subject_member`; the shipped
default policy is updated, and an operator policy reading the old names now
denies rather than silently passing. Recognition no longer accepts the
`Verifiable`-prefixed tags.

Refs #1054, #1062, closes #1070

title: feat(relationships)!: issue the VRC under the relationship DID, not the persona (#255)
body:
feat(relationships)!: issue the VRC under the relationship DID, not the persona (#255)

The last half of #241, and the half that mattered most.

Relationship communication has defaulted to a pairwise R-DID since #254, but
the credential it produces did not. `prepare_accept_vrc_request` minted the VRC
with `issuer = persona_did`, signed with the persona key. The subject was
already the peer's R-DID, so only the issuer half was persona-attributed — and
that was enough: the pairwise channel led straight back to the persona.

It is the worst place to leak it. The handshake DIDs are observed once, by the
mediator, at establishment. The VRC is the durable artifact both parties retain
and may publish to a community trust graph, where it correlates every
relationship a persona holds for as long as anyone keeps a copy. #241 said the
same: "The handshake persona DID is observed once; a published VRC correlates
indefinitely."

This could not be fixed here before now. The VTC pinned a published VRC's
issuer to the authenticated session DID, so a VRC issued under a relationship
DID was rejected outright — the only enforcement that existed forbade pairwise
identifiers rather than requiring them. Lifted in
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1061, which separates membership (proven
by the session) from the identifier the credential carries.

Both ends move together, so this is breaking on the wire:

- **Issuance** signs as whichever identity the relationship uses, keyed on
  `is_persona_did` — the same discriminator `listener_id_for_did` routes sends
  on. A relationship established without a dedicated R-DID still signs with the
  persona key, unchanged.
- **`vet_vrc_issued` gate 2** now requires the issuer to be the sender's DID in
  *this* relationship rather than their persona DID. That is strictly tighter
  as well as more private: gate 1 already matched the authenticated DIDComm
  sender against the same field, so the credential is pinned to the channel it
  arrived on instead of to a persona that could have issued it anywhere.
  Relationships with no R-DID are unaffected — `remote_did` equals
  `remote_p_did` there, and a test pins that.

The `#key-1` verification-method convention that `generate_did_peer_from_secrets`
imposes was already load-bearing in two places and spelled out longhand in
both. It is now named — `relationship_signing_vm_id` — with the secret lookup
beside it in `openvtc-core`, so the TUI crate does not reach into the secrets
resolver directly.

Docs: the note deferring "full pairwise operation, including the VRC issuer
field" to upstream work is replaced by what actually happens, including why the
issuer field mattered more than the handshake routing does. The example
credential showed a `did:webvh` issuer; it now shows the `did:peer` one it
would really carry.

What #241 leaves open after this is the handshake routing itself, which is
intrinsic — the mediator must route request/accept/finalise before a pairwise
channel exists — and worth closing as accepted rather than outstanding.

BREAKING CHANGE: a VRC issued by a peer running an older build carries their
persona DID and is now refused, and one issued by this build is refused by
older peers. Nothing is published yet, so no compatibility window is provided.

Refs #241, OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1054
