title: fix(deps): take the patched h2, and document the line that has no patch
body:
## The advisory

**RUSTSEC-2026-0258** — h2 accepts and queues empty DATA frames without limit.
A peer that never drains can drive unbounded memory growth, or a panic if the
length overflows. Upstream rates it **Low** and patched it in **0.4.16**.

The graph carried two h2 lines. They end differently, and the difference is the
whole PR.

## 0.4.14 → 0.4.16 — fixed

A straight bump to the patched release.

The lockfile moves **exactly one package**. I checked this rather than eyeball
the diff, because the raw diff also shows `windows-sys`, `syn` and `socket2`
lines that look like downgrades — they are dependency-list ordering inside
packages that already had both versions in the graph:

```
REMOVED: ['h2@0.4.14']
ADDED:   ['h2@0.4.16']
```

## 0.3.27 — cannot be fixed here, now an explicit exception

There is no version to move to: **0.3.27 is the newest 0.3**, and upstream
patched only the 0.4 line.

It arrives as `hyper 0.14 → hyper-tls 0.5 → reqwest 0.11 → ssi-dids-core 0.1.3
→ affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk`, reaching **`trust-tasks-tsp`** (via
`affinidi-tsp`) and **`trust-tasks-proof`**. That is the *normal* graph, not a
dev-dependency — crates we publish link it.

Nothing in this repo can shorten that chain:

- our requirements are already open — `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk = "0.8"`,
  `affinidi-tsp = "0.1"`
- every 0.8.x of the resolver SDK **up to and including the newest, 0.8.22**,
  requires `ssi-dids-core ^0.1`
- `ssi-dids-core 0.1` is what pins reqwest 0.11, hence hyper 0.14, hence h2 0.3

I tried bumping the Affinidi crates (0.8.7 → 0.8.13, affinidi-tsp 0.1.6 →
0.1.14). It does not clear the advisory and churns the lockfile substantially,
so it is deliberately **not** in this PR.

### Exposure, stated rather than waved away

`reqwest` is an HTTP **client** here, used to resolve DIDs. Reaching the flaw
needs a hostile or compromised resolution endpoint, and the cost is
availability only — memory growth or a panic, with no confidentiality or
integrity component. That is the entire argument for accepting it, and it is an
argument for accepting it *temporarily*.

### Why this exception is different from the others

Every entry already in `deny.toml`'s ignore list is a **maintenance-status**
notice that says "no active CVE". This is the first that is a real
vulnerability. The comment marks it as such so nobody reads the list as
uniformly harmless, and states the clearing condition: it goes when
`affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` moves to `ssi-dids-core 0.3+`, which is on
reqwest 0.12 / hyper 1.x and so on the patched h2 line. Worth re-checking
whenever the Affinidi crates are bumped.

## Why this is a separate PR

It surfaced on #240, but that PR only adds JSON Schemas and touches neither
`Cargo.lock` nor `Cargo.toml`. The advisory was published after main's last
green run, so **main fails it too** — this is not a regression from #240 and
should not be buried in a spec change.

## Test

- `cargo deny check` — clean across advisories, bans, licenses, sources
- `cargo test --workspace` — **493 passing, 0 failures**

title: spec(vta): an application-state store, versioned and namespaced
body:
Adds `vta/app-state/{get,put,list,delete,get-many,put-many}/1.0` — a third store on the VTA, beside the secrets vault and the credential vault, for versioned, namespaced, per-context JSON that an application owns and the VTA does not interpret.

Input for this is the design note [`docs/05-design-notes/appstate-store.md`](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/blob/main/docs/05-design-notes/appstate-store.md) in `OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure`, which is §7 step 1 of the sequence tracked by [#1029](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/issues/1029).

## Why a third store

Records are addressed by `(contextId, namespace, key)`. The namespace scopes one application so several tools can share a context without colliding, and is the seam a per-namespace grant would later use — which is why it is part of the address rather than a prefix convention on the key.

Agent memory (`vta/memory/*`) is the closest existing fit and is the wrong home for three reasons, the first of which settles it on its own:

- **"Forget everything" must stay safe to ask an agent.** It must not take an account's community memberships with it.
- `MemoryItem` is `{key, value}` — no version, nothing to hang a precondition on.
- `list` returns every entry in the context. Application state and agent memory grow independently, so every application read would pay for the agent's memory.

The secrets vault is shaped as a password manager (`secret_kind`, site-oriented `targets`); the credential vault is right for VCs, and application metadata is *about* credentials rather than being one.

## Three properties that make this a store rather than a field

**`version` is a per-`(contextId, namespace)` counter, not per record.** This is the one refinement over the design note, and it is load-bearing. A record's `version` is the counter value its most recent write took, so one number is simultaneously the optimistic-concurrency token `expectedVersion` compares against and the watermark `sinceVersion` compares against. A per-record counter serves the first but cannot serve the second: two records' per-record counters are not comparable to each other, so no single number could mean "everything changed after this point". The cost is that a record's version jumps between writes, which the shared schema states normatively.

**A failed precondition returns the current version *and value*.** A bare rejection obliges the caller to re-read, and between the rejection and the re-read the record can change again — the pattern has no fixed point under contention. Returning the winner's view with the rejection removes the race rather than narrowing it. This is normative, not a courtesy.

**`delete` leaves a versioned tombstone.** Without one, a consumer pulling from a watermark learns of every create and update and never of a deletion, so deleted records resurrect on its next rebuild and it disagrees with peers that saw the delete live. Retrofitting this later silently invalidates every watermark already in the field. Recommended retention is 30 days, and `list` refuses a `sinceVersion` older than the oldest retained tombstone with `watermarkTooOld` rather than serving an incomplete feed.

## Decisions worth review

- **`list` has two modes and the split is explicit.** Without `sinceVersion` it is a key-ordered snapshot; with it, a version-ordered change feed that always includes tombstones. `includeDeleted: false` together with `sinceVersion` is refused as a contradiction rather than honoured — a change feed that omits deletions cannot converge.
- **`highWatermark` on the response** is what a consumer stores, *not* `max(version)` over the returned records, which is wrong whenever a `prefix` filtered a later change out and undefined when the page is empty.
- **`put-many` defaults to `independent`.** An atomic default would let one stale record silently wedge an entire flush, and the caller could not distinguish a wedged flush from a slow one. `atomic` is available and reports per-record outcomes (`skipped` for writes not attempted) through `atomicBatchRejected`.
- **`get-many` accounts for every requested key** in exactly one of `records` / `missing` / `deferred`. `deferred` exists because the per-record cap times the key ceiling exceeds any sane response limit, and the alternative — refusing the whole batch — makes a caller bisect for a workable size.
- **Recommended per-record cap of 65536 bytes**, refused loudly with both `limitBytes` and `actualBytes`. A limit that drops a write silently has already cost a real deployment a lost join.
- **Blobs are deliberately out of scope in 1.0.** Adding a `blobRef` later is additive, and nothing in the first consumer's requirements needs one.
- **Namespaces are collision avoidance, not a trust boundary, in 1.0.** Both `put` and `delete` say so in `## Authorization`: mutually distrusting applications go in separate contexts. The address supports a future per-namespace grant, which is why namespace names should be chosen as though one existed.

## A codegen property this surfaced

A JSON-Schema `default:` is materialised by the codegen into a non-`Option` field with no `skip_serializing_if`, so an example omitting that member can never round-trip — the generated conformance test fails. `vault/list` avoids this only by accident: its request examples sit under `## Examples` rather than the `## Request` heading the codegen harvests from, so only its responses are round-trip tested.

Resolved deliberately here: `put-many.mode` keeps its schema `default` (which mode is the default is the spec's central claim, and a client transmitting it explicitly is correct) and its example states it; the convenience booleans carry their defaults in prose instead, matching what `list.includeDeleted` already did.

Worth a separate look, not fixed here: `checkExampleDocuments()` in `scripts/build-registry.mjs` compiles envelope validators only for `['0.1','0.2','0.3']`, so a `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.4"` document resolves to no validator and is silently skipped. That is currently every 0.4-targeting spec — 16 before this PR. The examples added here were validated against `_framework/0.4/trust-task.schema.json` out of band (56 documents, 0 failures), along with their payloads against their own payload schemas (30 payloads, 0 failures).

## Verification

- `npm run build` — 343 specs validated, 64 shared schemas indexed, no new warnings
- `npm run check-bindings` — 343 specs against 343 TS and 338 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — 450 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo test --workspace` — green

Bindings regenerated; `trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.1 → 0.11.2 and `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.12.1 → 0.12.2 (additive, patch per this crate's versioning policy).

title: release: publish the six siblings that now require trust-tasks-rs 0.11
body:
## The bug

#245 and #246 moved the sibling crates' `trust-tasks-rs` requirement to 0.11
**without moving their own versions**. `cargo publish` skips a version already
on crates.io, so none of them republished:

| crate | local | published | requires |
|---|---|---|---|
| trust-tasks-didcomm | 0.9.0 | 0.9.0 | trust-tasks-rs 0.11 |
| trust-tasks-https | 0.9.0 | 0.9.0 | trust-tasks-rs 0.11 |
| trust-tasks-proof | 0.9.0 | 0.9.0 | trust-tasks-rs 0.11 |
| trust-tasks-tsp | 0.9.0 | 0.9.0 | trust-tasks-rs 0.11 |
| trust-tasks-capability-client | 0.8.0 | 0.8.0 | trust-tasks-rs 0.11 |
| trust-tasks-didcomm-v1 | 0.8.0 | 0.8.0 | trust-tasks-rs 0.11 |

main requires 0.11; the registry still serves tarballs built against 0.9.

**That's not cosmetic.** A consumer taking trust-tasks-rs 0.11 together with any
of these gets two semver-incompatible copies of the same types. This is how it
was found — from `vtc-service`, trying to move VTI onto 0.11:

```
error[E0308]: expected `TrustTask<Value>`, found a different `TrustTask<Value>`
```

Minor bumps, because these crates carry `trust_tasks_rs` types in their public
APIs, so a semver-incompatible move of that dependency is breaking for their
consumers.

## The guard I added in #245 should have caught this

It didn't, and the reason matters: it watched `trust-tasks-rs/src/specs` only.
A change that alters **what a crate publishes without touching its source** —
which is exactly what a dependency-requirement bump is — was invisible to it.

It now checks **every publishable workspace member** against any change under
its directory. That's the shape the TDK's equivalent guard has had all along,
and what I should have written the first time. Twice now this guard has been
too narrow; the general form is the correct one.

## Verification

Replayed on the committed tree:

```
ok   trust-tasks-https             0.9.0 -> 0.10.0
ok   trust-tasks-proof             0.9.0 -> 0.10.0
ok   trust-tasks-didcomm           0.9.0 -> 0.10.0
ok   trust-tasks-didcomm-v1        0.8.0 -> 0.9.0
ok   trust-tasks-tsp               0.9.0 -> 0.10.0
ok   trust-tasks-capability-client 0.8.0 -> 0.9.0
```

`cargo build --workspace` clean.

## Note

Raised from a git worktree — this repo's shared checkout is in use by another
agent working on `spec/webvh-retire-orphan`, and we collided in it earlier
today. Nothing from that work is in this PR.

title: spec(vta): withdraw an extended code the framework already names
body:
Follow-up to #252, fixing a defect in the error taxonomy it published. Found while implementing the slice in `OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure` ([#1029](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/issues/1029)) — the implementation could not emit two of the codes the specs declared, which is the useful kind of feedback an implementation gives a spec.

## `vta/app-state:permissionDenied` is withdrawn

It was declared as an **extended** code for a failure [SPEC §8.3](https://trusttasks.org/SPEC.md#83-standard-error-codes) already names as a **standard** one. Two consequences, both worse than the duplication:

- A consumer switching on the standard `permissionDenied` would not match it — exactly the consumer it was meant to serve.
- `TrustTaskCode::Extended` maps to `taskFailed` for status purposes, so emitting the extended form downgrades a 403-shaped refusal into a generic task failure.

A conforming VTA answers an unauthorized caller with the standard code, so the extended one was unreachable in practice as well as wrong in principle.

Note this pattern exists elsewhere in the registry (`vault/list:permissionDenied` and siblings). Not touched here — one slug per PR, per CONTRIBUTING — but worth a sweep if others agree it is the same defect.

## `vta/app-state:contextNotFound` is restated as OPTIONAL

Kept rather than removed: it is a real diagnostic where a maintainer's authorization model can distinguish "no such context" from "not permitted to reach it".

But where the ACL *enumerates* the contexts a caller may act in — the shape the reference VTA uses — a caller can only ever ask about contexts its grant names, so both conditions produce the same answer and the code is never emitted. The previous wording made it a `MUST` such a maintainer cannot satisfy, which is the kind of requirement that gets quietly ignored rather than met. It now reads as a `MAY`, with the standard `permissionDenied` named as the conforming answer to both.

## Scope

No payload, response, or generated-type changes — the declared `errorCodes` and the Conformance prose move, nothing on the wire does. `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` produces no diff under `trust-tasks-rs/src/`, which is the check that this is prose-only.

## Verification

- `npm run build` — 343 specs validated, no new warnings
- `npm run check-bindings` — 343 specs against 343 TS and 338 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — 450 passed, 0 failed

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.2 → 0.11.3 and `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.12.2 → 0.12.3.

title: test(approvals): prove a reprovision can be gated on a human, and say what that does not buy
body:
#1030 argues that self-service recovery is already just DTTE: register the
provisioning task URI as consent-requiring and the existing ceremony does the
rest. The argument is sound and had never been run, which is the condition every
bug `delegated_consent_e2e.rs` exists for was found in. So this runs it.
Closes #1030.

## What the test establishes

`provision/integration/0.2` is dispatched and classified `[Mutating Secret
false]`, so the PDP gate sees it and it is not ceremony-exempt. That makes
consent-gating *plausible*; it does not make it work. The new case drives the
whole ceremony over the real router: the reprovision is refused with
`auth:consent_required` and a challenge-salted digest, a VTA-signed
`task-consent/request` is minted for the nominated approver, the approver signs
a decision, and the same payload in a fresh envelope then executes.

The approver deliberately holds **no ACL entry** — approver-set membership alone
authorizes the decision (#907), which is the property that lets a recovery
approver be a device rather than an administrator. Without that, the phone
approving your laptop's recovery would need admin rights over the context, and
the whole arrangement would be worse than the operator it replaces.

## The framing correction

The issue reads as though this delivers recovery for a new install. It does not,
and the gap is worth stating where operators will read it rather than leaving it
to be discovered during one.

Consent is the *policy* gate. It sits behind the bearer/authcrypt gate that
authenticates the caller, so a brand-new install holding no credential cannot
dispatch the task at all — approval rule or not. What the rule buys is recovery
**without an operator**, not recovery **from nothing**: an already-enrolled
device relays the request for the new one, which is exactly the
relayer-is-not-the-holder split provisioning was built around. The docs now say
so, and add the practical consequence — nominate the approver set while you
still have two devices, because a set established at recovery time is not a
recovery mechanism.

## The wire shape, found rather than assumed

The first draft sent `contextId`, the spelling most neighbouring tasks use. The
published `provision/integration/0.2` schema is `additionalProperties: false`
and names it `context`, so the spine refused the document as malformed.

That is the whole reason the refusal assertion checks
`details.reason == "auth:consent_required"` rather than just "the call failed".
A malformed-request rejection satisfies "it was refused" perfectly well, and the
remaining four steps would then have been exercising a ceremony that never
started — a green test proving nothing, which is the failure mode this file's
header is about.

## Also

`sealed-bootstrap.md` said `Status: **Design — not yet implemented**`. It is
implemented, and the stale line cost a reader a wrong assumption in a downstream
design doc, which is what #1030 reported. Corrected against the tree rather than
from memory: `sealed_transfer` plus the `vta`/`pnm bootstrap` surfaces, the
unified `POST /bootstrap/request` with its single-use carve-out and the retired
`GET /attestation/admin-credential`, `keys/wrapping.rs` built on
`sealed_transfer`, and no plaintext bundle encode paths left in `vta-sdk`. The
phase plan is retained as the design record with a note not to read it as
outstanding work.

No production code changes.

title: Allow reprovision to run as a DTTE-consentable task, for self-service recovery
body:
## Summary

Recovering a lost client today needs an operator with `pnm`:

```
new install   pnm bootstrap request --out req.json
operator      pnm context reprovision --id <ctx> --recipient req.json
new install   pnm bootstrap open --bundle <f> --expect-digest <hex>
```

That works, and the out-of-band step is a genuine security boundary — anything that lets an unauthenticated caller re-issue an admin credential means anyone who knows your context id can become you.

But where the user can already prove a **second registered factor**, the human in the loop is not adding security, only friction.

## This is just DTTE

Approvals are already *"one rule list keyed on **Trust Task type URI**"* in the reserved `approvals` policy row; `requires: consent` routes through the PDP to the ceremony — `task-consent/request/0.1`, `task-consent/decision/0.1` (DI-signed by the approver), `task-consent/granted/0.1`. And provisioning is already dispatched: `TASK_PROVISION_INTEGRATION_0_2`.

So the ask collapses to: **register the provisioning task URI as consent-requiring, with a recovery approver set.** Everything else is existing behaviour.

Three properties make it the right fit rather than merely a convenient one:

- **Approver-set membership alone authorizes a decision — an ACL entry is not required** (#907). The phone approving your laptop's recovery need not itself hold admin rights over the context.
- **Consent binds to the payload digest, not a session.** The approver approves *this* reprovision — this context, this recipient key — rather than elevating anything. Delegated step-up was deliberately deleted in favour of exactly this, and for recovery it is the difference between "approve one act" and "grant a capability".
- The approver only ever sees the challenge-salted `wire_digest`.

## Side benefit

`task-consent/decision/0.1` is signed by the approver, so an approved recovery produces a **second independently verifiable artifact** alongside the sealed bundle's `ProducerAssertion` — proof that a human approved, and which one. Better evidence than an audit row, and it needs no change to the audit log.

## Caveats

- Approvals are inert unless `policy.enforcement = true`, which defaults false — so this is opt-in per deployment.
- The `pnm approvals` surface is Trust-Task transport only; the SDK's REST arm is unimplemented and a REST client gets a 404. Fine for DIDComm clients, but a REST-only VTA cannot configure this today.

## Not urgent

Convenience, not capability — the operator path already delivers the recovery story. Worth doing when a second enrolled device is normal, which today it usually is not.

## Also, while here

`sealed-bootstrap.md` still says **"Status: Design — not yet implemented"**. `pnm-cli` implements the whole Mode A flow. That header cost me a wrong assumption in a design doc; worth a one-line fix.

## Context

`docs/design/vta-authoritative-state.md` (E1, D23) in OpenVTC/openvtc. D23 there is the product half: an approver set established *at recovery time* is not a recovery mechanism, so OpenVTC would prompt to nominate one during setup.

title: spec(vta): an application-state store, versioned and namespaced (#252)
body:
spec(vta): an application-state store, versioned and namespaced (#252)

Applications built on a VTA have had nowhere to keep versioned metadata.
Adds `vta/app-state/{get,put,list,delete,get-many,put-many}/1.0` — a third
store beside the secrets vault and the credential vault, for JSON an
application owns and the VTA does not interpret.

Records are addressed by `(contextId, namespace, key)`. The namespace scopes
one application so several tools can share a context without colliding, and
is the seam a per-namespace grant would later use — which is why it is part
of the address rather than a prefix convention on the key.

Three properties are the reason this is a store rather than a field on an
existing one:

- `version` is a monotonic counter maintained per `(contextId, namespace)`,
  not per record. One number is therefore both the optimistic-concurrency
  token `expectedVersion` compares against and the watermark `sinceVersion`
  compares against; a per-record counter serves the first but cannot serve
  the second, because two records' counters are not comparable to each other.
- A failed precondition returns the maintainer's current version *and value*
  with the rejection. A bare rejection obliges a re-read, and the re-read
  races the next write — the pattern has no fixed point under contention.
- `delete` leaves a versioned tombstone. Without one a consumer pulling from
  a watermark learns of every create and update and never of a deletion, so
  deleted records resurrect on its next rebuild. Retrofitting tombstones
  later silently invalidates every watermark already in the field.

Agent memory is untouched and remains safe to clear, which is the settling
argument for not building this on it: "forget everything" is a reasonable
thing to ask an agent and must not take an account's memberships with it.

Blobs are deliberately out of scope in 1.0; adding a `blobRef` is additive.

`put-many` keeps a schema `default` on `mode` because which mode is the
default is the spec's central claim, and the generated clients transmit it
explicitly. The convenience booleans state their defaults in prose instead,
so that an example omitting them round-trips exactly.

Regenerates both bindings and bumps trust-tasks-rs 0.11.1 -> 0.11.2 and
@openvtc/trust-tasks 0.12.1 -> 0.12.2.

title: chore(deps): affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.19.10, so a refused socket says why
body:
Floor `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.19.9 → 0.19.10 (affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#718). Manifest note and lockfile only; no code changes.

## Why

Two instances of this app on the same persona reconnect-loop against each other and it presents as a **network fault** rather than as "you have this open twice". The cause is not the mediator's one-socket-per-DID rule — it is that nothing on either side ever said what happened.

- **Server half.** `WebSocketCommands::Close` carried no reason, so the handler answered all three of its senders identically — the `duplicate-channel` problem report and `"replaced by a newer connection"`. That includes a newcomer **refused** by the duel damper, whose own connection was never displaced: the exact inverse of true.
- **Client half.** The sdk's websocket transport matched the close frame as `Message::Close(_)` and discarded it, logging `WebSocket connection closed by server` at debug. So even a correct reason on the wire changed nothing here.

#718 gives `Close` a `CloseReason`, maps each to its own problem-report code and close text, and surfaces the close code and reason at WARN in the sdk.

## Compatibility

`duplicate-channel` is preserved verbatim for the genuinely-replaced case. This repo matches on it only in doc comments and `openvtc-core/tests/didcomm_transport_e2e.rs`, and those are unaffected — hence a floor bump with no code change.

The eviction **policy** is deliberately untouched upstream. Displacement is what triggers the mediator's `spawn_inbox_redelivery`, and this repo is not representative in pulling stored mail explicitly via `message_pickup` — refusing outright would silently drop the stored-mail re-cover for clients that don't.

## Known gap

The mediator half of #718 is `affinidi-messaging-mediator` 0.18.21, and the newest `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator` (0.2.52) still embeds 0.18.20. The `#[ignore]`d transport e2e therefore still exercises the old close behaviour until a fixture carrying 0.18.21 publishes; the new reasons reach a live client only against a deployed mediator ≥ 0.18.21.

## Verification

`cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and `cargo test --workspace` all pass locally.

Closes the client-side half of OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1028.

title: feat(audit)!: make the audit destination a deployment choice, not a protocol one
body:
`AuditLogEntry` is `{id, timestamp, action, actor, resource, outcome, channel,
contextId, detail}` — no signature, no hash chain. The log corroborates what
happened; it cannot prove it, and a compromised VTA can rewrite its own history.
The canonical `AuditEnvelope` already names the members that would change that
(`prevHash`, `entryHash`, `schemaVersion`) and records why this maintainer omits
them: its log is flat and unchained.

This does not add tamper-evidence, deliberately. It adds the seam, so an
operator who needs a stronger guarantee implements one — an append-only file, a
transparency log, a blockchain anchor, a hash chain filling in those three
members — without the VTA committing to any scheme. Closes #1031.

## The shape

`vta_audit::AuditSink` takes the whole entry, one method. `KeyspaceAuditSink` is
today's behaviour and **owns the `log:{ts:020}:{uuid}` key format**, because that
format is a property of that backend rather than of the caller — a remote or
anchored sink has no use for a key. `FanOutAuditSink` composes several.

Modelled on `vti_common::telemetry::TelemetrySink`, whose own docs already name
"append-only log, blockchain anchor" as the backends it exists to admit: shared
`Arc` on `AppState`, defaulted through `AppStateParts`, `None` → unchanged
behaviour. The two stay separate for the reason recorded there — telemetry is
high-volume and query-oriented, audit is security-relevant and durable.

## Writes go through the sink; reads and retention do not

`cleanup_expired_logs` and the audit-list query still take a `KeyspaceHandle`,
and `AppState` carries both `audit_ks` and `audit_sink`. This is the design, not
an omission. A sink is free to be write-only and remote, and "delete rows older
than N days" is not an operation an append-only or anchored backend can offer —
the immutability is the point. Retention therefore stays a property of the local
keyspace, which is what the retention API is documented to govern.

The consequence is that swapping the sink outright would take `GET /audit/logs`
and the retention sweep with it. `FanOutAuditSink` is the answer: keep the
keyspace sink, add the new backend beside it. Every sink is attempted and the
first error returned only after all of them have run — short-circuiting would let
a failing sink hide an entry from the ones behind it, which for an audit log is
the failure mode that matters.

## The sweepers get the same sink object

Built once in `run()` and handed to both `AppStateParts` and the storage thread,
rather than reconstructed there. A sweeper's `acl.expire` is an unattended
removal — nobody was watching when the entry vanished — which makes it precisely
the row an operator installs a tamper-evident backend to capture. Rebuilding a
sink on the storage thread would have routed it back to the keyspace whatever
they configured, and the gap would surface only when someone went looking for a
deletion that was never recorded. `VtaState` clones the same `Arc` for the same
reason it shares the config `RwLock` (P1.1): two transports resolving audit
differently is a gap you find during an incident.

## Tests

Three unit tests on the sink module, five integration tests in
`vta-service/tests/audit_sink.rs`. The load-bearing one asserts **both** halves —
the installed sink receives the row *and the keyspace does not*. Without the
second assertion it would pass on a sink that merely observes alongside an
unchanged keyspace write, which delivers none of the property this exists for.
The others pin the default (no sink installed → the keyspace, exactly as
before), the sweeper path, the shared `Arc` across transports, and the fan-out
composition keeping the query API alive.

`storage_key` is pinned separately: the retention sweep stops at the first key
past its cutoff and the list query is a prefix scan, so both are correct only
while the key sorts by time *as a string* — which is what the zero-padding buys.

## Breaking

`vta_audit::{record, record_with_detail, record_consent}` take a
`&SharedAuditSink` where they took a `&KeyspaceHandle`. The alternative — keeping
the old signature and adding a parallel sink-taking one — would leave a second
way to write an audit row that bypasses the sink entirely, and a
tamper-evidence backend with a bypass is not one.

Mechanically this moved ~57 call sites across 24 files and a dozen `Deps`
structs, because the audit keyspace was threaded by hand everywhere rather than
carried once. `vta_keyspaces::Keyspaces.audit` is deliberately untouched: that
bundle's audit handle is a keyspace because backup export dumps it.

title: Mediator should protect the established connection, not evict it for a newcomer
body:
## Summary

The mediator's ceiling is **one websocket per DID**, and it enforces that by **evicting the established connection** in favour of the newcomer. That is backwards.

The incumbent is authenticated, live, and possibly mid-exchange. The newcomer has proved only that it can *also* authenticate. Preferring the newcomer means any second process silently takes over a live session — and when both retry, they take turns doing it, forever.

## This is a live bug, not a hypothetical

Two OpenVTC instances presenting the same persona reconnect-loop indefinitely, and it presents as a **network fault** rather than as "you have this open twice". It is the listener-flapping class already debugged in OpenVTC/openvtc#231 and the upstream affinidi-tdk-rs `force_refresh` fix.

Anyone who opens the app twice hits it today.

## Requested

An established, authenticated connection for a DID is **kept**. A second attempt is **refused**, with a reason the client can render — "this DID already has a live connection" — so the newcomer can say so instead of looping.

## The carve-out is probably unnecessary

Displacing a socket is currently how stored-mail redelivery gets triggered (OpenVTC/openvtc#218), so the obvious worry is that refusing would regress it.

Checked, and it does not for OpenVTC: it already collects stored mail explicitly through the standard message-pickup protocol (`affinidi_messaging_sdk::protocols::message_pickup`, via `Messaging::pickup_stored`). Redelivery does not need eviction, because there is a pull for it.

**Worth confirming across other clients before removing it** — the check is "does anything actually depend on connect-time displacement", not "assume nothing does". If OpenVTC is representative, the rule can simply be that the incumbent wins, with no opt-in displacement flag needed at all.

## Context

Raised from OpenVTC's side while building multi-instance detection (OpenVTC/openvtc#246). OpenVTC now registers as a device and heartbeats, so it can *tell* the user another instance is live — but detection is a workaround for the eviction behaviour, not a fix. Design notes in `docs/design/vta-authoritative-state.md` (E3) in that repo.

title: Pluggable audit sink, so tamper-evidence can be a deployment choice
body:
## Summary

`AuditLogEntry` is `{id, timestamp, action, actor, resource, outcome, channel, contextId, detail}` — **no signature, no hash chain**. The log corroborates what happened; it cannot prove it. A compromised VTA can rewrite its own history.

This issue deliberately **does not ask for tamper-evidence in the protocol**. The more useful move is an extension point.

## Requested

An audit sink trait the VTA writes through, with today's database sink as one implementation. An operator who needs stronger guarantees can then add one — an append-only log, a transparency log, a blockchain anchor — without the VTA committing to any particular scheme.

That keeps the crypto decision out of the protocol and turns "make the audit tamper-evident" from a design argument into a deployment choice.

## Why it is not urgent

For the case that matters most — proving a *recovery* was authorised — the evidence already exists elsewhere and is signed: the sealed bundle opened during bootstrap carries a `ProducerAssertion` (`AssertionProof::DidSigned`, or an attestation quote for a TEE VTA), which is independently verifiable. OpenVTC intends to retain that as a recovery receipt.

So the property is obtainable today where it counts. This is about making the log itself evidence rather than testimony, for everything else it records.

## Context

`docs/design/vta-authoritative-state.md` (E4, D20) in OpenVTC/openvtc.

title: feat(audit)!: make the audit destination a deployment choice, not a protocol one (#1049)
body:
feat(audit)!: make the audit destination a deployment choice, not a protocol one (#1049)

`AuditLogEntry` is `{id, timestamp, action, actor, resource, outcome, channel,
contextId, detail}` — no signature, no hash chain. The log corroborates what
happened; it cannot prove it, and a compromised VTA can rewrite its own history.
The canonical `AuditEnvelope` already names the members that would change that
(`prevHash`, `entryHash`, `schemaVersion`) and records why this maintainer omits
them: its log is flat and unchained.

This does not add tamper-evidence, deliberately. It adds the seam, so an
operator who needs a stronger guarantee implements one — an append-only file, a
transparency log, a blockchain anchor, a hash chain filling in those three
members — without the VTA committing to any scheme. Closes #1031.

## The shape

`vta_audit::AuditSink` takes the whole entry, one method. `KeyspaceAuditSink` is
today's behaviour and **owns the `log:{ts:020}:{uuid}` key format**, because that
format is a property of that backend rather than of the caller — a remote or
anchored sink has no use for a key. `FanOutAuditSink` composes several.

Modelled on `vti_common::telemetry::TelemetrySink`, whose own docs already name
"append-only log, blockchain anchor" as the backends it exists to admit: shared
`Arc` on `AppState`, defaulted through `AppStateParts`, `None` → unchanged
behaviour. The two stay separate for the reason recorded there — telemetry is
high-volume and query-oriented, audit is security-relevant and durable.

## Writes go through the sink; reads and retention do not

`cleanup_expired_logs` and the audit-list query still take a `KeyspaceHandle`,
and `AppState` carries both `audit_ks` and `audit_sink`. This is the design, not
an omission. A sink is free to be write-only and remote, and "delete rows older
than N days" is not an operation an append-only or anchored backend can offer —
the immutability is the point. Retention therefore stays a property of the local
keyspace, which is what the retention API is documented to govern.

The consequence is that swapping the sink outright would take `GET /audit/logs`
and the retention sweep with it. `FanOutAuditSink` is the answer: keep the
keyspace sink, add the new backend beside it. Every sink is attempted and the
first error returned only after all of them have run — short-circuiting would let
a failing sink hide an entry from the ones behind it, which for an audit log is
the failure mode that matters.

## The sweepers get the same sink object

Built once in `run()` and handed to both `AppStateParts` and the storage thread,
rather than reconstructed there. A sweeper's `acl.expire` is an unattended
removal — nobody was watching when the entry vanished — which makes it precisely
the row an operator installs a tamper-evident backend to capture. Rebuilding a
sink on the storage thread would have routed it back to the keyspace whatever
they configured, and the gap would surface only when someone went looking for a
deletion that was never recorded. `VtaState` clones the same `Arc` for the same
reason it shares the config `RwLock` (P1.1): two transports resolving audit
differently is a gap you find during an incident.

## Tests

Three unit tests on the sink module, five integration tests in
`vta-service/tests/audit_sink.rs`. The load-bearing one asserts **both** halves —
the installed sink receives the row *and the keyspace does not*. Without the
second assertion it would pass on a sink that merely observes alongside an
unchanged keyspace write, which delivers none of the property this exists for.
The others pin the default (no sink installed → the keyspace, exactly as
before), the sweeper path, the shared `Arc` across transports, and the fan-out
composition keeping the query API alive.

`storage_key` is pinned separately: the retention sweep stops at the first key
past its cutoff and the list query is a prefix scan, so both are correct only
while the key sorts by time *as a string* — which is what the zero-padding buys.

## Breaking

`vta_audit::{record, record_with_detail, record_consent}` take a
`&SharedAuditSink` where they took a `&KeyspaceHandle`. The alternative — keeping
the old signature and adding a parallel sink-taking one — would leave a second
way to write an audit row that bypasses the sink entirely, and a
tamper-evidence backend with a bypass is not one.

Mechanically this moved ~57 call sites across 24 files and a dozen `Deps`
structs, because the audit keyspace was threaded by hand everywhere rather than
carried once. `vta_keyspaces::Keyspaces.audit` is deliberately untouched: that
bundle's audit handle is a keyspace because backup export dumps it.

title: chore(deps): affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.19.10, so a refused socket says why (#253)
body:
chore(deps): affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.19.10, so a refused socket says why (#253)

The transport matched the server's close frame as `Message::Close(_)` and threw
it away — `debug!("WebSocket connection closed by server")` — so every close
looked identical from here: the socket vanished and the reconnect loop went
again. Two instances of this app on one persona therefore duelled, and the user
was shown a transport error rather than "you have this open twice".

The mediator half was also lying. `WebSocketCommands::Close` carried no reason,
so all three of its senders got the same `duplicate-channel` problem report and
the same "replaced by a newer connection" close text — including a newcomer
*refused* by the duel damper, whose own connection was never displaced. That is
the inverse of what happened to it.

affinidi-tdk-rs #718 gives `Close` a reason, maps each to its own problem-report
code, and surfaces the close code and reason at WARN in the sdk.
`duplicate-channel` is preserved verbatim for the genuinely-replaced case, so
the places this repo matches on it are unaffected and no code change is needed
here — the floor and the manifest note are the change.

The eviction policy is deliberately untouched upstream: displacement is what
triggers the mediator's stored-mail redelivery, and this repo is not
representative in pulling explicitly via `message_pickup`. Raised from this side
as OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1028.

Not yet observable in the e2e fixture: the mediator half is 0.18.21, and the
newest `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator` (0.2.52) still embeds 0.18.20. The
`#[ignore]`d transport e2e keeps asserting the old behaviour until a fixture
carrying 0.18.21 publishes.

fmt, clippy -D warnings, and `cargo test --workspace` pass.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(service): retire routes and Trust Tasks on evidence, not on a hand audit
body:
Two gaps in how this workspace retires things, both surfaced while retiring
`vta/discovery/capabilities/1.0` (#1043, #1044). Closes #1045.

## The superseded-route table had no guard

`deprecation.rs` maps legacy REST routes to the Trust Task that supersedes them
so that removal can be gated on observed usage dropping to zero. #1042 deleted
`GET /capabilities` and left its row behind — a row matching a path that can
never be hit again reads zero forever, which is exactly the signal the table
exists to produce, emitted about something already deleted. It was noticed by
accident and removed by hand in #1044, because nothing tied the table to the
live router.

`every_superseded_row_names_a_live_route` now walks the assembled router and
asserts every row matches a live route. It asserts on `MatchedPath` rather than
on a status code, because `MatchedPath` is what `mark_superseded` matches on: a
row spelling a parameter differently — `/acl/{id}` where the router registered
`/acl/{did}` — attaches no header and counts nothing while the route goes on
answering, and a status-only probe reads green over that. The failure text says
which way to fix it. The reverse direction is deliberately not asserted; a live
route absent from the table is legitimate, and `deprecation.rs` already records
which routes are excluded and why.

## Trust Task URIs had no deprecation path at all

A task could be retired only by deleting it, and the only evidence available was
a source audit — grep the repos we can see and reason about the rest. That was
defensible for one task with zero consumers anywhere and does not generalise;
the next retirement may be one somebody is calling.

`SUPERSEDED_TASKS` gives them the route mechanism:
`deprecated_trust_task_requests_total` labelled by URI, the successor named in
the response so a client can act rather than guess, and removal on an observed
zero. Seeded with the eleven dispatched URIs already carrying `#[deprecated]` in
`vta_sdk::trust_tasks` — attributes that told a Rust caller to migrate, told a
wire caller nothing, and left no instrument saying whether anyone was still
sending them.

Checked against the framework first. The *registry* has the concept
(`status: retired` + `supersededBy`, how twelve `messaging/*` tasks were retired
upstream), but `trust-tasks-rs` 0.11 exposes none of it: `schema_index` is
URI → payload schema and nothing else, `Payload` carries no lifecycle constant,
and `trust-task-discovery/0.1`'s expanded `supportedTypes` entry is closed over
`{type, requiredExt}`. So this is invention rather than adoption; the vocabulary
matches the registry's so that adopting a published signal later is a rename.

The notice rides the response document's **top level**, not `payload.ext`. The
framework envelope keeps unrecognized top-level members in `TrustTask::extra`
and SPEC §7.1/§7.2 tells consumers to preserve rather than reject them, so a
member there cannot break a client that has never heard of it. `payload` can
make no such promise: every published payload schema is
`additionalProperties: false`, the generated `Response` types are
`deny_unknown_fields`, and the conformance sweep validates against both. This is
the Trust-Task analogue of putting the REST signal in a header — beside the
answer rather than inside it. A document carrying a `proof` is left untouched.

## Both tables are now pinned to what they describe

`superseded_tasks_are_dispatched` refuses a row nothing routes (that reads zero
forever, same defect as the dangling route row), `superseded_task_successors_are
_served` refuses a successor this VTA does not serve (a notice that sends a
migrating client onto an unsupported type), and
`every_dual_accepted_spec_marks_its_0_1_form_superseded` pins
`wire_v0_2::WIRE_SPECS_V0_2` against `SUPERSEDED_TASKS`, so a new dual-accept
cannot land without an instrument on the form it replaces.

Not covered, and said so in the source rather than papered over:
`auth/passkey/login/{start,finish}/0.1` are deprecated but reach neither
instrument. They are REST-routed on paths the route table excludes on purpose,
and one path serves both versions with the delta inside the body, so separating
them needs a counter in those two handlers.

Two things the tests found rather than confirmed. The signal is attached in
`dispatch_trust_task_inner` wrapping every exit out of the checks, not after
them — the spine has a dozen early returns, and a URI going quiet because its
callers are all being rejected before the hook would read as "nobody sends this
any more"; the first version had exactly that hole and the rejection test caught
it. And that split is `Box::pin`ed: the callee's state machine inlines every
handler's future through `dispatch_typed`, and awaiting it by value overflowed
the test-thread stack in `tests/mock_vta.rs` under `cargo test --workspace`,
where feature unification builds more of vta-service than `-p vta-service` does.

title: Deprecation gaps: the superseded-route table has no guard, and Trust Task URIs have no deprecation path at all
body:
Two gaps in how this workspace retires things, both surfaced while retiring `vta/discovery/capabilities/1.0` (#1043, #1044). Neither is urgent; both get worse the more we retire, and the direction of travel is clearly toward retiring more.

## 1. The superseded-route table has no guard

`deprecation.rs` maps legacy REST routes to the Trust Task that supersedes them, and its purpose is explicit:

> removal can be gated on **observed usage dropping to zero** rather than a guessed calendar date

#1042 deleted `GET /capabilities` and left its row in `SUPERSEDED` behind. The row matched a path that could never be hit again, so it would have read **zero usage forever** — which is precisely the signal the table exists to produce. It was removed by hand in #1044, having been noticed by accident.

**Nothing ties that table to the live router.** No test asserts every `(method, path)` in `SUPERSEDED` is a route the service actually serves, so a dangling row is silent, and a silent dangling row makes the metric say "safe to delete" about something already deleted.

### Requested

A test that walks the assembled router (`build_api_router` already exists and the OpenAPI assertions already introspect it) and asserts every `SUPERSEDED` entry corresponds to a live route. Failure text should say which way to fix it: if the route is gone, drop the row; if the row is a typo, correct it — do not delete the row to silence the test, because the row is what carries the successor URI.

Note the reverse direction is *not* wanted: a live route absent from the table is legitimate, and `deprecation.rs` already documents which routes are deliberately excluded and why.

## 2. There is no deprecation path for a Trust Task URI

`deprecation.rs` gives REST routes the full treatment — `Deprecation: true`, a `Link: rel="successor-version"` header, and a per-route hit counter, so removal is evidence-led.

**Trust Task URIs get none of it.** A task can be retired only by deleting it, and the only available evidence is a source audit: grep this repo and the ones we can see, and reason about the rest.

That is what #1044 did, and it was stated plainly there as the weaker instrument it is. It was defensible for that task — zero consumers anywhere, plus a member whose vocabulary corresponded to nothing — but it does not generalise. The next retirement may be one someone *is* calling, and we would find out from a support ticket.

### Requested

The Trust-Task equivalent of the REST mechanism:

- A `SUPERSEDED_TASKS` table — `(retired URI, successor URI, reason)`.
- The dispatch spine increments a counter, labelled by URI, when a retired task is dispatched, and includes the successor in the response so a client can act rather than guess. The Trust-Task error shape already carries a machine-readable code, so there is somewhere to put it.
- Retirement then follows the same rule as routes: delete on an observed zero.

Worth checking against the framework spec first — a deprecation signal may already be defined for Trust Tasks, in which case this is adoption rather than invention. That was the outcome for capability negotiation itself (#1042): `trust-task-discovery/0.1` already existed and we simply were not serving it.

### Interaction with the census

`UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` and `vtc-service`'s `UNPUBLISHED_CANONICAL_OK` both shrink monotonically by test, and #1044 showed a URI can leave those lists by *ceasing to exist* rather than by gaining a spec. A deprecation table would make that path explicit rather than inferred from a count that moved.

title: vta-service-v0.20.0
body:
### Added

- **discovery**: Serve canonical capability negotiation, drop the parallel REST route ([#1042](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1042))

* feat(discovery)!: serve canonical capability negotiation, drop the parallel REST route

  Clients had no way to ask a VTA which Trust Tasks it serves. Calling one it does
  not is a 30-second DIDComm timeout with no explanation — the failure mode
  `didhosting-083-retired-task-uris` describes.

  The answer already existed and we were not serving it. `trust-task-discovery/0.1`
  is a published family in the dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf registry, carried by the
  `trust-tasks-rs` we already depend on: a client sends slug-glob patterns (`*`,
  `acl/*`, or an exact slug) and gets back the Type URIs the responder serves plus
  the framework version it targets. Nothing needed inventing, and — unusually for a
  new family — nothing needed specifying upstream first.

  The VTA answers **from its own dispatch table**. `dispatched_uris()` was already
  generated by `dispatch_table!` from the same declarations that build the match
  arms; it is now available at runtime rather than only under `cfg(test)`. A
  hand-maintained list would be a second source of truth, and an overstated
  discovery response is worse than none: a client believes a task is available and
  finds out on a live call.

  **What this does not do.** It answers "do we both know this task, at this
  version". It does not answer "do we agree how its payload is spelled" — two peers
  can both serve `contexts/create/1.0` and still disagree about `basePath` vs
  `base_path`, which is what #1033 was. Said plainly on the SDK method, because the
  obvious misreading is that discovery makes wire skew detectable.

title: docs: design note for Trust Task version negotiation and its versioning contract
body:
Refs #1045. **Design only** — no code, no URIs, nothing dispatched.

Adds `docs/05-design-notes/task-version-negotiation.md` and indexes it.

## The problem, live rather than hypothetical

A client sends whatever version it was compiled against:

```rust
self.dispatch_trust_task(trust_tasks::TASK_VAULT_LIST_0_1, filters, VAULT_TT_TIMEOUT)
```

`vault/list` is published at **0.1, 0.2 and 0.3**. This VTA serves 0.1 and 0.2. A client built against 0.3 gets `unsupported_type` — over DIDComm, a 30-second timeout with no explanation.

Everything needed to fix it already exists and is unused: discovery (#1042) says what a peer serves, `TypeUri` decomposes `(slug, major, minor)`. What is missing is the client choosing.

## Negotiation and versioning are one decision

Which is why they are one note. **Negotiation is tractable if and only if versions carry a compatibility contract** — without one, "negotiate" cannot mean better than "match exactly or fail".

### The contract: 1.0 is unremarkable

The notation is already semver. What is missing is a *promise*.

`vault/list` 0.1 and 0.3 have **identical payload shapes**. The only difference is enum values — `oauth-tokens` → `oauthTokens`. A breaking wire change shipped as a minor bump, twice.

**That is not a semver violation.** `0.x` explicitly guarantees nothing, so the registry is following semver correctly; semver at 0.x simply promises nothing to build on.

Proposed: drop the exemption. MAJOR for any wire-visible change that is not purely additive, MINOR for additive-only. A family at `7.2` is fine. No grammar change, no flag day — the rule binds the *next* change.

### Why not `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`

Considered and rejected. It is a framework grammar change — `TypeUri::parse_version` splits once and parses the remainder as `u32`, so `1.2.3` does not parse, and changing that touches SPEC §6.1 for every task in the registry.

The substantive objection is different: **a PATCH component carries no negotiation value and costs identity.** If PATCH is invisible on the wire then `1.2.3` and `1.2.4` are byte-identical — yet any matcher comparing Type URIs sees two different tasks. The URI *is* the wire identity.

And under the variant where MINOR is breaking too, a negotiator must match `MAJOR.MINOR` exactly — which is today's behaviour, for an extra component.

## The part I think is the good bit

**The sender speaks down**, and that resolves what looks like a hard conflict.

The payload schemas are `additionalProperties: false` and the generated types carry `deny_unknown_fields`. So a new client sending a new optional member to an old server is **rejected, not ignored** — which appears to rule out additive minors entirely.

It does not, because **nobody ever sends up-version**:

- Old client → new server: accepted, everything added since was optional. ✓
- New client → old server: would break — **but never happens**, the sender negotiated down first. ✓

So negotiation removes the need for forward tolerance, and `deny_unknown_fields` **stays**. That matters: it is a security requirement in CLAUDE.md, and #656/#658 are the scar where a silently-accepted unknown member minted a super-admin. Buying forward compatibility by tolerating unknown members would have given that up.

## What the note is careful about

- **The algorithm mirrors transport selection**, which CLAUDE.md already defines — intersect, take the highest common, typed error on empty, never silently downgrade. Consistency rather than invention.
- **The cost is stated**: negotiating down to 1.1 means holding a 1.1 encoder. The additive-only rule is what bounds it — bridging an additive minor is *dropping* members, not rewriting them. Contrast `wire_v0_2`, which rewrites enum values and has to carve out signed payloads because mutating those bytes voids the proof.
- **The rule needs teeth.** A minor bump is mechanically checkable against published schemas (added members optional, none removed, no enum-value changes). That census belongs upstream with the schemas.
- **What it does not solve**: two peers can both serve `contexts/create/1.0` and still disagree about `basePath` vs `base_path` (#1033). Discovery and negotiation do not make wire skew detectable.
- **Startup and staleness**: negotiation must not block boot (`server::run` has to reach its shutdown select), and a cached result must be able to go stale — R6.2, no latched status.

## Scope

§3 (negotiation) is entirely ours — client behaviour over an already-published discovery task.

§2 (the contract) is a **registry decision**. `vault/*`, `acl/*`, `keys/*` are canonical families in `trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`, and the deliberate direction since #840 has been to fold onto them, which means inheriting their versioning rules. The note flags checking the framework for existing versioning semantics before proposing anything — twice now the answer to "should we build this" has been "it already exists upstream and we were not using it", most recently `trust-task-discovery/0.1`.

## Four open questions (§6)

1. Ship negotiation first against exact-match semantics, or wait for the contract?
2. Negotiate every family, or only the five published at more than one version?
3. Empty intersection at startup — refuse to connect, or degrade to what did negotiate? The transport precedent refuses; a task surface is more granular.
4. Does `spec/vta/*` adopt the contract ahead of the registry, and what does being stricter than the families we fold onto mean?

Docs-only; no crate source touched, so no version bump.

title: Add the VDC (verifiable delegation credential) as a DTG edge credential
body:
## Problem

All six credential types in WD01 are **attestations** — each states that something is true about the graph, and a verifier evaluates it as a claim. Not one of them establishes that one entity may **act in another's name**. The VIC comes closest, but it is onboarding-shaped: its subject is by definition not yet in the graph, it is short-lived, and §Security says treat it as single-use.

Meanwhile delegation is already assumed by the specification's own vocabulary, with nothing to express it:

- `spec/terms-definitions/persona.md` — an identity controlled by the person "or their delegate"
- `spec/terms-definitions/personal_network_vault.md` — a person "may sometimes choose to delegate use of their credentials or keys to a VTA"
- `spec/intro.md` — AI agents are first-class DTG nodes, and an Agent Card VDS is planned

So today we can say "person P and agent A have a relationship" (VRC), but not "A may act in P's name, for these acts, until this date, and P can withdraw it."

## Delegation, not authority

The VDC is deliberately confined to **delegation**, and the PR adds an informative subsection, *Delegation and Authority*, saying so:

| Question | Answered by | The act is attributed to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| May this party do this thing, as itself? | authority — not defined in this specification | the party itself |
| May this party act in another's name? | delegation — the VDC | the entity in whose name it acts |

Neither implies the other. A service granted access to a person's mailbox may read that mail as itself; it has not thereby been appointed to send mail in that person's name. Conversely, a delegate appointed to correspond in a person's name holds that appointment whether or not it has access to any particular mailbox — and where it has not, the appointment gets it nowhere.

Two consequences are stated normatively:

- **A VDC never supplies authority.** A delegate cannot do in the delegator's name what the delegator could not do itself. A verifier must settle both questions separately, and a valid VDC is never on its own sufficient grounds to proceed (Security Considerations item 9).
- **The word "authority" is left free.** If the WG later wants a verifiable authority credential, it can be defined without reinterpreting the VDC or contending with it for the same semantic ground.

The subsection ends with a *when to use a VDC* test in the same style as the spec's existing credential/artifact test: **ask whose name the act is performed in.** The actor's own → a question of authority, not this credential. Another entity's, with the act attributed to that entity → delegation, and the VDC is what establishes it.

## How a delegation composes with authority

A second informative subsection answers the question a reviewer asks immediately after the first: if a VDC is not authority, does the delegate need authority of its own, or has the delegator handed its own over?

Neither. **A VDC moves the question; it does not answer it.** A verifier substitutes the delegator for the delegate and then asks the question it would have asked of the delegator directly. Three checks, each independent:

1. **Is this the delegate, and may it act in the delegator's name for this act?** — the VDC, plus chain and invocation binding. Defined here.
2. **May the delegator perform this act?** — membership, governance, an IDVC, a permission credential, verifier policy. Not defined here, and a VDC does not influence its outcome.
3. **Must the delegate independently qualify?** — a governance determination, now stated as such in §Governance Considerations.

The reach of a delegation is the **intersection** of what the delegator may do and what the VDC chain appoints the delegate for — never the union, and never more than either. Three consequences are spelled out:

- **Nothing the delegator holds is copied to the delegate.** A credential issued to the delegator stays the delegator's; the issuer's assurance about the delegator does not extend to the delegate, and a delegator cannot re-issue what it was itself issued. Delegation is a statement about who may speak in one's name, not a transfer of anything received.
- **Withdrawing the delegator's own permission stops the delegate immediately**, without revoking the VDC, because check 2 is evaluated at the time of the act. Revoking the VDC and withdrawing the underlying permission are different remedies with different reach.
- **A `scope` may exceed what the delegator itself may do**, which is not an error given that permissions change over the life of a durable appointment. Verifiers MUST NOT treat it as conferring anything beyond check 2; issuers SHOULD NOT do it.

This also rules out the alternative reading — a VDC as a container the delegator fills with its own permissions and hands over. That would make every issued authorization transferable by its holder, break the issuer's revocation reach, and attribute the act to the delegate rather than the delegator, which is the opposite of what delegation means.

## Why a new type rather than an existing one

Each overload fails, and the failures are informative:

- **VEC** — its `endorsement` object is community-defined and the spec explicitly says verifiability applies to the signature "not to the truth of the assertions." Putting representation inside a container whose stated semantics are *unverified opinion* means a verifier cannot distinguish "is good at Rust" from "may act as me."
- **VIC** — the least-bad overload, but its rules are terminal and onboarding-shaped, per above. Reusing it would mean redefining it.
- **VRC + a relationship-type field** — VRC currently carries no payload beyond `issuer` and `credentialSubject.id`. Adding semantics changes it from a bare edge to a typed one, which cuts against the ZKP predicate story, and imposes the bidirectional-pair requirement and the "new unique R-DID per counterparty" MUST on something inherently asymmetric.

The underlying reason is that a verifier evaluates an attestation by asking whether it is *true*. Representation asks something else — whether this party may stand in for that one, for this act, right now — and answering it requires scope containment, chain resolution, invocation binding and timely revocation. A distinct type string is what forces a verifier onto that path rather than the claim-evaluation one.

## What this PR does

Adds `DelegationCredential` (**VDC**) as a seventh concrete subtype and third edge credential.

**Applies the specification's own test.** §Credentials versus Trust Task Artifacts splits delegation cleanly, and the PR states this explicitly:

- the **grant** — "P appointed A to act in its name, for scope S, until T" — is true standing alone → credential, defined here
- the **invocation** — "A is acting in P's name, now, to do X" — is meaningful only in-exchange → trust task artifact, left to the DTG Core Trust Task Protocols spec

**Edge, with consent.** A grant plus a matching acceptance forms the edge, consistent with VRC/VMC pairing. A grant alone establishes what the delegator appointed, not what the delegate agreed to. This is the same consent question as #8 / #12 and is defined here in the same shape, without pre-empting that discussion.

**The machinery the six types do not have:**

- `delegation.scope` (REQUIRED, non-empty) — the acts the delegate may perform in the delegator's name; vocabulary governed by the VTC/VTN, exactly as VEC's `endorsement` is
- `delegation.parent` / `maxDepth` — attenuation-only re-delegation; a chain must resolve to a root delegation issued by the principal in whose name the acts would ultimately be performed. `parent` reuses the VWC `digest` encoding (SHA-256 over JCS) rather than introducing a second convention
- **Invocation binding** — a VDC is not a bearer token; the delegate must demonstrate key control at request time
- `validUntil` REQUIRED — an appointment with no expiry cannot be reasoned about by a verifier that cannot reach the delegator
- `credentialStatus` REQUIRED — see the note below

**Security considerations added:** misreading a VDC as a claim, treating a delegation as a permission, chain escalation, revocation latency, bearer use, and personhood laundering. The last is worth flagging on its own: a PHC asserts one membership per real person, and because a delegate's acts are attributable to the delegator, a verifier that cannot distinguish the two may credit several agents of one person as several people.

**Privacy considerations added:** delegation correlation (prefer R-DIDs), and scope terms as identifiers.

**Prior art:** ZCAP-LD and UCAN are cited in an informative subsection. The VDC reuses their *mechanics* — attenuation, root resolution, invocation binding — while noting the semantics differ: those models chain permissions, the VDC chains representation. It expresses those mechanics natively rather than embedding an opaque token, because scope is precisely the payload holders need to prove over in zero knowledge.

## Note on `credentialStatus`

`credentialStatus` currently appears **nowhere** in the specification. §Security Considerations tells verifiers to "check applicable revocation status via the governing trust registry," but no property tells them where to look. For attestations that is survivable; for a delegation — where revocation is the delegator's only means of withdrawing an appointment already made — it is not.

This PR therefore makes `credentialStatus` REQUIRED on the VDC only, and deliberately does not touch §Base Structure. The spec-wide question is worth its own issue and I'm happy to raise it separately.

## Also updated

Abstract, intro, taxonomy diagram and type hierarchy, `dtg_edge_credential` term (two subtypes → three), `specs.json` description, and a new `verifiable_delegation_credential` term definition. `CONTEXT.md` gains VDC and delegation-vs-authority language entries.

Renders clean with `npm run render`: no unresolved term references, all JSON examples parse, and the only dangling definitions reported are the five pre-existing ones.

## Open questions for the WG

1. **Scope vocabulary** — left entirely to VTC/VTN governance, mirroring VEC. Should the core spec instead define a minimal baseline so cross-community delegation is meaningful?
2. **A companion authority credential** — this PR reserves the ground rather than filling it. Is a verifiable authority credential wanted, and if so should the two be specified together so the boundary is drawn once?
3. **Delegate eligibility** — check 3 above is left to governance. Should the core spec instead take a position, e.g. requiring that a delegate acting within a community hold a VMC of its own?
4. **Acceptance strictness** — this draft requires the acceptance for a *complete edge* but lets a verifier rely on a grant alone where delegate consent isn't material. Should acceptance be unconditionally REQUIRED?
5. **`maxDepth` default** — this draft prohibits re-delegation when `maxDepth` is absent. Fail-closed seems right; confirming it is intended.
6. **ZKP constructions** — a delegation predicate is added to the list in §Zero-Knowledge and Selective Disclosure, but the constructions themselves are not worked out. Likely interacts with #9.
7. **Naming** — VDC is free, but sits close to VDS (verifiable data structure). Worth a look.

Opened as a draft for WG discussion — happy to split the `credentialStatus` point out, or to restructure if the group would rather see delegation land in a companion specification.

title: refactor(discovery)!: retire vta/discovery/capabilities — every member had a better home
body:
Closes #1043.

Follow-up to #1039, which reduced `spec/vta/discovery/capabilities/1.0` to `version` + `webvhServers` + `didCreationModes` and left the question open: **does what remains still earn a task?**

Audited each member against the rest of the surface. The answer is no — every one of them has a better home or describes nothing.

## `version` — duplicated at `GET /health/details`

`HealthDetailsResponse` already carries it, from the same `env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")`, at the same auth level (`health_details` takes `AuthClaims`).

The weakest of the three findings: both read the same constant, so unlike `services` they cannot disagree. Duplicated, not wrong.

## `webvhServers` — a *lossy* duplicate of `webvh/servers/list/1.0`

| | shape |
|---|---|
| capabilities | `WebvhServerInfo { id, label }` |
| `webvh/servers/list/1.0` | `WebvhServerRecord { id, did, label, createdAt, updatedAt }` |

Same underlying `webvh_store::list_servers` call. The dedicated task returns a strict superset.

The obvious objection is authorization — a cheap summary for callers who cannot see the full list — and **it does not hold**. `operations::did_webvh::list_webvh_servers` is commented *"Any authenticated user can list servers"*, exactly the gate capabilities used.

No production code read it from capabilities. `vtc-service/src/setup/wizard.rs` already calls `list_webvh_servers()`.

## `didCreationModes` — dead, and misleading

- **No consumer** in this repo or in OpenVTC.
- Derived entirely from `cfg!(feature = "webvh")` — the same species as the `features` booleans #1039 removed, reporting what the binary *could* do rather than what it does.
- Its vocabulary — `vta-built` / `template` / `final` / `user-specified-keys` — **appears nowhere else in the codebase**. It dates to #22 (April) and predates `WebvhPathMode`, which is the axis DID creation actually turns on now.
- The fixtures "covering" it assert `["webvh"]` — a *fourth* vocabulary, matching neither the code nor anything else. Its test coverage was fiction, the same defect class as #1033.

## Conclusion: retire the task

Every member migrates or dies:

| member | goes to |
|---|---|
| `version` | `GET /health/details` |
| `webvhServers` | `webvh/servers/list/1.0` (strict superset, same auth) |
| `didCreationModes` | nothing — it describes nothing |

This closes the `registry-drift-triage.md` row as **fold/delete**, which was its original recommendation before #1039 recorded "keep the delta".

The `discovery/1.0/*` DIDComm protocol beside it goes too — it was routed **unauthenticated**, which is worth noting on the way out.

Only consumer to migrate: `vta-mcp`'s `vta_capabilities` tool.

## On retiring rather than deprecating

`deprecation.rs` sets this repo's practice for removing a REST route — mark it, count usage, delete on an *observed zero* rather than a guessed date. **There is no equivalent for Trust Task URIs**, so that instrument is not available here.

The justification is therefore the audit above rather than a metric: zero consumers across both repos, plus a member whose vocabulary corresponds to nothing. That is a weaker instrument than the REST routes get, and worth stating rather than glossing.

If that is too weak a basis, the alternative is to build task-level deprecation signalling first — which is a larger piece of work and probably worth doing on its own merits.


---

## What the change does

Removes the task, the `discovery/1.0/*` DIDComm protocol beside it, and the types behind them: `CapabilitiesResponse`, `CapabilitiesBody`, `FeaturesInfo`, `ServicesInfo`, `WebvhServerInfo`, and `VtaClient::capabilities`.

`vta-mcp`'s `vta_capabilities` becomes **`vta_supported_tasks`**. Not a rename — the old tool promised four answers, three better held elsewhere and one describing nothing. The new description says what an agent actually needs to know before calling an operation, including that calling an unserved task fails as a *transport timeout* rather than a clear error, which is the reason to ask first.

Also discharges the `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` entry **by deletion rather than by a spec** — the cheaper way to shrink that list when the answer is "this should not exist".

## A dangling row #1042 left behind

`deprecation.rs` still carried a `GET /capabilities` row after #1042 deleted the route — matching a path that can never be hit again. **Nothing catches that**: no test ties the superseded-route table to the live router. Removed by hand here.

Worth a follow-up on its own: that table is meant to gate route removal on observed-zero usage, and a row for a route that no longer exists silently reads as "zero" forever.

## Tests

Rewritten rather than deleted, because the properties survive their subject:

- `capabilities_requires_auth` → **`trust_tasks_require_auth`**. The property was the dispatch spine's, not that task's.
- `capabilities_via_didcomm` → **`supported_trust_tasks_via_didcomm`**. Same property — a discovery answer survives the DIDComm round trip — asked of the task with a canonical answer.
- `with_didcomm_sequential_cycles_for_same_did_do_not_duel` repointed. It is about session lifecycle, not about what was asked; discovery suits because it needs no responder state.
- New: `supported_trust_tasks_decodes_without_a_framework_version`, because `frameworkVersion` is **OPTIONAL in 0.1** — an older responder omitting it must decode, not error.

## Verification

- `cargo check --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` all clean.
- Full `cargo test --workspace` green except the four `vtc-service` `admin_ui::tests`, which fail on `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1` leaving the embedded dir empty — the flag, not this change.
- Net **−172 lines**.

Rebased onto `main` after #1042 merged, so this is no longer stacked.

## Breaking change

Flagged as `BREAKING CHANGE:` in the commit body. Migration: `trust-task-discovery/0.1` (`VtaClient::supported_trust_tasks`) for what an agent serves, `GET /health/details` for its version, `webvh/servers/list/1.0` for its webvh hosts. No `version =` touched.

title: Retire vta/discovery/capabilities/1.0 — every remaining member has a better home
body:
Follow-up to #1039, which reduced `spec/vta/discovery/capabilities/1.0` to `version` + `webvhServers` + `didCreationModes` and left the question open: **does what remains still earn a task?**

Audited each member against the rest of the surface. The answer is no — every one of them has a better home or describes nothing.

## `version` — duplicated at `GET /health/details`

`HealthDetailsResponse` already carries it, from the same `env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")`, at the same auth level (`health_details` takes `AuthClaims`).

The weakest of the three findings: both read the same constant, so unlike `services` they cannot disagree. Duplicated, not wrong.

## `webvhServers` — a *lossy* duplicate of `webvh/servers/list/1.0`

| | shape |
|---|---|
| capabilities | `WebvhServerInfo { id, label }` |
| `webvh/servers/list/1.0` | `WebvhServerRecord { id, did, label, createdAt, updatedAt }` |

Same underlying `webvh_store::list_servers` call. The dedicated task returns a strict superset.

The obvious objection is authorization — a cheap summary for callers who cannot see the full list — and **it does not hold**. `operations::did_webvh::list_webvh_servers` is commented *"Any authenticated user can list servers"*, exactly the gate capabilities used.

No production code read it from capabilities. `vtc-service/src/setup/wizard.rs` already calls `list_webvh_servers()`.

## `didCreationModes` — dead, and misleading

- **No consumer** in this repo or in OpenVTC.
- Derived entirely from `cfg!(feature = "webvh")` — the same species as the `features` booleans #1039 removed, reporting what the binary *could* do rather than what it does.
- Its vocabulary — `vta-built` / `template` / `final` / `user-specified-keys` — **appears nowhere else in the codebase**. It dates to #22 (April) and predates `WebvhPathMode`, which is the axis DID creation actually turns on now.
- The fixtures "covering" it assert `["webvh"]` — a *fourth* vocabulary, matching neither the code nor anything else. Its test coverage was fiction, the same defect class as #1033.

## Conclusion: retire the task

Every member migrates or dies:

| member | goes to |
|---|---|
| `version` | `GET /health/details` |
| `webvhServers` | `webvh/servers/list/1.0` (strict superset, same auth) |
| `didCreationModes` | nothing — it describes nothing |

This closes the `registry-drift-triage.md` row as **fold/delete**, which was its original recommendation before #1039 recorded "keep the delta".

The `discovery/1.0/*` DIDComm protocol beside it goes too — it was routed **unauthenticated**, which is worth noting on the way out.

Only consumer to migrate: `vta-mcp`'s `vta_capabilities` tool.

## On retiring rather than deprecating

`deprecation.rs` sets this repo's practice for removing a REST route — mark it, count usage, delete on an *observed zero* rather than a guessed date. **There is no equivalent for Trust Task URIs**, so that instrument is not available here.

The justification is therefore the audit above rather than a metric: zero consumers across both repos, plus a member whose vocabulary corresponds to nothing. That is a weaker instrument than the REST routes get, and worth stating rather than glossing.

If that is too weak a basis, the alternative is to build task-level deprecation signalling first — which is a larger piece of work and probably worth doing on its own merits.

refactor(discovery)!: retire vta/discovery/capabilities — every member had a better home (#1044)

* refactor(discovery)!: retire vta/discovery/capabilities — every member had a better home
